feedback.feed_forward: Reread the final paragraph for missing stops first.

title: Using a and an the first time you mention one of something

point_json.grammar_name: The indefinite article: a and an

teach.can_do: I can put a or an in front of a thing I am mentioning for the first time.
teach.why_it_matters: English will not let a single countable thing stand bare. Leaving the small word out is quiet and constant, and a reader notices it in every sentence.
teach.meaning: When you name one thing and your listener has not met it yet, English puts a small word in front of it: a. Say I caught a bus and the listener knows there was one bus and that this is the first they have heard of it. The word becomes an when the next word begins with a vowel sound, purely so the two words do not collide in the mouth. It is used for one countable thing only, never for more than one and never for something you cannot count.

form.pattern: a + a naming word starting with a consonant sound · an + a naming word starting with a vowel sound
notes: The choice is made by sound and not by spelling: a university, a one-way street, an hour, an honest answer.
Only ever for one countable thing. Never with the more-than-one shape, and never with words like advice or luggage.
If a describing word comes first, the small word sits in front of that instead: a busy kitchen, an empty plate.
form.negative: The small word stays where it is when the sentence goes negative: there is not a bus until seven.
form.question: Ask two things: is it one of them, and is my listener meeting it for the first time? Two yeses means a or an.

left.role: the next sound is a consonant
left.text: a ticket · a hostel · a university

right.role: the next sound is a vowel
right.text: an hour · an office · an umbrella

spec.caption: Say the two words out loud. Your mouth chooses this one, not your eyes.

worked_example.sentence: Bea took an early train and found a seat by the window.
worked_example.why_this_form: The listener has met neither the train nor the seat before, and there is one of each. An goes with early because that word opens on a vowel sound.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Drop both small words and the sentence still makes sense, but it now reads as scribbled notes, and that is exactly how a reader receives it.

notice_set.sentence: Kwame ordered a coffee and a slice of toast.
notice_set.question: How many drinks did he order?
notice_set.why: This small word always means one of them, so the number is settled the moment it appears.

notice_set.sentence: There is an hour between the two trains.
notice_set.question: How long is the wait?
notice_set.why: Hour opens on a vowel sound even though it starts with an h on the page, so the mouth wants an.

notice_set.sentence: Lena wants a flat near the college.
notice_set.question: Does she already have one?
notice_set.why: The small word introduces something nobody has met yet, so whether she has found it is left open.

notice_set.sentence: Kwame asked for information about the evening menu.
notice_set.question: How many separate facts did he ask for?
notice_set.why: This word cannot be counted, so nothing counts it and no number is being claimed.

notice_set.sentence: Bea works as a chef in a hotel kitchen.
notice_set.question: What is her job?
notice_set.why: English puts the small word in front of a job when it names one, and the job named here is chef.

teach.rule_line: One of them, and new to your listener? Put a in front, or an before a vowel sound.
teach.false_rule: That an goes before the letters a, e, i, o and u. It goes before vowel sounds: a university, an hour. Say the word and listen to it.

errors.wrong: Kwame works as chef in a hotel on the seafront.
errors.right: Kwame works as a chef in a hotel on the seafront.
errors.why_it_happens: Many languages name a job with nothing in front of it, so the sentence feels complete because the meaning is complete. English hears a hole where the small word should be.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: a.
errors.l1_note: Very common for speakers of Russian, Polish, Japanese and Korean.

errors.wrong: The tutor gave Marta an information about the deadline.
errors.right: The tutor gave Marta some information about the deadline.
errors.why_it_happens: These small words count to one, so they attach themselves to anything that feels like a single item. This word cannot be counted at all, so nothing is allowed to count it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: an becomes some.

errors.wrong: We waited a hour and a half for the replacement bus.
errors.right: We waited an hour and a half for the replacement bus.
errors.why_it_happens: The choice was made by looking at the letter on the page. The h in hour is silent, so the mouth arrives at a vowel and wants the other form.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: a becomes an.

pays_in.note: Naming your job, your home or your journey needs it in nearly every clause.
pays_in.model: I work in a small kitchen and I take a bus in at five.

pays_in.note: A letter about a problem introduces one new thing after another.
pays_in.model: There is a crack in the bathroom ceiling and a draught under the door.

pays_in.note: It marks a first mention, which tells you what is new in a passage.
pays_in.model: The team built a shelter above the tideline before the survey began.

used_in.quote: Talking about what you cook and where you buy it introduces a new thing in almost every sentence.

payload.sentence: Gethin ordered a soup and a bread roll.
payload.question: How many bowls of soup did he order?

feedback.why_key: The small word counts to one every time it appears, so the number was settled before the food was even named.
feedback.feed_forward: Read a as the number one wearing a smaller coat.

payload.sentence: The café sells bread from the bakery next door.
payload.question: How many loaves does this tell you about?

feedback.why_key: Nothing counts this word, so the sentence describes what the café sells without ever claiming a number.
feedback.feed_forward: Notice when a bare word is naming a kind, not a count.

items.decision_cue: works as cook at the harbour café

payload.context: From a first draft of a letter about a job.
payload.sentence: My brother works as cook at the harbour café.
reasons: a single job named like this needs a small word in front of it
the café has been put in the wrong place
the sentence needs a full stop in the middle
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The job is perfectly clear without it, which is why the gap survives every reread. English still refuses to leave the space bare.
feedback.feed_forward: Put a in front of every job you name.

payload.context: From a note left for the next shift.
payload.stem: The delivery is running ___ hour late again.

expected: an

feedback.why_key: The h makes no sound here, so the next thing the mouth meets is a vowel and the longer form is needed.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the next word aloud before you choose.

payload.context: Telling a friend about a weekend away.
payload.stem: We found ___ small hostel just behind the harbour.

expected: a

feedback.why_key: One hostel, and the listener is hearing about it for the first time, so the shorter form goes in front of the describing word.
feedback.feed_forward: Place the small word ahead of any describing word.

payload.context: Build one sentence describing the kitchen at the back of the café.

expected: there is an oven and a fridge in the back room

feedback.why_key: Two new things, two small words, and each one is chosen by the sound that comes straight after it.
feedback.feed_forward: Give every newly named thing its own small word.

payload.given: Bea has a job at the hotel. Her job is cooking.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence naming the job she does.

expected: as a chef
as a cook
as a chef at the hotel
as a cook at the hotel

feedback.why_key: English names a job with a small word in front of it, even though only one person is being talked about.
feedback.feed_forward: Say as a before the name of any job.

payload.audio_text: We waited an hour for a table by the window.

expected: we waited an hour for a table by the window

feedback.why_key: Both small words are unstressed and almost swallowed, and both change the count of what the speaker is describing.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the tiny word in front of each thing.

payload.sentence: The office gave us an advice about the closing date.

expected: advice
some advice

feedback.why_key: It was one piece of guidance, which is why the counting word feels honest. This word simply cannot be counted in English.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete the counting word in front of advice.

payload.context: From a draft description of a ferry journey.
payload.sentence: The crossing takes a hour and twenty minutes in good weather.
reasons: the small word was chosen by the letter rather than by the sound
the crossing has been put in the wrong place
the sentence needs a full stop in the middle
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The spelling starts with a consonant and the sound does not, and English follows the sound every time.
feedback.feed_forward: Test the next word with your mouth, not your eyes.

payload.context: Two lines from a note left on the counter.
sentences: We need a coffee for table four.
We need coffee for the whole week.
meanings: One cup is wanted, and it is wanted now.
A supply of it is wanted, and no number is being given.

feedback.why_key: The same word means a cup when something counts it and a substance when nothing does.
feedback.feed_forward: Check whether anything in front is doing the counting.

payload.prompt_text: You have just moved into a rented flat and two things are missing from the kitchen. Write one sentence telling the landlord what is not there.

feedback.why_key: Both things are new to the landlord, so both arrive with a small word in front of them and the sentence sounds finished.
feedback.feed_forward: Introduce each missing thing with a or an.

payload.prompt_text: Take the Part 1 card about food and cooking. Speak for forty seconds. Listen back and mark every single thing you named for the first time with nothing in front of it.

feedback.why_key: The small word is unstressed, so it is the first thing speed removes, and its absence is what makes fluent speech still sound foreign.
feedback.feed_forward: Slow down at the moment you name something new.

title: Putting describing words in front of the thing, and never adding an s to them

point_json.grammar_name: Adjective position and invariability

teach.can_do: I can put a describing word in the right place and keep it the same shape however many things there are.
teach.why_it_matters: Two reds cars is a first-week slip that survives to a high level if nobody names it. It is cheap to fix now and expensive to leave alone.
teach.meaning: A describing word says what something is like: cold, empty, expensive. In English it goes in front of the thing it describes, and it never changes shape at all. It does not grow an s when there are three things instead of one, and it does not take a different ending for a man or a woman. Many languages do both of those, which is why both feel natural to write. The describing word can also come after is or are, and there too it stays exactly as it was.

form.pattern: describing word + naming word — a cold room, two cold rooms
notes: It comes first and never afterwards: never a room cold.
It never takes the mark for more than one: two cold rooms, and never two colds rooms.
It never changes for a man or a woman: a tall woman, a tall man, the same word both times.
After is or are it keeps the same shape: the rooms are cold.
form.negative: not goes with the word carrying the sentence rather than with the describing word: the room is not cold.
form.question: Ask what is it like. Put that word straight in front of the thing, and then leave it completely alone.

left.text: cold · empty · expensive

right.text: room · rooms · flat · flats

spec.caption: The left box never changes, however much the right box does.

worked_example.sentence: The two empty flats above the shop need new windows.
worked_example.why_this_form: Empty and new both sit in front of the things they describe, and neither of them grows an s even though flats and windows both did.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Write two emptys flats and a reader still understands you perfectly, which is the trap: the meaning arrives and the mistake stays put.

notice_set.sentence: Ottoline rents two small rooms above the bakery.
notice_set.question: How many rooms does she rent?
notice_set.why: The number is carried by the thing itself, so the word describing it has nothing to do and does not change.

notice_set.sentence: The old lifts in the north block are slow.
notice_set.question: What are the lifts like?
notice_set.why: One describing word comes in front of the lifts and the other comes after are, and both describe the same lifts.

notice_set.sentence: Gethin bought an expensive coat for the winter.
notice_set.question: How many coats did he buy?
notice_set.why: The counting is done by the small word at the front. Expensive says nothing at all about number.

notice_set.sentence: The tall man in the blue coat runs the stall.
notice_set.question: What is the man wearing?
notice_set.why: Two describing words, each in front of the thing it describes, and neither changed for the man.

notice_set.sentence: The rooms upstairs are cold in winter.
notice_set.question: What are those rooms like in winter?
notice_set.why: Here the describing word arrives after are instead of in front, and it still keeps exactly the same shape.

teach.rule_line: Describing words go in front of the thing and never change shape, however many things there are.
teach.false_rule: That a describing word has to match the thing it describes, the way it does in Spanish, French or Arabic. English describing words never move and never change.

errors.wrong: The two reds cars were parked across the entrance.
errors.right: The two red cars were parked across the entrance.
errors.why_it_happens: The mark for more than one is spread across the whole group, because in many languages that is exactly what happens. English puts it on the naming word only.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one letter: the s on reds.
errors.l1_note: Very common for speakers of Spanish, French, Italian and Arabic.

errors.wrong: Ottoline rents two rooms small above the bakery.
errors.right: Ottoline rents two small rooms above the bakery.
errors.why_it_happens: In many languages the describing word follows the thing, so the sentence reads as perfectly ordinary to the writer. English readers stumble over it every time.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: small goes in front of rooms.
errors.l1_note: Very common for speakers of Spanish, French, Arabic and Persian.

errors.wrong: Gethin bought expensive coat for the winter.
errors.right: Gethin bought an expensive coat for the winter.
errors.why_it_happens: The describing word arrives first and fills the space where the small word belongs, so the front of the group feels occupied and nothing seems missing.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: an.

pays_in.note: A long turn describing a place is a run of these, said quickly.
pays_in.model: It was a narrow street with two old cafés and a small market at the end.

pays_in.note: Describing what is wrong with a flat needs one in nearly every clause.
pays_in.model: The back windows are draughty and the front door has a broken lock.

pays_in.note: Describing words carry the writer's attitude, and the questions test it.
pays_in.model: The report describes a modest rise and a sharp fall in the same year.

used_in.quote: Answering this card means describing rooms, and every description hangs on one of these words sitting in the right place.

payload.sentence: The three empty flats face the yard.
payload.question: How many flats are empty?

feedback.why_key: The number sits on the thing being described, never on the word describing it, so empty stays as it is.
feedback.feed_forward: Count from the naming word, not from the describing word.

payload.sentence: Imre rents two narrow rooms over the workshop.
payload.question: What are the rooms like?

feedback.why_key: The word standing directly in front of the rooms is the one describing them, which is where English always puts it.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the word immediately before the thing.

payload.context: From a first draft of a letter to a landlord.
payload.sentence: The flat has two olds radiators and a broken window.
reasons: a describing word has been given the mark for more than one
the window has been put in the wrong place
the sentence needs a full stop in the middle
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: There really are two of them, so the mark feels owed. Only the naming word is allowed to carry it.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the mark on the thing and off the description.

payload.context: From a description of a flat above a shop.
payload.stem: The flat has four ___ (cold) rooms on the north side.

expected: cold

feedback.why_key: Four rooms sit right after it and it still does not move a letter. That is the whole habit being built here.
feedback.feed_forward: Type the describing word exactly as it was given.

payload.context: Describing a street you remember from a trip.
payload.stem: There were two ___ (old) cafés at the far end.

expected: old

feedback.why_key: Two cafés, one unchanged describing word. The number has already been announced twice and does not need announcing again.
feedback.feed_forward: Leave the describing word untouched after a number.

payload.context: Build one sentence about a repair that has been done.

expected: the landlord replaced the two broken locks last week

feedback.why_key: The describing word slots in between the number and the thing, and there is nowhere else in the sentence it can legally sit.
feedback.feed_forward: Slide the describing word in just before the thing.

payload.given: The kitchen has a window. The window is small and it does not open.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that puts the describing word in front of the thing.

expected: a small window that does not open
a small window which does not open
one small window that does not open

feedback.why_key: Moving the description forward turns two flat statements into one, and the small word still has to come before it.
feedback.feed_forward: Move the description in front and keep the small word first.

payload.audio_text: There are two old radiators and a cracked tile.

expected: there are two old radiators and a cracked tile

feedback.why_key: You will hear an s on radiators and none on old, and that difference is the entire lesson in one short line.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for which word in the group carries the s.

payload.sentence: The town has three olds hotels and a new one by the pier.

expected: three old hotels

feedback.why_key: The second half of the sentence got it right, which shows the writer knows the rule and lost it under speed.
feedback.feed_forward: Strip any s from a word that is only describing.

items.decision_cue: a room large at the back

payload.context: From a draft advertisement for a flat.
payload.sentence: The flat has a room large at the back and two small ones upstairs.
reasons: one describing word has been put after the thing it describes
the flat has been put in the wrong place
the sentence needs a full stop in the middle
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The second half of the sentence puts small in front, so the writer already knows where it goes and slipped once.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that no description trails behind its thing.

items.decision_cue: The flat has a small kitchen

payload.context: Two lines taken from different advertisements.
sentences: The flat has a small kitchen.
The flat has small kitchens.
meanings: There is one kitchen, and it is not large.
There is more than one kitchen, and none of them is large.

feedback.why_key: The describing word is identical in both lines. Everything about the number is carried by the thing and the word in front of it.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the naming word for the count, every time.

payload.prompt_text: You are advertising a room to rent. Write one sentence describing the room and the street it stands on, using at least three describing words.

feedback.why_key: Three descriptions in one sentence is where the s starts creeping onto the wrong words, because the sentence is long enough to lose track of.
feedback.feed_forward: Reread each describing word and delete any s.

payload.prompt_text: Take the Part 1 card about your home and the space in it. Speak for forty seconds about one room. Listen back and check that no describing word grew an s and that none of them arrived after the thing it described.

feedback.why_key: Describing a room out loud means stacking these words fast, and speed is where the wrong ending and the wrong position both appear.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the description before the thing, every time.

title: Saying that something exists somewhere: there is and there are

point_json.grammar_name: Existential there

teach.can_do: I can say that something exists somewhere, and match the small word to how many there are.
teach.why_it_matters: It is how English announces that something exists at all, and the word after there is decided by what comes next, which is the opposite of every other sentence.
teach.meaning: To announce that something exists somewhere, English does not begin with the thing. It begins with there, which points at nothing whatever, then puts is or are, and only then names the thing. There is a night bus. There are two night buses. Because the real thing arrives after the word that has to match it, you have to look forward rather than back, and this is the one place in the language where that happens.

form.pattern: There is + one thing · There are + more than one thing
notes: Choose is or are by looking forward at the thing that follows, never back at there.
With a list, match the first thing named: there is a table and four chairs.
Out loud it becomes there's for one thing. For more than one, speakers say there are in full.
form.negative: There is not a bus until seven. There are no seats left on the early train.
form.question: Turn the two words round: Is there a lift in the building? Are there any seats left?

left.role: the word that opens the door and means nothing at all
left.text: There

right.role: the thing that actually exists, and the word it chose
right.text: is a night bus · are two night buses

spec.caption: The thing on the right decides the word on its left. Read forward, then go back.

worked_example.sentence: There are four bus routes into Ashfield and one of them runs all night.
worked_example.why_this_form: Four routes come after the gap, so are was chosen by looking forward at them. Nothing about the opening word itself decides anything.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Write there is and the sentence promises one route and then names four, so the reader stops to work out which number to believe.

notice_set.sentence: There are three cafés on the square.
notice_set.question: How many cafés does the square have?
notice_set.why: The small word before the number had already told you to expect more than one.

notice_set.sentence: There is a chemist at the end of the street.
notice_set.question: How many chemists is this about?
notice_set.why: The small word announces a single thing, and a single chemist duly arrives after it.

notice_set.sentence: There are no seats left on the early train.
notice_set.question: Could you sit down on that train?
notice_set.why: The word no wipes the seats out entirely, so the sentence says they do not exist.

notice_set.sentence: It is a long walk from the station to the depot.
notice_set.question: What is this sentence telling you?
notice_set.why: This opening describes something. The other opening would have announced that the walk was there at all.

notice_set.sentence: There is a lift in the north block, but it is out of order.
notice_set.question: Can you use the lift?
notice_set.why: The first half says the lift is there and the second says it does not work. Being there and working are two claims.

teach.rule_line: Open with there, look forward at the thing, and let the thing choose is or are.
teach.false_rule: That there is and it is do the same job. There is announces that something exists. It is describes something the listener has already got.

errors.wrong: There is four bus routes into Ashfield.
errors.right: There are four bus routes into Ashfield.
errors.why_it_happens: The choice is made before the thing has been named, because everywhere else the deciding word comes first. Here it comes second and the writer has already committed.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: is becomes are.

errors.wrong: There is, along the coast road, several closed cafés.
errors.right: There are, along the coast road, several closed cafés.
errors.why_it_happens: Five words stand between the choice and the thing that decides it, and by the time the thing arrives the sentence has already moved past the decision.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: is becomes are.

errors.wrong: It is a chemist on the corner by the school.
errors.right: There is a chemist on the corner by the school.
errors.why_it_happens: Both openings park a small word in the front seat and both feel like the same move. Only one of them announces that something is there.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: It becomes There.
errors.l1_note: Common where the first language uses one verb, often have, for both jobs.

pays_in.note: Opening a map or process description almost always announces what is there.
pays_in.model: There are three stages in the process and two of them run at the same time.

pays_in.note: Describing your home town means saying what the place has got.
pays_in.model: There's a market on Saturdays and there are two parks near the river.

pays_in.note: The opening is squeezed to one sound and it warns you a list is coming.
pays_in.model: There's a form to fill in and there are two people to see first.

used_in.quote: A map description opens by announcing what the place contains, and every one of those sentences is this shape.

payload.sentence: There are four benches along the harbour path.
payload.question: How many benches does the path have?

feedback.why_key: The small word after there had already promised more than one before any number appeared.

payload.sentence: There's a chemist at the end of our street.

feedback.why_key: Squeezed down to one sound, the small word still announces a single thing and a single chemist follows it.

payload.context: From a first draft describing a station map.
payload.sentence: There is four platforms and a footbridge between them.
reasons: the small word was chosen before the thing that decides it was named
the footbridge has been put in the wrong place
the sentence needs a full stop in the middle
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.feed_forward: Look ahead to the thing before you write is.

payload.stem: There ___ two car parks and a bus stand near the pier.

expected: are

payload.context: Describing the block of flats you live in.
payload.stem: There ___ a lift in the entrance, but nobody uses it.

expected: is

feedback.why_key: One lift follows the gap, so the gap takes the word that goes with a single thing.
feedback.feed_forward: Count the thing after the gap before filling it.

payload.context: Build one sentence describing what the town has.

expected: there are two markets in the town and one closes in winter

feedback.feed_forward: Start with there, then let the thing follow.

payload.given: The square has four benches.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it so that the sentence announces that the benches are there.

expected: are four benches in the square

payload.audio_text: There's a market on Saturdays and there are two parks.

expected: there's a market on saturdays and there are two parks
there is a market on saturdays and there are two parks
theres a market on saturdays and there are two parks

feedback.why_key: The first opening is squeezed into one syllable and the second is not, and the difference is the count of what follows each one.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for whether the opening is squeezed or full.

payload.sentence: There is, on the far side of the estate, two empty shops.

expected: there are

feedback.why_key: Seven words separate the decision from the thing that decides it, and nothing in between offers a warning.
feedback.feed_forward: Read to the end of the sentence before fixing the opening.

items.decision_cue: It is a crack in the ceiling

payload.context: From a draft letter to a landlord about repairs.
payload.sentence: It is a crack in the ceiling above the bath.
reasons: this opening describes something rather than announcing that it is there
the ceiling has been put in the wrong place
the sentence needs a full stop in the middle
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: As written, the sentence answers a question nobody asked, about what some already-known thing turns out to be.
feedback.feed_forward: Use there when the reader has not met the thing.

payload.context: Two lines from different reports on the same street.
sentences: There is a bus stop outside the college.
It is a bus stop outside the college.
meanings: The writer is telling you that a stop is there at all.
The writer is telling you what a thing already mentioned turns out to be.

feedback.why_key: One line brings a stop into the conversation and the other explains a thing that was already in it.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the thing is new before you choose.

payload.prompt_text: A map shows a small coastal town with a harbour, two car parks and a new footbridge. Write one sentence opening a description of what the town has.

feedback.why_key: An opening sentence has to bring several things into the reader's head at once, and this shape is built for exactly that.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the opening word to the first thing you name.

title: Saying who something belongs to, with my, your, her and the added 's

point_json.grammar_name: Possessive determiners and possessive 's

teach.can_do: I can say who something belongs to, with a short word in front of it or with an added 's.
teach.why_it_matters: English marks ownership in front of the thing and never after it, and the word is chosen by the owner rather than by the thing owned.
teach.meaning: English has two ways of saying who something belongs to, and both of them go in front of the thing. The first is a short word: my, your, his, her, its, our, their. The second is an added 's on the owner: Nils's boots, the club's rules. Whichever you use, the choice is settled by the owner and never by the thing owned. His car and his keys are both his because he owns them; the car and the keys get no say in it.

form.pattern: my · your · his · her · its · our · their + the thing — or — the owner + 's + the thing
notes: Chosen by the owner: her brother, her brothers, her house, all her, because she is the owner.
Add 's to a person, an animal or a group: Nils's coach, the team's kit. Use of for a thing: the roof of the station.
its means belonging to it. it's means it is. Two different words that sound identical.
After the short word you never also use the: never the my coat.
form.negative: not belongs to the word carrying the sentence: that is not my bag.
form.question: Ask whose. The answer goes in front of the thing, as a short word or with an added 's.

left.text: Nils · the team · she

right.text: Nils's boots · the team's kit · her boots

spec.caption: The owner always comes first, and the thing owned never gets a vote.

worked_example.sentence: Nils lost his boots the week before the club's first match.
worked_example.why_this_form: His is chosen because Nils is the owner, and the club takes an added 's because it owns the match. Both sit in front of what is owned.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Write her boots and the sentence quietly hands them to somebody else, and no reader could tell that anything had gone wrong.

notice_set.sentence: Nils cleaned his boots after the match.
notice_set.question: Whose boots did he clean?
notice_set.why: The short word points back to Nils, who is the last person named.

notice_set.sentence: Marta borrowed her sister's bike for the race.
notice_set.question: Who owns the bike?
notice_set.why: The added 's sits on the sister, so the sister owns it and Marta only borrowed it.

notice_set.sentence: The club's changing rooms are locked at nine.
notice_set.question: Who do the changing rooms belong to?
notice_set.why: The added 's marks the club as the owner of whatever follows it.

notice_set.sentence: Their coach lives on the far side of town.
notice_set.question: How many people share this coach?
notice_set.why: This short word is the one English uses when more than one person is the owner.

notice_set.sentence: Its front wheel is buckled and the frame is bent.
notice_set.question: What is this sentence about?
notice_set.why: Without a mark between the two letters the word means belonging to it, so something was named just before.

teach.rule_line: Ask whose, then put the answer in front of the thing, as a short word or with 's.
teach.false_rule: That the word changes to match the thing owned, the way it does in French or Spanish. The owner alone decides it: her brothers, his sisters.

errors.wrong: Marta forgot his kit and had to borrow one from the coach.
errors.right: Marta forgot her kit and had to borrow one from the coach.
errors.why_it_happens: The word is being matched to the thing owned, which is what happens in French, Spanish and Italian. English matches it to the owner instead.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: his becomes her.
errors.l1_note: Very common for speakers of French, Spanish, Italian and Arabic.

errors.wrong: That is the my bag on the bench by the door.
errors.right: That is my bag on the bench by the door.
errors.why_it_happens: Two words that both point at the thing get stacked in front of it, because plenty of languages use them together and it sounds fuller that way.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: the.

errors.wrong: The roof from the station leaks over the ticket hall.
errors.right: The roof of the station leaks over the ticket hall.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer reaches for the word meaning coming out of, because belonging feels like coming from. English uses of when a thing owns a part of itself.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: from becomes of.

errors.wrong: Its a long walk to the ground from the bus stop.
errors.right: It's a long walk to the ground from the bus stop.
errors.why_it_happens: The two spellings sound identical and the one without a mark looks tidier, so it gets written. One means belonging to it and the other means it is.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one apostrophe to Its.

pays_in.note: Telling a story about people means saying whose thing you mean, constantly.
pays_in.model: I borrowed my brother's bike and left it outside the club's back gate.

pays_in.note: A letter about a shared building needs one in almost every sentence.
pays_in.model: My flat is above the shop and its front window faces the road.

pays_in.note: Tracking who owns what is how you follow a passage with two people in it.
pays_in.model: The captain's decision was overruled by the committee that ran the club.

used_in.quote: A long turn about a sport is full of other people's equipment, other people's coaching and your own gaps.

payload.sentence: Nils cleaned his boots after the match.
payload.question: Whose boots did he clean?

feedback.why_key: The short word points back to the last person named, and that person is Nils.
feedback.feed_forward: Trace the short word back to the nearest owner.

payload.sentence: Marta borrowed her sister's bike for the race.
payload.question: Who owns the bike?

feedback.why_key: The added mark sits on the sister, so she is the owner and Marta is only the rider.
feedback.feed_forward: Look for the word carrying the added 's.

payload.context: From a first draft of a message to a club secretary.
payload.sentence: I left the my kit in the changing room on Saturday.
reasons: two words doing the same job are stacked in front of the thing
the changing room has been put in the wrong place
the sentence needs a full stop in the middle
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Both words point at the kit, and English lets only one of them stand in that space.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose either the or the ownership word, never both.

payload.context: From a note about something left behind at the ground.
payload.stem: Marta cannot find ___ (she) training shoes.

expected: her

feedback.why_key: The owner is Marta, so the word is chosen from her and not from the shoes standing next to it.
feedback.feed_forward: Pick the word from the owner, not from the thing.

payload.context: Talking about a team you used to play for.
payload.stem: We trained at ___ (the club) old ground by the river.

expected: the club's
the clubs

feedback.why_key: A group owns things the same way a person does, so the added mark goes straight onto it.
feedback.feed_forward: Add 's to a group exactly as you would to a person.

payload.context: Build one sentence about a repair the club needs.

expected: the roof of the clubhouse leaks above the kit room

feedback.why_key: A building is not a person, so the part it owns is joined on with of rather than with an added mark.
feedback.feed_forward: Use of when the owner is a thing, not a person.

payload.given: Marta has a sister. The sister owns the bike Marta rode.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence saying whose bike Marta rode.

expected: her sister's bike
her sisters bike

feedback.why_key: Two owners stack up in front of one bike, and each of them is chosen by who owns what comes next.
feedback.feed_forward: Build the group from the owner inwards to the thing.

payload.audio_text: Their coach kept his notes in the team's old bag.

expected: their coach kept his notes in the team's old bag
their coach kept his notes in the teams old bag

feedback.why_key: Three owners in nine words, and every one of them is a short unstressed sound you have to catch to know who had what.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the small word in front of each thing.

payload.sentence: The gates from the ground are locked an hour after the whistle.

expected: the gates of the ground
the ground's gates
the grounds gates

feedback.why_key: Coming from a place and belonging to a place are different claims, and only one of them is true of a gate.
feedback.feed_forward: Change from to of when you mean belonging.

payload.context: From a draft report on the club's equipment.
payload.sentence: Its front wheel is buckled and the frame has a crack in it.
reasons: the word needs a mark between the two letters
the wheel has been put in the wrong place
the sentence needs a full stop in the middle
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Here the word really does mean belonging to it, and belonging is the one meaning that takes no mark at all.
feedback.feed_forward: Test it by reading the word as it is.

payload.context: Two lines from a report on the same afternoon.
sentences: Nils took his sister's bike.
Nils took her sister's bike.
meanings: The bike belongs to a sister of Nils.
The bike belongs to the sister of some other woman already named.

feedback.why_key: The word does not describe the sister at all. It says whose sister she is, and that changes who owns the bike.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the short word as naming the owner behind it.

payload.prompt_text: You have left two things behind at a sports club: one of your own and one you had borrowed from a friend. Write one sentence saying what is missing and whose it is.

feedback.why_key: Two owners in one sentence is where the words start being chosen by whatever is nearest instead of by who actually owns the thing.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the owner in your head before each thing.

payload.prompt_text: Take the Part 2 card about a sport you would like to be better at. Speak for forty seconds. Listen back and check that every his, her and their points at the person you actually meant.

feedback.why_key: In a long turn with two people in it, these small words drift onto the wrong owner and the listener quietly loses the thread.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the owner aloud whenever the story changes person.

title: Saying that something happened and finished, using the -ed ending

point_json.grammar_name: Past simple: regular verbs

teach.can_do: I can say that something happened and is over, using the -ed ending.
teach.why_it_matters: This ending is how English says the thing is done. Leave it off and every sentence you write drifts back into today.
teach.meaning: Adding -ed to a verb makes one claim and one only: this happened, and the happening is behind us. It does not say how long it took, whether it happened once or forty times, or whether anybody can still see the result. It marks the whole thing as closed. English puts that mark on the verb, once, whether or not the sentence ever says when.

form.pattern: verb + -ed  (walk → walked, ask → asked)
notes: A verb already ending in e just adds d: close → closed
A consonant plus y turns into ied: study → studied, carry → carried
One short vowel and one final consonant doubles it: stop → stopped, plan → planned
Three sounds, one spelling: worked ends in a t sound, filled in a d sound, and wanted adds a whole extra beat
form.negative: did not walk / didn't walk — the ending comes off, because did is now carrying it (unit point four)
form.question: Did you walk ...? — again the plain verb, because did has taken the job

marks.label: the sentence stops well short of here

spec.caption: The ending puts a lid on the event. Nothing about today is being claimed.

worked_example.sentence: The college moved its evening classes to the harbour campus.
worked_example.why_this_form: The move happened and finished. One ending on one verb tells the reader that, without any date being named at all.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Moves would turn it into something the college does again and again, as a matter of policy, and would say nothing about any particular move.

notice_set.sentence: The library closed at four during the exam weeks.
notice_set.question: Does the library still close at four?
notice_set.why: The ending shuts the whole thing away in a finished stretch of time. Today is not part of the claim.

notice_set.sentence: We walked to the study group together.
notice_set.question: Did this happen once, or many times?
notice_set.why: The ending says finished, not how often. Only extra words can tell you that.

notice_set.sentence: The tutor emailed the results and everybody opened them at once.
notice_set.question: Which happened first?
notice_set.why: Two closed events, told in the order they happened. English lets the order of the words do that work.

notice_set.sentence: She wanted a place on the course.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker say whether she got one?
notice_set.why: The ending closes the wanting. What came after it is a different sentence.

notice_set.sentence: The two colleges shared a library for years.
notice_set.question: Do they share it now?
notice_set.why: Closing the years off is a way of saying the arrangement is over. If it were still running the speaker could not have shut it.

teach.rule_line: If it happened and it is over, put -ed on the verb, once.
teach.false_rule: That you only need the ending when the sentence names a time. Most past sentences name none, and the ending goes on anyway.

errors.wrong: I joined the study group and we walk to the library every Thursday.
errors.right: I joined the study group and we walked to the library every Thursday.
errors.why_it_happens: The first verb was chosen carefully and the second was not. Every Thursday feels like a habit, and habits pull the speaker back into the present without warning.
errors.smallest_fix: Add two letters: walk becomes walked.

errors.wrong: The bus stoped outside the college gates.
errors.right: The bus stopped outside the college gates.
errors.why_it_happens: The rule the learner has is add -ed, and it is the right rule. The doubling is a spelling habit nobody mentions until it is already wrong on paper.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one letter: stoped becomes stopped.

errors.wrong: We studyed the same subject for two years.
errors.right: We studied the same subject for two years.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner applies the ending exactly as taught. Nothing in add -ed warns them that a consonant plus y behaves differently.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one letter: the y becomes an i.

errors.wrong: The course started in October. It lasts ten weeks and finished before the holiday.
errors.right: The course started in October. It lasted ten weeks and finished before the holiday.
errors.why_it_happens: Facts that are still true about the course, like its length, feel present to the writer even inside a report about a course that has ended.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one letter: the s becomes a d.

pays_in.note: Any example from your own experience is written in this form from start to finish.
pays_in.model: When the council opened the riverside path, local shops reported far more passing trade.

pays_in.note: The long turn is almost always a story, and a story runs on this ending.
pays_in.model: I signed up for the evening class and travelled across town twice a week for a year.

pays_in.note: The ending is often a single consonant and it is easy to miss entirely.
pays_in.model: They finished the survey and posted the results to every household.

used_in.quote: A skill you learned outside school is a finished story, and every sentence in it carries this ending.
Every year on the graph has closed, so every movement described in the answer is reported with this form.

payload.sentence: The college opened a second entrance on the harbour side.
payload.question: Is the opening still to come?

feedback.why_key: The ending puts the whole event behind the speaker. Nothing about it is still waiting to happen.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the ending as a lid on the event.

payload.sentence: I walked to my classes.
payload.question: Where does this sit?
options: a closed stretch of the past
a habit the speaker still has

feedback.why_key: The ending shuts the habit away. Whether the speaker still walks is a separate sentence they have not said.
feedback.feed_forward: Place the event on the line before you think about now.

items.decision_cue: and we travel to the coast

payload.context: From a paragraph about the writer's first year at college.
payload.sentence: I signed up for the field trip and we travel to the coast together.
reasons: the second verb slipped back into today
the writer did not join the group
a group cannot walk anywhere
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Both events belong to the same closed year. One of them has been left standing in the present.
feedback.feed_forward: Read your verbs on their own, in order, before you move on.

payload.context: From a short report on an evening course.
payload.stem: Twenty-two students ___ (enrol) in September and eighteen finished the year.

expected: enrolled

feedback.why_key: One short vowel and one final consonant, so the consonant doubles before the ending.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the verb aloud and listen for a short vowel before you spell it.

payload.context: From a note on a walking scheme in Ashfield.
payload.stem: The clinic ___ (copy) the results to the council before the deadline.

expected: copied

feedback.why_key: A vowel before the y keeps it; a consonant before the y turns it into an i.
feedback.feed_forward: Look at the letter before the y, then spell the ending.

payload.given: The tutor emails the reading list and the students print it in the library.

feedback.why_key: Two verbs, two endings. Moving one and leaving the other is the commonest way this goes wrong.
feedback.feed_forward: Change every verb in the sentence, not the first one.

payload.audio_text: They finished the project and waited for the marks.

expected: they finished the project and waited for the marks

feedback.why_key: One ending is a single hiss at the end of a word; the other adds a whole beat. Same spelling, two sounds.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen to the end of each verb, not the middle.

payload.context: Build one sentence about work that was completed in Verdon.

expected: the council planted four hundred trees along the river path

feedback.why_key: The ending sits on the verb and nowhere else, right after the thing that did it.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the doer first, then the verb with its ending.

items.decision_cue: The college closes on the first Friday of every month.

payload.context: Two lines taken from different college notices.
sentences: The college closes on the first Friday of every month.
The college closed on the first Friday of every month.
meanings: This is the arrangement now, and you can plan around it.
That was the arrangement during a stretch of time that has ended.

feedback.why_key: One ending is the whole difference between a notice you can act on and a fact about a past year.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the arrangement is still running.

payload.sentence: We applyed for the same course and both of us started in the autumn.

expected: applied

feedback.why_key: The rest of the sentence is fine. A consonant sits in front of the y, so the y cannot stay.
feedback.feed_forward: Check the letter before a final y before you add the ending.

payload.context: From a report on a walking scheme that ran two winters ago.
payload.sentence: The scheme opened in October. It runs for ten weeks and reached four hundred households.
reasons: one verb in the middle is still standing in the present
the scheme never started
ten weeks is too long for a scheme

title: Using the past of the verbs that refuse the -ed ending

point_json.grammar_name: Past simple: irregular verbs

teach.can_do: I can use the past of the common verbs that do not take the -ed ending.
teach.why_it_matters: The verbs that break the rule are the ones you need most: go, take, make, buy, eat. Every second sentence of a story leans on one of them.
teach.meaning: About ninety everyday verbs do not build their past by adding anything. They swap to a different word: go becomes went, buy becomes bought, eat becomes ate. The meaning is exactly the meaning of the -ed ending — it happened, it is closed — but the shape has to be learned one verb at a time. There is no rule waiting to be discovered here. There is a list, and it is short, and you already know half of it.

form.pattern: a separate past word, learned verb by verb  (go → went · buy → bought · eat → ate)
notes: Learn them in sound families rather than alphabetically: bring/brought, buy/bought, think/thought
A second family swaps one vowel: drink/drank, sing/sang, begin/began
A third family does nothing at all: cut/cut, put/put, let/let, cost/cost
Six of them cover most of what you will say: went, had, said, made, took, got
form.negative: did not go / didn't go — the special past word disappears and did carries the past instead
form.question: Did you go ...? — the plain verb comes back for the same reason

left.text: eat · buy · go · take

right.role: the past word you have to learn
right.text: ate · bought · went · took

spec.caption: Nothing is added and nothing is spelled out. One word is exchanged for another.

worked_example.sentence: We ate at the stall by the fish market and paid four pounds each.
worked_example.why_this_form: Ate is the whole past of eat; there is nothing to add to it. Paid sits beside it doing the same job with a different shape.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Eat would leave the meal in the speaker's ordinary week, as something they do rather than something they did on one occasion.

notice_set.sentence: The bakery sold out before ten.
notice_set.question: Could you still buy bread there at eleven?
notice_set.why: Sold is the past of sell, and the sentence closes the morning's stock before eleven arrives.

notice_set.sentence: They put the vegetables outside every morning that summer.
notice_set.question: Is this about one morning or about a run of mornings?
notice_set.why: Put looks the same in both places. Every morning that summer is what tells you the rest.

notice_set.sentence: The café kept its old sign when the owners changed.
notice_set.question: Is the sign still up?
notice_set.why: Kept closes the keeping at the moment the owners changed. Anything after that is a different sentence.

notice_set.sentence: I made the same soup for a week and got very tired of it.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker still want that soup?
notice_set.why: Two swapped past words in one sentence, and the second one lands on the speaker's feelings at the end of that week.

notice_set.sentence: The market began at six and the traders left by two.
notice_set.question: How many separate events are being reported?
notice_set.why: Began and left are two closed events with a gap between them, and neither takes an ending.

teach.rule_line: Some verbs swap to a different word for the past. Learn them in small families.
teach.false_rule: That there is a pattern underneath, and that once you find it you will not need the list. There is no pattern. Learning the list is the work.

errors.wrong: We eated at the harbour café before the film.
errors.right: We ate at the harbour café before the film.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner applies the rule they were given, and the rule is a good one. It is simply not the rule this verb obeys, and nothing in the sentence warns them.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: eated becomes ate.

errors.wrong: She buyed the bread from the stall at the end of the row.
errors.right: She bought the bread from the stall at the end of the row.
errors.why_it_happens: Buy sounds regular and looks regular. The past word shares almost no letters with it, so there is nothing to jog the memory in the middle of a sentence.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: buyed becomes bought.

errors.wrong: The café opened at six and we come in for breakfast every morning of that week.
errors.right: The café opened at six and we came in for breakfast every morning of that week.
errors.why_it_happens: Come and came differ by one letter and the base form already sounds finished, so the ear accepts it. Habit words like every morning make it worse.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: come becomes came.

errors.wrong: He putted the tray down on the counter and went back for the rest.
errors.right: He put the tray down on the counter and went back for the rest.
errors.why_it_happens: A past with no visible mark feels unfinished, so the learner adds one to be safe. Adding it is the error the safety produces.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete three letters: putted becomes put.

pays_in.note: The verbs that carry a spoken story are almost all on this list.
pays_in.model: I took the coast road, got there far too early and sat outside for an hour.

pays_in.note: One wrong past word in an example is the most visible slip on the page.
pays_in.model: When the council brought the market indoors, the number of stalls fell by half.

pays_in.note: Some of these differ from their plain form by a single vowel and go past fast.
pays_in.model: They ran the stall for years and then sold it to a neighbour.

used_in.quote: A meal you enjoyed with other people is told with went, had, made, took and ate, and almost nothing else.
The passage narrates a stretch of the river's history, and the narration runs on these swapped past words.

payload.sentence: The stall sold out before the market closed.
payload.question: Was there anything left at the end?

feedback.why_key: Sold is the past of sell, and selling out empties the stall before the closing time arrives.
feedback.feed_forward: Recognise the past word first, then read what it claims.

payload.sentence: We put the chairs outside as soon as the rain stopped.
payload.question: Where does this sit?
options: a closed stretch of the past
something the speaker does every day

feedback.why_key: Put never changes shape, so the sentence next to it is what places the moment. Stopped has closed it.
feedback.feed_forward: When a verb never changes, read the verbs around it.

payload.context: Idris is telling a friend about a morning at the market.
payload.sentence: I buyed the bread from the stall on the corner.
reasons: buy has its own past word and does not take the ending
bread cannot be bought at a stall
the speaker should be talking about today
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The rule is right and the verb is the exception. Buy exchanges itself for bought and takes nothing extra.
feedback.feed_forward: Check any verb you use often against the list before you trust the ending.

payload.context: Two friends talking about a meal at the harbour.
payload.stem: We ___ (eat) outside because the room upstairs was full.

expected: ate

feedback.why_key: Eat swaps to ate. Nothing is added and nothing is doubled.
feedback.feed_forward: Recall the past word before you reach for the ending.

payload.context: From a short piece about a market in Ashfield.
payload.stem: The council ___ (bring) the whole market indoors and half the traders left.

expected: brought

feedback.why_key: Bring belongs to the family that ends in ought: bring, buy, think and fight all land in the same place.
feedback.feed_forward: Learn this verb with the other ought verbs, not on its own.

payload.context: From a letter about a weekend away.
payload.stem: The cottage ___ (cost) less than the hotel and had a much better view.

expected: cost

feedback.why_key: Cost is one of the verbs that does nothing at all. Writing costed is the error that safety produces.
feedback.feed_forward: Leave the do-nothing verbs alone: cut, put, let, cost.

payload.given: The owners take the tables in at six and the square goes quiet.
payload.instruction: Move the whole sentence into a summer that has ended.

expected: took the tables in at six and the square went quiet

feedback.why_key: Both verbs swap words rather than take endings, and the second one is the one people leave behind.
feedback.feed_forward: Swap every verb in the sentence, not the first.

payload.audio_text: They ran the stall for years and then sold it.

expected: they ran the stall for years and then sold it

feedback.why_key: Run and ran are one vowel apart, and at speed the vowel is the only evidence you get.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen to the vowel in the middle of short verbs.

expected: put

feedback.why_key: Went is already right, so the sentence knows it is in the past. Put needs no help at all.
feedback.feed_forward: Take the ending off the do-nothing verbs.

payload.context: From a paragraph about a week spent working near the docks.
payload.sentence: The bakery started at five and we come in for rolls before every shift.
reasons: the second verb is still standing in the present
cafés do not open at six
the week is not named clearly enough
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Come and came are one letter apart, and the base form is quiet enough to slip past the writer's ear.
feedback.feed_forward: Check come, run and become twice; they hide well.

items.decision_cue: The kitchen cuts the bread each morning.

sentences: The kitchen cuts the bread each morning.
The kitchen cut the bread each morning.
meanings: This is what happens here, and it will happen again tomorrow.
This is what used to happen during a stretch that has ended.

feedback.why_key: The verb never changes for the past, so the single letter on the present form is carrying the whole difference.
feedback.feed_forward: With do-nothing verbs, read the small letters closely.
