notice_set.why: The plain past simply reports the six years. Whether they moved is a separate sentence.

notice_set.sentence: Every summer we would walk the ridge path before breakfast.
notice_set.question: Is this about one walk or about a habit?
notice_set.why: The summer sets the scene first, and only then can this word take on repeated actions inside it.

notice_set.sentence: I used to know the whole street by name.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker still know everybody's name?
notice_set.why: This works with a state as easily as with an action, which is exactly where the other option cannot follow.

notice_set.sentence: The rent went up three times that year.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker telling you the rises have stopped?
notice_set.why: A stated number of occasions is a report, not a habit, and the plain past is the only honest choice for it.

teach.rule_line: Used to means it was the case then, and it is not the case now.
teach.false_rule: That used to and would are two ways of saying the same thing. Would cannot carry a state at all, and that single rule decides most of the cases you will meet.

errors.wrong: There use to be a bakery on the corner of Bridge Street.
errors.right: There used to be a bakery on the corner of Bridge Street.
errors.why_it_happens: The d is silent in front of to, so the ear never hears it. The learner writes exactly what they say, which is the right instinct and the wrong spelling.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one letter: use becomes used.

errors.wrong: We used to living above the shop on Bridge Street.
errors.right: We used to live above the shop on Bridge Street.
errors.why_it_happens: To is followed by an -ing word in several phrases the learner already owns, such as look forward to. The pull of that pattern is strong and nothing here resists it.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: living becomes live.

errors.wrong: Did you used to rent out the top floor?
errors.right: Did you use to rent out the top floor?
errors.why_it_happens: The phrase is stored as one lump with its d attached, so it comes out whole even after the helper word has already taken the past away.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one letter: used becomes use.

errors.wrong: The flats would be cheaper before the new line opened.
errors.right: The flats were cheaper before the new line opened.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has been told this word does past habits and applies it to a past situation. It only handles repeated actions, and being cheap is not an action anybody repeats.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: would be becomes were.

pays_in.note: Questions about how things have changed for you are answered with this.
pays_in.model: I used to cycle in every day, but the new junction put an end to that.

pays_in.note: Comparing then and now is half of Part 3, and this is the cheapest way in.
pays_in.model: Families used to stay in the same district for generations, which is much rarer now.

pays_in.note: A contrast between an older arrangement and the present one.
pays_in.model: Councils used to build housing directly, and most of that work has since passed to private developers.

used_in.quote: A place you used to go to as a child is this structure named in the card itself, and the answer collapses without it.
Something you believed as a child and no longer believe needs a state in a past stretch, which is precisely where the other option cannot follow.

payload.sentence: There used to be a bakery on the corner.
payload.question: Can you buy bread there today?

feedback.why_key: The phrase carries the second claim with it, so nobody has to add that the bakery has gone.
feedback.feed_forward: Read this phrase as then, and not now.

payload.sentence: We lived above the shop for six years.
payload.question: Does the speaker say whether they still live there?

feedback.why_key: The plain past reports the years and stops. Only the other phrase promises anything about today.
feedback.feed_forward: Notice what the plain past refuses to tell you.

payload.context: A neighbour talking about the shops at the end of the road.
payload.sentence: There use to be a chemist next to the post office.
reasons: the phrase is written with a d even though nobody says it
there was never a chemist there
the speaker should say the year
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The letter is silent in front of to, so the ear is no help at all and the spelling has to be learned by eye.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the d even though you cannot hear it.

payload.context: Someone describing a street that has changed completely.
payload.stem: There ___ (use) to be three shops between the bridge and the school.

expected: used

feedback.why_key: The written form keeps its d even though the sound of it disappears before to.
feedback.feed_forward: Spell it with the d, every time.

payload.context: From a question in a survey about the neighbourhood.
payload.stem: Did your family ___ (use) to rent from the council?

expected: use

feedback.why_key: The helper word has already taken the past, so the phrase gives up its d in exactly the way every other verb gives up its ending.
feedback.feed_forward: Drop the d whenever did is in the sentence.

payload.given: The council built housing directly. It no longer does.
payload.instruction: Put both facts into one sentence, using the phrase that carries the second one for free.

expected: used to build housing directly
used to build housing directly, but it no longer does

feedback.why_key: The phrase does the work of the second sentence, which is why one clause can replace two.
feedback.feed_forward: Let the phrase carry the change; do not say it twice.

payload.audio_text: We used to walk down to the harbour every evening.

expected: we used to walk down to the harbour every evening

feedback.why_key: You will hear two words with no d between them and you have to write three letters that are not there in the sound.
feedback.feed_forward: Hear use to, write used to.

payload.context: Build one sentence about something that stopped a long time ago.

expected: my grandmother used to keep chickens behind the house

feedback.why_key: The plain verb comes straight after to, with nothing added to it at either end.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the dictionary form of the verb after to.

items.decision_cue: with the number of years in each

payload.context: Halina is listing every place she has lived, with the number of years in each.
payload.stem: We ___ in the flat above the shop.

options.why_this_means: That this is one entry in a record, with no promise about how things are today.
That the arrangement has ended, and that the ending is the point of saying it.

expected: lived

feedback.why_key: A list of places with lengths attached is a record. Nothing in it is being contrasted with today.
feedback.feed_forward: Use the plain past when you are simply recording.

items.decision_cue: now that the shops have all changed hands

payload.context: Halina is explaining why the street feels strange to her now that the shops have all changed hands.
payload.stem: We ___ in the flat above the shop.

options.why_this_means: That this is one entry in a record, with no promise about how things are today.
That the arrangement has ended, and that the ending is the point of saying it.

expected: used to live

feedback.why_key: The whole sentence exists to set then against now, and only one of these two forms says so on its own.
feedback.feed_forward: Reach for the phrase when the change is the point.

items.decision_cue: a house in Marlow that has been in the family for decades

payload.context: Two cousins talking about a house in Marlow that has been in the family for decades.
payload.stem: My grandparents ___ the top floor to students.

options.why_this_means: That they did it during those years, and the sentence stops there.
That they did it for a stretch and that nobody rents the top floor now.

follow_up.question: Which version tells you the renting has stopped?

feedback.why_key: Both are correct and both are about the same grandparents. Only one of them tells you what the top floor is doing today.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose by what you want the listener to know about now.

payload.context: From a paragraph about a village shop that closed.
payload.sentence: There would be a bakery on the corner and everybody would walk down for bread.
reasons: the first half is a state, and that word cannot carry a state
the second half is a repeated action and does not belong
the bakery should be named
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The walking is a repeated action and survives. The bakery simply being there is not an action anybody repeats, so it has to change.
feedback.feed_forward: Test each half: is it a state or a repeated action?

payload.sentence: Did you used to rent out the top floor before the survey was done?

expected: did you use to

feedback.why_key: The helper word has already taken the past, so the phrase behind it gives up its letter exactly as any other verb gives up its ending.
feedback.feed_forward: Strip the d whenever did is in front.

payload.prompt_text: Something about your home area that has changed. Write two sentences: one about a state that has ended, and one about an action you repeated when the scene was already set.

feedback.why_key: The state forces one choice and the repeated action allows two, which is the whole shape of this decision in two sentences.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask state or action before you choose the words.

payload.prompt_text: You have two minutes on the card A place you used to go to as a child. Use the phrase at least twice for states that have ended, and let the plain past carry anything you did on one particular visit. One minute to plan.

feedback.why_key: The card is built out of this choice, and mixing the three ways of saying a past habit is what makes an answer sound settled rather than rehearsed.
feedback.feed_forward: Separate the standing state from the one particular day.

title: Choosing between the event and the scene it happened inside

point_json.grammar_name: Past simple vs past continuous

teach.can_do: I can decide whether to report an event or paint the scene it happened inside.
teach.why_it_matters: Both forms are correct English and you can already build both. What costs marks is choosing the wrong one, and it happens in every story anybody tells.
teach.meaning: These two forms do not describe different events. They describe the same event from two distances. The plain past treats it as a whole thing that landed and finished, so the story can move on to the next item. Was or were plus -ing holds the same thing open and unfinished, so that something else can happen inside it. Choose the first for what happened; choose the second for what was already going on when it happened.

form.pattern: the event: plain past  ·  the scene: was / were + -ing
notes: A chain of finished events is all plain past, one after another
The scene usually comes first and the event lands inside it
Two scenes can run side by side; two events cannot happen at once unless you say so
The state verbs stay out of the -ing form no matter which job they are doing
form.negative: did not check  ·  was not checking
form.question: Did you check ...?  ·  Were you checking ...?

left.text: The guide was checking the tickets.

right.text: The guide checked the tickets.

spec.caption: The event drops into the scene. Reverse them and the story stops making sense.

worked_example.sentence: The rain was coming straight off the sea when the coach finally pulled in.
worked_example.why_this_form: The rain was there before the coach and stayed after it. Holding it open is what lets the arrival land inside it.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Came would make the rain a second event, so the reader would understand that it began at the moment the coach appeared.

notice_set.sentence: We were queuing outside the museum when the doors opened.
notice_set.question: Had the queuing begun before the doors opened?
notice_set.why: The queue is held open, so the opening of the doors lands somewhere in the middle of it.

notice_set.sentence: We queued outside the museum and the doors opened.
notice_set.question: Which order does this sentence put things in?
notice_set.why: Two closed events in a row are read in the order they are written. Nothing sits inside anything else.

notice_set.sentence: The guide was talking to the driver and nobody heard the announcement.
notice_set.question: Was the talking finished before the announcement?
notice_set.why: The talking is held open across the announcement, which is exactly why it swallowed it.

notice_set.sentence: It rained on the second day of the trip.
notice_set.question: Does the sentence hand you a picture of the rain, or a fact about it?
notice_set.why: The closed form counts the rain as one whole item in the record of the trip.

notice_set.sentence: We booked the tickets, packed on the Friday and left before six.
notice_set.question: How many separate steps are being reported?
notice_set.why: A chain of finished steps is all in the closed form, and that is what makes it read as a chain.

discovery.prompt: The sentences on the left and on the right describe the same trip. What is different about how the speaker is standing?
pairs: We were queuing outside the museum when the doors opened.
We queued outside the museum and the doors opened.
The guide was talking to the driver.
The guide talked to the driver.
It was raining on the second day of the trip.
It rained on the second day of the trip.

candidate_rules.text: On the left the speaker is inside the moment, watching something that has not finished.
On the left the actions lasted longer than the ones on the right.
On the left the sentence has a word like while or suddenly somewhere in it.

teach.rule_line: Ask: is this the event, or the scene the event happened inside?
teach.false_rule: That the -ing form is for long actions and the plain past for short ones. Length has nothing to do with it. A two-second action can be held open and a ten-year one can be closed.

contrast.question: Is this the event, or the scene the event happened inside?

fork.answer: The event: it lands, it is finished, and the story moves on to the next thing
The scene: it was already running, and something else happens inside it
fork.selects: was or were plus the -ing word

a.text: When the coach arrived, the guide checked the tickets.
a.means: The coach came first and the checking started afterwards. Two steps, in that order.

b.text: When the coach arrived, the guide was checking the tickets.
b.means: The checking was already under way, and the coach turned up in the middle of it.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You chose was collecting. That says the collecting was still running when the coach pulled out, so somebody was left behind on the pavement. If the collecting finished first, the closed form is the honest one.

edge_case.text: A run of completed events is all plain past, every one of them. Learners who fall in love with the -ing form narrate whole holidays in it, and the result is a page of scenery in which nothing ever happens.

contrast.stronger_test: Cover the rest of the sentence and ask what a photograph of that instant would show. If the photograph would catch something half-done, hold it open. If it would show a thing already over, close it.

worked_pairs.a: We were queuing for the boat when the storm warning went up.
worked_pairs.b: We queued for the boat and walked back to the hotel.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: when the storm warning went up
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: and walked back to the hotel
worked_pairs.gloss: The first drops a moment into the queue. The second counts the queue as one finished item and moves straight on to the next.

worked_pairs.a: The guide was pointing at the ruins, so nobody noticed the path.
worked_pairs.b: The guide pointed at the ruins and everybody looked up.
worked_pairs.gloss: Held open, the pointing covers the whole moment and hides the path. Closed, it is one gesture that gets one response.

worked_pairs.a: It was raining hard in Sandmouth that morning.
worked_pairs.b: It rained hard in Sandmouth that morning.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first is a scene waiting for something to happen in it. The second is a closed fact about the weather and the morning is over.

errors.wrong: The coach was arriving at the terminal and we climbed on board.
errors.right: The coach arrived at the terminal and we climbed on board.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer wants the sentence to feel vivid, and the held-open form feels more vivid. Two events in a chain do not need atmosphere; they need order.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: was arriving becomes arrived.

errors.wrong: We were leaving the hotel, we were catching the ferry and we were reaching the island before noon.
errors.right: We left the hotel, caught the ferry and reached the island before noon.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has been taught the -ing form as the storytelling form and applies it to the whole story. Every event turns into scenery, and a reader is left waiting for something to happen.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: were leaving becomes left, and the rest follow.

errors.wrong: I read the guidebook when the lights went out in the carriage.
errors.right: I was reading the guidebook when the lights went out in the carriage.
errors.why_it_happens: The reading feels like the important action, so it takes the strong closed form. That turns it into a response to the darkness rather than the thing the darkness interrupted.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: read becomes was reading.

pays_in.note: The long turn is a narrative, and a narrative needs both jobs done separately.
pays_in.model: The market was closing as we got there, so we ate at a stall by the gate instead.

pays_in.note: An example from experience needs a background before the point lands.
pays_in.model: Numbers were falling steadily, and the council closed two of the three visitor centres that spring.

pays_in.note: A true or false stem often turns on whether an action had finished.
pays_in.model: The survey team was still measuring the estuary when the funding was withdrawn.

used_in.quote: A time when the weather changed your plans is this choice made six or seven times: the weather is the scene and the change of plan is the event.
The passage narrates a sequence of decisions against a background that was already running, and two questions depend on telling them apart.

payload.sentence: We were queuing outside the museum when the doors opened.
payload.question: Had the queue formed before the doors opened?

feedback.why_key: The queue is held open, so the doors opening lands somewhere inside it rather than before it.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask which of the two things was there first.

payload.sentence: We queued outside the museum and the doors opened.
payload.question: Which order does the sentence put these in?

feedback.why_key: Two closed events in a row are read in the order they are written, with nothing sitting inside anything else.
feedback.feed_forward: Read a chain of closed events straight through, in order.

payload.context: From a paragraph telling the story of a day trip to the island.
payload.sentence: We were leaving the hotel at eight, we were catching the ferry and we were reaching the island before noon.
reasons: a chain of finished steps belongs in the closed form
the trip took too long for one day
the hotel should be named
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Every step has been turned into scenery, so the paragraph has three backgrounds and no story in front of them.
feedback.feed_forward: Close every step in a chain of events.

payload.context: From an account of a delayed trip to the island.
payload.stem: It ___ (rain) hard while we waited on the quay, and the crossing was cancelled.

expected: was raining

feedback.why_key: The rain surrounds the waiting rather than following it, which is what the held-open form is for.
feedback.feed_forward: Hold the weather open when something else happens in it.

payload.context: From the same account, two sentences later.
payload.stem: We ___ (book) a room by the harbour and slept for eleven hours.

expected: booked

feedback.why_key: Two finished steps, one after the other. Nothing here is being interrupted by anything else.
feedback.feed_forward: Close each step when the next one follows it.

payload.given: The guide talked to the driver. Nobody heard the announcement.
payload.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence in which the talking is what covered the announcement.

expected: was talking to the driver, so nobody heard the announcement
was talking to the driver and nobody heard the announcement

feedback.why_key: Holding the talking open is what lets it swallow the announcement instead of following it.
feedback.feed_forward: Open the action that has to cover the other one.

payload.audio_text: The market was closing when we got to the square.

expected: the market was closing when we got to the square

feedback.why_key: One small word decides whether the market shut before you arrived or was shutting as you walked up.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the small word in front of the -ing word.

items.decision_cue: the moment the announcement came over the speakers

payload.context: Ines is describing the moment the announcement came over the speakers.
payload.stem: I ___ the tickets at the desk.

options.why_this_means: That the collecting was over and done before anything else happened.
That the collecting was still going on, so the announcement landed in the middle of it.

expected: was collecting

feedback.why_key: The sentence exists to place the announcement, and it can only land inside something that is still open.
feedback.feed_forward: Hold the action open when another event lands in it.

items.decision_cue: the three jobs she finished before the coach left

payload.context: Ines is listing the three jobs she finished before the coach left.
payload.stem: I ___ the tickets at the desk.

options.why_this_means: That the collecting was over and done before anything else happened.
That the collecting was still going on, so the announcement landed in the middle of it.

expected: collected

feedback.why_key: A finished job on a list of finished jobs. Holding it open would mean she never got to the end of it.
feedback.feed_forward: Close the action when it is one item on a list.

items.decision_cue: as they came out of the museum

payload.context: A description of what the group saw as they came out of the museum.
payload.stem: The guide ___ by the coach door.

options.why_this_means: That the waiting is one completed item in the account of the afternoon.
That the waiting was already under way and the group walked into the middle of it.

expected: was waiting

feedback.why_key: The sentence reports what the group walked out into, and that has to be something already running.
feedback.feed_forward: Open the action that was there before the moment described.

payload.context: An account of the guide's afternoon, one finished job after another.
payload.stem: The guide ___ by the coach door.

options.why_this_means: That the waiting is one completed item in the account of the afternoon.
That the waiting was already under way and the group walked into the middle of it.

expected: waited

feedback.why_key: Inside a chain of completed jobs the waiting is itself a job, so it closes like the rest of them.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the form to the job the sentence is doing.

items.decision_cue: what the weather did when their coach pulled in

payload.context: Two travellers describing the same afternoon in Brackenfield, and what the weather did when their coach pulled in.
payload.stem: It ___ when the coach pulled in.

options.why_this_means: That the rain began at that point: the coach arrived and the weather turned.
That the rain was already falling before the coach got anywhere near the square.

follow_up.question: Which version tells you the rain started only after the coach arrived?

feedback.why_key: Both are correct English about a real afternoon. They describe two different afternoons, and the form is the only thing telling them apart.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide what you want to say about the timing, then choose.

items.decision_cue: The engineers were checking the bridge that morning.

payload.context: Two sentences taken from different reports on the same bridge.
sentences: The engineers checked the bridge that morning.
The engineers were checking the bridge that morning.
meanings: The check was carried out and the morning's job is complete.
The check was under way, and the sentence never says it was finished.

feedback.why_key: Only one of these tells you the bridge was actually signed off, and it is the shorter one.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the sentence lets the job reach its end.

payload.sentence: I read the guidebook when the lights went out in the carriage.

expected: was reading the guidebook

feedback.why_key: As written, the darkness comes first and the reading is somehow a response to it. The reading has to be open for the darkness to interrupt it.
feedback.feed_forward: Open the action the interruption lands in.

payload.prompt_text: A trip where the weather changed your plans. Write one sentence with both forms in it: what was already going on, and the thing that happened inside it.

feedback.why_key: One sentence carrying both jobs is the smallest complete piece of narrative English has.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the scene first, then drop the event into it.

parts: Visitor numbers fell for three winters in a row.
The council closed two of the three visitor centres.
The remaining centre took on all the school bookings.
model_combinations: Visitor numbers were falling for the third winter in a row when the council closed two of the three centres, and the survivor took on all the school bookings.
While visitor numbers were falling, the council closed two of the three visitor centres, leaving the third to absorb every school booking.
Visitor numbers were still falling when two of the three centres closed, and the remaining one took on all the school bookings.

feedback.why_key: The falling numbers are the background the closure decision sits inside, and only one of the three facts belongs in the held-open form.
feedback.feed_forward: Pick the one fact that is background, then close the rest.

payload.prompt_text: You have two minutes on the card A time when the weather changed your plans. Open with the scene, keep the chain of events closed, and do not let the whole story slide into the held-open form. One minute to plan.

feedback.why_key: Under pressure the two jobs collapse into one form, and the answer becomes either a list with no atmosphere or scenery with no story.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the scene once, then keep every event closed.

title: Telling a past story in an order a listener can follow

point_json.grammar_name: Narrative sequence: the past chain and its joining words

teach.can_do: I can tell a past story so that a listener always knows which part came first.
teach.why_it_matters: The two-minute long turn is a narrative task. A story told out of order costs marks nobody will ever explain to you, because the listener simply stops following.
teach.meaning: A story is a chain: finished event, finished event, finished event, told in the order they happened. The plain past carries the chain, one link at a time. The held-open form drops in wherever you want the listener to see the scene rather than the next step, and the joining words tell them where they are standing. Change nothing about the verbs and the order still works, because English trusts the order of the sentences.

form.pattern: plain past + plain past + plain past, with the joining words between
notes: First, After that and In the end open a sentence and take a comma
While plus was or were plus -ing gives the scene the next event lands in
Keep the events in the order they happened unless you say plainly that you are jumping back
Two or three joining words in a whole story is plenty; one on every sentence reads like a recipe
form.negative: did not tell the rest of it until later
form.question: What happened after that?

spec.caption: Three crosses in a row are the chain. The bar underneath them is the scene they happened in.

worked_example.sentence: We reached the square at seven, found a place near the railings and waited for the procession.
worked_example.why_this_form: Three finished steps in the order they happened, joined without fuss. The listener never has to work out what followed what.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Were reaching, were finding and were waiting would turn all three steps into scenery, and the listener would still be waiting for the story to begin.

notice_set.sentence: The drummers started, the lights went down and the crowd went quiet.
notice_set.question: Which happened first?
notice_set.why: Nothing tells you the order except the order, and in a chain of finished steps that is enough.

notice_set.sentence: The square was filling up while we looked for a place at the front.
notice_set.question: Was the square empty when they arrived?
notice_set.why: The filling is held open around the looking, so it was already under way before they got there.

notice_set.sentence: We got there late. The procession had passed an hour earlier.
notice_set.question: Which happened first?
notice_set.why: Here the order of the sentences and the order of events come apart, and the second sentence has to say so.

notice_set.sentence: After that, nobody moved for twenty minutes.
notice_set.question: Does the sentence tell you what came before it?
notice_set.why: A joining word points backwards without repeating anything, which is exactly why a story needs a few of them.

notice_set.sentence: In the end we walked home along the harbour.
notice_set.question: Is this near the start or near the finish of the story?
notice_set.why: Some joining words carry a position in the story as part of their meaning, and a listener uses them to know when to relax.

teach.rule_line: Keep the chain in the plain past and let the joining words carry the order.
teach.false_rule: That a story sounds livelier told in the held-open form. A story told entirely in it has scenery on every side and no events anywhere.

errors.wrong: The procession finished and after that everybody was going home.
errors.right: The procession finished and after that everybody went home.
errors.why_it_happens: The last step of a story often gets stretched for effect, as if a slow ending were a better one. It stops the chain from closing and leaves the listener waiting.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: was going becomes went.

errors.wrong: The drummers started, the lights went down and the crowd goes quiet.
errors.right: The drummers started, the lights went down and the crowd went quiet.
errors.why_it_happens: The last link in a chain is chosen when the writer is already thinking about the next sentence, and it defaults to the shape they use most often.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: goes becomes went.

errors.wrong: We arrived at the hall, and after that everybody is finding a seat.
errors.right: We arrived at the hall, and after that everybody found a seat.
errors.why_it_happens: The joining word feels as if it has already done the work of placing the sentence in time, so the verb is left to look after itself and does not.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: is finding becomes found.

pays_in.note: The whole long turn is this, from the first sentence to the last.
pays_in.model: We got there at six, waited near the railings and left before the crowd did.

pays_in.note: An example is a small story, and it fails if the order fails.
pays_in.model: The council trialled the scheme for a year, published the figures and quietly dropped it.

pays_in.note: Ordering questions turn on the joining words rather than on the events.
pays_in.model: After that the group moved to the second hall, and the talk started twenty minutes late.

used_in.quote: A time you took part in a traditional occasion is a chain of finished steps with one scene behind it, which is this point exactly.
The order of the steps in the enrolment is what several answers depend on, and the joining words are the only signposts given.

payload.sentence: The drummers started, the lights went down and the crowd went quiet.
payload.question: Which of these happened first?

feedback.why_key: Nothing states the order except the order itself, and in a chain of finished steps that is all a listener needs.
feedback.feed_forward: Read a chain straight through and trust the order.

payload.sentence: The square was filling up while we looked for a place at the front.
payload.question: Was the square empty when they arrived?

feedback.why_key: The filling is held open around the searching, so it had started before they got anywhere near the front.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the scene before you place the steps.

payload.context: Somebody telling the story of an evening at a street festival.
payload.sentence: The band came on, the doors closed and the crowd goes quiet.
reasons: the last link in the chain has slipped into the present
the doors should not have closed
the crowd went quiet too early
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Two links are closed and the third is not, so the story stops being a story halfway through the sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Check the last verb of every chain you write.

payload.context: From an account of an evening at the arts centre in Verdon.
payload.stem: We reached the hall at seven and ___ (find) a seat near the back.

expected: found

feedback.why_key: Two finished steps in a row, so the second one closes exactly as the first did.
feedback.feed_forward: Match every link in the chain to the one before it.

payload.context: From the same account, three sentences later.
payload.stem: The hall ___ (fill) up while the first group tuned their instruments.

expected: was filling

feedback.why_key: This one is the scene rather than a step, and the tuning is what happens inside it.
feedback.feed_forward: Hold the scene open and close the steps.

payload.context: Build the next sentence of a story that already has two steps in it.

expected: after that the procession turned into the harbour road

feedback.why_key: The joining word opens the sentence and points backwards without repeating a word of what came before.
feedback.feed_forward: Open with the joining word, then give the next step.

payload.given: The rain started. We were standing at the front of the crowd.
payload.instruction: Join these into one sentence in which the standing is the scene and the rain is the event.

expected: were standing at the front of the crowd when the rain started
were standing at the front of the crowd when it started to rain

feedback.why_key: The scene has to be open for the event to land in it, and putting the scene first is what tells a listener which is which.
feedback.feed_forward: Scene first, then the event that lands in it.

payload.audio_text: After that we walked home and nobody said much.

expected: after that we walked home and nobody said much

feedback.why_key: The ending on the first verb is a single consonant at speed, and it is the only thing keeping the sentence in the story.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the ending you heard, not the one you expected.

payload.context: From the middle of a story about a village hall meeting.
payload.sentence: We arrived at the hall, and after that everybody is finding a seat.
reasons: the joining word cannot place the sentence in time on its own
the meeting was not in a hall
arriving and sitting down are the same step
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The joining word points backwards but it does not carry the past. Only the verb can do that.
feedback.feed_forward: Place the verb yourself; the joining word will not.

payload.sentence: The procession finished and after that everybody was going home.

expected: went home

feedback.why_key: The last step of a story has to close, or the listener is left standing in the square waiting for the rest.
feedback.feed_forward: Close the final step of every story.

items.decision_cue: We got to the square and the procession passed.

payload.context: Two versions of the same evening, written by two people who were there.
sentences: We got to the square and the procession passed.
We got to the square. The procession had passed an hour earlier.
meanings: They arrived first and saw the procession go by afterwards.
They missed it: the procession was over before they arrived.

feedback.why_key: In the first, the order of the sentences is the order of events. In the second, the writer has to say plainly that it is not.
feedback.feed_forward: Say so explicitly whenever you jump backwards.

parts: The first speaker arrived twenty minutes late.
model_combinations: The hall was filling up slowly when the first speaker arrived twenty minutes late, and nobody complained.
The hall filled up slowly, the first speaker arrived twenty minutes late and nobody complained about the delay.
While the hall was still filling up, the first speaker arrived twenty minutes late, and not one person complained.

feedback.why_key: One of the three facts is the scene and the other two are steps, and choosing which is which is the whole task.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide which fact is the scene, then chain the rest.

payload.prompt_text: An occasion you took part in. Write three short sentences telling what happened, in order, with one joining word and no more.

feedback.why_key: Three closed steps and one signpost is the whole shape of a spoken story, and adding more signposts makes it worse rather than clearer.
feedback.feed_forward: Use one joining word; let the order do the rest.

payload.prompt_text: You have two minutes on the card A time you took part in a traditional occasion. One scene at the start, then a chain of closed steps, then a closed ending. Two joining words at most. One minute to plan.

feedback.why_key: This is the task the whole unit has been building towards: a scene, a chain and an ending that actually ends.
feedback.feed_forward: Plan three steps before you start speaking.

title: Saying what is already in the diary with a time and usually another person

point_json.grammar_name: Present continuous for fixed future arrangements

teach.can_do: I can say what is already arranged for later, with a time attached and usually somebody else expecting me.
teach.why_it_matters: This is the shape English uses for a diary, and learners who do not have it say everything about next week with will, which sounds like nothing has been settled.
teach.meaning: The -ing shape normally says that something is going on around now. Pointed at later, it says something slightly different but very close: the arrangement is going on around now, even though the event itself is not. A time has been picked, a place is usually known, and somebody else is involved and expecting you. That is why it feels solid. You are not saying what you believe or what you have decided alone; you are reading out something that already exists between you and another person.

form.pattern: am / is / are + the -ing verb, with a later time said or understood
notes: the shape is exactly the one you use for things going on around now; the time word is what points it forward
without a later time in the sentence or in the conversation, a listener will hear it as right now
verbs about states rather than doings resist the -ing shape here as much as anywhere else
form.negative: am not / isn't / aren't + the -ing verb: We aren't running the Tuesday session this month.
form.question: Am, is or are + person + the -ing verb: Are you seeing the supervisor on Friday?

left.text: the arrangement, with a time and another person in it

right.text: the event itself

spec.caption: The thing that is going on around now is the arrangement, not the event.

worked_example.sentence: I'm seeing the site manager at four to go through the survey.
worked_example.why_this_form: A time has been agreed and somebody else has it written down too. The speaker is reading out something that already exists between them.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: I'll see the site manager at four would sound as if the speaker had just thought of it and the manager knew nothing about it.

notice_set.sentence: Halvard is starting at the Norland office on the ninth.
notice_set.question: Do other people already know about this?
notice_set.why: A date this exact does not exist unless somebody else has agreed to it.

notice_set.sentence: We're taking the last train back on Sunday evening.
notice_set.question: Has a time already been settled?
notice_set.why: The train has a departure time and the speakers have picked it, so the arrangement exists before the sentence does.

notice_set.sentence: Lenka is moving into the flat above the bakery.
notice_set.question: Is this happening at this exact moment, or later?
notice_set.why: The shape is the same for both. What decides it is the time word, or the conversation it sits in.

notice_set.sentence: The clinic isn't taking walk-in patients next Thursday.
notice_set.question: Is this something the clinic has decided in advance?
notice_set.why: A named day tells you the arrangement was made before anyone said this sentence.

notice_set.sentence: Bo and I are meeting the landlord about the damp.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker alone in this?
notice_set.why: Two other people are inside the arrangement, which is the usual situation for this shape.

teach.rule_line: If a time is agreed and somebody else expects you, use the -ing shape.
teach.false_rule: That the -ing shape can only mean right now. Point it at a day next week and it says the day is already fixed.

errors.wrong: I meeting my supervisor at half four on Wednesday.
errors.right: I'm meeting my supervisor at half four on Wednesday.
errors.why_it_happens: The -ing verb carries all the meaning, so the small word in front carries none and quietly falls out, especially in speech where it is barely audible in the first place.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: am.

errors.wrong: We are having the laboratory results by Friday afternoon.
errors.right: We will have the laboratory results by Friday afternoon.
errors.why_it_happens: Having here means simply possessing, not doing anything, and a verb that describes a state rather than an activity will not go into the -ing shape however firmly the day has been agreed.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: are having becomes will have.

errors.wrong: Rents in the city are rising sharply next year.
errors.right: Rents in the city will probably rise sharply next year.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer knows the shape points forward and stops there. Nobody arranges the rent market, so the sentence claims a diary entry that could not exist.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: are rising becomes will probably rise.

errors.wrong: Sorry, I can't come, I will help my sister move house on Saturday.
errors.right: Sorry, I can't come, I'm helping my sister move house on Saturday.
errors.why_it_happens: Will is the future the learner reaches for first, so a promise already made to somebody else comes out sounding as if it were being invented on the spot as an excuse.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: will help becomes am helping.

pays_in.note: Any question about your week is answered in this shape.
pays_in.model: I'm doing an evening class on Tuesdays until the end of March.

pays_in.note: A letter changing or confirming an arrangement runs on it.
pays_in.model: I'm arriving on the Thursday evening rather than the Friday morning.

pays_in.note: Booking and enrolment conversations state the settled dates this way.
pays_in.model: You're joining the intermediate group, and that one meets on Mondays.

used_in.quote: Telling a friend that the plan has changed means stating what was arranged and what is arranged now, both in this shape.
The enrolment conversation settles a day and a time, and the settled version is announced in exactly this way.

payload.sentence: Nuria is presenting the flood figures at the Tuesday briefing.
payload.question: Does anybody besides Nuria already know about this?

feedback.why_key: A briefing with a day on it has been organised, and organising it took more than one person.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask who else would have to know for this to be true.

payload.sentence: The department is closing the library annexe over the summer.
payload.question: Where does this sit?

feedback.why_key: The decision and the dates are in place today. Only the closing itself is still waiting to happen.
feedback.feed_forward: Separate when it was settled from when it happens.

payload.context: Somebody explaining why they cannot make Thursday.
payload.sentence: I seeing the physiotherapist on Thursday morning.
reasons: a small word is missing before the -ing verb
the appointment has not been arranged
Thursday is already over
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The -ing verb cannot stand on its own. Something in front of it has to say who and when.
feedback.feed_forward: Say am, is or are out loud before the -ing verb.

payload.context: Turning down an invitation for the weekend.
payload.stem: I can't, my brother ___ (get) married on the Saturday.

expected: is getting
's getting
s getting

feedback.why_key: A wedding is the most arranged thing there is, so the sentence reads out a date that already exists.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose is, am or are to fit the person in front.

payload.context: From a short message confirming a visit.
payload.stem: Two of us ___ (travel) up on the Wednesday and staying overnight.

expected: are travelling
're travelling
re travelling

feedback.why_key: The message is confirming something already agreed, which is why the writer can name the day without hedging it.

title: Saying what a timetable does, when the clock belongs to somebody else

point_json.grammar_name: Present simple for timetables and scheduled events

teach.can_do: I can talk about a future set by a timetable, using the same shape I use for things that are generally true.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the smallest of these futures and the one learners skip, so they say the bus will leave at eleven and sound as if they decided it themselves.
teach.meaning: This is the future that belongs to an organisation rather than to a person. A railway, a college, a cinema, a court, a tide table: something outside everybody in the conversation has fixed the clock, published it, and will run to it whether or not anyone in the room turns up. Because it is treated as simply how things are, English uses the same shape it uses for permanent facts. Nobody is predicting and nobody is deciding. The time already exists in print.

form.pattern: the ordinary present shape, with the later time said or understood
notes: he, she, it and any single thing still add -s, exactly as they always do
the negative and the question still use do and does, exactly as they always do
it works only where a timetable really exists: transport, courses, performances, opening hours, tides
form.negative: doesn't / don't + the plain verb: The office doesn't open until ten on Saturdays.
form.question: What time does + person or thing + the plain verb: What time does the last ferry leave?

right.text: the ordinary present shape, pointed at a later day

title: Choosing which way to point forward, by asking where the future actually lives

point_json.grammar_name: will vs going to vs the -ing shape vs the plain present

teach.can_do: I can pick the right way of pointing forward by asking where the future I am describing actually comes from.
teach.why_it_matters: English has no single future. It has four, and the one you pick tells your listener how settled the situation already is, whether you meant that or not.
teach.meaning: Every sentence about later carries a second message underneath it: how much of this is already real. Say it out of your own head and you are giving an opinion or making up your mind on the spot. Say it with going to and you are pointing back at a decision you already took, or at something in front of you both. Say it with the -ing shape and you are reading out an arrangement another person is expecting you to keep. Say it plainly and you are quoting a printed timetable. Same afternoon, four different claims about how settled it is.

form.pattern: will + plain verb · am/is/are going to + plain verb · am/is/are + -ing verb · the ordinary present shape
notes: all four are ordinary, correct English; nothing here is more advanced than anything else
the choice is about where the future came from, not about how far away it is
an essay prefers will with a softening word for a prediction, and treats going to as speech
form.negative: each of the four goes negative in its own ordinary way; the choice itself does not change.
form.question: Ask yourself the question in the rule line before you open your mouth, not afterwards.

spec.label: how settled is this, and who settled it?

steps.gloss: nobody has settled anything; this is my head, right now
I settled it earlier, or something in front of us points at it
another person settled it with me, and there is a time
an organisation settled it and printed it

worked_example.sentence: I'm collecting the samples at seven, so I'll set an alarm.
worked_example.why_this_form: The collection is arranged with the lab and has a time on it. The alarm is a decision the speaker takes in the middle of the sentence, which is why the two halves are not alike.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: I'll collect the samples at seven would make the whole thing the speaker's own idea, and nobody at the lab would be expecting them.

notice_set.sentence: We're taking the early boat across on Friday.
notice_set.question: Has this been settled with anybody else?
notice_set.why: A named day and a named boat mean the speakers are working to something already agreed.

notice_set.sentence: Those cracks are going to spread if nobody repoints the wall.
notice_set.question: Can the speaker point at a reason while they say it?
notice_set.why: The cracks are the reason, and they are on the wall in front of whoever is listening.

notice_set.sentence: I think the scheme will run out of money before the second phase.
notice_set.question: Is anyone in charge planning it that way?
notice_set.why: I think puts the whole thing inside the speaker's head, where no plan and no printed date can live.

notice_set.sentence: The clinic opens at eight on the first of the month.
notice_set.question: Could somebody else check this?
notice_set.why: Opening hours are published by whoever runs the building, so anybody can look them up.

notice_set.sentence: Fine, I'll take the Wednesday slot instead.
notice_set.question: When did the speaker make up their mind?
notice_set.why: Fine is the sound of somebody giving way, which places the decision inside this exchange.

notice_set.sentence: The tide turns at twenty past five tomorrow afternoon.
notice_set.question: Did anybody decide this?
notice_set.why: Nothing in the conversation controls the water. The time is simply printed in a table.

discovery.prompt: All six sentences are about later. Sort them into groups and say what makes each group hang together.

Fine, I'll take the Wednesday slot instead.
Those cracks are going to spread if nobody repoints the wall.
The clinic opens at eight on the first of the month.
I think the scheme will run out of money before the second phase.
The tide turns at twenty past five tomorrow afternoon.

candidate_rules.text: The shapes differ by how much of the situation was already settled, and by who settled it.
The shapes differ by how far away in time the event is.
The shape is decided by the time word in the sentence: on Friday, at eight, next month.

teach.rule_line: Ask who has already settled this: nobody, only me, another person, or an organisation.
teach.false_rule: That will is the neutral one and the others are decorations you can skip. Skipping them means every sentence you say sounds equally unsettled.

contrast.question: Where does this future live: my head, my plans, our diary, or their timetable?

fork.answer: In my head, right now — I believe it, or I am making up my mind as I speak
In something that already exists — a decision I took earlier, or a sign in front of us
In somebody else's clock — a person expecting me, or a printed timetable if it is an organisation
fork.selects: the -ing shape, or the plain present when nobody in the conversation set the time

a.text: I'll speak to the site manager about the leak.
a.means: The speaker has thought of it this second and is offering to do it.

b.text: I'm speaking to the site manager about the leak.
b.means: It is already arranged, and the manager has it written down too.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You chose will. That tells your listener the idea has just occurred to you and nobody else knows about it. If the meeting was fixed last week, they will now ask you to arrange it, and you will have to explain twice.

edge_case.text: Shall survives in offers and suggestions, mostly as a question: Shall I carry that? Elsewhere in modern British English will has taken over. Recognise it when you hear it, and do not go looking for places to use it.

contrast.stronger_test: Ask who you would have to tell if you changed your mind. Nobody, because you have only just thought of it, gives you will. Only yourself gives you going to. One named person gives you the -ing shape. Nobody at all, because an organisation owns the time and cannot be argued with, gives you the plain present.

worked_pairs.a: I'll ring the letting agent, I've just thought of it.
worked_pairs.b: I'm ringing the letting agent at nine tomorrow.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first call does not exist yet anywhere except in the speaker's head. The second is a fixed point in the morning.

worked_pairs.a: We're going to convert the loft, we settled it in the spring.
worked_pairs.b: We're converting the loft in October, the builder is booked.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: we settled it in the spring
worked_pairs.gloss: Both families have made up their minds. Only one of them has another person holding a date.

worked_pairs.a: The results come out on the twelfth.
worked_pairs.b: The results are going to be poor, attendance has been down all year.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: attendance has been down all year
worked_pairs.gloss: One sentence quotes an institution. The other reads the evidence the speaker has been watching pile up.

errors.wrong: Slow down, we will come off the road on this bend.
errors.right: Slow down, we're going to come off the road on this bend.
errors.why_it_happens: Will arrives first because it was learned first. The speaker can see the bend and feel the speed, and the sentence throws all of that away and offers a private opinion instead.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: will come becomes are going to come.

errors.wrong: I can't make the Friday session, I will collect my daughter from the airport.
errors.right: I can't make the Friday session, I'm collecting my daughter from the airport.
errors.why_it_happens: The arrangement was made days ago with somebody who is counting on it, but the learner reaches for the shape that means deciding on the spot, and the excuse sounds invented.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: will collect becomes am collecting.

errors.wrong: If nothing changes, coastal populations are going to shrink by the middle of the century.
errors.right: If nothing changes, coastal populations will probably shrink by the middle of the century.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer has evidence in mind and reaches for the shape that admits evidence. In a formal argument that shape reads as somebody speaking aloud rather than as a case being set out.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: are going to shrink becomes will probably shrink.

errors.wrong: Small towns will disappear completely once the last bank branch shuts.
errors.right: Small towns will struggle badly once the last bank branch shuts.
errors.why_it_happens: Having finally chosen the right shape, the writer forgets that the shape alone does not license the size of the claim, and an absolute word turns a reasonable point into one nobody can defend.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: disappear becomes struggle.

reasons: nobody has arranged this, so it cannot be stated as settled
the sentence is about something already finished
the -ing verb is built wrongly
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The -ing shape claims a diary entry. No committee anywhere has written the cost of sea defences into one for 2050.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask who could have arranged it before you use that shape.

items.decision_cue: the brackets have already come away from the wall

payload.sentence: Careful, that shelf will fall, the brackets have already come away from the wall.

expected: is going to fall
's going to fall
s going to fall

feedback.why_key: The second half of the sentence hands over the evidence, so the first half has no business sounding like a private opinion.
feedback.feed_forward: When you can point at the reason, say going to.

payload.prompt_text: Your team has just been told the office is moving. Write two sentences: one about what you had already decided to do about your journey to work, and one about what you expect will happen to everyone else.

feedback.why_key: Your own decision and your guess about other people are two different kinds of future, and the two sentences should not look alike.
feedback.feed_forward: Change shape between your own plan and your guess.

payload.prompt_text: Speak for ninety seconds on how far ahead people where you live tend to plan. Use at least three of the four shapes, and afterwards say in one sentence why you chose each one.
