title: Keeping will out of the half of the sentence that starts with when, until or as soon as

point_json.grammar_name: Present forms after when, as soon as, before, after, until, once and by the time

teach.can_do: I can join two future events with when, until or as soon as, and put will in only one of them.
teach.why_it_matters: One of the most common errors at this level, and invisible to the person making it, because the broken version sounds perfectly logical in their head.
teach.meaning: Some sentences carry two future events: one is the moment, and the other is what happens at that moment. English marks the future only once. The half that starts with when, until, before, once, after, as soon as or by the time is the moment, and English treats a fixed future moment as though it were already here, so it uses the ordinary present shape. All the pointing forward is done by the other half. Saying it twice does not make the sentence more future; it makes it wrong.

form.pattern: when / before / after / until / once / as soon as / by the time + ordinary present shape ... will + plain verb
notes: the two halves can go in either order; whichever half starts with one of those words keeps the present shape
when the joining half comes first, a comma follows it: Once the results are in, we will decide.
the same words after a verb of knowing or asking are a different job, and there will is normal: nobody knows when it will reopen
form.negative: the joining half goes negative in the ordinary present way: until the road doesn't flood any more.
form.question: What will you do when the contract ends? — the asking half keeps will, the joining half does not.

left.text: when the funding arrives — ordinary present shape, no will

right.text: we will start the second phase — will lives here

spec.caption: One future, marked once. The half with the joining word never gets to carry it.

worked_example.sentence: As soon as the tide drops, the divers will go back down.
worked_example.why_this_form: The dropping tide is the moment the sentence is pointing at, and a moment is treated as fixed. The going down is the news, so that is where the pointing forward happens.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: As soon as the tide will drop would leave the reader waiting for a main piece of news that never comes, because both halves would be busy announcing the future.

notice_set.sentence: We will move the equipment once the floor dries.
notice_set.question: Has the floor dried yet?
notice_set.why: Both events are still ahead. The drying is simply being treated as the fixed point the moving hangs on.

notice_set.sentence: Ring me when you reach the depot.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker asking about now or about later?
notice_set.why: The arrival has not happened. The sentence borrows the everyday shape for a moment that is still ahead.

notice_set.sentence: Nobody knows when the crossing will reopen.
notice_set.question: Is the sentence about the moment something else happens, or about the reopening itself?
options: About the moment something else happens
notice_set.why: Here the reopening is the whole point of the sentence, not the peg another event hangs on.

notice_set.sentence: By the time the inspectors get here, we will have the paperwork ready.
notice_set.question: Which happens first, in the world?
notice_set.why: By the time sets a deadline, so everything the other half describes has to be done before it.

notice_set.sentence: I won't sign anything until the surveyor sends the report.
notice_set.question: Will the speaker sign if the report never comes?
notice_set.why: Until makes the report the condition, and the sentence says plainly what happens without it.

teach.rule_line: Mark the future once. The half with when, until or as soon as never carries it.
teach.false_rule: That a sentence about the future needs a future word in both halves. English marks it once and lets the joining word do the rest.

errors.wrong: I'll ring you when I will get to the station.
errors.right: I'll ring you when I get to the station.
errors.why_it_happens: Both events are genuinely in the future, so marking both feels honest and complete. Nothing in the sentence sounds odd afterwards, which is why it survives every re-reading.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: will.
errors.l1_note: Many languages do mark the future in both halves, so this transfers straight across.

errors.wrong: As soon as the figures will arrive, the committee will publish them.
errors.right: As soon as the figures arrive, the committee will publish them.
errors.why_it_happens: The joining half comes first, so the learner starts the sentence in future mode and stays there. By the time the real news arrives, the future has already been announced once.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: will.

errors.wrong: We can't begin until the surveyor will arrive on site.
errors.right: We can't begin until the surveyor arrives on site.
errors.why_it_happens: Until feels like a word about waiting, and waiting feels like the future, so the future gets marked again inside the waiting half where it does not belong.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: will.

errors.wrong: By the time the auditors get here, we finish the whole review.
errors.right: By the time the auditors get here, we will have finished the whole review.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has learned to strip the future out of the joining half, and strips it out of the other half too. The rule has been over-applied rather than misunderstood.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: will.

pays_in.note: Any argument about what must happen before something else improves needs it.
pays_in.model: Charging schemes will only work once the alternatives are genuinely usable.

pays_in.note: Answers about conditions and consequences are built on these joins.
pays_in.model: People will give up their cars when the buses run often enough to trust.

pays_in.note: Instructions and arrangements are sequenced with these words.
pays_in.model: Wait in the foyer until the previous group comes out.

used_in.quote: The whole argument turns on what has to happen first, which is this join made five or six times.
Talking about how people plan means sequencing two future events in one sentence, over and over.

payload.sentence: Text me when you land and I'll come out to the car park.
payload.question: Has the landing happened?

feedback.why_key: Nothing in this sentence has happened. The everyday shape is being used for a moment that is still ahead.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the whole sentence before you place it in time.

payload.sentence: Once the ring road opens, traffic in the old town will drop sharply.
payload.question: Which of the two happens first?
options: they happen at the same moment

feedback.why_key: Once names the moment everything else waits for, so the opening has to come first for the sentence to make sense.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the joining word and put its event first.

payload.context: Somebody explaining what they intend to do at the end of a contract.
payload.sentence: I'll take a fortnight off when I will finish this contract.
reasons: the future is marked twice in one sentence
the contract has already finished
the two halves are in the wrong order
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: One sentence gets one mark for the future, and the half beginning with when has already given up its claim to it.
feedback.feed_forward: Strip will out of the half beginning with when.

payload.context: From a note on a river restoration scheme.
payload.stem: The fish will return as soon as the water ___ (clear).

expected: clears

feedback.why_key: The clearing is the moment the return hangs on, so it is treated as a fixed point rather than announced as news.
feedback.feed_forward: Use the ordinary present shape after as soon as.

payload.context: Somebody giving instructions in a kitchen.
payload.stem: Take it out of the oven before the top ___ (start) to darken.

expected: starts

feedback.why_key: Before names a moment that has not arrived, and English still treats that moment as a fixed point on the clock.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the present shape after before.

payload.given: The grant money arrives in June. After that, the workshops reopen.
payload.instruction: Join them into one sentence, marking the future once, with the joining half first.

expected: the grant money arrives in june, the workshops will reopen
the grant money arrives, the workshops will reopen
the grant money arrives in june the workshops will reopen

feedback.why_key: The arrival becomes the peg and the reopening becomes the news, which is why only one half is left pointing forward.
feedback.feed_forward: Put will in the half that carries the news.

payload.context: Build one sentence stating what happens at the end of a trial.

expected: we will publish the data when the trial ends

feedback.why_key: Will sits in the first half with the news, and the half after when keeps its plain ending and nothing else.
feedback.feed_forward: Place will before when, never after it.

payload.audio_text: I'll let you know as soon as I hear back.

expected: i'll let you know as soon as i hear back
ill let you know as soon as i hear back
i will let you know as soon as i hear back

feedback.why_key: One small sound at the front carries the future for the whole sentence, and the second half has nothing at all on it.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the first half's small sound, then leave the second bare.

items.decision_cue: until the charging network will be

payload.context: From a body paragraph about electric vehicles.
payload.sentence: Sales will stay flat until the charging network will be dense enough to rely on.
reasons: the future has been marked in both halves of the sentence
the two events are in the wrong order
the sentence is about something already finished
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The first half is already pointing forward. The half after until only has to name the moment, and naming a moment needs no extra machinery.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete the second will and leave the first alone.

items.decision_cue: before the new rota will come

payload.sentence: The team needs training before the new rota will come into force in March.
payload.error_span: before the new rota will come

expected: before the new rota comes

feedback.why_key: March is doing all the work of pointing forward already. The extra word adds nothing and breaks the join.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete will from the half that starts with before.

payload.context: Two lines from the same report on a delayed instrument.
sentences: We will start the tests when the equipment arrives.
Nobody knows when the equipment will arrive.
meanings: The arrival is the peg the tests hang on, so it is treated as a fixed point.
The arrival is the thing being asked about, so the sentence leaves it pointing forward.

feedback.why_key: The same word does two different jobs. In one line it hangs an event on a moment; in the other it is the question itself.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the joining word is naming a moment or asking one.

payload.prompt_text: Think of something in your work or your studies that you are waiting on. Say in one sentence what you will do at the moment it finally happens.

feedback.why_key: You are naming a moment and hanging a plan on it, which is the exact shape this point exists for.
feedback.feed_forward: Mark the future once, in the half with the plan.

payload.prompt_text: Write two sentences for an essay on free public transport, each saying what has to happen before the policy could work. Use a different joining word in each. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: An argument about conditions is nothing but these joins, and a reader who meets two broken ones stops following the order of events.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the condition first, then the consequence with will.

title: Saying what will be going on at a moment later, and asking without pressing

point_json.grammar_name: Future continuous: will be + the -ing verb

teach.can_do: I can say what will already be going on at a particular moment later, and I can ask about someone's plans without sounding as though I want a favour.
teach.why_it_matters: The second job is the one nobody teaches and the one that saves you socially: it lets you ask about somebody's afternoon without them hearing a request coming.
teach.meaning: Pick a moment in the future and stand in it. This shape says that the thing was already under way when you arrived and had not finished. It is the difference between arriving and starting. There is a second job, and in speech it is the more useful one: because the sentence describes a situation rather than a decision, it takes all the pressure out of a question. Asking somebody what they will be doing on Friday enquires about their afternoon. Asking what they will do on Friday sounds like the beginning of a favour.

form.pattern: will be + the -ing verb
notes: the small word be never changes and is never dropped, however fast the sentence is said
in speech the whole opening runs together as one blurred sound before the -ing verb
verbs that describe a state rather than an activity stay out of this shape, exactly as they do everywhere else
form.negative: won't be + the -ing verb: The office won't be taking deliveries over the holiday.
form.question: Will + person + be + the -ing verb: Will you be using the van on Thursday?

marks.label: the moment you are talking about

spec.caption: You arrive in the middle of it. It did not start when you got there and it does not stop.

worked_example.sentence: At six on Friday we will still be loading the last of the samples.
worked_example.why_this_form: Six o'clock is a moment the speaker is standing in, and the loading is neither beginning nor ending there. It is simply in progress around it.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: We will load the last of the samples at six would say the loading begins at six, which is a promise about a start rather than a picture of a moment.

notice_set.sentence: At eleven tomorrow the surveyors will be walking the north boundary.
notice_set.question: Do they begin at eleven?
notice_set.why: Eleven is a moment inside the walk, not the start of it. They set off earlier.

notice_set.sentence: Will you be using the meeting room this afternoon?
notice_set.question: Is the speaker asking for something, or just checking?
notice_set.why: The question describes a situation rather than requesting a decision, so nobody feels pushed by it.

notice_set.sentence: Will you use the meeting room this afternoon?
notice_set.question: Could the listener hear a request coming?
notice_set.why: This one asks the listener to commit, and a commitment question usually has something behind it.

notice_set.sentence: This time next month Kwame will be teaching in Norland.
notice_set.question: Will he have started before that moment?
notice_set.why: The picture is of a job already under way, so the start is somewhere behind the moment named.

notice_set.sentence: The clinic won't be running its evening sessions in August.
notice_set.question: Is this about one evening or about a stretch of weeks?
notice_set.why: The shape stretches an activity out, so August is being described as a whole rather than dated.

teach.rule_line: Stand in a moment later and describe what is already going on around you.
teach.false_rule: That this is just a longer, politer will. It draws a picture of a moment; the politeness is a side effect of describing rather than asking.

errors.wrong: At nine tomorrow we will loading the containers at the north gate.
errors.right: At nine tomorrow we will be loading the containers at the north gate.
errors.why_it_happens: The two small words in the middle carry no meaning of their own and run together in speech, so one of them drops out and the writer's ear does not miss it.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: be.

errors.wrong: By this time next year I will be knowing whether the appeal succeeded.
errors.right: By this time next year I will know whether the appeal succeeded.
errors.why_it_happens: Knowing feels like something you do over a long stretch, so the shape that stretches things out looks right. Knowing is a state you are in, not an activity you perform.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: be.

errors.wrong: By Friday afternoon I will be finishing the whole review.
errors.right: By Friday afternoon I will finish the whole review.
errors.why_it_happens: By Friday points at a deadline, which is about getting something done. The shape chosen points at something still in progress, so the sentence promises the opposite of what the writer meant.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: be.

errors.wrong: Will you drive past the depot on Thursday? I need a favour.
errors.right: Will you be driving past the depot on Thursday? I need a favour.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner asks the direct question because it is shorter, and it lands as a demand for a commitment before the listener has heard what is being asked of them.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: be.

pays_in.note: Describing a normal day at a named hour, without turning it into a plan.
pays_in.model: At that hour I'll usually be finishing off whatever came in overnight.

pays_in.note: Describing what a society will be doing at a future point, with no agent deciding it.
pays_in.model: In twenty years more people will be working several short contracts at once.

pays_in.note: Announcements use it to describe a period rather than a moment.
pays_in.model: Staff will be checking tickets at the platform entrance throughout the morning.

used_in.quote: Describing how working life looks a decade from now needs a picture of a moment, not a list of decisions.
The welcome talk describes what staff will be doing across a whole morning, which is the stretching job this shape does.

payload.sentence: At noon on the fourteenth the team will be sampling the upper reach.
payload.question: Do they begin at noon?

feedback.why_key: Noon is a moment inside the work. The shape puts you in the middle of it rather than at the start.
feedback.feed_forward: Place the named hour inside the activity, not at its edge.

payload.sentence: Will you be going past the print room later?
payload.question: Is the speaker asking the listener to commit to something?

feedback.why_key: The question asks what the afternoon looks like, so nothing has been demanded and the listener can answer freely.
feedback.feed_forward: Notice how the shape removes the pressure from a question.

items.decision_cue: crews will working on the line

payload.context: From a notice about weekend engineering work.
payload.sentence: Between Saturday and Monday, crews will working on the line north of Ashfield.
reasons: a small word is missing between will and the -ing verb
the work has already been done
the two dates are the wrong way round
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Will cannot sit straight against an -ing verb. Something has to stand between them and hold the two together.
feedback.feed_forward: Say be out loud between will and the -ing verb.

payload.context: From a message telling a colleague when not to call.
payload.stem: Don't ring between two and four, I ___ (drive) back from the coast then.

expected: will be driving
'll be driving
ll be driving

feedback.why_key: The two hours are a stretch the drive fills, so the sentence paints the period rather than dating a departure.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep be between will and the -ing verb.

payload.context: Somebody describing where they expect to be in a year.
payload.stem: By next autumn I ___ (study) somewhere a good deal colder than here.

expected: will be studying
'll be studying
ll be studying

feedback.why_key: The course will already have started, so next autumn finds the speaker in the middle of it rather than at the door.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the thing has started before the moment named.

payload.given: The broadcast starts at seven. It runs for two hours. Somebody switches on at eight.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence describing what the station is doing at eight, from the point of view of somebody arriving then.

expected: will be broadcasting
will still be broadcasting
will be broadcasting the programme
will still be broadcasting the programme

feedback.why_key: Eight o'clock falls inside the two hours, so the sentence describes a moment in the middle rather than an event with edges.
feedback.feed_forward: Stand in the named hour and describe what surrounds you.

payload.context: Build one sentence describing a scene at an arrivals hall.

expected: my parents will be waiting at the barrier

feedback.why_key: The three words come in a fixed order and nothing is allowed between them, which is what makes the shape easy once you trust it.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the three words together in that order.

payload.audio_text: They'll be painting the stairwell most of next week.

expected: they'll be painting the stairwell most of next week
theyll be painting the stairwell most of next week
they will be painting the stairwell most of next week

feedback.why_key: Three words collapse into roughly one sound in ordinary speech, and the middle one is the one that disappears first.
feedback.feed_forward: Slow the replay and listen for the middle word.

payload.context: From a paragraph about changes in how people work.
payload.sentence: Within a decade far fewer households will be owning a second vehicle.
reasons: owning is a state, and a state cannot be shown in progress
the sentence points at the wrong stretch of time
a small word is missing after will
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Nobody performs owning. Nothing is going on that a picture of a moment could show, so the shape has nothing to paint.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether anybody is actually doing anything.

payload.sentence: The department will be completing the audit before the end of the financial year.

expected: will complete the audit
'll complete the audit
ll complete the audit

feedback.why_key: Before the end of the year is a deadline, and a deadline is about being done. A picture of work in progress says the opposite.
feedback.feed_forward: Drop be when the sentence is about getting something finished.

payload.context: Two ways of opening the same conversation with a colleague.
sentences: Will you be working in the archive on Friday?
Will you work in the archive on Friday?
meanings: The speaker wants to know what Friday looks like, and nothing is being asked of the listener yet.
The speaker is asking the listener to agree to something, and the favour is on its way.

feedback.why_key: One version describes the listener's Friday. The other asks them to commit to it, and everybody hears the difference immediately.
feedback.feed_forward: Describe their day before you ask them for anything.

payload.prompt_text: Pick an hour of tomorrow and describe what will already be going on around you at that moment, without saying when it starts or ends.

title: Saying whether a small amount is enough or is a shortage

point_json.grammar_name: a few and few, a little and little, and the language of proportion

pays_in.note: Proportion language is most of what a chart answer needs above the numbers themselves.
pays_in.model: The majority of journeys were made on foot, and a significant proportion by bicycle.

pays_in.note: The difference between conceding a point and dismissing it is one word.
pays_in.model: A few schemes have worked, but little of that success has been repeated elsewhere.

pays_in.note: Discussion answers need a way to grant part of a case without granting all of it.
pays_in.model: A few people manage it, but not many, and that's the whole problem.

pays_in.note: A true or false stem often turns on whether the passage said few or a few.
pays_in.model: Few of the original buildings survived the redevelopment.

teach.can_do: I can say that a small amount is enough, or that it is a shortage, and be understood the way I meant.
teach.why_it_matters: One missing word turns good news into a complaint. It is the cheapest meaning reversal in English and nobody warns learners about it.
teach.meaning: A few and few describe the same quantity and take opposite views of it. A few looks at what there is: some, enough to work with. Few looks at what there is not: hardly any, and the sentence is a complaint. A little and little do the same job for measured nouns. Nothing else in the sentence changes, so the only thing telling the reader which way you meant it is one small word at the front.

form.pattern: a few / few + counted noun  ·  a little / little + measured noun
notes: with the a, the sentence is positive: a few stalls stayed open, a little time is left
without it, the sentence is negative: few stalls stayed open, little time is left
the bare versions are formal and belong in writing rather than in conversation
for a large share without a number: the majority of, a significant proportion of, plenty of
the majority of takes its verb from the noun after of: the majority of households were, the majority of the money was
form.negative: few of the stalls stayed open, and little of the money was spent locally
form.question: How many of the stalls stayed open?

ends: there is enough to work with

worked_example.sentence: A few of the older traders are still there, so the market has kept some of its character.
worked_example.why_this_form: The second half of the sentence is positive, so the first half has to be too. The a is what makes the two halves agree.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Take the a away and the opening becomes a complaint, and the sentence then argues with itself halfway through.

notice_set.why: The same clock, and this version is telling you to give up on it.

notice_set.why: It is the useful way to report a large share when the exact number is not worth giving.

teach.rule_line: The a turns a shortage into a supply. Nothing else in the sentence changes.
teach.false_rule: That few and a few are one word with an optional article. They point in opposite directions, and a reader follows whichever one you wrote.

contrast.question: Am I saying there is some, or am I saying there is almost none?

fork.answer: Some, enough to work with, and I am pleased about it
Almost none, and I am pointing at the shortage
A large share, and I do not want to give a number
fork.selects: the majority of, a significant proportion of

a.text: A few of the stalls stayed open through the winter.
a.means: Some stayed open. The market kept going and the sentence is pleased about it.

b.text: Few of the stalls stayed open through the winter.
b.means: Almost all of them shut. The market emptied and the sentence is reporting a loss.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: Writing few when you meant a few does not read as a slip. It reads as a complaint, and the rest of your paragraph then argues against a shortage you never intended to report.

edge_case.text: Without the a, both words are formal and suit writing. In conversation people reach for hardly any or not many, and that is the right choice there, not a lesser one.

contrast.stronger_test: Put but on the end and see which way the sentence wants to go. A few stayed open, but... expects a problem. Few stayed open, but... expects a consolation.

title: Running one three-question check in front of every noun I write

point_json.grammar_name: The article decision: a, the, or nothing

pays_in.note: You will run this check forty or fifty times in one answer.
pays_in.model: A degree taught in a second language costs students time before it saves them any.

pays_in.note: Chart language moves constantly between categories and particular figures.
pays_in.model: Cycling accounted for a small share of journeys, and the share fell after 2018.

pays_in.note: General claims in a discussion need the empty space, and examples need the pointer.
pays_in.model: People generally trust a doctor more than they trust the health service as a whole.

pays_in.note: A passage signals whether a claim is general or particular with these words alone.
pays_in.model: The scheme described in the previous section was never repeated.

teach.can_do: I can run one short check in front of any noun and come out with the right word every time.
teach.why_it_matters: Articles are among the last things any learner gets reliable, so what you need is not a feeling but a procedure you can run in three seconds under pressure.
teach.meaning: You have met the three choices separately. Putting them together is one question asked in a fixed order, and the order matters, because the first question that gets a yes ends the check. Ask whether you mean the category as a whole. If not, ask whether your reader can pick out which one you mean. If not, you are introducing one of several, and what happens then depends only on whether the noun is one English counts.

form.pattern: Q1 category? nothing.  Q2 identifiable? the.  Q3 otherwise: a with a singular counted noun, nothing with a plural or a measured one
notes: question one: renewable energy is expensive to store
question two: the storage problem described above is the reason
question three, singular counted: a battery lasts about ten years
question three, plural or measured: batteries lose capacity, storage costs money
a singular counted noun can never stand alone: not battery lasts ten years
form.negative: a battery does not last for ever
form.question: How long does a battery last?

rungs.text: Q1  Do I mean the whole category?  ->  nothing
Q2  Can my reader pick out which one?  ->  the
Q3  Neither: singular counted  ->  a, otherwise nothing

worked_example.sentence: Renewable energy is expensive to store, and a battery big enough for a house still costs more than the roof it sits under.
worked_example.why_this_form: The first noun is a whole category, so nothing goes in front. The second is one of many, so it takes a. The third is narrowed by the words after it, so it takes the.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: The renewable energy would point at one particular supply, which is not a claim anybody could check, and battery on its own is a shape English does not have.

notice_set.sentence: Renewable energy is expensive to store.
notice_set.question: Is this about one supply or about the whole idea?
notice_set.why: The first question gets a yes, so the check stops there and the space stays empty.

notice_set.sentence: The storage problem described above is the main obstacle.
notice_set.question: Can a reader tell which problem is meant?
options: Only if they know the subject
notice_set.why: The words after the noun narrow it to one, which is the second question answered yes.

notice_set.sentence: A battery large enough for a house costs about as much as a small car.
notice_set.question: Is one particular battery meant?
options: No, any one of that kind
notice_set.why: Neither of the first two questions gets a yes, the noun is singular and counted, so it takes the third answer.

notice_set.sentence: Batteries lose capacity as they age.
notice_set.question: How many batteries are being talked about?
notice_set.why: The first question again, and a plural noun making a general claim takes nothing in front.

notice_set.sentence: Battery lasts about ten years.
notice_set.question: Does this sound like something an English speaker would write?
notice_set.why: A singular counted noun cannot stand on its own, whichever of the three answers you were aiming at.

teach.rule_line: Category, then identifiable, then one of several. Stop at the first yes.
teach.false_rule: That articles are a feel you pick up by reading. Reading helps and is not enough: the decision is taken faster than noticing works, so you need a check.

contrast.question: Whole category, one my reader can pick out, or one of several?

fork.answer: The whole category, with a plural or a measured noun
One my reader can pick out from what they already have
One of several, singular and counted

b.text: The buses in Marlow run every ten minutes.
b.means: The particular service we have been discussing, which the reader already has in mind.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: Both versions are correct English and they answer different questions. If your paragraph is about what the town is like, the pointer narrows a general claim into a timetable, and your reader takes away a smaller point than you made.

edge_case.text: Two places where the check does not help: fixed phrases like at home, by car, in bed and at school, and names, which have to be learned one at a time. Neither is worth arguing with. Learn them as words.

contrast.stronger_test: If the noun is singular and counted, something has to go in front of it, whatever the rest of the check said. That one fact catches more mistakes than the whole of the rest of the procedure.

title: Saying whether somebody went and came back, or is still there

point_json.grammar_name: has been to and has gone to

teach.can_do: I can say whether someone went somewhere and came back, or is there at this moment.
teach.why_it_matters: One syllable decides whether your listener expects to see the person this afternoon. It is a small point and it goes wrong constantly.
teach.meaning: Both sentences describe a journey that has already started, and they disagree about where the traveller is standing while you read them. Been says the journey is finished in both directions: they went, they came back, and the trip is now part of what they have done. Gone says the journey is only half over: they set off and they have not returned, which is usually the reason they are being mentioned at all.

form.pattern: have / has been to + a place, or have / has gone to + a place
notes: been to takes to when you mean the trip: I have been to Marlow, not I have been in Marlow
you can count trips that are over, so been to takes twice, three times, several times; gone to cannot
been is also the plain third form of be, so it turns up in sentences with no travel in them at all
form.negative: haven't been to is the everyday negative; hasn't gone to usually means they never set off.
form.question: Have you ever been to ...? Where has she gone?

worked_example.sentence: Two of the surveyors have been to the Norland reserve, so they know the access track.

worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Gone would put both surveyors out at the reserve right now, and the second half of the sentence would have nobody left to know anything.

notice_set.sentence: Marek has gone to the harbour office.
notice_set.question: Can you speak to him where you are?
notice_set.why: The half-finished journey leaves him at the other end of it, which is why somebody said this to you in the first place.

notice_set.sentence: Marek has been to the harbour office.
notice_set.question: Can you speak to him where you are?
notice_set.why: The round trip is complete, so the office visit is behind him and he is back where you are.

notice_set.sentence: Have you ever been to a night market?
notice_set.question: What is the question about?
options: whether it has ever happened in your life
notice_set.why: Ever throws the question across a whole life, and only the completed round trip can be counted that way.

notice_set.sentence: It has been cold since the weekend.
notice_set.question: Is this sentence about a journey?
notice_set.why: Been here is just the plain third form of be. The travelling meaning only appears when to and a place follow it.

teach.rule_line: Been means they went and came back; gone means they are still at the other end.
teach.false_rule: That been and gone are two spellings of one idea. They put the traveller in two different places, and only one of them is in the room with you.

contrast.question: Is the person back, or are they still at the other end?

fork.answer: Back, and the trip is now part of what they have done
Still there, and that is exactly why they are not in front of you

a.text: Halida has been to the site office.
a.means: She went and she is back. You could turn round and ask her about it.

b.text: Halida has gone to the site office.
b.means: She is at the site office now, which is why you cannot find her.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote has gone. Your listener now expects an empty chair and starts planning round it. If she is sitting two desks away, been is the word that says so, and the whole difference is one syllable.

edge_case.text: Been is also the plain third form of be, so it appears in sentences with no travelling in them: it has been cold all week. And in speech been to happily takes a place that is really an appointment: I've been to the dentist.

contrast.stronger_test: Try adding and she's back now on the end. If the sentence takes it without complaint, been was the word you wanted. Gone refuses it outright.

worked_pairs.b: Kester has gone to the Verdon gorge for the weekend.
worked_pairs.gloss: You can count trips that are over. A trip somebody is still on has no count yet, only a length.

errors.wrong: Nuala isn't at her desk. She has been to the wholesaler.

errors.why_it_happens: Been is the word learners meet first, in the question about experience, so it becomes the default for anything involving travel. Nothing in the sentence corrects it, and the result is a clear sentence saying the wrong thing.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: been becomes gone.

errors.wrong: I went to Sandmouth three times, so I know the coast road well.

errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: went becomes have been.

errors.wrong: Have you ever gone to the Norland reserve?
errors.right: Have you ever been to the Norland reserve?
errors.why_it_happens: The question asks about a whole life of chances, but gone insists the person is away at this exact moment, which cannot be true of somebody standing in front of you answering it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: gone becomes been.

title: Talking about an activity that has been running up to now and still shows

point_json.grammar_name: Present perfect continuous

teach.can_do: I can talk about an activity that has been running up to now and still shows.
teach.why_it_matters: It answers how long you have been doing something, and it explains the state you or a place are in without your having to name the state.
teach.meaning: This form points at the activity rather than at anything the activity produced. It says something has been going on across a stretch reaching up to this moment, and it very often exists to explain something the listener can see: the mud on the boots, the empty shelf, the tiredness. It makes no promise that the activity is finished, and quite often the whole point is that it is not.

form.pattern: have / has been + the -ing form
notes: Three parts and all three are needed: the helper, been, and the -ing form
've been and 's been in speech, and both are short enough to disappear entirely
Verbs about states rather than activities refuse this form: know, own, belong, mean
form.negative: haven't been + the -ing form: I haven't been sleeping properly.
form.question: How long have you been + the -ing form ...?

marks.label: and runs all the way along here
which is why things look like this

spec.caption: The arrow is the activity. The mark at the end is the state it has left behind, and that state is usually why anybody said it.

worked_example.sentence: The team have been sampling the estuary since first light, which is why the boat is filthy.
worked_example.why_this_form: The sentence is about the work itself and the mess it made, not about a finished set of samples. Nobody is counting anything here.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Have sampled would put a finished set of samples on the table and leave the state of the boat out of the sentence entirely.

notice_set.sentence: Idris has been repainting the survey hut.
notice_set.question: Is the hut finished?
notice_set.why: The form points at the work rather than at a result, so whether it is done is simply not part of the claim.

notice_set.sentence: Idris has repainted the survey hut.
notice_set.question: Is the hut finished?
notice_set.why: Without been and the -ing, the sentence hands you the finished hut and says nothing about the afternoon that produced it.

notice_set.sentence: The pump has been running since Tuesday.
notice_set.question: Is it running at this moment?
notice_set.why: The activity is drawn as a line reaching the present moment, and nothing in the sentence cuts it off before then.

notice_set.sentence: You've been working outside, haven't you?
notice_set.question: How does the speaker know?
options: they can see the result on the person
notice_set.why: This is the form's commonest job: reading backwards from a state you can see to the activity that caused it.

notice_set.sentence: We have been waiting for the results for three weeks.
notice_set.question: Have the results come?
notice_set.why: The waiting is drawn as still running, and waiting that is still running has nothing at the end of it yet.

teach.rule_line: Use it for the activity itself, running up to now and often still going.
teach.false_rule: That it simply means for a long time. A three-minute activity takes it perfectly well when the activity is the thing you are pointing at.

errors.wrong: I have been knowing the family since I was small.
errors.right: I have known the family since I was small.
errors.why_it_happens: The stretch really does run up to now, and this is the form that draws a stretch, so it is a reasonable guess. Knowing is not an activity anyone performs, so English refuses to view it as one.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: have been knowing becomes have known.

errors.wrong: The clinic has been treating four hundred patients this month.
errors.right: The clinic has treated four hundred patients this month.
errors.why_it_happens: A counted total is a result, and this form is not looking at results. The number makes the sentence sound like a report while the verb is still pointing at the activity behind it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: has been treating becomes has treated.

errors.wrong: I've written since two o'clock and I still have two sections left.
errors.right: I've been writing since two o'clock and I still have two sections left.
errors.why_it_happens: The simple form has been learned as the safe one and gets used everywhere. Here the sentence is about the afternoon and the state it has left behind, and the simple form throws both of those away.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word and one ending: written becomes been writing.

pays_in.note: It answers how long questions and explains why things look as they do.
pays_in.model: I've been commuting right across the city for about two years now.

pays_in.note: Describing a long project needs the activity, not only the result.
pays_in.model: I've been learning to sail since the spring and I am still nowhere near good.

pays_in.note: A trend that is still running wants the activity form.
pays_in.model: Governments have been subsidising rail travel for decades without closing the gap.

used_in.quote: Every answer on this card is about something still in progress, which is exactly what this form was built to say.

payload.sentence: You've been working outside, haven't you?
