title: Choosing between pointing at the finished thing and pointing at the doing

point_json.grammar_name: Present perfect simple vs continuous

teach.can_do: I can choose between pointing at a finished result and pointing at the activity behind it.
teach.why_it_matters: Both forms are correct English and they answer different questions. The wrong one tells your listener the job is finished when it is not, or the reverse.
teach.meaning: Both forms reach from an earlier moment up to now, and when they arrive they look at different things. The simple form looks at what the activity produced: the finished thing, the total, the number done. The continuous looks at the activity itself: how long it has run, whether it is still going, and what state it has left everything in. Ask what you are pointing at and the choice makes itself.

form.pattern: simple: have / has + third form. continuous: have / has been + the -ing form
notes: A counted result pushes you towards the simple: I have sent four emails
A length, or an explanation of how things look, pushes you towards the continuous: I have been sending emails since eight
State verbs have no continuous at all, so the choice never arises with know, own, belong or mean
form.negative: haven't + third form for the result; haven't been + the -ing form for the activity.
form.question: How much have you done? asks for the simple. What have you been doing? asks for the continuous.

left.role: the simple: look at what came out of it
left.text: I have marked twelve essays.

right.role: the continuous: look at the doing and the state it left
right.text: I have been marking essays since six.

spec.caption: Same evening, same essays. One sentence hands you the pile and the other hands you the person.

worked_example.sentence: I have been marking essays since six, and I have finished eleven of them.
worked_example.why_this_form: The first half explains the state of the room and the person, so it takes the activity. The second half hands over a number, so it takes the result.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Swap them and the sentence claims the evening produced nothing, and that eleven essays were somehow an activity rather than a total.

notice_set.sentence: The council has repaired the footbridge.
notice_set.question: Can you walk over it this morning?
notice_set.why: The simple form hands you the finished bridge, and a finished bridge is one you can cross.

notice_set.sentence: The council has been repairing the footbridge.
notice_set.question: Can you walk over it this morning?
notice_set.why: This one reports the work rather than the bridge. Whether the barriers have come down is outside what it claims.

notice_set.sentence: Halida has been writing her report.
notice_set.question: Is the report finished?
notice_set.why: The activity is in view and the document is not, so the sentence is silent about it either way.

notice_set.sentence: Halida has written her report.
notice_set.question: Is the report finished?
notice_set.why: The simple form exists to hand over the product, and here the product is a finished report.

notice_set.sentence: We have owned the shop for eleven years.
notice_set.question: Why is there no continuous version of this sentence?
options: owning is not something you do
the sentence is in the wrong tense
notice_set.why: The continuous draws activities. Owning is a state that is simply true, so there is no activity for it to draw.

teach.rule_line: Point at the result with the simple; point at the doing with the continuous.
teach.false_rule: That the continuous means unfinished and the simple means finished. The continuous does not say either way. It is simply not looking at that.

contrast.question: Am I pointing at what is done, or at the doing?

fork.answer: At what is done: a result, a total, a number, a finished thing
fork.selects: the simple, as in have marked

fork.answer: At the doing: how long it ran, whether it is still going, why things look like this
fork.selects: the continuous, as in have been marking

a.text: Idris has marked the essays.
a.means: Every essay is done and the pile is ready to hand back.

b.text: Idris has been marking the essays.
b.means: That is what he has been doing, which is why he looks like that. Whether the pile is finished is not said.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You chose has been marking. Your reader now expects an unfinished pile and asks how far you got. If every essay is done, the simple form says so and stops there.

edge_case.text: With live, work and study the two forms mean almost exactly the same thing and nobody will notice which you chose. Verbs about states, like know, own and belong, refuse the continuous outright, and that is a rule rather than a preference.

contrast.stronger_test: Try dropping a number into the sentence. If a count sits comfortably, you are in the simple. The continuous does not want counting; it wants a length.

worked_pairs.a: I have read three of the six chapters.
worked_pairs.b: I have been reading since the train left.
worked_pairs.gloss: A count belongs to a result. A length belongs to an activity.

worked_pairs.a: The council has repaired the footbridge.
worked_pairs.b: The council has been repairing the footbridge.
worked_pairs.gloss: One says you can walk across it this morning. The other says the barriers may well still be up.

worked_pairs.a: Halida has written her report and left it on your desk.
worked_pairs.b: Halida has been writing her report, so do not disturb her.
worked_pairs.gloss: The second half of each sentence tells you which form the first half needed.

errors.wrong: I have been reading three of the six chapters.
errors.right: I have read three of the six chapters.
errors.why_it_happens: The reading really has gone on across a stretch, so the activity form feels honest. The counted chapters are a result, and a result cannot sit inside a form that refuses to look at results.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: have been reading becomes have read.

errors.wrong: Sorry about the flour everywhere. I have baked since lunchtime.
errors.right: Sorry about the flour everywhere. I have been baking since lunchtime.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner reaches for the shorter and safer form. The sentence exists to explain the mess, and only the activity form points back at the afternoon that made it.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word and one ending: baked becomes been baking.

errors.wrong: The same family have been owning the shop for eleven years.
errors.right: The same family have owned the shop for eleven years.
errors.why_it_happens: Eleven years is a stretch running up to now, which is exactly what the continuous draws, so it is a fair guess. Owning is not something anybody performs; it is a state that is simply true.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: have been owning becomes have owned.

pays_in.note: Questions about length and questions about progress want opposite forms.
pays_in.model: I've been taking an evening course, and I've finished two of the four modules.

pays_in.note: A trend still running and a total already reached are two sentences.
pays_in.model: Councils have been cutting rural routes for a decade and have removed nearly half of them.

pays_in.note: Whether a job is done or still in progress can turn on the word been.
pays_in.model: They've been resurfacing the road, so expect delays.

used_in.quote: Talking about something you have been getting to grips with needs both forms in the same minute, one for the effort and one for what you can now do.
The essay has to separate what has been going on from what has actually been achieved, and that separation is this choice.

payload.sentence: The council has been repairing the footbridge.
payload.question: Can you walk over it this morning?

feedback.why_key: This form reports the work rather than the bridge, so the state of the barriers is simply outside the claim.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether you are being handed a thing or an activity.

payload.sentence: The council has repaired the footbridge.
payload.question: Can you walk over it this morning?

feedback.why_key: The simple form hands over the finished bridge, and a finished bridge is one you can cross.
feedback.feed_forward: The simple form gives you the product.

payload.context: From an essay about small businesses on the high street.
payload.sentence: The same family have been owning the shop for eleven years.
reasons: owning is not an activity, so it refuses this form
the stretch of time is already finished
the helper is the wrong one
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The continuous draws activities. Nobody performs owning, so there is no activity for it to draw here.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the verb is something you could stop doing.

payload.context: From a tutor's note at the end of a working day.
payload.stem: I ___ (mark) eleven of the twenty essays.

expected: have marked
've marked

feedback.why_key: Eleven of twenty is a total, and a total is what the activity has produced rather than the activity itself.
feedback.feed_forward: A number in the sentence pulls you to the simple.

payload.context: A tutor explaining the state of a very untidy office.
payload.stem: I ___ (mark) essays since six, so ignore the mess.

expected: have been marking
've been marking

feedback.why_key: The mess is the reason for the sentence, and only the activity form reaches back to the hours that produced it.
feedback.feed_forward: If you are explaining a state, use the activity form.

payload.given: Waiting times started rising in 2019. They are still rising now.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that points at the rising itself rather than at any total.

expected: have been rising since 2019
have been rising steadily since 2019
have been rising ever since 2019

feedback.why_key: Nothing has been completed and no figure is being offered, so all the sentence has to point at is the stretch of rising.
feedback.feed_forward: Draw the stretch when nothing has finished.

payload.audio_text: They've been resurfacing the road, so expect delays.

expected: they've been resurfacing the road so expect delays
they have been resurfacing the road so expect delays
theyve been resurfacing the road so expect delays

feedback.why_key: Drop the been and the sentence says the road is finished, which is the opposite of the warning it is carrying.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for been; it is the word that changes the message.

items.decision_cue: holding out a stapled document across the desk

payload.context: A colleague is holding out a stapled document across the desk.
payload.stem: Halida ___ the report.

options.why_this_means: That the report exists as a finished thing you could pick up.
That writing is what she has been doing, with nothing claimed about a finished report.

expected: has written

feedback.why_key: There is a document in somebody's hand, so the sentence is about the product rather than about the hours behind it.
feedback.feed_forward: If you can hold it, use the simple form.

items.decision_cue: nodding at a closed door and saying not to knock

payload.context: A colleague is nodding at a closed door and saying not to knock.
payload.stem: Halida ___ the report.

options.why_this_means: That the report exists as a finished thing you could pick up.
That writing is what she has been doing, with nothing claimed about a finished report.

expected: has been writing

feedback.why_key: A shut door and a warning are about a person mid-activity, and the activity form is the one that leaves the outcome open.
feedback.feed_forward: If the person is still at it, keep the outcome open.

items.decision_cue: handing the finished file to the client

payload.context: The team leader is handing the finished file to the client.
payload.stem: We ___ the survey data.

options.why_this_means: That the checking is done and the data can be relied on.
That checking is what has been filling the time, with no verdict offered yet.

expected: have checked

feedback.why_key: A file being handed over is a finished product, and a finished product needs the form that points at products.
feedback.feed_forward: Handing something over calls for the simple form.

items.decision_cue: why nobody has left the office

payload.context: The team leader is explaining why nobody has left the office.
payload.stem: We ___ the survey data.

options.why_this_means: That the checking is done and the data can be relied on.
That checking is what has been filling the time, with no verdict offered yet.

expected: have been checking

feedback.why_key: The sentence is explaining where the evening went, not delivering a verdict, and only the activity form does that job.
feedback.feed_forward: Explaining the evening means drawing the activity.

items.decision_cue: the same evening in the workshop

payload.context: Kester is telling a friend about the same evening in the workshop.
payload.stem: I ___ on the boat.

options.why_this_means: That the work is done and there is something to show for it.
That the evening went on it, with nothing said about whether anything is finished.

follow_up.question: Which one leaves it open whether the boat is finished?

feedback.why_key: Both sentences are true about the same evening. They differ in whether anybody is being promised a result at the end of it.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide whether you are promising a result.

payload.context: Two messages left by the same person on the same evening.
sentences: I have written to the landlord.
I have been writing to the landlord.
meanings: The letter has gone and there is nothing left to do about it.
This has been going on for a while and it is plainly not over.

feedback.why_key: One message closes a job and the other opens a complaint. The words in between them are identical.
feedback.feed_forward: Read for whether anything was produced.

payload.context: From a form filled in by a site inspector.
payload.sentence: I have been visiting four of the six sites on the list.
reasons: a counted total belongs to the other form
the helper is the wrong one
the stretch of time is already finished
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Four out of six is a score, and a score is a result. This form is not looking at results, so the number has nowhere to go.
feedback.feed_forward: Counted things take the simple form.

payload.sentence: Sorry about the flour everywhere. I have baked all afternoon.

expected: i have been baking
i've been baking

feedback.why_key: The sentence exists to account for the flour, and only the activity form reaches back to the afternoon that spread it about.
feedback.feed_forward: Explain a mess with the activity form.

payload.prompt_text: Think of a course or a project you are in the middle of. Say one sentence about the activity and one that gives a number of things done.

feedback.why_key: Putting both forms side by side in one answer is what shows you are choosing between them rather than defaulting to one.
feedback.feed_forward: Activity first, then the count.

payload.prompt_text: Talk for a minute about a piece of technology you have been getting to grips with. Use the activity form at least twice and give one total. One minute.

feedback.why_key: An answer that separates the effort from what was actually achieved sounds honest, and it happens to demonstrate the whole point at the same time.
feedback.feed_forward: Say what you have been doing, then what you have done.

title: Building a sentence around the thing something was done to

point_json.grammar_name: The passive: what it does to a sentence

pays_in.note: Process and map answers are written almost entirely in this shape.
pays_in.model: Seawater is drawn into the plant through a screen at the intake.

pays_in.note: It lets a paragraph hold one topic in the subject slot throughout.
pays_in.model: The scheme was funded out of the transport budget rather than from reserves.

pays_in.note: Question stems flip a passage sentence into this shape and back again.
pays_in.model: The ridge was replanted after the fire of 2019.

teach.can_do: I can build a sentence around the thing something happened to, instead of around whoever did it.
teach.why_it_matters: Every process description and a great deal of academic prose is built this way. The form is small; what it does to a sentence is not.
teach.meaning: An ordinary English sentence starts with the doer: the council, the machine, the storm. Sometimes the doer is not what you want to talk about. This shape lets you move the thing that was affected to the front and make it the subject, so the sentence is now about that thing. The event itself does not change. What changes is where the reader's attention starts, and whether the doer appears in the sentence at all.

form.pattern: be + past participle
notes: be carries the time, exactly as it does anywhere else: is checked, was checked, will be checked
the past participle after it never changes shape
the doer, if you still want it, goes at the end after by
form.negative: be + not + past participle: the gates are not opened at night
form.question: Is the channel dredged every autumn?

left.text: the maintenance crew

right.text: the sluice gates

spec.caption: The right-hand box moves to the front of the sentence and takes the subject slot. The left-hand box steps back, or leaves altogether.

worked_example.sentence: The sluice gates are checked twice a day.
worked_example.why_this_form: The note is about the gates and their upkeep, not about which crew is holding the spanner, so the gates take the front of the sentence.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Two engineers check the sluice gates twice a day makes the engineers the subject, and a reader would then expect the next line to carry on about them.

notice_set.sentence: The old pumping station at Verdon was demolished last spring.
notice_set.question: Does the sentence tell you who knocked it down?
notice_set.why: Nobody is named. The building stands at the front because the building is what the sentence is about.

notice_set.sentence: A contractor from Norland knocked the pumping station down.
notice_set.question: Which does this sentence put first, the building or the people?
notice_set.why: The doer is in front, so a reader expects the next line to carry on about the contractor.

notice_set.sentence: Rainwater is collected on the roof and piped to a tank under the yard.
notice_set.question: Does it matter here who installed the pipes?
options: Yes, the sentence depends on it
No, the sentence works without it
notice_set.why: The interest is in where the water goes. Naming an installer would add a person nobody asked about.

notice_set.sentence: The proposal was rejected six weeks later.
notice_set.question: What is this sentence about?
options: The people who turned it down
notice_set.why: Putting the proposal in the subject slot keeps a paragraph about the proposal about the proposal.

notice_set.sentence: Two thousand trees were planted along the Ashfield ridge.
notice_set.question: Could you say who planted them from this sentence alone?
notice_set.why: The number and the place survive; the planters do not. That is the trade this shape makes.

notice_set.sentence: The storm brought down forty of the new trees.
notice_set.question: Does this sentence name what caused the damage?
notice_set.why: When the cause is the news, English puts it at the front and the sentence stays in its ordinary shape.

teach.rule_line: Decide what the sentence should be about, then put that first.
teach.false_rule: That this shape is a way of making writing sound clever. It is a way of choosing the subject. Any formality is a side effect of that choice.

errors.wrong: The pumping station demolished last spring.
errors.right: The pumping station was demolished last spring.
errors.why_it_happens: Demolished looks like a finished verb on its own, so nothing feels missing to the writer until a reader asks what the station demolished.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: was.

errors.wrong: Forty of the young trees were broke in the storm.
errors.right: Forty of the young trees were broken in the storm.
errors.why_it_happens: Broke is the shape the learner uses in ordinary past sentences and it arrives first. The second form of an irregular verb is stored far more weakly than the first.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: broke becomes broken.

errors.wrong: The old mill was collapsed during the storm.
errors.right: The old mill collapsed during the storm.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has decided this shape belongs in reports and applies it to every verb in one. Collapse has nothing to move to the front, because the mill is already the thing that came down.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: was.

used_in.quote: Every stage of the heat-pump diagram is written in this shape, from the first sentence to the last.

payload.sentence: The reservoir above Verdon was drained over the summer.
payload.question: Does the sentence name anyone who did the draining?

feedback.why_key: The doer has been left out on purpose. What survives is the reservoir and what happened to it.
feedback.feed_forward: Check whether a doer is named before deciding what the sentence is about.

items.decision_cue: what happened to the depot yard

payload.context: Sam is describing what happened to the depot yard.
payload.sentence: The yard resurfaced in June.
reasons: the yard is shown as doing the work
the time named is wrong
this verb cannot take an object
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: As written, the yard is out there resurfacing something. One short word puts it back on the receiving end.
feedback.feed_forward: Add be when the subject is on the receiving end.

payload.context: From a note on the Verdon water works.
payload.stem: Silt ___ (remove) from the intake channel every autumn.

expected: is removed

feedback.why_key: Silt does not remove anything. It is what gets removed, so the sentence is built round it.
feedback.feed_forward: Match be to the time and leave the participle alone.

payload.context: Two neighbours are talking about the flats behind the station.
payload.stem: The whole block ___ (paint) last year and it still looks new.

expected: was painted

feedback.why_key: Last year fixes when it happened, and the block is on the receiving end, so was carries the date.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the time on be, never on the word after it.

payload.given: The council widened the approach road in March.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it so that the sentence is about the road.

expected: was widened in march
was widened by the council in march
was widened in march by the council
the approach road was widened in march

feedback.why_key: Moving the road to the front leaves nothing for it to do, so be steps in and the road becomes what the sentence reports on.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the affected thing first, then add be.

payload.context: A warden explaining the routine at the Verdon channel.

expected: every autumn the channel is dredged
the channel is dredged every autumn

feedback.why_key: Both orders are ordinary English. What neither of them does is tell you who runs the dredger.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep is and the participle together, wherever the time phrase goes.

payload.audio_text: The roof was checked before the tenants moved in.

expected: the roof was checked before the tenants moved in

feedback.why_key: Was is one unstressed syllable in the middle of a sentence, and it is the only thing marking the roof as the thing that got checked.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a short be in front of the -ed word.

payload.sentence: The intake screen cleaned every morning, and the debris is carted away.

expected: the intake screen is cleaned

feedback.why_key: The second half of the line shows the shape the first half is missing. Debris does not cart itself and screens do not clean themselves.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the two halves against each other before you submit.

payload.prompt_text: At a recycling plant, glass is sorted by colour before it goes into a crusher. Write one sentence about what happens to the glass. Do not mention the staff.

feedback.why_key: Nobody reading a process wants to meet the staff. Holding the glass in the subject slot is the whole register.
feedback.feed_forward: Start with the material, not with the plant.

payload.prompt_text: Take the first two stages of the dried pasta diagram and write them again as two sentences, keeping the wheat as the thing each sentence reports on. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: Two stages in a row in one voice is what a process answer sounds like, and it is what a single sentence cannot show you.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that both sentences still open with the wheat.

title: Putting a sentence of that kind into whatever time I need

point_json.grammar_name: The passive across the tenses

pays_in.note: A map answer moves between what stood there once and what stands there now.
pays_in.model: The old goods yard has been replaced by a park-and-ride.

pays_in.note: One topic can be held across several times inside a single paragraph.
pays_in.model: The charge was brought in during 2018 and has been increased twice.

pays_in.note: Travel announcements are almost all built this way, and the first word carries the news.
pays_in.model: The next two services have been cancelled.

teach.can_do: I can move this shape into any time, from what is happening now to what will happen next year.
teach.why_it_matters: There is one thing to learn here, not six. Learners who find this hard are finding be hard, and be is already known.
teach.meaning: Once you can build one sentence of this kind you can build all of them, because only one word does the work of placing it in time. Be moves exactly as it moves in an ordinary sentence, and the word after it sits still. So the difference between a job that is happening, a job that is finished and a job that is promised is carried entirely by the first word of the pair.

form.pattern: be, in any time you like, + past participle
notes: now, as a routine: is repaired, are repaired
in the past: was repaired, were repaired
happening as we speak: is being repaired
finished and still relevant: has been repaired
after will, must, can and to, be keeps its plain shape: will be repaired, to be repaired
form.negative: be + not + past participle: the line was not reopened until May
form.question: Has the line been reopened?

spec.caption: Only the first word travels. The word after it never leaves its place.

worked_example.sentence: The signal box at Sandmouth is being rebuilt.
worked_example.why_this_form: The work started and has not finished, and the speaker is standing in the middle of it, so being is what reports that.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Has been rebuilt would close the job and hand you a finished box, which is not what a passenger looking at the scaffolding would say.

notice_set.sentence: The signal box at Sandmouth is being rebuilt.
notice_set.question: Is the work finished?
notice_set.why: Being tells you the work is under way at the moment of speaking.

notice_set.sentence: The box at Sandmouth has been rebuilt.
notice_set.question: Is the work finished?
notice_set.why: Been closes the job and leaves the result standing in front of you.

notice_set.sentence: Three of the level crossings will be closed for good.
notice_set.question: Have those crossings shut yet?
notice_set.why: Will puts the whole event ahead of now, so nothing has happened so far.

notice_set.sentence: Freight was diverted through Brackenfield for eleven weeks.
notice_set.question: Is freight still going that way?
notice_set.why: Eleven weeks is named and closed, so the arrangement ended when they did.

notice_set.sentence: Tickets can be bought at the machine on platform two.
notice_set.question: Does the sentence say anybody has bought one?
notice_set.why: It reports what is possible, not what has happened.

teach.rule_line: Put the time on be and leave the word after it alone.
teach.false_rule: That each time has its own version to memorise. There is one version. Be does the moving, and you already know how be moves.

errors.wrong: The bridge has been rebuild since the flood.
errors.right: The bridge has been rebuilt since the flood.
errors.why_it_happens: Three words are stacked up and only the first two get any attention. After been, nothing is allowed to stay in its plain shape.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: rebuild becomes rebuilt.

errors.wrong: The branch line will reopened in the spring.
errors.right: The branch line will be reopened in the spring.
errors.why_it_happens: Will already feels like the whole of the future, so be looks like a spare part. It is the part that puts the line on the receiving end.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: be.

errors.wrong: The depot was extended in 2019. New sidings are laid the following winter.
errors.right: The depot was extended in 2019. New sidings were laid the following winter.
errors.why_it_happens: The shape stays identical across the two sentences, so the writer stops noticing that the time has to be carried across as well.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: are becomes were.

used_in.quote: Every change between the two maps is reported in this shape, and only the first word of the pair changes.

payload.sentence: The Ashfield line has been closed since the landslip.
payload.question: Are trains running on it today?

feedback.why_key: Been holds the closure against the present, so the line is still shut as you read.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the first word of the pair: it says where in time you are.

payload.context: Ravi is telling a friend about the flat he has just moved into.
payload.sentence: The kitchen was fitted last month, so everything in it is new.
reasons: the time is wrong
the word after was is wrong
be is missing
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Was carries a closed month and fitted is the right second form. There is nothing here to repair.
feedback.feed_forward: Check be and the word after it separately, then stop looking.

payload.context: From a notice on the Brackenfield branch.
payload.stem: The signal box ___ (rebuild) at the moment, so the branch is on single-line working.

expected: is being rebuilt

feedback.why_key: At the moment puts the work under way as you write, and being is what reports under way.
feedback.feed_forward: Use being when the job is still going on as you speak.

payload.context: A supervisor going through the rules on a first day.
payload.stem: Nobody goes up onto the gantry until the harness ___ (check).

expected: has been checked
is checked

feedback.why_key: The check has to be over before anyone climbs, so the version that closes the job is the safer one.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the job must be finished before the next thing starts.

payload.given: Contractors will remove the old filter beds next year.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it so the sentence reports on the filter beds.

expected: will be removed next year
will be removed by contractors next year
will be removed next year by contractors
the old filter beds will be removed next year

feedback.why_key: Will needs be after it before the beds can sit on the receiving end of anything.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep be in its plain shape whenever will comes first.

payload.context: A guide showing visitors round a small dairy.

expected: the cheese is turned by hand every morning
every morning the cheese is turned by hand

feedback.why_key: By hand here is not a person. It is how the job is done, and it stays put whichever order you choose.
feedback.feed_forward: Move the time phrase freely; keep is and the participle together.

payload.audio_text: The last two services have been cancelled.

expected: the last two services have been cancelled

feedback.why_key: Have been is two weak syllables that vanish at speed, and they are the difference between a delay you can wait out and a train that is not coming.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the pair have been in front of the -ed word.

payload.sentence: The depot was extended in 2019, and new sidings are laid the following winter.

expected: were laid

feedback.why_key: The two halves of the sentence sit in different years and only one of them says so.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the dates first, then read the first word of each pair.

payload.prompt_text: A square in Marlow held a car park in 1990 and holds a market hall today. Write one sentence reporting that change, keeping the square as the thing the sentence is about.

feedback.why_key: A change of use is something done to a place, and the place is what the reader is looking at on the map.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose the time first, then build be to match it.

payload.prompt_text: Write the second paragraph of the Sandmouth maps answer: three changes, all reported as things done to the village, all sitting in the same time. Four minutes.

feedback.why_key: Three sentences is where drift starts, because the shape stops feeling like a decision and starts feeling like a habit.
feedback.feed_forward: Read your three first words in a row and check they match.

title: Telling a piece of a sentence apart from a whole one

point_json.grammar_name: Main clauses, subordinate clauses, and what makes a fragment

teach.can_do: I can tell whether a group of words can stand alone as a sentence or needs to lean on another one.
teach.why_it_matters: Nearly every broken sentence in a written answer is one of these two pieces being used as if it were the other.
teach.meaning: A clause is a group of words with a subject and its own verb: the fare rose. That is the smallest thing English accepts as a sentence, and a clause that stands on its own like that is called a main clause. Now put one small word in front of it — because, although, when, if — and it can no longer stand up. It still has its subject and its verb, but it now leans on a main clause and cannot be left alone with a full stop after it. That leaning kind is called a subordinate clause.

form.pattern: main clause = subject + verb, able to stand alone. subordinate clause = joining word + subject + verb, unable to stand alone.
notes: The joining word is what makes the difference, not the length. Because it rained is short and still cannot stand alone.
A subordinate clause can come first or second: because the road flooded, the coach was late — or — the coach was late because the road flooded.
When it comes first, a comma marks where it ends. When it comes second, usually no comma is needed.
One sentence needs exactly one main clause. It may have none, one or several subordinate clauses hanging off it.
form.negative: Both kinds go negative in the ordinary way: although the road was not flooded, the coach was still late.
form.question: Ask of any group of words: could I put a full stop after this and walk away?

left.text: the coach was late

right.text: because the road flooded

spec.caption: Both have a subject and a verb. Only one of them can be left alone with a full stop.

worked_example.sentence: Although the college added an evening class, the waiting list did not get any shorter.
worked_example.why_this_form: Although turns the first clause into the leaning kind, so the sentence still needs the second clause to stand on. The comma shows where the leaning part stops.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Delete although and you have two clauses that can each stand alone, and a comma between them is no longer enough to hold them together.

notice_set.sentence: Because the grant was withdrawn.
notice_set.question: Could this be a sentence on its own?
notice_set.why: It has a subject and a verb, but because leaves it leaning on something that never arrives.

notice_set.sentence: The grant was withdrawn.
notice_set.question: Could this be a sentence on its own?
notice_set.why: Subject, verb, and nothing in front of it asking for more. That is a whole sentence.

notice_set.sentence: When the results came out, half the class had already left.
notice_set.question: How many clauses are in this sentence?
notice_set.why: Two subjects and two verbs, joined by when. One of them leans and one of them stands.

notice_set.sentence: The results came out. Half the class had already left.
notice_set.question: Is anything broken here?
options: Yes, one part cannot stand alone
No, both parts are whole sentences
notice_set.why: Nothing is leaning, so two full stops are perfectly correct. It simply does not tell you how the two facts relate.

notice_set.sentence: Which explains why the scheme was quietly dropped.
notice_set.question: Could this be a sentence on its own?
notice_set.why: Which is a joining word too, so this piece is still waiting to be attached to whatever it explains.

notice_set.sentence: Fewer students took physics last year, although the department had opened two new labs.
notice_set.question: Which part could stand alone?
notice_set.why: The second part has although in front of it, so it leans. Cover it and the first part is still a sentence.

discovery.prompt: Every group of words on the left can be a sentence. None of the ones on the right can, even though all of them have a subject and a verb. What has been done to them?
pairs: the ferry stopped running
because the ferry stopped running
the tunnel was widened in 2018
when the tunnel was widened in 2018
the fee was reduced
although the fee was reduced

candidate_rules.text: One extra word at the front takes away the clause's ability to stand alone.
The ones on the right are about reasons and times, and reasons and times are never sentences.
A group of words cannot stand alone if it begins with because, when or although.

teach.rule_line: Could I put a full stop after this and walk away? If not, it is leaning on something.
teach.false_rule: That a long group of words is a sentence and a short one is not. Length has nothing to do with it: I agree is a sentence, and although the entire scheme was funded from the outset is not.

errors.wrong: Because the tuition fee rose again in September. Many applicants withdrew.
errors.right: Because the tuition fee rose again in September, many applicants withdrew.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner puts the full stop where they would take a breath, and the first piece is long enough to feel finished. Nothing in it sounds incomplete until you cover the piece that follows.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one mark: the full stop becomes a comma.

errors.wrong: The department opened two new labs, fewer students took physics.
errors.right: Although the department opened two new labs, fewer students took physics.
errors.why_it_happens: Both facts are true and they clearly belong together, so a comma feels like enough. Making one of them lean is the move the learner has never been shown.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: although.

errors.wrong: The lab was refitted over the summer the equipment arrived in October.
errors.right: The lab was refitted over the summer, and the equipment arrived in October.
errors.why_it_happens: Two clauses were written straight through without the writer noticing there was a seam. There is no punctuation error to see, which is why proofreading rarely catches it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: and.

errors.wrong: Despite the department opened two new labs, applications fell.
errors.right: Although the department opened two new labs, applications fell.
errors.why_it_happens: Despite and although both signal that a turn is coming, so they feel interchangeable. Nobody has told the learner that only one of the two can have a subject and a verb after it.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: despite becomes although.

pays_in.note: Every complex sentence you will ever write is these two pieces in some arrangement.
pays_in.model: Although the fee was reduced, the number of applications barely moved.

title: Pinning one event to another with when, while, before, after and until

point_json.grammar_name: Time clauses: when, while, as, before, after, until, as soon as

teach.can_do: I can attach a time clause to a sentence and keep the verb inside it in the right form.
teach.why_it_matters: Time clauses are where will turns up and should not, and where a whole sentence quietly loses the part that can stand alone.
teach.meaning: A time clause is a leaning clause whose joining word answers when. When, while, as, before, after, until and as soon as each fix the second event against the first: at the same moment, earlier, later, or right up to a point and no further. Because the clause leans, it always travels with a clause that stands. And there is one habit here that catches everybody: when the whole sentence is about the future, the time clause itself stays in the present.

form.pattern: when / while / as / before / after / until / as soon as + subject + verb, + main clause
notes: Future meaning, present form: I will call you when the results arrive — never when the results will arrive.
While and as suit an activity that was already running; when suits a single moment.
Until means right up to a point and stops there: we waited until the last train left.
The time clause can go first or second. A comma is needed only when it goes first.
form.negative: The clause goes negative in the ordinary way: while the office was not open, deliveries were left at the gate.
form.question: Questions ask about the main clause, not the time clause: what did you do while the line was down?

spec.caption: Each joining word pins the second event to a different place against the first.

worked_example.sentence: We will move the servers as soon as the new room is ready.
worked_example.why_this_form: The whole sentence is about the future and the main clause already says so. The time clause takes the present because the future has been stated once and does not need saying twice.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: As soon as the new room will be ready is not a stronger or a politer version. It is simply not English, and it is one of the most visible errors at this level.

notice_set.sentence: As soon as the survey closed, the figures were published.
notice_set.question: Which happened first?
notice_set.why: As soon as puts the second event immediately after the first, with nothing in between.

notice_set.sentence: While the line was closed, the freight went by road.
notice_set.question: Did the freight move during the closure or after it?
notice_set.why: While covers a stretch of time, and the second event sits inside that stretch.

notice_set.sentence: The office had emptied before the storm reached the coast.
notice_set.question: Was anyone still in the office when the storm arrived?
notice_set.why: Before puts the emptying earlier, so the storm found the office already empty.

notice_set.sentence: I will send the file when the meeting ends.
notice_set.question: Is the meeting over?
notice_set.why: Ends looks like a present form, but the sentence is about the future. The time clause simply does not repeat it.

notice_set.sentence: We stayed until the last bus had gone.
notice_set.question: Did they leave before the last bus?
notice_set.why: Until marks the point at which the staying stopped, so they were still there when the bus went.

teach.rule_line: In a sentence about the future, the time clause stays in the present.
teach.false_rule: That every clause in a sentence about the future needs will. English states the future once, in the main clause, and the time clause does not repeat it.

errors.wrong: I will let you know as soon as the results will arrive.
errors.right: I will let you know as soon as the results arrive.
errors.why_it_happens: The sentence really is about the future and the learner is being consistent, which is exactly the reasoning that produces it. Nothing in the usual teaching says the time clause is the one place where consistency is wrong.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: will.

errors.wrong: After the depot closed in March. The drivers were moved to Ashfield.
errors.right: After the depot closed in March, the drivers were moved to Ashfield.
errors.why_it_happens: The time clause is long enough to feel like a finished thought, and after is not heard as a word that leaves anything hanging.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one mark: the full stop becomes a comma.

errors.wrong: When the alarm went off, everyone is outside within a minute.
errors.right: When the alarm went off, everyone was outside within a minute.
errors.why_it_happens: The two clauses are chosen one at a time and nobody reads the sentence as a single unit. The main clause slips back to the form the learner uses most.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: is becomes was.

errors.wrong: We waited when the last train left.
errors.right: We waited until the last train left.
errors.why_it_happens: When and until both point at a moment and when is far commoner, so it arrives first. When names the moment something happened; until names the moment something stopped.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: when becomes until.

pays_in.note: A two-minute story is a chain of events, and time clauses are the links.
pays_in.model: While we were waiting for the parts to arrive, the whole line stood idle.

pays_in.note: Predictions almost always need a moment attached, and that is where will doubles up.
pays_in.model: Employers will only change their hiring once the shortage starts costing them contracts.

pays_in.note: An instruction in a talk is often a time clause, and the answer sits inside it.
pays_in.model: Before you submit the form, check that the reference number matches the letter.

used_in.quote: Any answer about what will happen next needs a moment pinned to it, and the extra will appears there every time.
Two of the answers are inside time clauses, and the speaker gives the moment before the fact.

payload.sentence: While the shop was being refitted, the staff worked from the unit next door.
payload.question: Where were the staff during the refit?

feedback.why_key: While covers the whole stretch of the refit, and the second clause tells you what filled it.
feedback.feed_forward: Read while as during the whole of that.

payload.sentence: The system will switch to the new server when the tests finish.
payload.question: Have the tests finished?

feedback.why_key: Finish looks present, but the whole sentence sits in the future and the time clause simply does not repeat it.
feedback.feed_forward: Read a present-form time clause as future when the main clause is future.

items.decision_cue: when the new contract will start

payload.sentence: We will move the accounts across when the new contract will start.
reasons: the future is stated twice
the time clause is in the wrong place
the main clause needs a comma
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.feed_forward: State the future once, in the main clause.

payload.context: From a note to a team about an office move.
payload.stem: We will hand over the keys as soon as the survey ___ (finish).

expected: finishes
is finished
has finished

feedback.why_key: The main clause has already put the sentence in the future, so the time clause takes the plain present.
feedback.feed_forward: Never put will inside a time clause.

payload.context: Two colleagues talking about a bad week at the clinic.
payload.stem: When the second nurse ___ (arrive), the queue had gone right round the corner.

expected: arrived

feedback.why_key: The queue formed first, so the arrival is the later of the two events and takes the simple past.
feedback.feed_forward: Fix the earlier event first, then choose the form for the later one.

payload.given: The last ferry left at six. We were still queuing on the slip road.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence beginning with a time clause that puts the queue at that exact moment.

expected: the last ferry left at six we were still queuing on the slip road
the last ferry left at six, we were still queuing on the slip road

feedback.why_key: The time clause pins the queue to the moment the ferry went, which two separate sentences leave the reader to work out.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the moment in the leaning clause and the news in the main one.

payload.context: Build one sentence about a flood warning system.

expected: the alarm will sound before the level reaches the top gauge

feedback.why_key: Will sits in the main clause and nowhere else. Before takes the plain present even though both events are still ahead of us.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep will out of any clause starting with before.

payload.audio_text: As soon as we'd signed it off, the invoice went out.

expected: as soon as we'd signed it off the invoice went out
as soon as we had signed it off the invoice went out
as soon as wed signed it off the invoice went out

feedback.why_key: The 'd is one small sound and it carries the whole order of events. Lose it and the two things start happening at once.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a 'd riding on the subject inside a time clause.

payload.sentence: The old system will stay in use until the licence will expire in June.

expected: until the licence expires
until the licence has expired

feedback.why_key: The sentence has already been put in the future once. Repeating it inside the time clause is the single most visible error in this area.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete will from any clause beginning when, until, before or after.

payload.sentence: After the depot closed in March. Forty drivers were moved to the Ashfield site.

title: Choosing the right word to attach a reason or a result

point_json.grammar_name: Reason and result: because, since, as, so, therefore, consequently

teach.can_do: I can attach a reason or a result to a sentence with the right kind of word, in the right place.
teach.why_it_matters: These words look interchangeable and are not: one joins two clauses, one starts a new sentence, and mixing them is where comma splices come from.
teach.meaning: Cause and effect can be written from either end: name the reason, or name the result. English gives you three different kinds of word for it and they are not swappable. Because, since and as go in front of a clause and make it lean; they introduce the reason. So goes between two clauses that both stand; it introduces the result. Therefore and consequently are not joining words at all — they are adverbs, and they need a full stop in front of them.

form.pattern: reason: because / since / as + clause. result: main clause + , so + clause. adverb: full stop + Therefore, + clause.
notes: Because introduces the reason and so introduces the result. They face in opposite directions and you never need both.
Since and as also mean because, but they suit a reason the reader already knows.
Therefore and consequently cannot hold two clauses together. Put a full stop in front and a comma after.
form.negative: The reason clause goes negative as usual: because the funding was not renewed, the class closed at half term.
form.question: Ask which half is the reason and which is the result before you choose the word.

left.text: because the funding was withdrawn

right.text: so the evening class closed

spec.caption: One arrow, two ways to write it. The word you choose depends on which end you are standing at.

worked_example.sentence: Because the funding was withdrawn in April, the evening class closed at half term.
worked_example.why_this_form: The withdrawal is the reason, and because is the word that puts a reason into a leaning clause. The comma marks where the leaning part ends.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: So in that slot would claim the withdrawal was the result of the closure, which turns the whole sentence round.

notice_set.sentence: The bridge was closed for repairs, so the diversion added twenty minutes.
notice_set.question: Which part is the result?
notice_set.why: So always introduces the result, and the result always comes second.

notice_set.sentence: Because the diversion added twenty minutes, the school bus arrived late.
notice_set.question: Which part is the reason?
notice_set.why: Because always introduces the reason, and here the reason has been put first.

notice_set.sentence: The rent rose again in March. Therefore, two of the shops did not renew.
notice_set.question: Could that full stop be a comma instead?
notice_set.why: Therefore is an adverb, not a joining word, so it cannot hold two clauses together across a comma.

notice_set.sentence: As the site had no drainage, the first winter flooded it.
notice_set.question: Does as mean at the same time here, or because?
notice_set.why: As has both meanings. The reason reading is the natural one when the second clause is plainly a consequence.

notice_set.sentence: Since the depot moved, the village has lost its only employer.
notice_set.question: Is since about time here, or about a reason?
notice_set.why: Since is genuinely ambiguous here, and that ambiguity is a good reason to write because when the reason is the point.

notice_set.sentence: The line was single track, so trains could not pass each other.
notice_set.question: Is the second clause the cause or the effect?
notice_set.why: After so, you are always reading an effect. Nothing else can follow it.

discovery.prompt: Each pair says the same thing twice. Work out what has to change when the word changes.
pairs: Because the fare rose, fewer people travelled.
The fare rose, so fewer people travelled.
Because the mill shut, the village lost its shop.
The mill shut, so the village lost its shop.
Because the survey was late, the report missed its date.
The survey was late, so the report missed its date.

candidate_rules.text: Because goes in front of the reason and so goes in front of the result, so the two clauses swap places.
Because goes at the start of a sentence and so goes in the middle of one.
Use because when the sentence is about the past and so when it is about the present.

teach.rule_line: Because points at the reason. So points at the result. Therefore needs a full stop.
teach.false_rule: That because, so and therefore are three ways of writing one word. They are three different grammatical classes and they sit in three different places.

contrast.question: Am I about to write the reason or the result?

fork.answer: The reason, and I want it in a leaning clause
fork.selects: because, since or as in front of the clause

fork.answer: The result, and both halves are staying as full clauses
fork.selects: so between them, after a comma

fork.answer: The result, and I want a fresh sentence for it
fork.selects: a full stop, then therefore or consequently

a.text: The evening class closed because the funding ran out.
a.means: The money went first. The closure is what followed from it.

b.text: The evening class closed, so the funding ran out.
b.means: The closure came first, and losing the money is what followed from that.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote so. That tells your reader the closure came first and the money went because of it. The facts are unchanged and the arrow has been turned round, which is far harder to spot than a broken form.

edge_case.text: As and since also mean because, and as also means at the same time. In a timed answer that ambiguity costs you nothing if you simply write because whenever the reason is the point.

contrast.stronger_test: Say the two halves out loud with and because of that between them. Whichever half sits second is the result, and that is the half so belongs in front of.

worked_pairs.a: Rents rose sharply, so two of the independent shops did not renew.
worked_pairs.b: Rents rose sharply because two of the independent shops did not renew.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: so two of the independent shops did not renew
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: because two of the independent shops did not renew
worked_pairs.gloss: The first blames the rents for the closures. The second blames the closures for the rents, and that is a different town.

worked_pairs.a: The path floods every winter, so the council has fenced it off.
worked_pairs.b: Because the path floods every winter, the council has fenced it off.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: so the council has fenced it off
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: Because the path floods every winter
worked_pairs.gloss: Same arrow, two ways of writing it. The second puts the reason first, which leaves the fencing as the news.

worked_pairs.a: The line was never electrified. Therefore, journey times have not moved since the 1980s.
worked_pairs.b: The line was never electrified, so journey times have not moved since the 1980s.
worked_pairs.gloss: Both are correct. The first is two sentences and reads formally; the second is one and reads plainly. What you may never do is put therefore where so is.

errors.wrong: The rent rose again in March, therefore two of the shops did not renew.
errors.right: The rent rose again in March. Therefore, two of the shops did not renew.
errors.why_it_happens: Therefore means what so means, so it feels as though it can stand in the same place. Nobody has told the learner that meaning and grammatical class are two separate facts about a word.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one mark: the comma becomes a full stop.

errors.wrong: Because the mill shut, so the village lost its only shop.
errors.right: Because the mill shut, the village lost its only shop.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner marks the relation twice to be certain the reader sees it. Both words are correct on their own and in English exactly one of them has to go.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: so.
errors.l1_note: Marking the pair on both clauses is the standard pattern in several Asian languages.

errors.wrong: The evening class closed, so the funding ran out.
errors.right: The evening class closed because the funding ran out.
errors.why_it_happens: Under time pressure the learner writes the two facts in the order they thought of them and reaches for the commonest joining word. So then quietly reverses the cause and the effect without breaking anything.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: so becomes because.

errors.wrong: Because of the funding was withdrawn, the class closed.
errors.right: Because the funding was withdrawn, the class closed.
errors.why_it_happens: Because of is stored as one unit and comes out whole. It takes a noun, not a clause, and here a clause with its own subject and verb has been put after it.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: of.

pays_in.note: A problem-and-solution answer is a chain of reasons and results end to end.
pays_in.model: Because deliveries are now priced as free, the number of separate vans on each street has doubled.

pays_in.note: Part 3 asks why about everything, and a bare fact does not answer why.
pays_in.model: Rents went up faster than wages, so a lot of people my age are still at home.

pays_in.note: A True or False stem often reverses the arrow the passage drew.
pays_in.model: The scheme was withdrawn because take-up never reached a third of the target.

used_in.quote: The prompt asks for causes and then for consequences, which is this point twice in each paragraph.
The passage explains a closure and one question turns on which of the two facts caused the other.

payload.sentence: Rents rose sharply, so two of the independent shops did not renew.
payload.question: Which came first?

feedback.why_key: So always puts the result second, so whatever sits in front of it is the earlier event.
feedback.feed_forward: Read so as and because of that.

payload.sentence: We moved out to Brackenfield because the rent went up twice in one year.
payload.question: Why did they move?

feedback.why_key: Because introduces the reason, and the reason here is the rent, not the place they went to.
feedback.feed_forward: The clause after because is always the reason.

therefore is the wrong meaning here
the comma is in the wrong place

feedback.feed_forward: Put a full stop in front of therefore.

feedback.feed_forward: If the second half is the consequence, use so.

payload.context: From a paragraph on independent shops.
payload.stem: ___ the business rate was cut, three empty units were taken within a month.

expected: because
since
as

feedback.why_key: The rate cut is the reason and the lettings are the result, so the reason clause is the one that leans.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the reason in the leaning clause.

payload.given: The line was never electrified. Journey times have not changed since the 1980s.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that presents the second fact as the result of the first.

expected: so journey times have not changed since the 1980s

feedback.feed_forward: Use so when both halves stay as full clauses.

payload.audio_text: The van hadn't turned up, so we'd started without it.

expected: the van hadn't turned up so we'd started without it
the van had not turned up so we had started without it
the van hadnt turned up so wed started without it

feedback.why_key: So is a single unstressed sound at the seam. If you do not hear it you write two sentences and the cause disappears.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the small word at the seam between two clauses.

payload.stem: The evening class closed, ___ the funding ran out.

options.why_this_means: That the closure came first and the money stopped as a result of it.

expected: because

feedback.why_key: The grant went in March and the class stopped in May, so the money is the reason and the closure is what followed.

feedback.why_key: The freeze was announced at the start of the year and the rise was counted at the end of it, so the rise is what followed.

items.decision_cue: asked the mayor to hold fares

options.why_this_means: That the freeze came first and the extra passengers are what it produced.
That the passengers came first and holding the fares was the response to them.

feedback.why_key: The rise came first and it is why the fares were held, so the second clause is the reason and not the result.

items.decision_cue: does not say which came first

payload.context: From a draft paragraph on small towns.
payload.sentence: Because the mill shut, so the village lost its only shop.
reasons: the relation is marked twice
the two clauses are the wrong way round
the comma is unnecessary
nothing wrong, it's fine

items.decision_cue: Because of the grant was withdrawn

because of the withdrawal of the grant

One sentence, plainer in tone, with the link carried by a joining word after a comma.
