title: Admitting a fact that works against you and still keeping your point

point_json.grammar_name: Contrast clauses: although, even though, though, while, whereas

teach.can_do: I can put a fact that works against my point inside the same sentence and still keep my point.
teach.why_it_matters: Conceding something and then holding your ground is the shape of a strong body paragraph, and it is one leaning clause away.
teach.meaning: Sometimes two facts are both true and one of them makes the other surprising. Although, even though, though, while and whereas put the surprising fact into a leaning clause, so the reader knows immediately which of the two you are actually arguing for: the main clause always wins. Whereas is slightly different from the rest. It sets two things side by side and compares them, rather than admitting one in order to keep the other.

form.pattern: although / even though / though / while / whereas + clause, + main clause
notes: The main clause is the one you mean. The leaning clause is the fact you are giving away.
Even though is the strong version of although; though is the informal one and often comes at the end in speech.
Whereas compares two different subjects: online sales rose, whereas footfall fell.
One contrast word per sentence. Although at the front and but in the middle is one too many.
form.negative: The leaning clause takes its negative in the ordinary way: although the trial did not finish, the results were published.
form.question: Ask which of the two facts you want your reader to walk away with. That one goes in the main clause.

left.role: the concession, in the leaning clause
left.text: although the app was free

right.role: the point you are making, in the main clause
right.text: very few people kept it past a week

spec.caption: Both facts are true. The one in the main clause is the one you are arguing for.

worked_example.sentence: Although the app was free to download, very few people kept it past the first week.
worked_example.why_this_form: The free download is the fact that works against the point, so it goes into the leaning clause and the abandonment is left standing as the news.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Swap the two clauses over and the sentence becomes an argument for the app: the abandonment turns into a detail and the free download becomes the point.

notice_set.sentence: Although the tablets were handed out in September, the reading scores did not move.
notice_set.question: Which fact is the writer arguing for?
notice_set.why: The main clause carries the point; the leaning clause holds the fact being conceded.

notice_set.sentence: Even though the trial ran for three years, the findings were never published.
notice_set.question: Is three years a long time for this writer's argument?
options: Yes, and that is the job even though is doing
notice_set.why: Even though marks the concession as a strong one, which makes the main clause more surprising.

notice_set.sentence: Online sales rose by a fifth, whereas footfall in the shops fell.
notice_set.question: Are these two facts about the same thing?
options: No, two different things are being compared
notice_set.why: Whereas sets two subjects side by side rather than conceding one in order to keep the other.

notice_set.sentence: While the software was easy to install, the training took a fortnight.
notice_set.question: What does while mean here?
notice_set.why: While has a time meaning and a contrast meaning. Nothing here is happening at the same time, so only the contrast reading is available.

notice_set.sentence: The training took a fortnight, though the software installed in an hour.
notice_set.question: Where has the contrast word gone?
notice_set.why: Though is happy to sit in the middle, and in speech it will even come at the very end of the sentence.

teach.rule_line: The fact you are conceding goes in the leaning clause. Your point stays in the main one.
teach.false_rule: That although and but are two spellings of one word. Although makes a clause lean; but joins two clauses that both stand. Use one or the other, never both.

errors.wrong: Although the app was free, but almost nobody kept it.
errors.right: Although the app was free, almost nobody kept it.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner marks the turn twice so the reader cannot miss it, and in several languages that doubling is the correct pattern. In English one of the two words is always redundant.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: but.
errors.l1_note: The doubled pattern is standard in several South and East Asian languages.

errors.wrong: Although the high cost, the scheme went ahead.
errors.right: Although the cost was high, the scheme went ahead.
errors.why_it_happens: Although has been stored as a contrast word rather than as a clause word, so it is put in front of whatever the contrast is about. What follows here is a noun phrase with no verb in it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: was.

errors.wrong: Although the reading scores did not move, the tablets were handed out in September.
errors.right: Although the tablets were handed out in September, the reading scores did not move.
errors.why_it_happens: Both clauses are true, so the sentence sounds fine when it is read back. The learner has put the news in the leaning clause and the concession in the main one, and the argument now runs backwards.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: although goes in front of the other clause.

errors.wrong: The software installed in an hour, the training took a fortnight.
errors.right: Although the software installed in an hour, the training took a fortnight.
errors.why_it_happens: The contrast between the two facts is obvious to the writer, so it feels as though it has been stated. Nothing on the page states it, and a comma cannot hold two stand-alone clauses together.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: although.

pays_in.note: A paragraph that never concedes anything reads as if the other side was never considered.
pays_in.model: Although phones are a genuine distraction in class, a blanket ban moves the problem to the school gate.

pays_in.note: Part 3 rewards an answer that admits the obvious objection before answering it.
pays_in.model: Even though it costs more up front, you get the money back over about four years.

pays_in.note: The writer's real claim is always in the clause without the contrast word.
pays_in.model: While the scheme met its recycling target, the cost per tonne doubled.

used_in.quote: A discussion answer has to state the other view fairly before it disagrees, and that is a leaning clause.
The follow-up questions push for both sides, and the neat answer concedes one and keeps the other.

payload.sentence: Although the tablets were issued to every pupil, reading scores did not move.
payload.question: What is the writer's point?
options: That the scores did not move

feedback.why_key: The main clause carries the point. The leaning clause is the fact being given away on the road to it.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the main clause as the writer's actual claim.

payload.sentence: The pay is better, though the shifts are a lot longer.
payload.question: Would the speaker recommend the job?

feedback.why_key: Though puts the longer shifts into the leaning clause, so the better pay is what the speaker is really saying.
feedback.feed_forward: The clause without the contrast word is the one that counts.

items.decision_cue: Although the app was free to download, but

payload.context: From a first draft on free software.
payload.sentence: Although the app was free to download, but almost nobody kept it past a week.
reasons: the contrast is marked twice
the two clauses do not contrast
the comma should not be there
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Although has already turned the sentence. But then tries to turn it again, and the second turn has nothing left to work on.
feedback.feed_forward: Use although or but, never both in one join.

payload.context: From a paragraph on school tablets.
payload.stem: ___ every pupil was given a tablet, only a third of them used it for schoolwork.

expected: although
though
even though
while

feedback.why_key: The giving out is the fact being conceded, so it is the clause that leans.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the contrast word in front of the fact you are giving away.

payload.context: From a description of two lines on a chart.
payload.stem: Online sales rose by a fifth, ___ footfall in the town centre fell for the fourth year running.

expected: whereas
while

feedback.why_key: Two different things are being set side by side and compared, which is exactly what whereas is for.
feedback.feed_forward: Use whereas when you are comparing two subjects rather than conceding one.

payload.given: The software installed in under an hour. The training took a fortnight.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence in which the quick install is the fact you are giving away.

expected: the software installed in under an hour the training took a fortnight
the software installed in under an hour, the training took a fortnight

feedback.why_key: The concession leans and the fortnight is left standing, which is the shape of an argument rather than a list.
feedback.feed_forward: Concede in the leaning clause, argue in the main one.

payload.context: Build one sentence about a kerbside recycling scheme.

expected: even though the bins were emptied weekly the recycling rate barely moved

feedback.why_key: Even though needs a subject and a verb behind it, and the sentence still has to finish with a clause that stands alone.
feedback.feed_forward: Give the contrast word a full clause, not a noun.

payload.audio_text: Even though we'd asked twice, they'd sent the wrong part.

expected: even though we'd asked twice they'd sent the wrong part
even though we had asked twice they had sent the wrong part
even though wed asked twice theyd sent the wrong part

feedback.why_key: Both 'd sounds ride on the pronoun and vanish in ordinary speech, and with them goes the order of the two events.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a 'd attached to the subject in each clause.

items.decision_cue: Although the high cost of the licences

payload.sentence: Although the high cost of the licences, the college renewed all of them.
payload.error_span: Although the high cost of the licences

expected: although the licences were expensive
although the cost of the licences was high
despite the high cost of the licences
although the licences cost a lot

feedback.why_key: Although needs a subject and a verb behind it. A noun phrase on its own leaves the clause with nothing to lean with.
feedback.feed_forward: Give although a clause, or change it to despite.

payload.context: From a paragraph whose argument is that a new timetable failed.
payload.sentence: Although attendance fell every term, the timetable was redesigned in September.
reasons: the writer's point has ended up in the leaning clause
the contrast word is the wrong one
the two clauses need a full stop between them
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The paragraph is arguing that the timetable failed and the falling attendance is the evidence. Putting it in the leaning clause gives the evidence away.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that your main clause carries the claim you are making.

payload.context: Two lines from different reports on the same region.
sentences: Although the city added four thousand jobs, the smaller towns lost more than that.
The city added four thousand jobs, whereas the smaller towns lost more than that.
meanings: The region is worse off, and the city's growth is being conceded on the way to saying so.
Two places are being compared and neither is being conceded to the other.

feedback.why_key: Although hands one fact away in order to make a point. Whereas holds both facts up and simply compares them.
feedback.feed_forward: Use whereas to compare and although to concede.

payload.prompt_text: A city has spent heavily on free public wi-fi and the number of people using its libraries has kept falling. Write one sentence that concedes the spending and still makes the point about the libraries.

feedback.why_key: Conceding first and arguing second is what makes an argument read as considered rather than one-sided.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the fact against you in the leaning clause.

payload.prompt_text: Open your paragraph on phones in schools. Find the strongest objection to your view and write one sentence that concedes it and then answers it. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: A paragraph that never concedes anything reads as though the writer has not thought about the other side at all.
feedback.feed_forward: Concede once per paragraph, inside a leaning clause.

title: Saying why something was done, and choosing between to and so that

point_json.grammar_name: Purpose: to, in order to, so as to, so that

teach.can_do: I can say why something was done, and pick the right shape depending on who does the second thing.
teach.why_it_matters: For to improve and for improving are among the most stubborn errors at this level, and the fix is one question about who does what.
teach.meaning: A purpose answers why. English has two shapes for it and the choice between them is mechanical. If the same person does both things, the second one goes into a bare to-infinitive: the council widened the path to slow the cyclists down. If somebody else does the second thing, a to-infinitive has nowhere to put that new subject, so you need so that and a full clause: the council widened the path so that walkers could pass safely. The deciding question is not formality. It is whether the subject changes.

form.pattern: same subject: main clause + to / in order to / so as to + verb. different subject: main clause + so that + subject + verb.
notes: In order to and so as to are the formal versions of to. They add no meaning at all.
The clause after so that almost always carries can, could, will or would.
For + -ing says what a thing is for, not why somebody acted: this valve is for releasing pressure.
form.negative: The negative purpose is so as not to or in order not to: we left early so as not to miss the last bus.
form.question: Ask who does the second action. The same person means to; a different person means so that.

left.text: the clinic opened on Saturdays to reach shift workers

right.text: the clinic opened on Saturdays so that shift workers could attend

spec.caption: Who does the second action decides the shape. Nothing else does.

worked_example.sentence: The clinic began opening on Saturdays so that shift workers could see a nurse without losing pay.
worked_example.why_this_form: The clinic opens and the shift workers do the seeing. Two different subjects, so the purpose needs a clause of its own with could inside it.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: To see a nurse would attach the seeing to the clinic, and the sentence would end up claiming the clinic wanted to be examined.

notice_set.sentence: The council widened the path to slow the cyclists down.
notice_set.question: Who slows the cyclists down?
notice_set.why: A to-infinitive has no subject of its own, so it borrows the one standing in front of it.

notice_set.sentence: The council widened the path so that walkers could pass safely.
notice_set.question: Who passes safely?
notice_set.why: So that opens a full clause with its own subject, which is exactly why the subject is allowed to change.

notice_set.sentence: The hospital extended its opening hours to reduce the queue.
notice_set.question: Could so that replace to here without changing the meaning?
options: Yes, if a subject is added
notice_set.why: So that the queue would be shorter says the same thing in more words. Both are correct; to is shorter.

notice_set.sentence: We left an hour early so as not to miss the ferry.
notice_set.question: What does so as not to mean here?
options: We wanted to avoid missing it
notice_set.why: So as not to is the standard negative purpose, and it is what keeps for not missing off the page.

notice_set.sentence: This valve is for releasing pressure.
notice_set.question: Is this a purpose clause?
options: Yes, it says why somebody did something
No, it says what a thing is for
notice_set.why: For plus -ing describes a function. It cannot say why an action was taken.

notice_set.sentence: The trust bought two vans in order to reach the outlying villages.
notice_set.question: How does in order to differ from plain to here?
options: It is more formal, and nothing else
It changes who does the reaching
notice_set.why: In order to is a longer, more formal to. It adds no meaning whatsoever.

discovery.prompt: Three of these six are correct and three are not. Work out what the correct ones have in common.
pairs: The clinic opened late to reach shift workers.
The clinic opened late for reaching shift workers.
The clinic opened late so that shift workers could attend.
The clinic opened late to shift workers could attend.
We left early so as not to miss the ferry.
We left early for not missing the ferry.

candidate_rules.text: To takes a bare verb when the subject stays the same; so that takes a full clause when the subject changes.
For plus an -ing form is always wrong after a main clause.
Use to in short sentences and so that in long ones.

teach.rule_line: Same person doing both things? Use to. A different person? Use so that.
teach.false_rule: That for plus an -ing form is the way to say why. For plus -ing says what something is for. Why somebody acted needs to or so that.

contrast.question: Does the same person do both actions?

fork.answer: Yes — one subject does both of them
fork.selects: to, in order to or so as to, plus a bare verb

fork.answer: No — somebody else does the second one
fork.selects: so that plus a full clause, usually with can or could

a.text: The clinic opened on Saturdays to see more patients.
a.means: The clinic does the seeing. It wanted a bigger caseload.

b.text: The clinic opened on Saturdays so that more patients could be seen.
b.means: The patients are the ones who get seen. The clinic did it for them.

minimal_pair.only_difference: to see / so that ... could be seen

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote to see more patients. That hands the seeing to the clinic and turns a service into an ambition. If the people you are writing about are the ones who benefit, the purpose needs a subject of its own.

edge_case.text: So that will drop its that in speech, and in order that survives in very formal writing. Neither changes the decision, which is only ever about whether the subject stays the same.

contrast.stronger_test: Put a subject in front of the second verb and see whether it is the same one as the first. If you had to write a new subject, you have to write so that.

worked_pairs.a: The trust bought two vans to reach the outlying villages.
worked_pairs.b: The trust bought two vans so that the outlying villages could be reached.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: so that the outlying villages could be reached
worked_pairs.gloss: In the first the trust does the reaching. In the second the villages are reached, and the sentence needs a clause to say so.

worked_pairs.a: The council fenced the path to keep walkers off the cliff edge.
worked_pairs.b: The council fenced the path so that walkers would keep off the cliff edge.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: so that walkers would keep off
worked_pairs.gloss: Both are correct and they credit the keeping-off to different people: the council in the first, the walkers themselves in the second.

worked_pairs.a: We left an hour early so as not to miss the ferry.
worked_pairs.b: We left an hour early so that the children would not miss the ferry.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: so that the children would not miss
worked_pairs.gloss: The negative works the same way. As soon as the subject changes, the infinitive cannot carry it and a clause has to.

errors.wrong: The clinic opened on Saturdays for reaching shift workers.
errors.right: The clinic opened on Saturdays to reach shift workers.
errors.why_it_happens: For is the everyday purpose word in most languages, and for plus -ing is a shape English really does use, for what a thing is for. The learner is generalising a pattern that genuinely exists.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one phrase: for reaching becomes to reach.
errors.l1_note: Almost universal where the first language uses one preposition for purpose.

errors.wrong: The council widened the path for to slow the cyclists down.
errors.right: The council widened the path to slow the cyclists down.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner knows the purpose word is for and also knows the verb needs to, so both arrive together. Only one of them is doing any work.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: for.

errors.wrong: The clinic opened on Saturdays so that to reach shift workers.
errors.right: The clinic opened on Saturdays to reach shift workers.
errors.why_it_happens: Both shapes are known and neither has been chosen, so they are stitched together. So that is waiting for a subject that never arrives.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one phrase: so that.

errors.wrong: The trust bought two vans so that reach the outlying villages.
errors.right: The trust bought two vans so that the villages could be reached.
errors.why_it_happens: So that has been treated as a longer spelling of to, and the clause it opens has therefore been left with no subject in it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one subject: the villages.

pays_in.note: A solution paragraph is a list of measures and what each one is meant to achieve.
pays_in.model: Councils could subsidise evening buses so that shift workers were not forced to drive.

pays_in.note: Any answer beginning why do people is a purpose clause waiting to happen.
pays_in.model: A lot of people cycle in now to avoid the cost of parking rather than for the exercise.

pays_in.note: Who benefits from a measure is usually carried by the shape of its purpose clause.
pays_in.model: The gates were fitted so that residents could reach the towpath after dark.

used_in.quote: Every proposal in the answer has to state what it is meant to achieve, and for whom.
The examiner asks why schemes are set up, and the answer is a purpose clause with a subject in it.

payload.sentence: The clinic opened on Saturdays to see more patients.
payload.question: Who does the seeing?

feedback.why_key: A to-infinitive has no subject of its own, so it takes the one standing in front of it.
feedback.feed_forward: Trace a bare to-verb back to the nearest subject.

payload.sentence: The clinic opened on Saturdays so that shift workers could be seen.
payload.question: Who gets seen?

feedback.why_key: So that opens a clause with its own subject, and that is the only way the subject is allowed to change.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the subject inside the so that clause before you decide who benefits.

items.decision_cue: for reducing the number of cars

payload.context: From a first draft on city centre traffic.
payload.sentence: The council raised the parking charge for reducing the number of cars in the centre.
reasons: for plus an -ing form cannot say why somebody acted
the two halves do not belong together
the verb reducing is the wrong form of the word
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: For plus -ing states what a thing is for. Why the council acted needs to reduce or so that the number would fall.
feedback.feed_forward: Replace for plus -ing with to plus a bare verb.

payload.context: From a paragraph on rural health services.
payload.stem: The trust bought two vans ___ (reach) the outlying villages.

expected: to reach
in order to reach
so as to reach

feedback.why_key: The trust does the buying and the trust does the reaching, so one subject covers both verbs and a bare infinitive is enough.
feedback.feed_forward: One subject for both verbs means to plus the bare verb.

payload.context: The same paragraph, one sentence later.
payload.stem: The trust bought two vans ___ patients in the outlying villages could reach the surgery.

expected: so that

feedback.why_key: The patients do the reaching, not the trust, so the purpose needs a clause with its own subject in it.
feedback.feed_forward: A new subject after the gap means so that.

payload.given: The council fenced the towpath. It wanted walkers to keep away from the crumbling edge.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence in which the walkers are the ones doing the keeping away.

expected: so that walkers would keep away from the crumbling edge
so that walkers could keep away from the crumbling edge
so that walkers would stay away from the crumbling edge

feedback.why_key: The subject changes from the council to the walkers, and only a full clause can carry that change.
feedback.feed_forward: When the doer changes, open a clause with so that.

payload.audio_text: We'd set off early so as not to miss the last ferry.

expected: we'd set off early so as not to miss the last ferry
we had set off early so as not to miss the last ferry
wed set off early so as not to miss the last ferry

feedback.why_key: So as not to runs together into almost one word in speech, and it is the shape that keeps for not missing off the page.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for three small unstressed words before the verb.

items.decision_cue: pays for all the fuel itself

payload.context: The depot pays for all the fuel itself and wanted its own running costs down.
payload.stem: The depot fitted trackers to the vans ___ cut the fuel bill.

options.why_this_means: That the depot is doing the cutting, because it is the depot's bill.
That the drivers are doing the cutting, on bills of their own.

expected: to

feedback.why_key: The depot fits the trackers and the depot saves the money, so one subject covers both verbs.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask who ends up better off before you choose the shape.

items.decision_cue: buys their own fuel out of the day rate

payload.context: Every driver at the depot is self-employed and buys their own fuel out of the day rate.
payload.stem: The depot fitted trackers to the vans ___ cut the fuel bill.

options.why_this_means: That the depot is doing the cutting, because it is the depot's bill.
That the drivers are doing the cutting, on bills of their own.

expected: so that the drivers could

feedback.why_key: The depot fits the trackers but the drivers pay the bill, so the second verb needs a subject of its own.

items.decision_cue: carrying equipment up two flights of stairs

payload.context: The nurses had been carrying equipment up two flights of stairs a dozen times a day.
payload.stem: The clinic moved to the ground floor ___ reach the treatment rooms more easily.

That the people coming in are the ones with the easier journey.

expected: to

feedback.why_key: The nurses are the ones climbing the stairs, and the nurses are the clinic, so the subject never changes.

items.decision_cue: arrive with walking frames or in wheelchairs

payload.stem: The clinic moved to the ground floor ___ reach the treatment rooms more easily.

options.why_this_means: That the clinic staff are the ones with the easier journey.

items.decision_cue: where the cliff edge had crumbled

payload.stem: The council fenced the path ___ keep walkers off the edge.

title: Saying how much of something there was and what it led to

point_json.grammar_name: Degree and result: so ... that, such ... that, too ... to, enough ... to

teach.can_do: I can say that there was so much of something that it produced a result, or so much that it blocked one.
teach.why_it_matters: It turns a bare adjective into a claim with a consequence attached, which is the difference between describing a problem and arguing about one.
teach.meaning: Very tells your reader the amount. So, such, too and enough tell them what the amount did. So and such report an amount that produced a result: the hall was so cold that half the class went home. Too reports an amount that blocked one: the hall was too cold to sit in, and nobody sat in it. Enough reports an amount that was sufficient, and the result did happen. Choosing between them is not about strength of feeling. It is about whether the thing happened or not.

form.pattern: so + adjective / adverb + that + clause | such + a / an + adjective + noun + that + clause | too + adjective + to + verb | adjective + enough + to + verb | enough + noun + to + verb
notes: So goes in front of an adjective or an adverb. Such goes in front of a noun phrase: so cold, but such a cold hall.
Enough goes after an adjective and in front of a noun: warm enough, but enough chairs.
Too and enough take a bare to-infinitive with no that: too cold to sit in, warm enough to sit in.
So and such take a full clause after that, and in speech the that is often dropped.
form.negative: Too already carries a negative result, so the clause after it stays positive: it was too cold to sit in, never too cold not to sit in.
form.question: Did the thing happen? If it did not, the sentence needs too.

spec.label: how much, and what the amount did

steps.text: not enough space to seat them
steps.gloss: there was too little, so it did not happen
there was too much of the wrong thing, so it did not happen
the amount was sufficient, and it happened

steps.text: so big that it seated them twice over
steps.gloss: the amount was striking, and here is what it produced

worked_example.sentence: The lecture hall was so cold that a third of the group left before the break.
worked_example.why_this_form: Something did happen because of the cold, and the sentence names it. So plus that is the shape for an amount that produced a result.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Too cold to stay would say that nobody stayed at all. The cold would have blocked the sitting rather than merely driving some people out.

notice_set.sentence: The hall was too small to take the whole year group.
notice_set.question: Did the whole year group fit in?
notice_set.why: Too always reports something that did not happen. The size is what stopped it.

notice_set.sentence: The hall was small enough to heat on one boiler.
notice_set.question: Was one boiler enough?
notice_set.why: Enough reports an amount that was sufficient, and what follows it did happen.

notice_set.sentence: The reading list was so long that most students never finished it.
notice_set.question: Did anyone finish it?
notice_set.why: So plus that reports a result that really happened, and most is not all.

notice_set.sentence: It was such a long reading list that most students never finished it.
notice_set.question: What is different from the sentence before?
options: Only the shape, because the adjective now sits in front of a noun
notice_set.why: Such is what you use when the adjective has a noun attached to it. The claim is unchanged.

notice_set.sentence: There were not enough chairs to seat the whole group.
notice_set.question: Did everyone get a chair?
notice_set.why: Enough in front of a noun counts the things, and not enough says the count fell short.

discovery.prompt: Each pair uses the same adjective about the same hall. Work out what changes between the left and the right.
pairs: The hall was too small to take the year group.
The hall was small enough to heat on one boiler.
The list was too long to finish in a term.
The list was so long that most students never finished it.
It was too cold to sit through the lecture.
It was so cold that a third of them left early.

candidate_rules.text: On the left the amount stopped it happening; on the right something did happen.
Too is used for bad things and enough for good ones.
Too goes with an infinitive and so goes with that, so the shape decides the meaning.

teach.rule_line: Did it happen? If it did not, you need too. If it did, you need so, such or enough.
teach.false_rule: That too is simply a stronger very. Very reports an amount and claims nothing else. Too reports that the amount stopped something from happening.

contrast.question: Did it happen, or did the amount stop it happening?

fork.answer: It happened, and I want to say how striking the cause was
fork.selects: so + adjective + that, or such + a + noun + that

fork.answer: It did not happen: there was too much of something in the way
It happened because there was as much as was needed
fork.selects: adjective + enough + to, or enough + noun + to

a.text: The hall was too small to heat on one boiler.
a.means: One boiler was not used, because the size ruled it out.

b.text: The hall was small enough to heat on one boiler.
b.means: One boiler was used, and the size is exactly why it worked.

minimal_pair.only_difference: too small to / small enough to

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote too small to heat on one boiler. That says the heating never happened and blames the size for it, which is the opposite of what you meant. Too always reports a failure, whatever the adjective in front of it.

edge_case.text: Enough goes after an adjective and in front of a noun: warm enough, but enough chairs. It is the one placement rule in this area and it catches everybody exactly once.

contrast.stronger_test: Ask whether the thing actually took place. If it did not, the sentence needs too. If it did, it needs so, such or enough, and nothing else will do.

worked_pairs.a: The reading list was too long to finish in one term.
worked_pairs.b: The reading list was so long that most students never finished it.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: so long that most students never finished it
worked_pairs.gloss: The first says nobody finished it, as a matter of arithmetic. The second says most did not, as a matter of fact, and leaves room for the ones who did.

worked_pairs.a: It was so cold in the hall that a third of them left early.
worked_pairs.b: It was such a cold hall that a third of them left early.
worked_pairs.gloss: Identical claims. So sits in front of a bare adjective; such sits in front of an adjective with a noun behind it.

worked_pairs.a: There were not enough places to take everyone who applied.
worked_pairs.b: There were too few places to take everyone who applied.
worked_pairs.gloss: Both are correct and both report the same shortfall. Not enough counts up from nothing; too few counts down from what was needed.

errors.wrong: The hall was enough warm to work in all afternoon.
errors.right: The hall was warm enough to work in all afternoon.
errors.why_it_happens: Every other word of this kind goes in front of the adjective — very warm, too warm, quite warm — so enough is put there too. It is the one that goes behind.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: enough goes after warm.

errors.wrong: It was so a cold hall that a third of them left early.
errors.right: It was such a cold hall that a third of them left early.
errors.why_it_happens: So is the commoner word and it has already been learned as the degree word. Nothing in the way it is taught says that a noun after the adjective switches it to such.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: so becomes such.

errors.wrong: The reading list was too long that most students never finished it.
errors.right: The reading list was so long that most students never finished it.
errors.why_it_happens: Too and so both report a striking amount, so they feel interchangeable, and that is dragged across from the so pattern. Too never takes that.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: too becomes so.

errors.wrong: The hall was too big to hold the whole year group, so everyone got a seat.
errors.right: The hall was big enough to hold the whole year group, so everyone got a seat.
errors.why_it_happens: Too is heard as a strong very and the writer means the size was impressive. The sentence then reports a failure in its first half and a success in its second.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one phrase: too big becomes big enough.

pays_in.note: It states a problem and its consequence in one sentence instead of two.

pays_in.note: It is the natural shape for the why part of a two-minute answer.

pays_in.note: A True or False stem often turns on whether the passage said something happened or did not.

used_in.quote: The answer has to say what the shortage has actually produced, not simply that it is large.
Saying why you would recommend it is a degree and a result held together in one sentence.

title: Putting a question inside a sentence without it behaving like a question

point_json.grammar_name: Embedded questions and other noun clauses

teach.can_do: I can drop a question into the middle of a sentence and keep the word order straight.
teach.why_it_matters: It is one of the most visible errors a listener notices, it happens in almost every polite request, and the repair is a single move.
teach.meaning: A clause can do the job of a noun. Instead of naming a thing, it names a piece of information: where the office is, whether the funding will continue, what the council intends. When a question goes into that slot it stops being a question and becomes a thing your sentence is talking about, so it loses the swapped word order that questions carry. The question word stays. The swap goes.

form.pattern: verb / adjective + question word or whether + subject + verb ...
notes: no swapping: where the office is, not where is the office
no do, does or did inside the clause: how much it cost, not how much did it cost
when there is no question word, use whether or if: I am not sure whether it is worth it
the clause can also be the subject of the sentence: what the council intends is anybody's guess
form.negative: The negative sits on the outer sentence or inside the clause, not on both: I do not know why they left.
form.question: Ask what the sentence is about. If the answer is a piece of information, that information is behaving like a noun.

left.text: Where is the ticket office?

right.role: the same question sitting inside a sentence
right.text: Could you tell me where the ticket office is?

spec.caption: Once the question is inside another sentence, it stops behaving like a question.

worked_example.sentence: Nobody can tell me how long the repairs will take.
worked_example.why_this_form: The question has become the thing the sentence is about, so it sits where a noun would sit and takes ordinary subject-before-verb order.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: How long will the repairs take is a question being asked out loud. Inside this sentence it leaves the reader waiting for a question mark that never comes.

notice_set.sentence: Could you tell me where the ticket office is?
notice_set.question: Is the speaker asking for directions?
notice_set.why: The whole sentence is a request, even though the part about the office has stopped looking like a question.

notice_set.sentence: She asked me whether the office was open on Saturdays.
notice_set.question: Did she already know the answer?
notice_set.why: Asking is what you do when the information is missing, and whether marks the gap as a yes-or-no one.

notice_set.sentence: I can't remember how much the repairs cost.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker know the figure?
notice_set.why: The missing piece of information is the amount, and the sentence is a statement about not having it.

notice_set.sentence: Nobody has explained why the meeting was moved.
notice_set.question: Was the meeting moved?
notice_set.why: The clause takes the move for granted. What is missing is only the reason for it.

notice_set.sentence: It is not clear whether the funding will continue.
notice_set.question: Has a decision been announced?
notice_set.why: Whether marks an open question, so nothing has been settled either way.

teach.rule_line: Once a question sits inside a sentence, put the subject before the verb.
teach.false_rule: That a question word always brings question order along with it. The question word stays; the swapped order is left behind.

errors.wrong: Could you tell me where is the ticket office?
errors.right: Could you tell me where the ticket office is?
errors.why_it_happens: The learner is asking a question, so the question shape fires automatically. The shape belongs to the outer sentence, which already has it, and the inner clause never needed it.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: is goes to the end.

errors.wrong: Nobody knows how much did it cost.
errors.right: Nobody knows how much it cost.
errors.why_it_happens: Did is stored as part of the question, not as a signal of question order, so it travels inside with the question word and nothing flags it as redundant.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: did.

errors.wrong: She asked me if would I be free on Thursday.
errors.right: She asked me if I would be free on Thursday.
errors.why_it_happens: If already feels like the start of a question, so the swap comes with it. The learner is repeating the shape of the original question rather than reporting its content.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: would goes after I.

errors.wrong: I explained her where the office was.
errors.right: I explained to her where the office was.
errors.why_it_happens: Explain looks like tell and behaves like say, and nothing about its meaning warns the learner that it refuses a person straight after it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: to.

title: Saying which person or thing I mean by hanging a clause on it

point_json.grammar_name: Defining relative clauses

teach.can_do: I can add a clause after a noun to say exactly which person or thing I mean.
teach.why_it_matters: This is the cheapest complex sentence in English and the safest one to risk. Two short sentences become one, and the reader stops asking which one you meant.
teach.meaning: This kind of clause does one job: it narrows a noun down until only the right thing is left. Say the driver and your listener has a whole depot to choose from. Say the driver who took the Ashfield run and there is one. The clause is not decoration you could lift out. Take it away and the sentence stops identifying anything, which is why nothing is allowed to separate it from its noun.

form.pattern: noun + who / which / that + the rest of the clause
notes: who for people, which for things, and that for either of them in this kind of clause
the relative word stands in for the noun inside the clause, so the noun is never said twice
the verb inside the clause agrees with the noun outside it, however far back that noun is
form.negative: The inside of the clause goes negative in the ordinary way: the driver who does not take the Ashfield run.
form.question: Ask which one? about the noun. Turn the answer into who took it or which arrived late, and hang it straight on the noun.

left.text: the driver

right.role: the clause that narrows it to one
right.text: who took the Ashfield run

spec.caption: Nothing comes between the two boxes. No comma, no pause, no breath.

worked_example.sentence: The engineer who checked the Ashfield line has written the report.
worked_example.why_this_form: On its own, the engineer could be any of nine people on that team. The clause cuts nine down to one, and then the sentence can get on with its news.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Two separate sentences would still be true, but they make the reader hold a person in mind and wait to find out which one was meant.

notice_set.sentence: The drivers who finished the safety course start on the new route in April.
notice_set.question: Do all the drivers start on the new route in April?
notice_set.why: Only the drivers picked out by the extra words start. The others are outside what the sentence is talking about.

notice_set.sentence: The lift that serves the north platform is out of order.
notice_set.question: Can you use a different lift?
notice_set.why: One lift has been picked out. Whether the station has any others is simply left open.

notice_set.sentence: The road that runs along the Verdon floods twice a winter.
notice_set.question: Does the road beside the river flood?
notice_set.why: The added words are how you know which road is meant, and that road is the one beside the river.

notice_set.sentence: Passengers who booked online can board first.
notice_set.question: Can a passenger who paid at the desk board first?
notice_set.why: The permission is attached to one group only, and paying at the desk puts you outside it.

notice_set.sentence: The clinic treats patients who live inside the county.
notice_set.question: Would the clinic treat someone from three counties away?
notice_set.why: Living inside the county is what makes someone one of the patients the sentence means.

teach.rule_line: If taking the words out leaves the reader asking which one, weld them on.
teach.false_rule: That who is for people and that is only for things. That works for people too here, and speakers use it constantly.

errors.wrong: The engineer who I trained him last year has taken over the depot.
errors.right: The engineer who I trained last year has taken over the depot.
errors.why_it_happens: Plenty of languages keep the pronoun inside the clause. The learner builds a complete clause and then adds the relative word in front of it, and nothing feels missing, because nothing is.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: him.
errors.l1_note: Very common for speakers of Arabic, Persian and several South Asian languages.

errors.wrong: The inspector which signed the report has retired.
errors.right: The inspector who signed the report has retired.
errors.why_it_happens: Which arrives first because it is the word learners meet most in written English. The check for whether the noun is a person happens later, once the sentence is already moving.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: which becomes who.

errors.wrong: The reports that covers the Sandmouth crossing arrive on Friday.
errors.right: The reports that cover the Sandmouth crossing arrive on Friday.
errors.why_it_happens: The verb inside the clause has to agree with a noun that is now several words behind, and the last thing the learner heard in their head was a singular word.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one letter: the s on covers.

errors.wrong: The scheme which the council approved in March. It has already run over budget.
errors.right: The scheme which the council approved in March has already run over budget.
errors.why_it_happens: The added clause makes the first group of words long enough to feel like a whole sentence, so a full stop goes in and the real news is left stranded in a new one.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one full stop and let the sentence carry on.

pays_in.note: Every sentence in a body paragraph that defines who you are talking about.
pays_in.model: The households that struggle most with fuel bills are the ones least able to pay for insulation.

pays_in.note: It is how you identify a person or a place inside a long turn.
pays_in.model: The teacher who taught me to swim was the one everybody at the pool was frightened of.

pays_in.note: Passages define their key terms this way, and the questions test the definition.
pays_in.model: The technique that the survey team adopted had been abandoned almost everywhere else.

used_in.quote: You cannot argue about which services a small town should keep without a sentence that says which services you mean.
The passage introduces its central term and then narrows it with a clause, which is exactly what the first question turns on.

payload.sentence: The trains that stop at Brackenfield are always the slow ones.
payload.question: Is every train on this line slow?

feedback.why_key: Only one group of trains has been picked out, and it is the group that stops at Brackenfield.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the added words as a filter on the noun, not as extra news.

payload.sentence: Staff who work nights are offered a free eye test each year.
payload.question: Does a day-shift nurse get the free eye test?

feedback.why_key: Working nights is what makes someone one of the staff the sentence is about, so the offer stops at the edge of that group.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask who is inside the group before you decide what is being promised.

payload.context: From a first draft of a report on shift patterns.
payload.sentence: The supervisor who I interviewed her last week runs the whole night team.
reasons: the person is named twice inside the same clause
the wrong relative word has been chosen
the two halves need a comma between them
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Who already stands in for the supervisor. Her says it again, and the clause ends up with one person too many in it.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the clause on its own and delete anything that repeats the noun.

payload.context: From a paragraph about small towns losing their bus routes.
payload.stem: The residents ___ rely on the last bus have no other way of getting home.

expected: who
that

feedback.why_key: Residents are people, so who is the natural choice, and that is equally at home in this kind of clause.
feedback.feed_forward: Check whether the noun is a person before you reach for which.

payload.context: A student explaining how her course is organised.
payload.stem: The modules that ___ (run) in the evening fill up first.

expected: run

feedback.why_key: The verb inside the clause points back to modules, which is plural, even though evening is the nearest word to it.
feedback.feed_forward: Look back to the noun the clause hangs on, not to the nearest word.

payload.context: Build one sentence about equipment on the Verdon survey.

expected: the sensors that the team installed in march have already failed

feedback.why_key: The clause sits straight after sensors and stops there. The main verb of the sentence is still waiting behind it.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the clause next to its noun, then finish the sentence you started.

payload.given: Some passengers change at Marlow. Those passengers lose forty minutes.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that says which passengers lose the time.

expected: who change at marlow lose forty minutes
that change at marlow lose forty minutes
changing at marlow lose forty minutes

feedback.why_key: One sentence now does both jobs: it says which passengers are meant and it says what happens to them.
feedback.feed_forward: Fold the second sentence into the noun it describes.

payload.audio_text: The neighbours who've just moved in keep the yard gate open.

expected: the neighbours who've just moved in keep the yard gate open
the neighbours who have just moved in keep the yard gate open
the neighbours whove just moved in keep the yard gate open

feedback.why_key: In speech who've is a single syllable. If you never hear it you will write who just moved in and lose the link.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a small extra sound riding on the relative word.

payload.sentence: The software which the depot ordered it last spring has never been switched on.

expected: which the depot ordered
that the depot ordered
the depot ordered

feedback.why_key: Which is already the software. Saying it again gives the clause two objects and one of them has to go.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete the pronoun that repeats the noun in front of the clause.

payload.context: Two lines from a timetable notice at Sandmouth.
sentences: The ferries that serve the islands run all winter.
The ferry that serves the islands runs all winter.
meanings: Several boats do this crossing, and none of them stops for the season.
One boat does this crossing, and it does not stop for the season.

feedback.why_key: Both verbs agree with the noun the clause hangs on, so the endings tell you how many boats there are.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the verb endings backwards to the noun to count the things.

payload.prompt_text: A college wants to charge a small fee for evening classes. Write one sentence that says exactly which students would be hit hardest.

feedback.why_key: Naming the group precisely is the whole move here, and it is how a bare opinion becomes an argument a reader can follow.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the group, then narrow it with a clause before the main verb arrives.

payload.prompt_text: Take the body paragraph you wrote on rural services. Rewrite one sentence so that it names the exact group of people affected and finishes with the main point. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: The commonest way this goes wrong under time pressure is a full stop after the clause, leaving the sentence with nothing to say.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that the sentence still has a main verb after the clause ends.

title: Leaving out who, which or that when the clause already has a subject

point_json.grammar_name: Omitting the relative pronoun (contact clauses)

teach.can_do: I can drop who, which or that when someone else is already doing the verb in the clause.
teach.why_it_matters: It makes your English sound like English rather than like a grammar drill, and it is the shape most people are actually listening for.
teach.meaning: The relative word has a job inside its own clause. Sometimes it is the one doing the verb, and then it cannot leave, because the clause would have nobody in it. Sometimes another subject is already there, doing the verb, and the relative word is only the thing the verb happens to. Then it is carrying no weight, and English quietly drops it. The meaning does not change at all. Only the number of words does.

form.pattern: noun + (who / which / that) + subject + verb ...
notes: keep the word when nothing follows it but a verb: the tutor who marked my essay
drop it when a new subject follows: the essay the tutor marked
a preposition left at the end of the clause is normal and stays where it is: the flat we looked at
form.negative: Nothing changes when the clause is negative: the essay the tutor did not mark.
form.question: Put your finger on the word straight after who, which or that. Is it a verb, or is it somebody new?

ends: nobody else in the clause, so the word has to stay
somebody else is already doing the verb, so the word can go

marks.label: the tutor who marked my essay
the bus that goes past the school
the essay that the tutor marked

worked_example.sentence: The form I filled in on Tuesday has gone missing.
worked_example.why_this_form: I is already doing the filling in, so the relative word has nothing left to do in the clause, and English lets it disappear without a trace.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Putting that back in front of I changes nothing about the meaning. It only slows the sentence down by a syllable and makes it a shade more careful.

notice_set.sentence: The engineer the depot hired last month starts on Monday.
notice_set.question: Who did the hiring?
notice_set.why: The depot sits between the engineer and the verb, which puts the depot in charge of the hiring.

notice_set.sentence: The engineer who hired the new drivers starts on Monday.
notice_set.question: Who did the hiring?
notice_set.why: Nobody else appears before the verb, so the engineer is the one doing it.

notice_set.sentence: The report the council rejected ran to ninety pages.
notice_set.question: Who rejected it?
notice_set.why: The council has slipped straight in after the noun, and that is your signal about who acted.

notice_set.sentence: The tutor I emailed twice has finally replied.
notice_set.question: Who sent the emails?
notice_set.why: I is doing the emailing. The tutor is only on the receiving end of it.

notice_set.sentence: The parcel that arrived this morning is still on the desk.
notice_set.question: Did something arrive this morning?
notice_set.why: Nothing stands between that and arrived, so the parcel itself is what arrived.

teach.rule_line: Look at the word after the relative word. If it is a new subject, you can drop it.
teach.false_rule: That leaving it out is lazy or too informal for an essay. Careful written English drops it exactly as readily as conversation does.

errors.wrong: The bus goes past the school leaves at ten past eight.
errors.right: The bus that goes past the school leaves at ten past eight.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has stored the rule as the word is optional and applies it everywhere. Nothing in that stored version mentions who is doing the verb, so nothing fires to stop it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: that.

errors.wrong: The flat we looked at it on Saturday has already gone.
errors.right: The flat we looked at on Saturday has already gone.
errors.why_it_happens: With the relative word gone, the clause looks unfinished, so the learner puts an object back in to repair it. The repair is what creates the error.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: it.
errors.l1_note: Frequent for speakers of Arabic, Persian, Hebrew and several South Asian languages.

errors.wrong: The route the drivers complain about most. It has three level crossings.
errors.right: The route the drivers complain about most has three level crossings.
errors.why_it_happens: With no relative word to signal that the sentence has not finished, the run of words feels complete, a full stop goes in, and the actual news is stranded in the next sentence.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one full stop and run the two halves together.

pays_in.note: Short answers about your own life run on these almost continuously.
pays_in.model: The course I signed up for last autumn turned out to be mostly practical.

pays_in.note: It shortens a clumsy sentence without costing you any complexity.
pays_in.model: The measures governments announce most loudly are rarely the ones that change behaviour.

pays_in.note: Nothing marks the join, so a listener has to hear the second subject.
pays_in.model: The building the college bought last year is still empty.

used_in.quote: Describing a book you recommend needs a run of these: the book I read, the part I liked, the friend I lent it to.

payload.sentence: The tutor my sister recommended has a waiting list until March.
payload.question: Who did the recommending?

feedback.why_key: My sister has arrived before the verb, which means she is the one doing the recommending and the tutor is what she recommended.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the first subject after the noun and give the verb to it.

payload.sentence: The editor who commissioned the piece has since left the paper.
payload.question: Who commissioned the piece?

feedback.why_key: Nothing stands between who and commissioned, so the editor is doing the commissioning rather than receiving it.
feedback.feed_forward: Check whether a new subject appears before the verb.

payload.context: From a letter to a local paper.
payload.sentence: The service runs through Brackenfield was cut without any warning.
reasons: nobody else is doing the verb, so the word cannot be dropped
the object of the clause has been repeated
a comma is needed after the noun
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Runs has no subject of its own here, so the sentence gives the reader two main verbs and no way to sort them out.
feedback.feed_forward: Restore the word whenever a verb follows the noun directly.

payload.context: A tenant writing to a landlord. Put in the missing word only if the sentence needs one.
payload.stem: The damp ___ appeared in the back bedroom has now spread to the hallway.

expected: that
which

feedback.why_key: Appeared has nobody else to belong to, so the word has to stay and hold the clause together.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the word whenever a verb comes straight after the noun.

payload.given: The college bought a building last year. It is still empty.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence, and leave out the relative word if you are allowed to.

expected: the college bought last year is still empty
that the college bought last year is still empty
which the college bought last year is still empty

feedback.why_key: The college is already doing the buying, so nothing is lost when the relative word goes.
feedback.feed_forward: Drop the word once a second subject is in place.

payload.given: One instrument failed in the first week. That instrument had been borrowed.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence. Decide whether the relative word can go.

expected: that failed in the first week had been borrowed
which failed in the first week had been borrowed

feedback.why_key: The instrument is the thing doing the failing, so there is nobody to take the word's place and it has to stay.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask who fails, who buys, who writes, before you delete anything.

payload.context: Say one sentence about a recipe in your family.

expected: the dish my grandmother taught me takes two days

feedback.why_key: My grandmother slides in straight after dish with nothing to introduce her, and the sentence still finds its main verb at the end.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the second subject next to the noun and keep going.

payload.audio_text: The shift I'd swapped with him fell on the bank holiday.

expected: the shift i'd swapped with him fell on the bank holiday
the shift i had swapped with him fell on the bank holiday
the shift id swapped with him fell on the bank holiday

feedback.why_key: Nothing marks where the clause begins, so the only clue is the new subject arriving with a squashed auxiliary attached to it.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a new subject appearing straight after a noun.

payload.sentence: The path the guides recommend it in summer is closed for repairs.

expected: the guides recommend
that the guides recommend
which the guides recommend

feedback.why_key: The path is already the thing being recommended. Adding it gives the clause a second object and one of them has no home.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete any pronoun that repeats the noun the clause hangs on.

payload.context: Two lines from a court report.
sentences: The officers the magistrate criticised have been moved to other duties.
The officers who criticised the magistrate have been moved to other duties.
meanings: The magistrate did the criticising and the officers were on the receiving end.
The officers did the criticising and the magistrate was on the receiving end.

feedback.why_key: The same six words in a different order swap who acted and who was acted on, and only the position of the subject tells you which.
feedback.feed_forward: Locate the subject of the inner verb before you decide who did what.

payload.prompt_text: Think of something you were given as a child and still own. Say one sentence about it, and leave out the relative word.

feedback.why_key: Because someone else did the giving, the relative word is doing no work and the sentence sounds lighter without it.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the thing, add who acted on it, then finish the sentence.

payload.prompt_text: You have one minute on the long-turn card about a book you would recommend. Identify the book, the person who lent it to you and the part you remember, using three of these clauses. Speak it, do not write it.

feedback.why_key: Under real speaking pressure the object slips back in, because the clause feels unfinished without it. That is the habit this turn is hunting.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the clause once, then stop; do not repeat the thing.

title: Choosing between to work and working after the verb in front

point_json.grammar_name: Verb + to-infinitive vs verb + -ing

teach.can_do: I can pick the right shape, to do or doing, for the verbs I use most often.
teach.why_it_matters: The sentence still makes sense when this is wrong, so nobody stops you. It just leaks a small error through every paragraph you write.
teach.meaning: Most of the time this carries no meaning at all. The verb standing in front reaches for one shape or the other, and which one it reaches for is a fact about that verb rather than a fact about the world. Enjoy takes doing. Decide takes to do. Nothing about enjoying is longer or less finished than deciding. So the verb and its shape are learned together, as one piece, the way the word itself was learned.

form.pattern: verb + to + base verb   |   verb + verb-ing
notes: Reaches for to: decide, want, hope, plan, agree, offer, refuse, learn, manage, afford, promise, seem, tend, fail, expect
Reaches for -ing: enjoy, avoid, finish, suggest, mind, keep, practise, consider, risk, deny, admit, involve, imagine, delay
Takes either, with no change of meaning: begin, start, continue, prefer, like, hate, love
There is no third list to work out. A verb that is not in one of the first two has to be looked up once and then stored
form.negative: The word not goes in front of the shape, never inside it: we decided not to renew the contract; she admitted not checking the figures.
form.question: Ask the verb, not the sentence: what does this verb take?

left.text: decided to move, agreed to pay, managed to finish, refused to sign

right.text: avoided moving, suggested paying, finished writing, denied signing

spec.caption: Two piles, and no rule running between them. The verb on the left of the gap tells you which pile you are standing in.

worked_example.sentence: The Marlow depot managed to cut its fuel bill without losing a single route.
worked_example.why_this_form: Manage is one of the verbs that arrives with to already attached, the way depend arrives with on. The choice was made by the word manage, not by the situation.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Managed cutting means nothing at all. That is the useful half of this point: the wrong shape here is not a different meaning, it is no meaning.

notice_set.sentence: The council avoided closing the Marlow library.
notice_set.question: Did the library close?
notice_set.why: Avoid says the thing was kept from happening, and the verb after avoid always turns up in the -ing shape.

notice_set.sentence: The crew managed to repair the pump before the tide turned.
notice_set.question: Was the pump repaired?
notice_set.why: Manage says the hard thing was actually done. Manage always takes to, whatever the sentence is about.

notice_set.sentence: Our neighbours have offered to drive us to the station.
notice_set.question: Have they driven you to the station yet?
notice_set.why: An offer points forward, so nothing has happened yet. Offer is one of the to verbs.

notice_set.sentence: She kept apologising for the delay.
notice_set.question: How many times did she apologise?
notice_set.why: Keep says the action came round again and again, and keep is one of the -ing verbs.

notice_set.sentence: The firm denied causing any lasting damage to the river.
notice_set.question: Does the firm say it damaged the river?
notice_set.why: Deny pushes the thing away from the speaker, and deny takes the -ing shape every time.

notice_set.sentence: We cannot afford to lose another driver this winter.
notice_set.question: Has a driver left this winter?
notice_set.why: The sentence is about what would be too costly, not about what has happened. Afford is a to verb.

discovery.prompt: Every sentence below is correct English. Try to find the rule that puts a sentence in the left column rather than the right one.
pairs: They enjoy walking to work.
They want to walk to work.
We finished repairing the roof.
We agreed to repair the roof.
He avoided answering the question.
He refused to answer the question.

candidate_rules.text: There is no rule to find. The verb on the left of the gap belongs to a list, and the list is learned rather than worked out.
Verbs about liking or disliking something take the -ing shape.
The -ing shape is used when the action goes on for longer.

teach.rule_line: Ask the verb in front, not the sentence. Store each verb with its shape attached.
teach.false_rule: That -ing here means a longer or unfinished action. It does not. Finish takes -ing, and finishing is exactly what is over.

errors.wrong: The council suggested to build a second footbridge.
errors.right: The council suggested building a second footbridge.
errors.why_it_happens: Suggest means roughly what advise and recommend mean, and those feel like to verbs, so to is supplied by analogy. Meaning is doing the choosing here, and meaning has no vote.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: to build becomes building.

errors.wrong: We are considering to move the depot to Verdon.
errors.right: We are considering moving the depot to Verdon.
errors.why_it_happens: Consider points at something not yet done, and a not-yet action feels as though it should take the forward-looking to shape. Consider simply refuses it.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: to move becomes moving.

errors.wrong: She enjoys to cycle along the towpath at the weekend.
errors.right: She enjoys cycling along the towpath at the weekend.
errors.why_it_happens: To do is the shape a learner meets first, so it becomes the default filling for every gap. Enjoy is one of the commonest verbs that will not take it.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: to cycle becomes cycling.

errors.wrong: They decided to moving the market to Tuesdays.
errors.right: They decided to move the market to Tuesdays.
errors.why_it_happens: Both shapes have been half-learned and both arrive at once. It is the signature of a chunk that was never stored whole, only as two loose pieces.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete three letters: moving becomes move.

pays_in.note: Every policy sentence has one verb sitting on top of another.
pays_in.model: Councils that plan to cut bus subsidies rarely consider replacing them with anything.

pays_in.note: A two-minute answer is a chain of verbs following verbs.
pays_in.model: I kept going back because I enjoyed working with people who had done the job for years.

pays_in.note: Whether the second action happened is carried by the first verb.
pays_in.model: The company denied withholding the survey results for eight months.

used_in.quote: Both sides of this essay are built from verbs like plan, expect, avoid and involve, each dragging its own shape behind it.
Saying what you enjoy, what you have decided and what you keep doing uses three different shapes in one answer.

payload.sentence: My manager has offered to swap my Friday shift.
payload.question: Has the shift been swapped?

feedback.why_key: An offer is something put on the table and not yet taken up. Offer is one of the verbs that arrives with to attached.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the first verb for what happened, and take its shape as given.

payload.sentence: The report avoided naming the firm responsible for the spill.
payload.question: Does the report name the firm?

feedback.why_key: Avoid says the naming was kept from happening. The -ing shape after it is not adding anything; avoid always takes it.
feedback.feed_forward: Let the first verb tell you what happened, not the shape of the second.

payload.context: From a paragraph about a college trying to save money.
payload.sentence: The college suggested to reduce the number of evening classes.
reasons: suggest takes the -ing shape, not to
the sentence needs a person after suggested
reduce is the wrong verb here
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Suggest sits in the -ing pile. Nothing about the meaning of this sentence is wrong, which is exactly why the error survives so long.
feedback.feed_forward: Check suggest against the list before you write the second verb.

payload.context: From a letter about the last bus out of Verdon.
payload.stem: Passengers who miss it cannot afford ___ (wait) an hour for a taxi.

expected: to wait

feedback.why_key: Afford is a to verb, and it stays a to verb after cannot. The negative changes nothing about the shape.
feedback.feed_forward: Look past the negative to the verb that owns the shape.

payload.context: A cook talking about a busy Saturday.
payload.stem: I have finally finished ___ (plan) the menu for the weekend.

expected: planning

feedback.why_key: Finish sits in the -ing pile. The planning is over, so if -ing meant an unfinished action this sentence could not exist.
feedback.feed_forward: Store finish and its -ing shape as one chunk.

payload.context: From a maintenance note on the Verdon sensor trial.
payload.stem: The team keeps ___ (find) the same fault, and has agreed ___ (replace) the whole batch.

expected: finding, to replace
finding to replace

feedback.why_key: One sentence, two verbs, two different piles. Keep takes -ing and agree takes to, and neither choice is about the meaning.
feedback.feed_forward: Handle each verb separately; the sentence has no single setting.

payload.given: The landlord will not repair the boiler. He has said so twice.
payload.instruction: Write it as one sentence that starts with the landlord and uses refuse.

expected: to repair the boiler
to repair the boiler twice
twice to repair the boiler

feedback.why_key: Refuse belongs to the to pile, and it stays there whatever tense is wrapped round it.
feedback.feed_forward: Fix the shape from the verb, then worry about the tense.

payload.context: Build one sentence about a delay to the Ashfield recycling scheme.

expected: the council has postponed replacing the recycling bins

feedback.why_key: Postpone takes the -ing shape, and that shape sits directly against the verb with nothing between them.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the second verb straight after the first, in the shape the first one wants.

payload.audio_text: They've agreed to look at it, but they keep putting the meeting off.

expected: they've agreed to look at it, but they keep putting the meeting off
they have agreed to look at it, but they keep putting the meeting off
theyve agreed to look at it but they keep putting the meeting off

feedback.why_key: In speech the to after agreed is almost swallowed. If you never hear it you will never write it, and the sentence will come out as agreed look.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the small unstressed to riding between the two verbs.

payload.sentence: Most students avoid to ask questions in a full lecture theatre.

expected: avoid asking

feedback.why_key: Avoid is in the -ing pile. Nothing in the sentence signals it, which is why this one has to be retrieved rather than reasoned out.
feedback.feed_forward: When the fix is a list fact, retrieve it; do not argue from meaning.

payload.context: Someone talking about their shifts at the hospital.
payload.sentence: I've decided cutting down on nights, but I don't mind to work weekends.
reasons: both verbs have taken the wrong shape
only the first verb has taken the wrong shape
only the second verb has taken the wrong shape
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Decide belongs with to and mind belongs with -ing, so the sentence has them the wrong way round twice over.
feedback.feed_forward: Check each verb against its own pile before you move on.

payload.prompt_text: A town is about to start collecting food waste from every street. Write one sentence saying what households will have to stop doing and what the council has agreed to provide.

feedback.why_key: The prompt forces one verb from each pile into the same sentence, which is where the error normally appears.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the first verb, then ask it what shape it wants.

payload.prompt_text: Take the body paragraph you wrote on the four-day week. Rewrite two sentences so that each one has a verb sitting on top of another verb, and check both shapes before you stop. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: Under time pressure the default shape wins, and the default shape is to. Two sentences is enough to catch that habit in the act.
feedback.feed_forward: On the reread, look only at pairs of verbs standing next to each other.

title: Putting the -ing shape after every preposition, with no exceptions

point_json.grammar_name: The -ing form after a preposition

teach.can_do: I can put a verb after by, without, after, instead of or good at without stopping to think.
teach.why_it_matters: This is the one place in the whole area where a real rule exists, it never has exceptions, and it repairs a very common written error at the same time.
teach.meaning: A preposition is a word that expects a thing after it: after lunch, without a ticket, good at maths. When what follows is an action rather than a thing, English turns the action into a thing by adding -ing. That is all -ing is doing here. It is not saying the action is long, or repeated, or still running. It is the shape a verb wears when it has to stand where a noun would stand.

form.pattern: preposition + verb-ing
notes: Common ones: by, without, after, before, instead of, on, in, for, about, of, at, with, since, apart from
Despite and in spite of are prepositions, so they take -ing or a noun and never a full clause
A few phrases end in the word to and that to is a preposition: look forward to, object to, be used to, be committed to, in addition to. The verb after them is -ing
A preposition can never be followed by to plus the base verb. There is no sentence in English where it can
form.negative: The word not goes between the preposition and the -ing: she apologised for not telling us sooner.
form.question: Is the word in front of the gap a preposition? Then the question is already answered.

left.role: the word before the gap is a preposition
left.text: by / without / after / instead of / good at / look forward to

right.role: so the verb can only wear -ing
right.text: closing, saying, finishing, replacing, fixing, hearing

spec.caption: One arrow, no branches. This is the only part of the unit where knowing the rule is enough.

worked_example.sentence: The depot cut its emissions by replacing the two oldest vans.
worked_example.why_this_form: By is a preposition, so whatever follows it has to stand where a noun stands. Replacing is the verb replace wearing the shape that lets it do that.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: By to replace has no meaning available to it. The preposition has asked for a thing and been handed something that cannot be one.

notice_set.sentence: They cut costs by closing the two smallest depots.
notice_set.question: How were the costs cut?
notice_set.why: By names the method, and the action that is the method turns up in the -ing shape because by needs a thing after it.

notice_set.sentence: She left the meeting without saying anything.
notice_set.question: Did she say anything?
notice_set.why: Without is a preposition, so the action it rules out arrives as saying rather than as to say.

notice_set.sentence: After finishing the river survey, the team drove back to Verdon.
notice_set.question: Which happened first?
notice_set.why: After puts one thing before the other, and the thing it puts first is an action in the -ing shape.

notice_set.sentence: The scheme went ahead in spite of costing twice the estimate.
notice_set.question: Did the scheme cost more than expected?
notice_set.why: In spite of is a preposition, so the cost comes in as a thing. This is why despite cannot be followed by a full clause.

notice_set.sentence: I am looking forward to hearing from the housing office.
notice_set.question: Has the housing office written back yet?
notice_set.why: The to in look forward to is a preposition, not the to of to do. That is why hearing and not hear follows it.

notice_set.sentence: He apologised for arriving forty minutes late.
notice_set.question: Did he arrive late?
notice_set.why: For is a preposition, so the thing being apologised for is an action wearing the -ing shape.

discovery.prompt: One of these columns is impossible English. Work out what the left-hand words have in common.
pairs: We saved money by cycling.
We saved money to cycle.
She went out without locking up.
She went out without to lock up.
I object to paying twice.
I object to pay twice.

candidate_rules.text: By, without and object to all end in a preposition, and a preposition can only be followed by -ing.
Short linking words like by and without take -ing.
When the sentence contains the word to, the verb goes in its base form.
