teach.rule_line: If the word before the gap is a preposition, the verb after it must be -ing.
teach.false_rule: That the word to is always followed by the base verb. In look forward to, object to and be used to, to is a preposition.

errors.wrong: Despite the survey was finished on time, the report arrived in June.
errors.right: Despite finishing the survey on time, the report arrived in June.
errors.why_it_happens: Despite means what although means, so it inherits although's grammar. Nobody mentions that one is a preposition and the other joins clauses, and the meaning gives no clue.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: was finished becomes finishing, and the subject goes.

errors.wrong: I look forward to hear from you about the tenancy.
errors.right: I look forward to hearing from you about the tenancy.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner sees to and applies the only rule they have for it. The to in look forward to is a preposition and looks identical to the other one.
errors.smallest_fix: Add three letters: hear becomes hearing.

errors.wrong: The council reduced waste by to collect food scraps separately.
errors.right: The council reduced waste by collecting food scraps separately.
errors.why_it_happens: To do is the default shape for a second verb, and it goes in even after a preposition that has no room for it. The result is a shape English cannot read at all.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word and add three letters: by to collect becomes by collecting.

errors.wrong: She is used to work nights, so the shift does not bother her.
errors.right: She is used to working nights, so the shift does not bother her.
errors.why_it_happens: Be used to and used to look the same and are learned at the same time. One is a preposition phrase about being accustomed; the other is a past habit and takes the base verb.
errors.smallest_fix: Add three letters: work becomes working.

pays_in.note: Every sentence about method, cause or concession runs through a preposition.
pays_in.model: Cities have cut congestion by charging for road space rather than by widening it.

pays_in.note: The standard closing line of a formal letter turns on this rule.
pays_in.model: I look forward to receiving confirmation that the repairs have been booked.

pays_in.note: Explaining how something could be done needs by plus -ing.
pays_in.model: You could cut most of that waste just by planning the week's meals in advance.

pays_in.note: A concession clause built on despite compresses a whole claim.
pays_in.model: Despite falling steadily since 2016, the figure remains above the national average.

used_in.quote: Every solution sentence in this task is built on by plus an action, and the action has to be a thing before by will take it.

payload.sentence: We got the bill down by turning the heating off at night.
payload.question: What brought the bill down?

feedback.why_key: By points at the method, and the method is an action that has been turned into a thing so that by can hold it.
feedback.feed_forward: Read by as how, then expect an -ing straight after it.

payload.sentence: Despite cutting its staff by a third, the depot met every delivery slot.
payload.question: Did the depot lose staff?

feedback.why_key: Despite is a preposition, so the staff cut arrives as a thing. The sentence still asserts it happened.
feedback.feed_forward: Treat despite plus -ing as a fact the writer accepts.

payload.context: The last line of a letter to a letting agency.
payload.sentence: I look forward to hear from you before the end of the month.
reasons: the to in look forward to is a preposition, so it needs -ing
look forward is the wrong verb for a letter
the sentence needs a subject after hear
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Two identical-looking words are doing different jobs. This to is the kind that ends a phrase, not the kind that starts a verb.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the to belongs to the phrase in front of it.

payload.context: From a paragraph about a town-wide recycling trial.
payload.stem: Ashfield halved its landfill waste by ___ (sort) glass at the kerbside.

expected: sorting

feedback.why_key: By is a preposition and there is no second option. This is the one gap in the unit you can fill without knowing the verb.
feedback.feed_forward: Spot the preposition first; the shape follows automatically.

payload.context: Someone describing their commute since the tram opened.
payload.stem: I am used to ___ (stand) now, and I leave without ___ (check) the timetable.

expected: standing, checking
standing checking

feedback.why_key: Both gaps sit behind a preposition, and the to in am used to is one of them. Neither gap has a choice to make.
feedback.feed_forward: Check whether to belongs to a phrase before you treat it as an infinitive.

payload.given: Although the college raised its fees, applications went up.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it starting with despite, keeping the same meaning.

expected: raising its fees, applications went up
raising its fees, the college's applications went up
raising its fees applications went up

feedback.why_key: Despite cannot hold a clause, so the clause has to be squeezed into an -ing shape before it will fit.
feedback.feed_forward: Swap although for despite and the verb loses its subject and gains -ing.

payload.context: Build one sentence for a report on a small savings scheme.

expected: the fund grew without taking on any new risk

feedback.why_key: Without has to sit directly in front of the -ing shape. Nothing can come between a preposition and the thing it holds.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the preposition and the -ing word next to each other.

payload.audio_text: We cut the waste right down by planning the week's meals before shopping.

expected: we cut the waste right down by planning the week's meals before shopping
we cut the waste right down by planning the weeks meals before shopping

feedback.why_key: Two prepositions and two -ing shapes in one short sentence. In speech the endings are light, and light is exactly what learners stop writing.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the -ing ending even when you barely hear it.

payload.sentence: Many households now rent tools instead of to buy them outright.

expected: instead of buying

feedback.why_key: Instead of ends in the preposition of, and of will not hold an infinitive. The fix is the ending, not the word.
feedback.feed_forward: Look at the last word before the gap, not the first.

payload.sentence: Despite the rent was rising every year, most tenants stayed in the district.

expected: despite rising rents
although the rent was rising
despite the rising rent
despite the rent rising

feedback.why_key: Despite is holding a full clause, which it cannot do. Either the clause shrinks to a thing or the word changes to one that takes clauses.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide which side to move: shrink the clause or swap the connector.

payload.context: Someone talking about training for a half marathon.
payload.sentence: I used to running before work, but now I go at lunchtime.
reasons: this used to is the past habit one, so it takes the base verb
used to always takes -ing
the sentence needs but replaced with and
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Used to on its own is a past habit and takes run. It is only be used to, with a form of be in front, that ends in a preposition.
feedback.feed_forward: Look for a form of be before used to before you reach for -ing.

payload.prompt_text: Someone asks how an ordinary household could cut its water use. Answer in one sentence that begins with a method, using by.

feedback.why_key: By plus -ing is the fastest way to answer a how question, and it is available before you have decided how the sentence ends.
feedback.feed_forward: Open with by, then let the -ing word carry the idea.

payload.prompt_text: Go back to your food-waste answer. Rewrite one solution sentence so it names the method with by plus -ing, and one concession sentence so it opens with despite plus -ing. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: Despite plus a full clause is the error that survives longest, because it only appears when the sentence is long enough to forget how it started.
feedback.feed_forward: After writing despite, check that no subject follows it.

title: Deciding between despite and although by looking at what comes next

point_json.grammar_name: despite / in spite of + noun or -ing, versus although + clause

teach.can_do: I can choose between despite and although by looking at what I am about to write next.
teach.why_it_matters: Despite he was tired is one of the most common written errors at this level, and the fix is a question about the next four words, not about meaning.
teach.meaning: Despite, in spite of and although all mark the same turn, and almost no learner ever gets the meaning wrong. What goes wrong is the grammar on the right of the word. Although is a clause word: a subject and its verb must follow it. Despite and in spite of are prepositions: a noun, a pronoun or an -ing form must follow them, and never a subject with a verb. So the decision is not about what you mean at all. It is about what shape the next few words are going to take.

form.pattern: although + subject + verb ... | despite / in spite of + noun phrase or -ing form ...
notes: In spite of is three words and despite is one. There is no despite of.
To put a clause after despite you have to wrap it first: despite the fact that the cost rose. Correct, and four words longer than although.
Either can start the sentence or sit in the middle. The comma goes in only when the concession comes first.
form.negative: Negatives change nothing about the choice: although the funding was not renewed, or despite the loss of funding.
form.question: Ask what the word straight after the linker is going to be: a subject, or a noun?

left.role: although: a subject and a verb follow
left.text: although the cost rose

right.role: despite: a noun or an -ing form follows
right.text: despite the rising cost

spec.caption: Same meaning, two different shapes on the right-hand side. The shape is the whole decision.

worked_example.sentence: Despite the rise in fuel duty, freight traffic on the motorway kept growing.
worked_example.why_this_form: What follows the linker is a noun phrase — the rise — with no verb of its own, and a noun phrase is exactly what despite takes.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Although the rise in fuel duty is not a milder version of the same sentence. It is an unfinished clause, and the reader waits for a verb that never arrives.

notice_set.sentence: Despite the heavy rain, the survey went ahead.
notice_set.question: What comes straight after despite?
notice_set.why: The heavy rain has no verb in it, so it is a noun phrase, and that is what despite requires.

notice_set.sentence: Although it rained heavily, the survey went ahead.
notice_set.question: What comes straight after although?
notice_set.why: It rained is a subject and its verb, which is exactly what although requires.

notice_set.sentence: Despite losing two days to the weather, the team finished the survey.
notice_set.question: What comes straight after despite?
notice_set.why: Losing is an -ing form, and despite takes those as happily as it takes nouns.

notice_set.sentence: Despite the fact that it rained for three days, the survey went ahead.
notice_set.question: Why is the fact there?
options: To make the sentence more formal
To give despite a noun to hold on to
notice_set.why: The fact is the noun despite needs, and the clause is then hung on it. Correct, and four words longer than although.

notice_set.sentence: Although the heavy rain, the survey went ahead.
notice_set.question: Is this a sentence?
notice_set.why: Although has been given a noun phrase and is still waiting for a verb, so the first clause never finishes.

notice_set.sentence: In spite of the delay, the results were published on time.
notice_set.question: Could despite replace in spite of here?
notice_set.why: They are the same word in two lengths and they take exactly the same thing after them.

discovery.prompt: All six sentences mean the same thing. Three of them are correct and three are not. Work out what the correct ones have in common.
pairs: Despite the delay, the results were published.
Despite the results were delayed, they were published.
Although the results were delayed, they were published.
Although the delay, the results were published.
Despite being delayed, the results were published.
Despite they were delayed, the results were published.

candidate_rules.text: Despite is followed by a noun or an -ing form; although is followed by a subject and a verb.
Despite is for short concessions and although is for long ones.
Use despite at the start of a sentence and although in the middle of one.

teach.rule_line: Look right, not left. A subject and verb means although; a noun means despite.
teach.false_rule: That despite is the formal word and although the ordinary one, so despite is the safer choice in an essay. They are equally formal. Only the shape after them differs.

contrast.question: Is a subject and a verb coming next, or a noun?

fork.answer: A subject and its verb: the cost rose, they were delayed
A noun phrase or an -ing form: the rising cost, being delayed

a.text: Despite the sharp rise in fares, passenger numbers held up.
a.means: Correct English. A noun phrase follows the linker, and a preposition is what a noun phrase needs.

b.text: Although the sharp rise in fares, passenger numbers held up.
b.means: Broken English. Although is left waiting for a verb that never arrives.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote although in front of a noun phrase. Your reader now waits for a verb, does not get one, and has to go back to find where the first clause was supposed to end. The meaning was never in doubt; the shape was.

edge_case.text: Despite can carry a clause if you give it a noun to hold first: despite the fact that the cost rose. It is correct, it is four words longer than although, and in a timed answer it is rarely worth the space.

contrast.stronger_test: Cover everything to the left of the linker and read the next four words. If they could start a sentence on their own, you need although. If they could not, you need despite.

worked_pairs.a: Despite the closure of the coast road, the ferry kept its timetable.
worked_pairs.b: Although the coast road was closed, the ferry kept its timetable.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: the closure of the coast road
worked_pairs.gloss: The same fact twice: once as a noun with no verb, once as a clause with one. The linker follows the shape, not the meaning.

worked_pairs.a: In spite of losing two days to the weather, the team finished on time.
worked_pairs.b: Even though they lost two days to the weather, the team finished on time.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: losing two days to the weather
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: they lost two days to the weather
worked_pairs.gloss: An -ing form has no subject of its own, so it takes the preposition. Give it a subject and it needs the clause word instead.

worked_pairs.a: Despite the fact that the grant was cut, the survey continued.
worked_pairs.b: Although the grant was cut, the survey continued.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: the fact that the grant was cut
worked_pairs.gloss: Both are correct. The fact that is the scaffolding that lets a preposition carry a clause, and it costs four words you did not have to spend.

errors.wrong: Despite the cost was high, the scheme went ahead.
errors.right: Although the cost was high, the scheme went ahead.
errors.why_it_happens: Despite and although mean the same thing, so the learner takes whichever comes to mind and never checks the shape of what follows. Meaning is doing the choosing, and meaning is not the deciding factor here.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: despite becomes although.
errors.l1_note: Very frequent where the first language uses one word for both.

errors.wrong: Although the high cost of the works, the scheme went ahead.
errors.right: Despite the high cost of the works, the scheme went ahead.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has been told that although is the safe academic word and reaches for it first. Nothing then checks whether a verb is on its way.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: although becomes despite.

errors.wrong: Despite of the delay, the results were published on time.
errors.right: Despite the delay, the results were published on time.
errors.why_it_happens: In spite of ends in of and despite does not. The two are stored as one item with an of floating loose inside it, and the of surfaces in the wrong half.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: of.

errors.wrong: Despite the delay, but the results were published on time.
errors.right: Despite the delay, the results were published on time.
errors.why_it_happens: The turn feels as though it needs marking on both sides of the comma, and in several first languages it genuinely does.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: but.

pays_in.note: Concession appears in almost every body paragraph, and this is where it breaks.
pays_in.model: Despite the cost of the equipment, most farms recover it within four seasons.

pays_in.note: A chart description needs concession when one line refuses to follow the trend.
pays_in.model: Despite the overall fall, demand in the eastern region rose in every year shown.

pays_in.note: Recognising which shape follows the linker is how you parse a long sentence quickly.
pays_in.model: In spite of repeated warnings, the flood defences were not raised until 2021.

used_in.quote: Every solution paragraph has to concede a cost, and the concession is one of these two shapes.
Two sentences in the passage open with a concession, and the claim is in what follows the comma.

payload.sentence: Despite the heavy rain, the survey went ahead.
payload.question: What kind of words come straight after despite?
options: A noun phrase with no verb

feedback.why_key: The heavy rain has no verb in it, and a group of words with no verb is what a preposition takes.
feedback.feed_forward: Look for the verb before you name the shape.

payload.sentence: Although it rained for three days, the survey went ahead.
payload.question: What kind of words come straight after although?
options: A noun phrase with no verb

feedback.why_key: It rained is a subject with its own verb, and that is the one thing although insists on.
feedback.feed_forward: Check for a subject and a verb after although, every time.

payload.context: From a first draft on first-time buyers.
payload.sentence: Despite the rent was rising every year, most tenants stayed where they were.
reasons: despite has been given a subject and a verb
the two halves do not contrast
the comma is in the wrong place
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The rent was rising is a clause. Despite is a preposition and cannot take one, however clear the meaning is.
feedback.feed_forward: If a subject and verb follow, write although.

payload.context: From a report on a coastal survey.
payload.stem: ___ the loss of two working days to the weather, the team finished on schedule.

expected: despite
in spite of

feedback.why_key: The loss is a noun with no verb attached, so the linker has to be the preposition.
feedback.feed_forward: A noun after the gap means despite.

payload.context: The same report, one paragraph later.
payload.stem: ___ the team lost two working days to the weather, it finished on schedule.

expected: although
though
even though

feedback.why_key: The team lost is a subject with its verb, so only the clause word will fit in the gap.
feedback.feed_forward: A subject and a verb after the gap mean although.

payload.given: Although fuel duty rose sharply, freight traffic on the motorway kept growing.
payload.instruction: Write the same sentence again, starting with despite.

expected: the sharp rise in fuel duty freight traffic on the motorway kept growing
the sharp rise in fuel duty, freight traffic on the motorway kept growing
a sharp rise in fuel duty freight traffic on the motorway kept growing
the sharp rise in fuel duty, freight traffic on the motorway continued to grow

feedback.why_key: To move from although to despite you have to turn the clause into a noun phrase. That conversion is the whole exercise.
feedback.feed_forward: Turn the verb into a noun before you write despite.

payload.audio_text: Despite having warned them twice, we'd got the wrong delivery again.

expected: despite having warned them twice we'd got the wrong delivery again
despite having warned them twice we had got the wrong delivery again
despite having warned them twice wed got the wrong delivery again

feedback.why_key: Having is the -ing form despite needs, and in speech it is fast and easy to lose. Without it you are left with a preposition and a bare verb.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for an -ing form immediately after despite.

payload.context: A coastal survey ran through a wet October, and the weather was against them from the first day.
payload.stem: ___ the weather was against them, the team finished on time.

options.why_this_means: That a subject and its verb are about to follow, which is what this word requires.
That a noun phrase or an -ing form is about to follow, with no verb of its own.

expected: although

feedback.why_key: The weather was is a subject with its own verb, so only the clause word can sit in front of it.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the four words after the gap before you choose.

payload.context: A coastal survey ran through a wet October, with the weather against them from the first day.
payload.stem: ___ the weather, the team finished on time.

options.why_this_means: That a subject and its verb are about to follow, which is what this word requires.
That a noun phrase or an -ing form is about to follow, with no verb of its own.

expected: despite

feedback.why_key: The weather is a noun on its own with no verb behind it, so the preposition is the only word that fits.
feedback.feed_forward: A bare noun after the gap means the preposition.

payload.context: A clinic report notes that waiting times had doubled over two years and that satisfaction scores stayed flat.
payload.stem: ___ waiting times had doubled, satisfaction scores barely moved.

options.why_this_means: That a subject and its verb are about to follow, which is what this word requires.
That a noun phrase or an -ing form is about to follow, with no verb of its own.

expected: although

feedback.why_key: Waiting times had doubled has a subject and a verb, so the preposition has nothing it can attach to.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the verb after the gap; if there is one, use although.

payload.context: A clinic report notes the doubling of waiting times over two years and flat satisfaction scores.
payload.stem: ___ the doubling of waiting times, satisfaction scores barely moved.

options.why_this_means: That a subject and its verb are about to follow, which is what this word requires.
That a noun phrase or an -ing form is about to follow, with no verb of its own.

expected: despite

feedback.why_key: The doubling is a noun built out of a verb, and a noun is what the preposition needs. Nothing in the phrase is doing anything.
feedback.feed_forward: A noun made from a verb still counts as a noun.

payload.context: The grant was cut in April and the survey team stayed in the field until the autumn.
payload.stem: ___ the grant was cut, the survey continued to the end of the season.

options.why_this_means: The plain concession: two clauses, four words shorter, and nothing between the linker and the subject.
The same concession carried by a preposition, which needs the noun the fact before it can take a clause.

follow_up.question: Which version has given the preposition a noun so that it can carry a clause?

feedback.why_key: Both are correct. Despite the fact that is the scaffolding a preposition needs in order to take a clause, and it costs four words.
feedback.feed_forward: Use the fact that only when you really want the noun.

payload.sentence: Despite the rent was rising every year, most tenants stayed where they were.

expected: although the rent was rising
even though the rent was rising
despite the rising rent
despite the rise in the rent

feedback.why_key: Either the linker changes to match the clause, or the clause changes to match the linker. Both repairs are one edit and both are correct.
feedback.feed_forward: Fix the linker or fix the shape, whichever is shorter.

payload.sentence: Despite of the delay at the terminal, every connecting coach was held for us.

expected: despite the delay
in spite of the delay

feedback.why_key: The of belongs to in spite of and to nothing else. Despite already carries the meaning on its own.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete of after despite, or write in spite of in full.

payload.context: From a draft report on a river survey.
payload.sentence: Despite the delay, but the results were published before the end of the season.
reasons: the turn has been marked twice
despite has been given a clause
the comma should not be there
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Despite has already turned the sentence. But turns it a second time, and the second turn has nothing left to act on.
feedback.feed_forward: One turn per sentence, marked once.

payload.prompt_text: Farms upstream have been fined every year for run-off, and the river below them is no cleaner. Write the same idea twice: once beginning with despite and once beginning with although.

feedback.why_key: Writing the pair forces the conversion between a noun phrase and a clause, which is the only thing this choice is ever about.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the clause first, then turn it into a noun for despite.

payload.prompt_text: Open your paragraph on farm river pollution. Find every despite, in spite of and although, and check what follows each one. Fix any that have the wrong shape after them. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: This is a check you can run on any finished answer in twenty seconds, and it catches an error that appears in most of them.
feedback.feed_forward: Read four words to the right of every concession word.

title: Telling someone what another person said, in your own words

point_json.grammar_name: Reported statements

teach.can_do: I can tell someone what another person said, in my own words, without quoting them.
teach.why_it_matters: Almost every story you tell carries somebody else's words. Anchor them wrongly and your listener cannot work out who did what to whom.
teach.meaning: When you report what somebody said, you stop standing where they were standing and start standing where you are. Three things in their sentence were anchored to them: the person words, the time words and the place words. All three are re-anchored to you. The verb often steps back as well, because you are reporting from a later moment. None of this is decoration. Each shift tells your listener whose sentence they are currently inside.

form.pattern: reporting verb + (that) + a clause with ordinary statement word order
notes: that can be dropped in speech and in a friendly message; keep it in an essay
tell needs a listener straight after it (told me); say never takes one without to
the verb usually steps one place further back, and the person, time and place words move with it
here becomes there, tomorrow becomes the next day, this becomes that
form.negative: She said she had not seen the notice on the door.
form.question: Did she say the depot was closing, or did she only say it might?

left.role: what they said, anchored to where they were standing
left.text: "I am moving to Sandmouth in the spring."

right.role: what you say, anchored to where you are standing
right.text: She said she was moving to Sandmouth in the spring.

spec.caption: Nothing has been added and nothing has been lost. Everything that pointed at her now points from you.

worked_example.sentence: The site manager told us the scaffolding was coming down that week.
worked_example.why_this_form: Told takes a listener straight after it, and was coming steps back from is coming because you are passing this on from outside her week.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Keeping is coming and this week would put you back inside her week, as if you were relaying the message the same afternoon.

notice_set.sentence: The receptionist said the lift was out of order.
notice_set.question: Are these the receptionist's exact words?
options: No, her meaning in someone else's words
notice_set.why: There are no quotation marks and the pronouns have moved, so this is a report rather than a recording.

notice_set.sentence: Mina told her tutor she had finished the second reading.
notice_set.question: Which happened first, the reading or the telling?
notice_set.why: Had finished puts the reading behind the telling, which is the only job that form is doing here.

notice_set.sentence: Ravi said he was working in Sandmouth at the time.
notice_set.question: Is Ravi necessarily working in Sandmouth now?
options: No, the sentence only covers the stretch he spoke about
No, it says he has left
notice_set.why: The report is anchored to the moment he spoke, so it makes no claim at all about today.

notice_set.sentence: She said she would send the file the following day.
notice_set.question: The following day is counted from when?
options: from the day the file was needed
notice_set.why: Time words inside a report are measured from the reported moment, which is why tomorrow could not stay.

notice_set.sentence: Anya said she had been living there for a year.
notice_set.question: Had she moved out by the time she spoke?
notice_set.why: The year runs up to the moment she spoke, so she was still there when she said it.

notice_set.sentence: The email said the deadline had moved to the Friday.
notice_set.question: Is the Friday necessarily this week's Friday?
options: No, it is the Friday in the reported situation
notice_set.why: The article the points back into the reported week, not out into the reader's calendar.

discovery.prompt: Each pair says the same thing twice. Work out everything that changes on the way from left to right.
pairs: "I am waiting outside."
He said he was waiting outside.
"We finished the survey yesterday."
They said they had finished the survey the day before.
"I will bring the forms here tomorrow."
She said she would bring the forms there the next day.

candidate_rules.text: Everything anchored to the original speaker — the person, the time, the place — is re-anchored to whoever is reporting.
The verb moves one step further into the past.
If the sentence contains said, every verb after it must be in a past form.

teach.rule_line: Re-anchor the report to where you are standing: the person, the time, the place.
teach.false_rule: That reporting is a fixed list of swaps you apply without reading. The swaps follow the meaning, and when the anchor has not moved, nothing moves.

errors.wrong: The tutor said me that the deadline had moved.
errors.right: The tutor told me that the deadline had moved.
errors.why_it_happens: Say and tell come out as one verb in many languages, so the learner takes whichever surfaces first and hangs the listener on it. Say will not carry a listener unless to is there.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: said becomes told.

errors.wrong: Ravi said that I had already paid the deposit, so I stopped worrying.
errors.right: Ravi said that he had already paid the deposit, so I stopped worrying.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner keeps the pronoun the original speaker used. Inside the report, I now points at the reporter, and the sentence quietly hands the deposit to the wrong person.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: I becomes he.

errors.wrong: She told us she will look at the figures on Monday, but Monday came and went.
errors.right: She told us she would look at the figures on Monday, but Monday came and went.
errors.why_it_happens: The words come across from her mouth unchanged. It passes in speech and reads as a jolt on the page, because the sentence around it has already moved into the past.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: will becomes would.

errors.wrong: She explained that the office was short-staffed and the phones ring all morning.
errors.right: She explained that the office was short-staffed and the phones rang all morning.
errors.why_it_happens: The first verb gets re-anchored and the second is forgotten. The report starts in one time frame and finishes in another, and the reader is left to guess which was meant.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: ring becomes rang.

pays_in.note: Half of a two-minute talk about a person is what that person said.
pays_in.model: She told me the course was harder than she had expected, and she turned out to be right.

pays_in.note: It is how a second voice gets into an essay at all.
pays_in.model: Supporters of the scheme said it would pay for itself within a decade.

pays_in.note: Two students relaying a tutor's words is a standard section-three shape.
pays_in.model: He said the reading list had been shortened to four titles.

used_in.quote: Answers on this card are almost entirely about what other people say and how it lands, which is this point running for two minutes.
The prompt is about what gets passed on and how, so the essay reports claims in almost every body sentence.

payload.sentence: Kemi told me she had left the parcel with the neighbours.
payload.question: Who left the parcel?

feedback.why_key: She points back at Kemi, because inside a report every pronoun is measured from the person doing the reporting.
feedback.feed_forward: Trace each pronoun back to a name before you read on.

payload.sentence: The department said the fee had been waived for the second year.
payload.question: Where does the waiving sit?
options: at the moment the department spoke

feedback.why_key: Had been waived is the report's way of saying this was already done when the sentence was spoken.
feedback.feed_forward: Place the reported event against the moment of speaking, not against today.

payload.context: A new starter is telling a friend how the first shift went.
payload.sentence: The supervisor said me the rota was going up on Thursday.
reasons: say cannot take a listener without to
the rota is not going up on Thursday
the verb form of going is wrong
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Tell hands the words to a named listener; say only reports them. Said me tries to make one verb do the other's job.
feedback.feed_forward: If a listener is named, use told.

payload.context: Reporting a conversation that finished last week. Original: "I will confirm the room on Monday."
payload.stem: The office said they ___ (confirm) the room on Monday.

expected: would confirm
'd confirm
d confirm

feedback.why_key: Will belongs to the moment they spoke. From where you are standing that moment is behind you, so will steps back to would.
feedback.feed_forward: Step will back to would when the speaking is over.

payload.context: Two passengers on the platform. Original: "The Ashfield train has already left."
payload.stem: The guard told us the Ashfield train ___ (already leave).

expected: had already left
'd already left
d already left

feedback.why_key: The leaving was finished before he spoke, and the report keeps that order visible by putting the verb one place further back.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the earlier of two past events one step further back.

payload.given: Dev said: "I am training two new drivers here this month."
payload.instruction: Report what Dev said. You are writing about it later, somewhere else.

expected: he was training two new drivers there that month
that he was training two new drivers there that month

feedback.why_key: Three anchors move together: the person, the place and the month. Leave one behind and the sentence points in two directions at once.
feedback.feed_forward: Move the person, the place and the time in one pass.

payload.given: The letting agent to me: "Your deposit has gone back to your bank."
payload.instruction: Report it to a friend, naming yourself as the listener.

expected: me my deposit had gone back to my bank
me that my deposit had gone back to my bank

feedback.why_key: Told takes the listener bare and straight away, and your becomes my because the deposit is now being described from your side.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the listener immediately after told, with no to.

payload.context: Original: "The recording has been cut for time." Build the report.

expected: the presenter said the recording had been cut for time

feedback.why_key: Has steps back to had and nothing else in the clause moves, because statement word order was already there.
feedback.feed_forward: Change only the auxiliary; leave the word order alone.

payload.audio_text: She said she'd sent the photos to the group already.

expected: she said she'd sent the photos to the group already
she said she had sent the photos to the group already
she said shed sent the photos to the group already

feedback.why_key: The whole report hangs on one unstressed syllable. She'd sent and she sent are a week apart in meaning and almost nothing apart in sound.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the 'd before the main verb, not for the main verb.

payload.sentence: The editor said that I had already approved the caption, so I stopped chasing it.

expected: she had already approved
he had already approved
they had already approved

feedback.why_key: Two people cannot both be I in one sentence. The approving belongs to the editor, so the pronoun has to point back at her.
feedback.feed_forward: Change every I inside the report to the reported speaker.

items.decision_cue: and the vans arrive before seven

payload.context: Someone is describing a conversation that happened last winter.
payload.sentence: The depot manager said the yard was too small and the vans arrive before seven.
reasons: the second half of the report was never re-anchored
the yard is not too small
the vans do not arrive before seven
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The report starts last winter and ends this morning. A listener has to pick one and cannot tell which was meant.
feedback.feed_forward: Re-anchor every clause in the report, not just the first.

payload.context: Two sentences from different paragraphs of the same report on an admissions scheme.
sentences: The registrar said that fewer students had applied.
The registrar said that fewer students were applying.
meanings: The applications were counted and the count was already in before she spoke.
The falling off was going on around her as she spoke, with no total yet.

feedback.why_key: One report hands you a finished number; the other hands you a trend still running at the moment of speaking.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the reported event was finished or still running.

payload.prompt_text: A local reporter interviewed you last month about how you get your news. Write one sentence reporting something you told her, from where you are standing today.

feedback.why_key: You are now the person being reported, so every anchor in your own sentence has to move across to the reporter's side.
feedback.feed_forward: Check the pronouns last; they are the ones that slip.

payload.prompt_text: Take one body paragraph from your last Task 2 answer on this prompt and add two sentences reporting what somebody on the other side of the argument said. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: A paragraph that reports nobody is a paragraph with one voice in it, and one voice is the hardest thing to argue with or from.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the two new sentences alone and check every anchor.

title: Reporting a question without turning it back into a question

point_json.grammar_name: Reported questions

teach.can_do: I can report a question without turning it back into a question.
teach.why_it_matters: The word order slips back under pressure and it is the most audible error in this whole area. A listener hears it every single time.
teach.meaning: A reported question is not a question. Nobody in the room is being asked anything: you are telling someone what was once asked, and the sentence you produce is an ordinary statement. That is the whole idea, and every difference follows from it. The subject goes back in front of the verb where it lives in statements. The do, does or did that was holding the question together disappears, because the tense goes back onto the main verb. And the sentence ends with a full stop.

form.pattern: asked (+ person) + wh-word / if / whether + SUBJECT + VERB
notes: no do, does or did: where did she go becomes where she had gone
yes-no questions need if or whether, because there is no wh-word to hold the slot open
the sentence ends with a full stop, never a question mark
asked takes a person straight after it; wanted to know does not take one at all
form.negative: He asked why we had not signed the form.
form.question: The report is never a question. Turn it round to check: where does the bus leave from becomes he asked where the bus left from.

left.role: a question: the verb jumps in front of the subject
left.text: Where is the depot?

right.role: reported: the subject goes back in front
right.text: She asked where the depot was.

spec.caption: One move, and it is always the same move. The subject climbs back in front of the verb.

worked_example.sentence: The receptionist asked whether we had booked a slot.
worked_example.why_this_form: There was no wh-word in the original, so whether holds the slot open, and we sits in front of had exactly as it would in any statement.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Asked had we booked a slot sounds as though she is asking you now, in the middle of your own sentence, and the reader has to stop and start again.

notice_set.sentence: Ravi asked where the forms were kept.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker asking you a question?
options: No, they are telling you what Ravi asked
notice_set.why: The sentence is a statement about a question. Nobody in the conversation is being asked anything.

notice_set.sentence: She asked if I had finished the second draft.
notice_set.question: Was the original a yes-no question?
options: No, it started with a wh-word
notice_set.why: If is only ever there because there was no wh-word to hold the place open.

notice_set.sentence: He wanted to know how much the repair would cost.
notice_set.question: Who wants the information?
notice_set.why: Wanted to know is a reporting phrase like asked, and the person doing the wanting is the one who asked.

notice_set.sentence: The inspector asked what time the shift had started.
notice_set.question: Which happened first, the shift starting or the asking?
notice_set.why: Had started puts the shift behind the asking, which is why the verb sits one place further back.

notice_set.sentence: They asked whether the coast road was open.
notice_set.question: Does the sentence tell you whether the road was open?
notice_set.why: A reported question reports the asking and nothing else. The answer is simply not in the sentence.

notice_set.sentence: She asked me why I had changed courses.
notice_set.question: Who changed courses?
notice_set.why: I inside the report points at whoever is reporting, so the change of course belongs to the speaker.

discovery.prompt: Each question on the left has been reported on the right. Two things have gone missing on the way across. Find both.
pairs: "Where does the ferry leave from?"
He asked where the ferry left from.
"Have you signed the form?"
She asked whether I had signed the form.
"Why did the class finish early?"
They asked why the class had finished early.

candidate_rules.text: The subject goes back in front of the verb and the do, does or did drops out, because the sentence is no longer a question.
The question mark is removed.
Any sentence containing asked keeps question word order after the wh-word.

teach.rule_line: Once a question sits inside a bigger sentence, it takes statement word order.
teach.false_rule: That a reported question is still a question and keeps question word order. Nobody is being asked anything; the sentence is a statement about an asking.

errors.wrong: She asked me where was the nearest chemist.
errors.right: She asked me where the nearest chemist was.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner hears where and the question word order fires by itself, because that is the only pattern they have ever produced after a wh-word. It outlives the rule by years, since it is a habit and not a belief.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: was goes to the end.

errors.wrong: He asked what time did the coach leave.
errors.right: He asked what time the coach left.
errors.why_it_happens: Did is carried across from the original, where it was doing real work. Inside the report the tense has already moved onto the main verb, so did has nothing left to do but duplicate it.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: did, and put the tense on leave.

errors.wrong: She asked that I had brought my passport.
errors.right: She asked whether I had brought my passport.
errors.why_it_happens: A yes-no question has no wh-word, so the learner reaches for the that-frame they already own from reported statements. That introduces a statement; a question needs if or whether.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: that becomes whether.

errors.wrong: The clerk asked how long I am staying, and I said until Friday.
errors.right: The clerk asked how long I was staying, and I said until Friday.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner replays the question as it was heard. The rest of the sentence has already moved into the past, so the unshifted verb reads as a jump out of the story and back into the room.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: am becomes was.

pays_in.note: Retelling a conversation in a long turn is mostly reported questions.
pays_in.model: She asked me why I had chosen that course, and I did not have a good answer.

pays_in.note: Section three turns questions into reports constantly, and the word order says who asked.
pays_in.model: He asked whether the deadline had been moved.

pays_in.note: A letter answering an enquiry usually reports the enquiry first.
pays_in.model: Your office asked whether I had enclosed the original receipt.

used_in.quote: The card asks what makes a conversation go well, and answers fill up with what one person asked another.
Two students relay a tutor's questions to each other, and the reported word order is the only clue to who is asking.

payload.sentence: My neighbour asked when the bins were being collected.
payload.question: Does the speaker want you to answer?
options: No, they are reporting what the neighbour asked

feedback.why_key: The sentence is a statement about an asking, which is exactly why it does not sound like a question.
feedback.feed_forward: Read it as a statement, because that is what it is.

payload.sentence: The tutor asked whether anyone had read the second chapter.
payload.question: What kind of answer was the original question looking for?

feedback.why_key: Whether is only ever there because the original had no wh-word, and a question with no wh-word wants yes or no.
feedback.feed_forward: Read whether as the sign of a yes-no original.

payload.context: Someone describing a conversation on the concourse at Ashfield.
payload.sentence: A visitor asked me where was the ticket office.
reasons: the subject and verb are still in question order
the ticket office is not at Ashfield
asked cannot take me
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Nobody in this sentence is being asked anything, so the verb has no business standing in front of its subject.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the subject first after the wh-word.

payload.context: Original: "Have you kept the receipt?"
payload.stem: The office asked ___ I had kept the receipt.

expected: whether
if

feedback.why_key: There was no wh-word in the original, so something has to hold the slot open, and that is the only job whether has here.
feedback.feed_forward: Use if or whether when the original had no wh-word.

payload.context: Original: "Where are the spare keys kept?" Build the report.

expected: she asked where the spare keys were kept

feedback.why_key: The keys go in front of were, because after the wh-word the sentence behaves like every other statement you have ever built.
feedback.feed_forward: Build the clause as a statement, then put the wh-word on the front.

payload.context: Original: "Does the office close at four?" Build the report.

expected: he wanted to know if the office closed at four

feedback.why_key: The does has gone and its tense has landed on closed, which is the only place left for it once the question stops being a question.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete does and put its tense on the main verb.

payload.given: The interviewer asked: "Why did you leave your last position?"
payload.instruction: Report the question. You are writing about the interview afterwards.

expected: why i had left my last position
me why i had left my last position
why i left my last position
me why i left my last position

feedback.why_key: Did disappears and takes its tense onto the main verb, and I comes in front of it because this is now a statement.
feedback.feed_forward: Drop did first, then set the word order.

payload.given: My manager asked: "Are you free on Thursday morning?"
payload.instruction: Report it to a colleague later the same week.

expected: if i was free on thursday morning
whether i was free on thursday morning
me if i was free on thursday morning
me whether i was free on thursday morning

feedback.why_key: There is no wh-word to hold the slot, so if or whether steps in, and are steps back to was behind it.
feedback.feed_forward: Open a yes-no report with if or whether.

payload.audio_text: She asked me what I'd said to the landlord.

expected: she asked me what i'd said to the landlord
she asked me what i had said to the landlord
she asked me what id said to the landlord

feedback.why_key: In speech the subject and the 'd run together into one sound, and that sound is the whole difference between a report and a question.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the subject squeezed in after the wh-word.

payload.sentence: The producer asked how many people did watch the repeat, and nobody could tell her.

expected: how many people had watched
how many people watched

feedback.why_key: Did is left over from the question it used to be. Once the clause is inside a statement, the tense belongs on watch and did has no work.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete the leftover did and move its tense onto the verb.

items.decision_cue: when would the results be ready

payload.sentence: Everyone wanted to know when would the results be ready, so I asked at the desk.
payload.error_span: when would the results be ready

expected: when the results would be ready
when the results were going to be ready

feedback.why_key: Would has jumped in front of its subject out of pure habit. Nobody is being asked anything here, so the results come first.
feedback.feed_forward: Send the subject back in front of the modal.

payload.context: From a write-up of a lab visit.
payload.sentence: The technician asked that the samples had been logged before lunch.
reasons: a reported yes-no question needs if or whether, not that
the samples were not logged before lunch
had been logged is the wrong form
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: That introduces a statement, so the sentence currently reports the technician telling you something rather than asking you.
feedback.feed_forward: Use whether when the original wanted yes or no.

payload.prompt_text: Think of the last time somebody interviewed you, for a course or a job. Write one sentence reporting the hardest question they asked you.

feedback.why_key: You are describing an asking, not doing one, so the clause you build has to sit down as a statement.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the clause on its own first; if it sounds like a question, fix it.

payload.prompt_text: Take this Part 2 card and give the full two-minute answer. At least three sentences must report something somebody asked you. You will be judged only on the word order in those three.

feedback.why_key: Under time pressure the question order comes back, which is why this rung is timed and spoken rather than written and careful.
feedback.feed_forward: Slow down half a beat before every wh-word.

payload.injection: Ask the learner about a time somebody at work or on a course needed information from them, then ask what exactly that person wanted to know.

feedback.why_key: A live conversation is the only place this error really lives, because it is a habit that only fires when nobody is monitoring.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the subject first, even when you are hurrying.

title: Reporting an order, a request or a piece of advice

point_json.grammar_name: Reported commands, requests and advice

teach.can_do: I can report an instruction, a request or a piece of advice without turning it into a statement.
teach.why_it_matters: An instruction has no statement inside it, so there is nothing for that to introduce. Forcing one in is where the whole pattern collapses.
teach.meaning: An order, a request and a piece of advice are not statements about the world. They are attempts to move somebody, and English reports them with a shape that keeps the movement visible: a person, then to, then the thing they were being moved towards. The verb you choose in front of it records how hard the push was — advised is a suggestion you could ignore, asked is a request, told is an instruction, warned means something bad was waiting. The negative goes in front of to, never inside it.

form.pattern: told / asked / advised / warned / reminded + PERSON + to + verb
notes: the person is compulsory: you cannot say she told to wait
the negative goes in front of to: he told us not to wait
asked is a request, told is an instruction, advised is advice, reminded means you already knew, warned means danger
there is no that-clause here: not she told me that I wait
form.negative: The steward told us not to block the aisle.
form.question: Did she ask you to sign it, or did she tell you to sign it?

rungs.text: "You could sit here." → suggested sitting there
"You should sit down." → advised me to sit down
"Could you sit down?" → asked me to sit down
"Sit down." → told me to sit down
"Don't sit there." → warned me not to sit there

worked_example.sentence: The site manager asked us to keep the gate shut after six.
worked_example.why_this_form: It was a request rather than an order, so asked; the person comes straight after it, and the instruction itself sits inside the to-infinitive.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Told us to keep the gate shut reports the same words as an instruction and makes the manager sound as though refusing was never on offer.

notice_set.sentence: The nurse told him to stop taking the tablets.
notice_set.question: Was this a suggestion or an instruction?
notice_set.why: Told records a push he was not really invited to refuse.

notice_set.sentence: The nurse advised him to stop taking the tablets.
notice_set.question: Was this a suggestion or an instruction?
notice_set.why: Same shape, softer verb. Advised leaves the decision with him.

notice_set.sentence: She asked me not to mention the figures.
notice_set.question: What am I supposed to do?
notice_set.why: Not sits in front of to, so it covers the whole instruction rather than one word of it.

notice_set.sentence: The steward reminded us to keep our passes visible.
notice_set.question: Had we been told this before?
notice_set.why: Reminded only makes sense if the instruction was already somewhere in our heads.

notice_set.sentence: He warned the drivers not to use the coast road.
notice_set.question: What does warned add that told would not?
notice_set.why: Warn carries the reason for the instruction inside the verb: something bad was waiting.

notice_set.sentence: They asked us to send the receipts by Friday.
notice_set.question: Who sends the receipts?
notice_set.why: The person named after asked is the one who does the thing in the to-infinitive.

discovery.prompt: Each instruction on the left has been reported on the right. Work out where the instruction itself ends up.
pairs: "Wear the harness."
The supervisor told us to wear the harness.
"Could you send the receipts?"
They asked us to send the receipts.
"Don't lean on the doors."
The guard told us not to lean on the doors.

candidate_rules.text: The person being moved comes first, and the instruction goes into a to-infinitive after them.
The imperative verb keeps its own form and a to is added in front of it.
Any sentence with told needs a that-clause after the person.

teach.rule_line: Report an instruction with a person and a to-infinitive, and put any not in front of to.
teach.false_rule: That every report needs that. That introduces a statement, and an instruction has no statement in it for that to introduce.

errors.wrong: The supervisor told to us to wear the harness.
errors.right: The supervisor told us to wear the harness.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has said something to somebody a thousand times, and the to leaks forward onto the listener. Tell takes its listener bare; only say needs to in front of one.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: the first to.

errors.wrong: The guard told us to don't lean on the doors.
errors.right: The guard told us not to lean on the doors.
errors.why_it_happens: Don't is how the original was spoken, so it travels across in one piece. Inside the report the negative belongs in front of to, where it can cover the whole instruction.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one span: to don't lean becomes not to lean.

errors.wrong: She asked me that I should send the file again.
errors.right: She asked me to send the file again.
errors.why_it_happens: The that-clause is the only reporting frame the learner has practised, so a request gets forced into it and then needs should to carry the push. The infinitive does that job in three words fewer.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one span: that I should send becomes to send.

errors.wrong: The officer warned us against to park on the verge.
errors.right: The officer warned us against parking on the verge.
errors.why_it_happens: Every other verb in this family took a to-infinitive, so the learner reaches for one again. Warn against is a fixed pair, and after a preposition English takes only the -ing form.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: to park becomes parking.

pays_in.note: Talks about advice, teachers and first jobs are made of this shape.
pays_in.model: My first supervisor told me to write everything down, which I still do.

pays_in.note: A letter about repairs or a course reports what you were instructed to do.
pays_in.model: Your office asked me to send the meter reading before the end of the month.

pays_in.note: Instruction-heavy passages report requirements this way rather than as rules.
pays_in.model: Residents are reminded not to leave bicycles in the stairwell.

used_in.quote: The card is about advice and who gives it, so almost every answer reports somebody telling somebody else to do something.
The letter has to report what the landlord asked the writer to do before it can complain about what happened next.

payload.sentence: The physiotherapist told me to walk on it every day.
payload.question: Who does the walking?

feedback.why_key: The person named after told is the one who carries out whatever comes after to.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the named person as the doer of the to-verb.

payload.sentence: The office asked staff not to park in the loading bay.
payload.question: What are staff supposed to do?
options: keep out of the loading bay

feedback.why_key: Not sits in front of to, so it cancels the whole instruction rather than one word inside it.
feedback.feed_forward: Read not before to as covering everything after it.

payload.context: Someone describing being stopped at a level crossing.
payload.sentence: The signaller told to us to wait behind the barrier.
reasons: tell takes its listener with no to in front
the barrier was already up
wait is the wrong verb form
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The listener belongs immediately after told. The extra to has come across from say, which is a different verb with a different habit.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the listener straight after told, with nothing between.

payload.context: Original: "Please send the timesheets by Friday."
payload.stem: The payroll office asked us ___ (send) the timesheets by Friday.

expected: to send

feedback.why_key: The instruction goes inside the to-infinitive, which is where English keeps the thing somebody is being moved towards.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the instruction in a to-infinitive after the person.

payload.context: Original: "Don't lift anything heavy for a fortnight."
payload.stem: The doctor told me ___ (lift) anything heavy for a fortnight.

expected: not to lift

feedback.why_key: The negative goes in front of to so that it covers the whole instruction, not just the lifting.
feedback.feed_forward: Put not in front of to, never after it.

payload.given: The inspector to the driver: "Take the diversion at the roundabout."
payload.instruction: Report the instruction as an instruction, not as a request.

expected: the driver to take the diversion at the roundabout
him to take the diversion at the roundabout

feedback.why_key: Told records that the driver was not being offered a choice, which is exactly what a bare imperative does.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the reporting verb to how hard the push was.

payload.given: My neighbour to me: "You should get the gutters cleared before the autumn."
payload.instruction: Report it as advice you were free to ignore.

expected: me to get the gutters cleared before the autumn
me to clear the gutters before the autumn

feedback.why_key: Advised keeps the decision with you, which is what should was doing in the original.
feedback.feed_forward: Use advised when the original left the choice open.

payload.context: Original: "Don't leave the bay unlocked." Build the report.

expected: the supervisor told us not to leave the bay unlocked

feedback.why_key: Four things in a fixed order: verb, person, not, to. Move any of them and the sentence stops working.
feedback.feed_forward: Build it in that order every time: verb, person, not, to.

payload.audio_text: They've asked us not to book anything before the audit.

expected: they've asked us not to book anything before the audit
they have asked us not to book anything before the audit
theyve asked us not to book anything before the audit

feedback.why_key: Us not to runs together into one unstressed lump in speech, and it is the lump that carries the whole instruction.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the person and the not squeezed in before to.

payload.sentence: The conductor told passengers to don't board until the platform staff had finished.

expected: not to board

feedback.why_key: Don't belongs to the words as they were spoken. Inside the report the negative moves in front of to, where it covers the whole instruction.
feedback.feed_forward: Convert don't into not in front of to.

payload.context: From a clinic leaflet.
payload.sentence: The trust warned patients against to take the two tablets together.
reasons: against is a preposition, so it needs an -ing form after it
the two tablets can be taken together
warned cannot take an object
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Warn against is a fixed pair, and no preposition in English is ever followed by a to-infinitive.
feedback.feed_forward: After any preposition, use the -ing form.

payload.prompt_text: Your building manager gave everyone an instruction about the bins last month and nobody followed it. Write one sentence reporting the instruction, including what people were told not to do.

feedback.why_key: A negative instruction is where this pattern earns its keep, because that is where the shape most often falls apart.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that not is in front of to before you stop.

payload.prompt_text: Write the second paragraph of this letter. It must report at least two things you were asked or told to do, and one thing you were advised not to do. Six minutes.

feedback.why_key: A complaint only works if the reader can see what you were told to do and what you then did, in that order and in that shape.
feedback.feed_forward: Read back only the reporting verbs and check each has a person after it.

title: Choosing a linking word by what it means and by where it is allowed to stand

point_json.grammar_name: Connectors grouped by function and by grammatical class

teach.can_do: I can pick a linking word that says the right thing and put it where English allows it to stand.
teach.why_it_matters: Half of all linking-word errors are not about meaning at all. The writer picked the right relation and then put the word somewhere it is not allowed to go.
teach.meaning: A linking word does two separate jobs at once, and learners are usually only taught one of them. The first is the relation: does the next idea add, contrast, explain, follow from or qualify what came before? The second is grammatical: some of these words join two clauses inside one sentence, some open a fresh sentence and point back at the last one, and some take a noun and nothing else. Getting the relation right and the class wrong still breaks the sentence.

form.pattern: joins two clauses: because, although, while, whereas, so that · opens a sentence: however, therefore, in addition, even so · takes a noun: despite, because of, in spite of
notes: the joining kind can start the sentence or sit in the middle: although it rained, we went / we went although it rained
the sentence-opening kind needs a full stop or a semicolon in front of it, and usually a comma after
the noun kind will not accept a clause: despite the cost, never despite it cost
and, but, so and or join two clauses and stay between them
form.negative: The negative belongs inside a clause, not on the linking word: although the clinic did not close, hours were cut.
form.question: First ask what the relation is. Then ask what the word is standing next to: a clause, or a noun?

left.role: joins two clauses inside one sentence
left.text: although · because · while · whereas · so that

right.role: opens a new sentence and points back
right.text: however · therefore · in addition · even so

spec.caption: The relation is only half the choice. The other half is what the word is allowed to stand beside.

worked_example.sentence: The clinic opened a late surgery because so many of its patients work full time.
worked_example.why_this_form: Because joins the two clauses inside one sentence, so the reason and the decision arrive as a single idea rather than as two facts placed side by side.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Because of expects a noun and nothing else. Write because of so many patients work and the sentence falls over at the word work.

notice_set.sentence: The surgery stays open late because most of its patients work.
notice_set.question: Why does the surgery stay open late?
notice_set.why: Because always points backwards from the result to the reason, and the reason is the half that follows it.

notice_set.sentence: Most patients work; therefore the surgery stays open late.
notice_set.question: Which happened first?
notice_set.why: Therefore points forwards, so the half before it is the cause and the half after it is what followed.

notice_set.sentence: Although the surgery stays open late, few patients come in after six.
notice_set.question: Do many people use the late hours?
notice_set.why: Although warns you that the second half will not be what the first half led you to expect.

notice_set.sentence: The surgery stays open late despite the cost.
notice_set.question: Is the late opening expensive?
notice_set.why: Despite concedes something real. The cost is a fact the sentence is pushing past, not a fact it doubts.

notice_set.sentence: Fewer patients now miss appointments. In addition, the waiting list has shortened.
notice_set.question: How many improvements are mentioned?
notice_set.why: In addition promises another item of the same kind, so the second sentence has to be a separate piece of good news.

teach.rule_line: Choose the relation first, then check what the word is allowed to stand next to.
teach.false_rule: That however, but and although are three ways of saying one thing. They mean the same and stand in three different places, which is why swapping them breaks sentences.

errors.wrong: Despite the clinic was full, nobody waited more than ten minutes.
errors.right: Although the clinic was full, nobody waited more than ten minutes.
errors.why_it_happens: Despite and although carry the same relation, so whichever comes to mind first gets used. Despite is only allowed in front of a noun, and a whole clause has just turned up behind it.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: despite becomes although.

errors.wrong: The waiting list has shortened, however the staff shortage is worse than ever.
errors.right: The waiting list has shortened; however, the staff shortage is worse than ever.
errors.why_it_happens: However does the same job as but, so it feels like a joining word. It is not one, and neither is the comma, which leaves two whole sentences with nothing holding them together.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one comma into a semicolon.

errors.wrong: The trust closed two clinics. As a result, demand had been rising for years.
errors.right: Demand had been rising for years. As a result, the trust closed two clinics.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner can see that the two facts belong together and reaches for a connecting phrase without checking which way it points. As a result always runs from the cause to what followed it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one pair of sentences.

errors.wrong: Although the surgery stays open late, but few patients come in after six.
errors.right: Although the surgery stays open late, few patients come in after six.
errors.why_it_happens: Several languages mark both halves of a contrast, so leaving one half unmarked feels unfinished. English marks it once and reads the second marker as a stutter.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: but.
errors.l1_note: Very common for speakers of Chinese, Vietnamese and Turkish.

pays_in.note: Every body paragraph needs a reason and a contrast, correctly placed.
pays_in.model: Although the scheme cut traffic in the centre, it pushed the queues onto the ring road.

pays_in.note: The connector tells you whether the next sentence agrees or turns.
pays_in.model: The trial was halted early. Even so, the results were published in full.

pays_in.note: A lecture signals its shape with these, and the answers follow the signals.
pays_in.model: Now, having dealt with the causes, I want to turn to what can be done.

used_in.quote: A problem and solution answer is a chain of causes and consequences, so every join in it is one of these words.
The talk marks each new section with a connector, and two answers depend on hearing which one arrived.

payload.sentence: The pool closed for repairs. Consequently, the swimming club moved to Marlow.
payload.question: Why did the club move?

feedback.why_key: Consequently runs forwards from a cause, so whatever came before it is the reason for what comes after.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the connector as an arrow and check which way it points.

payload.sentence: Even though the gym is free for staff, hardly anybody uses it.
payload.question: Do many staff use the gym?

feedback.why_key: Even though warns you that the second half will go against what the first half sets up, so free does not lead to popular.
feedback.feed_forward: Expect the turn when a sentence opens with a concession.

payload.context: From a first draft about university costs.
payload.sentence: Despite the fees rose again in 2022, applications went up.
reasons: this word cannot have a whole clause after it
the relation between the two halves is the wrong way round
the two halves need a full stop between them
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The meaning is right and the class is wrong. Despite takes a noun, and the fees rose again is a clause.
feedback.feed_forward: Swap to although when a clause follows.

payload.context: From a paragraph about sitting all day at work.
payload.stem: ___ the health warnings, most office jobs still involve eight hours in a chair.

expected: despite
in spite of

feedback.why_key: The health warnings is a noun phrase with no verb in it, so only the noun-taking word will fit in front of it.
feedback.feed_forward: Check for a verb before you choose the word.

payload.context: From a paragraph about a river clean-up at Verdon.
payload.stem: Farm run-off has fallen sharply. ___, fish have returned to the upper river.

expected: as a result
consequently
therefore

feedback.why_key: The first sentence is the cause and the second is what followed, so the word between them has to point forwards.
feedback.feed_forward: Name which half is the cause before you choose.

payload.given: Despite the high cost, the trust kept the late surgery open.
payload.instruction: Say the same thing using a word that takes a whole clause.

expected: the cost was high, the trust kept the late surgery open
it was expensive, the trust kept the late surgery open
the cost was high the trust kept the late surgery open

feedback.why_key: Once the word takes clauses, the noun has to grow a verb, and the high cost becomes the cost was high.
feedback.feed_forward: Give the noun a verb when you switch to although.

payload.context: Say one sentence about a free sports club.

expected: although the club charges nothing, very few children join

feedback.why_key: One word marks the contrast and the second half carries no marker at all, which is what English expects.
feedback.feed_forward: Mark the contrast once and leave the other half bare.

payload.audio_text: The clinic's moved, so we'll have to book earlier from now on.

expected: the clinic's moved, so we'll have to book earlier from now on
the clinic has moved so we will have to book earlier from now on
the clinics moved so well have to book earlier from now on

feedback.why_key: So is one unstressed syllable and it is carrying the entire relation between the two halves of the sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a small word at the join of two clauses.

payload.sentence: The new flats filled within a month, however the rents rose again in the spring.

expected: ; however, the rents rose
. however, the rents rose
, but the rents rose

feedback.why_key: However points backwards but joins nothing, so the two halves need either a stronger mark or a word that really does join.
feedback.feed_forward: Change the comma to a semicolon, or swap however for but.

items.decision_cue: In spite of this, the shops that survived

payload.context: From a passage about a town centre after a retail park opened.
payload.sentence: Two thirds of the units on the main street stood empty by 2021. In spite of this, the shops that survived reported steady trade.
reasons: the relation between the two sentences is the wrong way round
this phrase cannot come at the start of a sentence
the two sentences should be joined with a comma
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Empty units would normally predict weak trade, and the second sentence goes against that, which is exactly what the phrase promises.
feedback.feed_forward: Accept the connector when the second half really does turn.

payload.prompt_text: Free exercise classes were offered at a local sports centre and hardly anybody came. Write one sentence about it, and pick a linking word that can sit in front of a subject and a verb.

feedback.why_key: The contrast is real and the only decision left is whether the word you chose can sit in front of a clause.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that a subject and a verb follow your linking word.

payload.prompt_text: Open your problem and solution answer on the sedentary working day. Underline every linking word and, for each one, write C if it joins two clauses, S if it opens a sentence and N if it needs a noun. Fix any that are in the wrong place. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: Sorting your own linking words into three classes takes two minutes and finds errors that reading for meaning never will.
feedback.feed_forward: Label each linking word by class before you reread for sense.

title: Pointing back at something so the reader lands on the right thing

point_json.grammar_name: Reference: pronouns, this, that, such

teach.can_do: I can point back at something I have already said and be sure my reader lands on the right thing.
teach.why_it_matters: This is what cohesion actually is. Not linking words, but a chain of pointing that never leaves the reader holding two candidates at once.
teach.meaning: Words like it, they, this and such carry no meaning of their own. They borrow it from something already on the page, and your reader resolves them without noticing, by taking the nearest thing that fits. That is where the risk lives. If two things fit, the reader picks one and never registers that they chose, and you never find out which. A pointing word is only safe when exactly one thing can be at the other end of it.

form.pattern: it / they / this / that / these / such (+ a noun that names what you mean)
notes: it and they point back at a single noun and must match it for number
this and that can point back at a whole idea, which is exactly why they go wrong
the safe habit is this plus a noun that names the idea: this closure, this refusal, this shift
such plus a noun does the same job at a higher register: such measures, such an approach
form.negative: Neither of these worked and none of them was cheap: the negative sits on the pointing word itself.
form.question: Cover everything before the pointing word. Could a stranger say what it means? If not, name it.

left.text: ... and this has never been explained.

right.text: ... and this refusal has never been explained.

spec.caption: One noun after this turns a guess into a fact.

worked_example.sentence: The council shut two of the four recycling points. This closure has doubled the queues at the two left open.
worked_example.why_this_form: Closure names what the second sentence is pointing at, so the reader is never briefly holding two candidates, the council and the shutting.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: A bare this would leave the reader to guess, and a fair share of them would land on the recycling points rather than on the decision.

notice_set.sentence: The clinic moved into the old library. It has been shut for a fortnight.
notice_set.question: What has been shut?
notice_set.why: Two single things have just been named and nothing in the second sentence chooses between them.

notice_set.sentence: The clinic moved into the old library. The clinic has been shut for a fortnight.
notice_set.question: What has been shut?
notice_set.why: Repeating the noun costs two words and removes the guesswork entirely.

notice_set.sentence: Rasheed told Emeka that his car had been towed.
notice_set.question: Whose car was towed?
notice_set.why: Both men have been named and both are equally available, so the sentence holds two readings at once.

notice_set.sentence: The council raised the charge and cut two routes. This has been widely criticised.
notice_set.question: What has been criticised?
