notice_set.why: Three things are on offer here: the charge, the cuts, and both together. Nothing narrows it down.

notice_set.sentence: The council raised the charge and cut two routes. This second decision has been widely criticised.
notice_set.question: What has been criticised?
notice_set.why: Second decision counts along the sentence before it and lands squarely on the route cuts.

teach.rule_line: Every pointing word needs exactly one possible owner. Two owners is a broken sentence.
teach.false_rule: That repeating a noun is clumsy and a pronoun is always tidier. A repeated noun is clear; an unclear pronoun costs far more than the repetition.

errors.wrong: The supplier sent the invoice to the contractor before it had been approved.
errors.right: The supplier sent the invoice to the contractor before the invoice had been approved.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer has one thing in mind and cannot see the other reading at all. The reader has two singular nouns to choose from and takes the nearer one, which is the contractor.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word for its noun: it becomes the invoice.

errors.wrong: Schools cut music and drama while protecting sport. This is short-sighted.
errors.right: Schools cut music and drama while protecting sport. This choice of priorities is short-sighted.
errors.why_it_happens: A bare this feels like a summary because the writer has just finished summarising in their own head. On the page it points at three or four things at once and settles on none of them.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one noun after this.

errors.wrong: In the article, it says that fewer teenagers are learning to drive.
errors.right: The article says that fewer teenagers are learning to drive.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has been taught to open with a phrase and then needs a subject, so it arrives to fill the slot. It now points at nothing, because the only candidate has been shut inside the opening phrase.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete two words: in and it.

errors.wrong: Councils tried three approaches. Second approach worked best.
errors.right: Councils tried three approaches. The second approach worked best.
errors.why_it_happens: The approaches have already been introduced, so they feel established to the writer. English marks an established thing with the, and without it the reader has nothing telling them to look back.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: the.
errors.l1_note: Very common for speakers of languages with no article system.

pays_in.note: Every second sentence of a paragraph points back at the first one.
pays_in.model: Fares rose twice in a single year. This second increase pushed regular users back into their cars.

pays_in.note: Reference questions ask what a highlighted word is pointing at.
pays_in.model: Such measures rarely survive a change of administration.

pays_in.note: A long answer falls apart the moment this stops having an owner.
pays_in.model: People shop online and go out less, and that combination has emptied the high street.

used_in.quote: One question on this passage asks what a highlighted pronoun refers to, which is this point tested directly.

payload.sentence: The firm replaced the old system with a cloud service. It has cut costs by a third.
payload.question: What has cut the costs?

feedback.why_key: The old system was thrown out, so it cannot be saving anybody money. Only one candidate survives the sentence before it.
feedback.feed_forward: Test every candidate against the verb before you settle.

payload.sentence: Tamsin rang her sister after she got back from Sandmouth.
payload.question: Who came back from Sandmouth?

feedback.why_key: Two women have been named and both fit. The speaker knows which one; the listener is quietly guessing.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the person again when two of them are in play.

payload.context: From a draft about phones in classrooms.
payload.sentence: Schools ban phones, teachers confiscate them, and parents complain. This is worrying.
reasons: the pointing word has three different things it could mean
the wrong pointing word has been used
the sentence needs a linking word in front of it
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The banning, the confiscating and the complaining are all available, and a bare this settles on none of them.
feedback.feed_forward: Add a noun after this that names what you mean.

payload.context: A firm moved its records online and lost three days of work when the service went down.
payload.stem: This ___ persuaded the directors to keep paper copies after all.

expected: failure
outage
breakdown
collapse

feedback.why_key: The noun names the event the sentence is pointing at, so the reader never has to choose between the move and the crash.
feedback.feed_forward: Follow this with a noun that names the event.

payload.given: The paper printed the correction on page nineteen. This annoyed the readers who had complained.
payload.instruction: Rewrite the second sentence so nobody has to guess what annoyed them.

expected: burial annoyed the readers who had complained
placement annoyed the readers who had complained
decision annoyed the readers who had complained

feedback.why_key: Naming the thing removes the choice between the correction itself and where the paper chose to put it.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the action, not the object, when the action is your point.

payload.given: The trust opened two walk-in centres. Second centre closed within a year.
payload.instruction: Fix the second sentence so it points back properly.

expected: second centre closed within a year
second of these closed within a year

feedback.why_key: The centres are already on the page, and the is the word that tells your reader to look back rather than forward.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the in front of anything you have already introduced.

payload.context: The paragraph before this one described three separate hold-ups in the fieldwork.

expected: such delays are rarely reported in the summary

feedback.why_key: Such plus a noun gathers up several things already mentioned and hands them to the reader as one labelled bundle.
feedback.feed_forward: Use such plus a noun to sum up a list you have just given.

payload.audio_text: They've fixed the router, but that hasn't helped the signal.

expected: they've fixed the router, but that hasn't helped the signal
they have fixed the router but that has not helped the signal
theyve fixed the router but that hasnt helped the signal

feedback.why_key: That is unstressed and easily heard as the, which would turn a pointing word into an article and lose the link between the two halves.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the vowel in that when it points backwards.

payload.sentence: The developer bought the mill from the trust two years before it was demolished.

expected: before the mill was demolished
before the building was demolished

feedback.why_key: A trust can be wound up and a mill can be knocked down, so both nouns survive the verb and the reader has to pick one.
feedback.feed_forward: Replace the pointing word with the noun when two candidates fit.

items.decision_cue: This shift has left small towns

payload.context: From the middle of a passage about where people now do their shopping.
payload.sentence: More households now buy their weekly food online. This shift has left small towns with empty units on the main street.
reasons: the pointing word has more than one owner
the noun after this does not match anything before it
the two sentences should be joined
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Shift names the change described in the sentence before, so there is exactly one thing at the far end of the pointing word.
feedback.feed_forward: Accept the reference when one noun names one prior idea.

payload.prompt_text: Write two sentences. The first says that many services can now only be booked online. The second must begin with This and a noun, and say what that has done to older users.

feedback.why_key: The noun you choose after This is the thing that tells your reader which part of the first sentence you are building on.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose the noun before you write the rest of the sentence.

payload.prompt_text: Open your paragraph on phones in schools. Circle every it, this and they, and for each one write down the single thing it points at. Rewrite any where you had to think. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: If you had to stop and think about your own sentence, a reader coming to it cold has no chance at all.
feedback.feed_forward: Rewrite any pointing word you had to pause over.

title: Standing at a point in the future and saying what is already finished by then

point_json.grammar_name: Future perfect: will have + past participle

teach.can_do: I can pick a point in the future, stand in it, and say what is already over by the time I get there.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the shape a projection wants. A chart running to 2040, or an essay forecasting, needs a sentence that looks back from a date nobody has reached.
teach.meaning: Every other way of pointing forward looks at something ahead of you. This one walks past it first. You choose a moment in the future, you stand in it, and from there you look backwards at something that is by then already over. The event itself may be tomorrow or twenty years away; what matters is that it is behind the moment you have chosen. That is why these sentences almost always carry a by: by June, by the time the survey closes, by the end of the decade.

form.pattern: will have + the past participle, which is the shape you already use after have
notes: the past participle is the same word you would use in have finished, have grown, have fallen
in speech will have shrinks to something like will've, and after a pronoun it can vanish almost completely
the sentence nearly always names the future point, usually with by, and it makes very little sense without one
form.negative: won't have + the past participle: The defences won't have failed by then, but they will be close.
form.question: Will + person + have + the past participle: Will the figures have stabilised by March?

marks.label: and is over before you arrive
the moment you stand in and look back from

spec.caption: Walk past the event first. Then turn round and describe it from there.

worked_example.sentence: By 2040 the catchment will have lost around a fifth of its winter rainfall.
worked_example.why_this_form: The sentence puts the reader in 2040 and looks back over everything that happened on the way there. The loss is not coming; from that vantage point it has already happened.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: The catchment will lose a fifth of its rainfall in 2040 would date the loss to that single year, which is a much narrower and much stranger claim.

notice_set.sentence: By the end of March the team will have surveyed every inlet on the coast.
notice_set.question: Is any surveying still going on at the end of March?
notice_set.why: The end of March is the point being looked back from, and the work is behind it.

notice_set.sentence: By the time the report lands, the money will have gone elsewhere.
notice_set.question: Which happens first?
notice_set.why: The looking-back shape always puts its own event behind the moment named.

notice_set.sentence: The gauges won't have failed by the summer, but they will be close to it.
notice_set.question: Are the gauges working in the summer?
notice_set.why: The sentence checks the state of the gauges at the summer and finds them still standing.

notice_set.sentence: Marta will have finished the fieldwork long before the funding runs out.
notice_set.question: Is the fieldwork over when the funding runs out?
notice_set.why: Long before puts a wide gap between the end of the work and the moment being looked back from.

notice_set.sentence: In ten years the town will have grown by half again.
notice_set.question: Is the growth spread over the ten years or squeezed into the last one?
notice_set.why: Looking back from the end of a stretch takes in everything that happened inside it.

teach.rule_line: Choose a moment later, stand in it, and describe what is already behind you.
teach.false_rule: That this is a grander, more academic way of saying will. Use it with no future point named and the sentence has nowhere to look back from.

errors.wrong: By June the team will finished the second phase of the survey.
errors.right: By June the team will have finished the second phase of the survey.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer knows the work is over by June and puts the verb into a finished shape, which feels like enough. The word that does the looking back is the one that carries no meaning of its own, so it is the one that goes missing.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: have.

errors.wrong: By 2050 the coastal population will have grew by nearly a third.
errors.right: By 2050 the coastal population will have grown by nearly a third.
errors.why_it_happens: Grew is the shape the writer uses far more often, so it arrives first. The shape needed after have is a different one, and for irregular verbs there is nothing in the sentence to remind you.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: grew becomes grown.

errors.wrong: I will have rung the office tomorrow evening about the readings.
errors.right: I will ring the office tomorrow evening about the readings.
errors.why_it_happens: The shape has been learned as the impressive one and gets used to sound more careful. With no later point to look back from, it leaves the reader hunting for a moment the sentence never names.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: have.

errors.wrong: By the time the grant will arrive, the project will have closed.
errors.right: By the time the grant arrives, the project will have closed.
errors.why_it_happens: The sentence contains two future events and the writer marks both. The half beginning with by the time is only naming the moment, and a named moment is treated as fixed.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: will.

pays_in.note: A chart with projected years is described from inside the projected year.
pays_in.model: By 2035 renewable sources will have overtaken gas in the electricity mix.

pays_in.note: A forecast paragraph needs a sentence that looks back from the date it is arguing about.
pays_in.model: By the middle of the century most coastal councils will have abandoned the smallest defences.

pays_in.note: A passage stating what is complete by a future date is often tested on the order of events.
pays_in.model: By the time the second survey began, the eastern colony will have moved twice.

used_in.quote: A line chart running into projected years is described from inside those years, which is what this shape is for.
The passage sets out what will be complete before the next stage begins, and the questions turn on that order.

payload.sentence: By the end of the decade the reserve will have doubled in size.
payload.question: Is the reserve still getting bigger at the end of the decade?

feedback.why_key: The sentence only reports the state of things at that point. What happens afterwards is left completely open.
feedback.feed_forward: Report only what the named moment can see.

payload.sentence: By the time the new terminal opens, the old one will have closed for good.
payload.question: Which happens first?

feedback.why_key: Looking back from the opening finds the closure already behind it, which is the whole job of this shape.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the looked-back event first on your line.

payload.context: From a description of a projected population chart.
payload.sentence: By 2045 the figure for the northern districts will risen above two million.
reasons: the word that does the looking back is missing
the year is too far away for this shape
the figure should be plural
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The finished shape of the verb is there, but nothing in front of it is holding the sentence at 2045 and looking back.
feedback.feed_forward: Put have between will and the finished verb.

payload.context: From a caption under a projection of glacier cover.
payload.stem: By 2060 the lower glaciers ___ (disappear) from the range altogether.

expected: will have disappeared

feedback.why_key: The caption stands the reader in 2060 and looks back at everything that has gone by then.
feedback.feed_forward: Build it in three pieces: will, have, finished verb.

payload.context: From a note on a projected trade chart.
payload.stem: By the final year of the forecast, exports ___ (fall) below the level of the first.

expected: will have fallen

feedback.why_key: The verb has to take the shape it always takes after have, and for this one that is not the shape you use for a plain past event.
feedback.feed_forward: Check the finished shape of an irregular verb before writing.

payload.given: The trial ends in August. The results are published in September.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence saying what is already over by September, looking back from that month.

expected: will have ended
will have finished
will have closed

feedback.why_key: September becomes the vantage point, and from there August is behind you rather than ahead.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the later month, then look back from it.

payload.context: Build one sentence about a regeneration scheme, looking back from a later date.

expected: most of the estate will have been rebuilt by then

feedback.why_key: Will, have and the finished verb come in that order and stay together, with the later point pinned on the end.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the three words in order and the date last.

payload.audio_text: They'll have signed it off by Thursday.

expected: they'll have signed it off by thursday
theyll have signed it off by thursday
they will have signed it off by thursday

feedback.why_key: In speech the middle word shrinks to almost nothing, and losing it is what produces the broken written version later.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the faint sound between the person and the verb.

items.decision_cue: I will have written to the clinic

payload.context: From a draft letter, where no later date is mentioned anywhere.
payload.sentence: I will have written to the clinic about the appointment.
reasons: there is no later moment for the sentence to look back from
the letter has already been written
the finished shape of the verb is wrong
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The shape promises a vantage point later on and then never supplies one, so the reader is left standing nowhere.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the later point, or drop back to plain will.

items.decision_cue: By the time the funding will arrive

payload.sentence: By the time the funding will arrive, the contractors will have left the site.
payload.error_span: By the time the funding will arrive

expected: by the time the funding arrives
when the funding arrives

feedback.why_key: The second half is doing the pointing forward for both. The first half only has to name the moment, and a named moment is treated as fixed.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete will from the half that names the moment.

payload.context: Two lines from different sections of the same forecast.
sentences: The eastern marshes will flood in 2050.
The eastern marshes will have flooded by 2050.
meanings: The flooding is dated to that single year and nothing is claimed about the years before it.
The flooding happens at some point on the way there, and by that year it is already behind us.

feedback.why_key: One line puts the event in a year. The other puts the reader in a year and finds the event already over.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide whether you are dating the event or the vantage point.

payload.prompt_text: Pick a date five years from now. Write one sentence about your studies or your work that would already be true by then, looking back from that date.

feedback.why_key: Naming the date first is what gives the sentence somewhere to stand, and without it the shape has nothing to look back from.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the date first, then the finished event.

payload.prompt_text: Look at the projected section of the electricity chart and write the two sentences that describe the final year. At least one must look back from that year at what is already over. Four minutes.

feedback.why_key: The projected part of a chart is exactly the part no other shape describes properly, because it has already happened from the chart's point of view.
feedback.feed_forward: Anchor on the final year, then report what is finished.

title: Saying that I arranged something rather than did it myself

point_json.grammar_name: have and get something done

pays_in.note: Questions about your home, your health or your things need it constantly.
pays_in.model: I had the kitchen done just before I moved in.

pays_in.note: A story about a problem usually involves somebody else fixing it.
pays_in.model: We got the whole thing looked at by someone in the village.

pays_in.note: It lets you write about what households arrange without inventing tradespeople.
pays_in.model: Owners are now required to have their properties assessed for insulation.

teach.can_do: I can say that I paid or asked somebody else to do a job, without naming them.
teach.why_it_matters: Without it, learners either claim they rewired their own flat or spend a clause naming a workman nobody asked about.
teach.meaning: There is a gap between doing a job yourself and having no connection to it at all, and most of adult life sits in that gap. This structure fills it. It says the job was arranged by you and carried out by somebody else, and it does that without naming the somebody else at all. The order matters and it is unusual: you, then the thing, then what happened to the thing.

form.pattern: have / get + the thing + past participle
notes: the thing comes between the two verbs, which is the part that feels wrong at first
have is neutral in speech and in writing; get is warmer and belongs in speech
the tense sits on have or get, never on the word at the end: I had the roof repaired, I am having it repaired
form.negative: we did not have the roof repaired until the spring
form.question: Where did you have the roof repaired?

left.text: we

right.text: the roof repaired

spec.caption: The person who did the work is nowhere in the sentence, and that is the whole reason the structure exists.

worked_example.sentence: They had the whole ground floor rewired before the tenants moved in.
worked_example.why_this_form: The owners paid for the work and did none of it, and the electrician's name is not part of the story anybody here is telling.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: They rewired the whole ground floor would claim the owners did the job themselves, which is a different weekend and a different set of skills.

notice_set.sentence: We had the roof repaired the week after the storm.
notice_set.question: Did these people climb onto the roof themselves?
notice_set.why: The structure says the job happened and somebody else did it, without ever introducing that somebody.

notice_set.sentence: We repaired the roof the week after the storm.
notice_set.question: Did these people climb onto the roof themselves?
notice_set.why: Nothing sits between the two parts, so the people at the front are the people on the ladder.

notice_set.sentence: I am getting my eyes tested on Friday.
notice_set.question: Who will do the testing?
notice_set.why: The speaker has made the appointment and will sit in the chair. The tester is not in the sentence and does not need to be.

notice_set.sentence: She had her bag stolen on the way home.
notice_set.question: Did she arrange this?
notice_set.why: The same shape also reports something bad that happened to you, which is the one use that has nothing to do with arranging anything.

notice_set.sentence: They are having the whole ground floor rewired this month.
notice_set.question: Is the work finished?
options: No, it is going on now
notice_set.why: The time sits on the first word of the pair, exactly as it does in any other sentence.

teach.rule_line: Put the thing in the middle: had the roof repaired, not had repaired the roof.
teach.false_rule: That have here means own or possess. It carries no meaning of its own in this structure. It is doing a job, and the job is arranging.

errors.wrong: We had repaired the roof the week after the storm.
errors.right: We had the roof repaired the week after the storm.
errors.why_it_happens: Every other structure the learner knows keeps the two verb parts together, so the thing gets pushed out to where it usually goes and the sentence quietly changes meaning.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one phrase: the roof goes between had and repaired.

errors.wrong: I am getting my eyes test on Friday.
errors.right: I am getting my eyes tested on Friday.
errors.why_it_happens: The last word is a long way from the verb that governs it, so the ending is dropped when attention runs out at the end of the clause.
errors.smallest_fix: Add two letters: test becomes tested.

errors.wrong: Residents got their meters replaced under a scheme funded by the council.
errors.right: Residents had their meters replaced under a scheme funded by the council.
errors.why_it_happens: Get is the version everybody hears and it arrives first. In a report it reads as chatty next to the formal vocabulary around it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: got becomes had.

used_in.quote: Almost any honest answer about work done to a flat needs this structure twice.

payload.sentence: We had the chimney repointed the week after the storm.
payload.question: Who went up the ladder?

feedback.why_key: The thing sitting in the middle is what tells you the speaker arranged the job rather than doing it.
feedback.feed_forward: Look for a noun between the two verbs.

payload.context: Marta is telling a colleague about an appointment she has booked.
payload.sentence: I am getting tested my eyes on Friday.
reasons: the thing is in the wrong place
the day is wrong
getting cannot be used here
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Everything in the sentence is a word this structure uses, and they are in an order it does not allow.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the thing before the last word, every time.

payload.context: Two colleagues talking about a flat that has just been sold.
payload.stem: They had the whole ground floor ___ (rewire) before it went on the market.

expected: rewired

feedback.why_key: The ending is the only thing marking the floor as the thing the electrician worked on.
feedback.feed_forward: Give the last word its ending even when the sentence is long.

payload.context: A student explaining why their laptop has been away for a week.
payload.stem: I am ___ (have) the screen replaced under the warranty.

expected: having

feedback.why_key: The time sits on the first word of the pair, so the -ing goes there and nowhere else.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the tense on have or get, never on the last word.

payload.given: A builder from the village repaired our chimney last autumn.
payload.instruction: Rewrite so that we are the ones arranging the work, and no builder appears.

expected: had our chimney repaired last autumn
we had our chimney repaired last autumn
had the chimney repaired last autumn

feedback.why_key: The builder disappears, the chimney moves into the middle, and the sentence is now about the household.
feedback.feed_forward: Move the thing into the middle when the doer leaves.

payload.context: Someone explaining what they are doing on Friday morning.

expected: i am getting my eyes tested on friday
on friday i am getting my eyes tested

feedback.why_key: The day can move to the front and the middle three words cannot move at all.
feedback.feed_forward: Fix the middle first, then place the time phrase.

payload.audio_text: We had the kitchen done just before we moved in.

expected: we had the kitchen done just before we moved in

feedback.why_key: Spoken at speed, had the runs together into a single sound, and it is the sound that carries the whole meaning.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a noun sitting between two verbs.

payload.sentence: Residents got their meters replaced under a scheme funded by the council.

expected: had their meters replaced

feedback.why_key: Nothing here is ungrammatical. One word is a level below everything around it, and that is what a reader hears.
feedback.feed_forward: Use had in a report and keep got for conversation.

payload.prompt_text: Think of one job in your home that somebody else did for you. Write one sentence about it that does not name the person who did it.

feedback.why_key: The person you would normally name is exactly the person this structure exists to leave out.
feedback.feed_forward: Say what was done, not who did it.

payload.prompt_text: You are asked about your home and what you have changed in it. Speak for forty-five seconds and use this structure at least twice, once about the past and once about something arranged for the near future.

feedback.why_key: Using it twice in one answer, in two different times, is where the word order stops needing thought.
feedback.feed_forward: Plan the two things first, then start the clock.

title: Choosing which of the two things in an event my sentence should be about

point_json.grammar_name: Active or passive: the five conditions

pays_in.note: A process or map answer lives or dies on this decision.
pays_in.model: The clay is pressed into moulds and then left to harden.

pays_in.note: It keeps one topic in the subject slot for the length of a paragraph.
pays_in.model: The levy was introduced without warning and has been raised twice since.

pays_in.note: Talking about what a society does needs a way to report effects without inventing a culprit.
pays_in.model: A lot of that work is done by volunteers now, which surprises people.

pays_in.note: A question stem often turns a passage sentence round to see whether you followed it.
pays_in.model: The eastern section was paid for out of a regional fund.

teach.can_do: I can work out which half of an event a sentence ought to be built around, and say why.
teach.why_it_matters: Both voices are correct English, so nothing here is about being allowed. What it is about is whether your paragraph holds together from one line to the next.
teach.meaning: Both shapes are correct, so the question is never which one is permitted. It is which of the two things in the event this sentence should be about, because English puts what a sentence is about at the front. If the doer is unknown, obvious, beside the point, very long, or simply not what this paragraph has been following, then the affected thing belongs at the front, and the passive is how you get it there.

form.pattern: be + past participle, with the doer dropped or moved to the end after by
notes: condition one: nobody knows or cares who did it
condition two: you are describing a made thing being made, not people at work
condition three: this sentence is about whatever the last sentence ended on
condition four: an institution is speaking and there is no I or we in it
condition five: the doer is a long heavy phrase that belongs at the end
if none of the five holds, the ordinary shape is shorter and clearer
form.negative: be + not + past participle: the tender was not awarded until June
form.question: Was the tender awarded in June?

ends: the affected thing is the news

marks.label: A firm from Norland won the tender.
The tender was won by a firm from Norland.
The tender was awarded in June.

worked_example.sentence: The proposal reached the panel in January. It was rejected six weeks later.
worked_example.why_this_form: The second line carries on with what the first line ended on, so the reader's attention never has to move and the paragraph stays in one place.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: The panel rejected it six weeks later swings the reader onto the panel for one line and then swings them back, which reads as a paragraph changing its mind.

notice_set.sentence: The gates are opened twice a day.
notice_set.question: Do you need to know who opens them to understand this?
notice_set.why: The routine is the information. A named operator would add a person the reader has no use for.

notice_set.sentence: A driver from the Marlow depot opened the gates early on Tuesday.
notice_set.question: Why does this sentence name the driver?
options: Because who did it is the news
notice_set.why: Something went wrong and a person is answerable for it. That is exactly when the doer belongs at the front.

notice_set.sentence: The proposal reached the panel in January. It was rejected six weeks later.
notice_set.question: What is the second of these two sentences about?
notice_set.why: It carries on with what the first sentence ended on, so nothing in the reader's head has to move.

notice_set.sentence: Applicants are notified by email within ten working days.
notice_set.question: Who is speaking here, a person or an organisation?
notice_set.why: Leaving the notifier out is what makes it institutional. Put we in and a person is suddenly writing to you.

notice_set.sentence: The footpath was blocked for most of the winter.
notice_set.question: Does the sentence blame anybody?
notice_set.why: This shape can report a problem without pointing at a person, which is sometimes tact and sometimes evasion.

notice_set.sentence: The consortium that funded the whole eastern section pulled out in May.
notice_set.question: Is the sentence easy to follow the first time you read it?
options: No, you wait a long time for anything to happen
notice_set.why: Nine words of subject arrive before any event does. Moving the heavy part to the end is one of the jobs this shape exists for.

discovery.prompt: Each pair says the same thing. Read the line before it, then decide why one version settles and the other jars.
pairs: The proposal reached the panel in January. It was rejected six weeks later.
The proposal reached the panel in January. The panel rejected it six weeks later.
Seawater enters through a screen. It is then forced across a membrane.
Seawater enters through a screen. Pumps then force it across a membrane.
The gates are opened twice a day.
A driver from the Marlow depot opened the gates early on Tuesday.

candidate_rules.text: The version that settles begins with whatever the sentence before it was already about.
The version that settles is the one with no person in it.
The version that settles is the one with is, are or was in front of the -ed word.

teach.rule_line: Begin with whatever the last sentence left the reader holding.
teach.false_rule: That academic writing should be passive throughout. A wall of it is harder to read than a mixture, and each one has to earn its place.

contrast.question: Which of the two things in this event should the sentence be about?

fork.answer: The doer, because who did it is the news or the paragraph is following them
The affected thing, because who did it is unknown, taken for granted or already old news
fork.selects: the passive, with no doer at all

fork.answer: The affected thing, but the doer is long and worth keeping
fork.selects: the passive with by at the end

a.text: The proposal reached the panel in January. The panel rejected it six weeks later.
a.means: The paragraph has turned to the panel, and a reader now expects to hear more about how the panel works.

b.text: The proposal reached the panel in January. It was rejected six weeks later.
b.means: The paragraph is still following the proposal, and a reader expects to hear what happened to it next.

minimal_pair.only_difference: the second sentence: The panel rejected it / It was rejected

contrast.wrong_choice_note: Taking the active here is not a grammar mistake and nobody will circle it. It moves the reader across to the panel for a single line and straight back, and a paragraph of that keeps changing its mind.

edge_case.text: Some style guides tell writers to delete every passive they find. That advice grew up in offices where writers used it to hide. In a description of a process, hiding the operator is the whole point. Follow the sentence, not the slogan.

contrast.stronger_test: Cover your sentence and read only the one before it. Whatever that sentence ended on is what this one should open with. If that thing is on the receiving end of the new event, you need the passive.

worked_pairs.a: Seawater is drawn through a fine screen and then forced across a membrane.
worked_pairs.b: Pumps draw seawater through a fine screen and then force it across a membrane.
worked_pairs.gloss: The diagram is about the water, not about the pumps. The first version keeps the water in front from the opening word to the last.

worked_pairs.a: The eastern section was funded by a consortium of regional transport authorities.
worked_pairs.b: A consortium of regional transport authorities funded the eastern section.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: by a consortium of regional transport authorities
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: A consortium of regional transport authorities
worked_pairs.gloss: Eight words of funder in front of a short subject makes the reader wait. The first version puts the heavy part where a reader can take it.

worked_pairs.a: Applicants are notified within ten working days.
worked_pairs.b: We notify applicants within ten working days.
worked_pairs.gloss: One of these is an institution speaking and the other is a person. Both are correct English, and only one of them belongs on a form.

errors.wrong: It was decided by our group that the survey would be repeated in the autumn.
errors.right: Our group decided to repeat the survey in the autumn.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has been told this is the academic voice and applies it to a sentence whose entire point is that the group made a decision. Seven words go on hiding a doer the reader wanted.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one opening: It was decided by our group that becomes Our group decided to.

errors.wrong: The estuary was polluted for eleven years and nothing was done about it.
errors.right: A tannery upstream polluted the estuary for eleven years and nothing was done about it.
errors.why_it_happens: Dropping the doer has become automatic, because that is how the shape was first taught. Here the doer is the accusation, and a sentence that hides it says almost nothing.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one subject: name the tannery and put it in front.

errors.wrong: The kitchen was refitted by the landlord before I was permitted to move in.
errors.right: The landlord did the kitchen up before I moved in.
errors.why_it_happens: Essay grammar is being exported into a conversation about the speaker's own flat. Doer-free sentences sound stilted out loud, and the first part of the test is a conversation.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one subject: put the landlord in front and delete was.

used_in.quote: The whole answer is one long chain of this decision, taken the same way at every stage.
Answers about what tourism does to a place need a way of reporting effects without naming a culprit who was never there.

payload.sentence: The gates on the Verdon cut are opened twice a day.
payload.question: Would knowing the name of the operator change what this tells you?

feedback.why_key: The routine is the whole of the information. A name would sit in the sentence doing nothing.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask what a reader would do with the doer before you put one in.

payload.sentence: A driver from the Marlow depot opened the gates early on Tuesday.
payload.question: Why is the driver named here?
options: Because who did it is the news

feedback.why_key: Somebody broke the routine and a person is answerable. When that is the story, the person goes at the front.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the doer whenever the doer is what went wrong.

payload.context: Amara is answering a question about the flat she lives in.
payload.sentence: The boiler was replaced by the owner shortly before I was permitted to collect the keys.
reasons: it sounds like a form rather than a person talking
the time is wrong
the word after was is wrong
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Every word of it is correct and none of it sounds like somebody talking about the flat they live in.
feedback.feed_forward: In speech, put the person in front and use ordinary verbs.

payload.context: From a description of a small dairy, written for visitors.
payload.stem: The milk ___ (heat) to eighty degrees before it goes into the vats.

expected: is heated

feedback.why_key: The paragraph is following the milk from the churn to the vat, so the milk stays where the reader last left it.
feedback.feed_forward: Follow the material, not the people around it.

payload.context: From a museum label beside a wooden fishing boat.
payload.stem: The hull ___ (build) from oak cut on the Norland estate.

expected: was built

feedback.why_key: The label is about the boat in front of you. Where the oak came from is worth the words; who sawed it is not.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the object in front when the object is the exhibit.

payload.given: Volunteers clear the beach at Sandmouth every April.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it so the beach is what the sentence is about, and leave the volunteers out.

expected: is cleared every april
the beach at sandmouth is cleared every april

feedback.why_key: With the volunteers gone the beach has nowhere to go but the front, and be arrives to hold it there.
feedback.feed_forward: Drop the doer first, then rebuild round what is left.

payload.audio_text: The whole stretch is inspected every spring.

expected: the whole stretch is inspected every spring

feedback.why_key: Is disappears almost completely between two stressed words, and it is the piece that tells you somebody comes out to do this.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the small word you half-heard; it is nearly always there.

items.decision_cue: The tender went out to eleven firms in the spring.

payload.context: The line before this one reads: The tender went out to eleven firms in the spring.
payload.stem: ___ in June.

options.text: A firm from Norland won it
options.why_this_means: That the news is which firm won, and the paragraph now turns to that firm.

options.text: It was won by a firm from Norland
options.why_this_means: That the paragraph is still following the tender, with the winner added at the end.

expected: it was won by a firm from norland

feedback.why_key: The reader has been holding the tender since the line before, so the tender opens the next one.
feedback.feed_forward: Open with the thing the reader is already holding.

items.decision_cue: A firm from Norland has taken three contracts in two years.

payload.context: The line before this one reads: A firm from Norland has taken three contracts in two years.
payload.stem: ___ in June.

options.text: A firm from Norland won it
options.why_this_means: That the news is which firm won, and the paragraph now turns to that firm.

options.text: It was won by a firm from Norland
options.why_this_means: That the paragraph is still following the tender, with the winner added at the end.

expected: a firm from norland won it

feedback.why_key: This paragraph has been following the firm, so the firm keeps the front and naming it again is not repetition, it is continuity.
feedback.feed_forward: Let the paragraph's subject, not the event, choose the shape.

items.decision_cue: The intake screen had been blocked for a fortnight.

payload.context: From a report on the Verdon works. The sentence before reads: The intake screen had been blocked for a fortnight.
payload.stem: ___ on the Thursday.

options.text: The Brackenfield crew cleared the screen
options.why_this_means: That the crew is now the subject and the report turns to what they did.
That the report is still on the screen, and who cleared it is not being asked.

expected: the screen was cleared

feedback.why_key: Nobody has been introduced yet, and the screen has been in front of the reader for a whole sentence already.
feedback.feed_forward: Do not introduce a doer the paragraph has not needed.

items.decision_cue: A crew from Brackenfield arrived on the Wednesday.

payload.context: Later in the Verdon report. The line before reads: A crew from Brackenfield arrived on the Wednesday.
payload.stem: ___ on the Thursday.

options.text: The Brackenfield crew cleared the screen
options.why_this_means: That the crew is now the subject and the report turns to what they did.
That the report is still on the screen, and who cleared it is not being asked.

expected: the brackenfield crew cleared the screen

feedback.why_key: The crew has just walked into the paragraph. Dropping them one line later wastes the introduction the reader just read.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep a doer you have only just introduced.

payload.context: Two openings taken from different drafts of the same report.
sentences: The panel rejected the proposal.
The proposal was rejected.
meanings: The next line will tell you more about the panel.
Whatever comes next will keep following the proposal.

feedback.why_key: Neither is a better sentence. They are promises about what comes next, and one of them is a promise you can keep.
feedback.feed_forward: Read your next sentence before you fix the shape of this one.

payload.context: A briefing note about a footbridge that a private trust paid for and the council now looks after.

options.why_this_means: That the note is about the trust and what its money has produced.
That the note is about the bridge, and the trust can wait for a later line.

follow_up.question: Which version would you use if the next sentence lists the trust's other projects?

feedback.why_key: Both are correct English and they set up different paragraphs. The choice is made by the sentence you have not written yet.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide what the paragraph is about, then write its first sentence.

payload.context: From a body paragraph about who should pay for public transport.
payload.sentence: It was decided by our group that fares should be frozen for two years.
reasons: the sentence hides the doer it is actually about
the word after was is wrong
the time is wrong
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Seven words go on pushing the group to the back of a sentence whose only news is that the group decided something.
feedback.feed_forward: Cut the passive whenever the doer is the news.

payload.prompt_text: Here is the sentence before yours: Waste paper arrives at the mill in bales. Write the next sentence so that it carries on with the paper and brings no staff into it.

feedback.why_key: The reader put the paper down at the end of the last line and expects to pick it up at the start of this one.
feedback.feed_forward: Open with the word the previous sentence ended on.

payload.prompt_text: Write the two middle stages of the desalination diagram as one short paragraph. Every sentence must keep the water as the thing it reports on. Four minutes.

feedback.why_key: Holding one subject across three sentences is the difference between a process answer and a list of events.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that each sentence opens with the water or with a part of it.

title: Deciding whether to name the doer at the end, or to leave it out

point_json.grammar_name: by + agent: keep it or cut it

pays_in.note: Process answers drop the doer everywhere and keep the method every time.
pays_in.model: The sheets are trimmed by a rotary blade before they are stacked.

pays_in.note: A responsibility argument collapses the moment the doer goes missing.
pays_in.model: Air quality on the site is checked by a body with no stake in it.

pays_in.note: A stem that adds or removes a doer is testing whether you read the end of the sentence.
pays_in.model: The survey was carried out by a team from the university.

teach.can_do: I can decide whether the doer at the end of a sentence is worth its words.
teach.why_it_matters: Most learners either keep every doer or drop every doer. Deciding one sentence at a time is what separates a paragraph that informs from one that pads.
teach.meaning: Once the affected thing is at the front, the doer has two possible fates: it disappears, or it comes back at the end after by. Neither is the default. Keep it when the doer is specific, unexpected, or the reason anyone is reading the sentence. Cut it when the doer is people in general, or so obvious from the job that naming it tells the reader what they already assumed before they started.

form.pattern: be + past participle (+ by + the doer)
notes: the by phrase always comes after the participle, at the end of the clause
by can also mark an instrument or a means rather than a person: cut by machine, warmed by the sun
an instrument is information, so it is almost never the thing you cut
form.negative: the hall was not funded by the council but by a private trust
form.question: Who was the hall funded by?

rungs.text: The footbridge was rebuilt.
The footbridge was rebuilt by a charity.
The footbridge was rebuilt by a charity nobody had heard of.

spec.top_label: the doer is worth a clause

worked_example.sentence: The market hall was rebuilt by a trust set up by former traders.
worked_example.why_this_form: Nobody would guess that a group of traders paid for a public building, so the doer is the surprise and the sentence exists to deliver it.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: The market hall was rebuilt would report only that the building went up, which is the part of the story that anybody standing in front of it can already see.

notice_set.sentence: The refuse bins are emptied on Thursdays.
notice_set.question: Do you learn anything if the sentence names the council?
options: No, you had already assumed it
notice_set.why: A reader supplies the council for free. Four words that tell you what you already knew are four words wasted.

notice_set.sentence: The refuse bins are emptied by a contractor from Brackenfield.
notice_set.question: Is that what you expected to hear?
notice_set.why: The doer is not what a reader would have guessed, and that is exactly what makes it worth naming.

notice_set.sentence: The tiles are cut by machine and then stacked by hand.
notice_set.question: Are these two by phrases naming people?
options: No, they name how the job is done
Only the first one names a person
notice_set.why: By does not always introduce a doer. Here it tells you the method, and the whole sentence is about the difference between the two methods.

notice_set.sentence: The footbridge was paid for by a charity nobody in the town had heard of.
notice_set.question: Where does the longest part of this sentence sit?
notice_set.why: A long doer at the front makes the reader wait. Sent to the end, it arrives once they know what it is doing there.

notice_set.sentence: The estuary was polluted for eleven years.
notice_set.question: Does the sentence tell you who was responsible?
notice_set.why: This is the case where dropping the doer costs the sentence its point, because responsibility was the point.

teach.rule_line: Delete the by phrase and reread. If nothing is missing, it never was.
teach.false_rule: That the passive means leaving the doer out. That is one thing you can do with it, and plenty of sentences are better with the doer kept.

contrast.question: Would naming the doer tell my reader something they do not already have?

fork.answer: No, it is people in general or it is obvious from the job
Yes, it is specific or unexpected, and the affected thing still leads
fork.selects: the passive with by at the end

fork.answer: Yes, and the doer is short and is the whole news

a.text: The market hall was rebuilt after the fire.
a.means: It went back up. Who paid for it is not part of what is being reported.

b.text: The market hall was rebuilt by a trust set up by former traders after the fire.
b.means: It went back up, and the surprise is who paid for it, which the rest of the paragraph will now explain.

minimal_pair.only_difference: by a trust set up by former traders

contrast.wrong_choice_note: Adding by the council to a sentence about a council building tells the reader what they assumed before they reached the verb. It costs three words and buys nothing, and a paragraph of those reads as padding rather than detail.

edge_case.text: By does not only introduce doers. Cut by machine, damaged by frost, warmed by the sun all name a means or a cause rather than a person, and those never come out, because they are the information.

contrast.stronger_test: Ask whether a reader could have guessed the doer from the subject alone. Bins and councils, exams and schools, roads and highway teams: if the pair is obvious, delete it.

worked_pairs.a: The refuse bins are emptied on Thursdays.
worked_pairs.b: The refuse bins are emptied by a contractor from Brackenfield.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first sentence answers when, which is the question a resident actually has. The second answers who, and is worth writing only if who was in doubt.

worked_pairs.a: The reed beds were poisoned over three successive summers.
worked_pairs.b: A dye works on the north bank poisoned the reed beds over three summers.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: A dye works on the north bank
worked_pairs.gloss: Where responsibility is the argument, hiding the doer empties the sentence. The second version is the one that can be answered, agreed with or denied.

worked_pairs.a: The tiles are cut to size and then stacked by hand.
worked_pairs.b: The tiles are cut to size by two workers and then stacked by hand.
worked_pairs.gloss: By hand survives because it is a method. By two workers goes, because a process description is not a staffing plan.

errors.wrong: The exam papers are marked by the examiners in the weeks after the test.
errors.right: The exam papers are marked in the weeks after the test.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner is proud of the by phrase because it looks like the complete version of the structure, and completeness feels safer than judgement.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one phrase: by the examiners.

errors.wrong: The whole eastern section was funded, which nobody expected.
errors.right: The whole eastern section was funded by a private consortium, which nobody expected.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has stored this shape as the one with no doer, so the doer is dropped even when the second half of the sentence is pointing straight at it.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one phrase: by a private consortium.

errors.wrong: The market hall was rebuilt by them after the fire of 2019.
errors.right: The market hall was rebuilt after the fire of 2019.
errors.why_it_happens: A pronoun is put in the doer slot to keep the structure complete, but a pronoun with nobody to point at gives the reader a puzzle instead of a fact.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one phrase: by them.

used_in.quote: The tile diagram has methods worth naming at three stages and no people worth naming anywhere.

payload.sentence: The recycling bins are emptied on Thursdays.
payload.question: Do you already know roughly who does this?
options: The sentence says a resident does

feedback.why_key: A reader supplies the answer without being told, which is why the sentence does not tell them.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask what the reader would guess before you write the doer in.

payload.sentence: Emissions from the estate are monitored by an independent body.
payload.question: Why is the monitor named in this one?
options: Because who checks is the whole point

feedback.why_key: Independence is the claim being made. Delete the phrase and the sentence stops making it.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the doer when the doer is what is being argued about.

items.decision_cue: how a household waste service works

payload.context: From a leaflet about how a household waste service works.
payload.sentence: Green bins are collected by refuse crews on alternate Tuesdays.
reasons: the doer adds nothing a reader did not assume
the time is wrong
the word after are is wrong
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Refuse crews are who collects bins everywhere there are bins. The phrase states a definition rather than telling the reader anything.
feedback.feed_forward: Cut a doer that the noun in front already implies.

payload.context: From a note about how a small factory works.
payload.stem: The panels ___ (cut) by machine and then finished by hand.

expected: are cut

feedback.why_key: Neither of the two by phrases here names a person. Both name a method, and the sentence exists to set the two methods side by side.
feedback.feed_forward: Use by for a method as readily as for a doer.

payload.context: From the opening of a research summary.
payload.stem: The fieldwork ___ (carry out) by a team from the coastal institute.

expected: was carried out

feedback.why_key: Who did the work is the first thing a reader of a summary wants, so the doer stays and it stays at the end.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the doer after the participle, never in front of it.

payload.given: The papers are marked by the examiners during the fortnight after the test.
payload.instruction: Cut the part that tells the reader nothing new, and change nothing else.

expected: are marked during the fortnight after the test
the papers are marked during the fortnight after the test

feedback.why_key: Everything the sentence was really reporting survives the cut, and that is the test of whether a phrase was earning its place.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete the phrase and reread before you decide.

payload.audio_text: The hall was paid for by a local trust.

expected: the hall was paid for by a local trust

feedback.why_key: Two small words land next to each other and neither is stressed, and together they are the whole of the money question.
feedback.feed_forward: Write both small words even when you only half-hear the second.

items.decision_cue: The market hall burned down in a single night.

payload.context: A short guide to the town centre for visitors. The line before reads: The market hall burned down in a single night.
payload.stem: It ___ two years later.

options.why_this_means: That the building went back up and nothing about who paid is being reported.

options.text: was rebuilt by a trust set up by former traders
options.why_this_means: That the surprise is who paid, and the paragraph is about to explain them.

expected: was rebuilt by a trust set up by former traders

feedback.why_key: A visitor guide is written to tell you what you could not work out from the front of the building, and the traders are exactly that.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the doer whenever it is the part a reader could not guess.

items.decision_cue: Every civic building is inspected each spring.

payload.context: A council maintenance schedule listing routine work. The line before reads: Every civic building is inspected each spring.
payload.stem: It ___ two years later.

options.why_this_means: That the building went back up and nothing about who paid is being reported.

options.text: was rebuilt by a trust set up by former traders
options.why_this_means: That the surprise is who paid, and the paragraph is about to explain them.

expected: was rebuilt

feedback.why_key: A schedule of routine work has no room for a story about traders. The document decides what counts as relevant, not the event.
feedback.feed_forward: Let the document you are writing decide what the reader needs.

items.decision_cue: The dried panels move on to the finishing bay.

payload.context: From a description of how ceramic panels are made. The line before reads: The dried panels move on to the finishing bay.
payload.stem: There they are trimmed ___.

options.why_this_means: That the method is what changes at this stage, and a reader following the process needs it.

options.text: by two workers on the late shift
options.why_this_means: That the staffing is what changes at this stage, which a process description does not track.

expected: by a rotary blade

feedback.why_key: A process description follows the material through the machines. Who is on shift is a different document.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the method in a process; leave the staffing out.

items.decision_cue: Labour is the largest single cost in the bay.

payload.context: From a note explaining why the finishing bay costs so much to run. The line before reads: Labour is the largest single cost in the bay.
payload.stem: There they are trimmed ___.

options.why_this_means: That the method is what changes at this stage, and a reader following the process needs it.

options.text: by two workers on the late shift
options.why_this_means: That the staffing is what changes at this stage, which a process description does not track.

expected: by two workers on the late shift

feedback.why_key: The same stage, a different question. A note about wages needs the people; the blade is now the part nobody asked about.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the doer you keep to the question the text is answering.

payload.context: Two lines lifted from separate parts of one environmental report.
sentences: The estuary was polluted for eleven years.
The estuary was polluted for eleven years by a tannery upstream.
meanings: A problem is described and no one is answerable for it.
A problem is described and a named party can be asked about it.

feedback.why_key: The three words at the end are the difference between a weather report and an accusation.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether your sentence needs somebody to answer for it.

items.decision_cue: a housing association repainted last month

payload.context: Two tenants talking about a stairwell that a housing association repainted last month.
payload.stem: The stairs ___ in April.

options.why_this_means: That the state of the stairwell is the news and nobody is being credited or blamed.
That the association doing something at last is the news, and the paint is the evidence.

follow_up.question: Which one would you say if the conversation is about how slow the association has been?

feedback.why_key: Both are ordinary spoken English. One is about a stairwell and the other is about a landlord, and only you know which conversation you are in.
feedback.feed_forward: Pick the version that matches what you are complaining about.

items.decision_cue: a fire and the rebuilding that followed it

payload.context: From a paragraph about a fire and the rebuilding that followed it.
payload.sentence: The market hall was rebuilt by them after the fire of 2019.
reasons: the doer named at the end points at nobody
the time is wrong
the word after was is wrong
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: A doer with nothing behind it is worse than no doer at all, because the reader stops to look for the person and finds nobody.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete a doer you cannot name.

payload.prompt_text: Air quality on the Norland estate is checked every month, and the checking is done by a body with no connection to the operator. Write one sentence that makes the independence part of the news.

feedback.why_key: Independence only exists in the sentence if the doer is in it, so this is a case where the end of the sentence carries the argument.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the claim you want to defend into the by phrase.

payload.prompt_text: You are asked what has changed about the place you live in. Give a forty-five second answer with two sentences of this kind in it: one where the doer is left out and one where the doer is worth naming. Say why you kept the second.

feedback.why_key: One answer is the smallest space in which the decision has to be taken twice and taken differently.
feedback.feed_forward: Drop the doer in your first sentence and name it in your second.

title: Describing a process from the first stage to the last in one steady voice

point_json.grammar_name: The process chain: present simple passive and its links

pays_in.note: A diagram answer is this point from the first line to the last.
pays_in.model: Used cans are sorted by weight before they are crushed into blocks.

pays_in.note: Technical passages describe how things are made in exactly this chain.
pays_in.model: The sheets are trimmed to size before they are stacked for delivery.

pays_in.note: A tour or a lecture describing how something works uses this shape throughout.
pays_in.model: The samples are sealed on site and sent to the laboratory the same day.

teach.can_do: I can describe a whole process, stage by stage, without changing voice or losing track of the material.
teach.why_it_matters: A diagram answer is not a set of separate sentences. It is one chain, and the marks come from the chain holding together across all of it.
teach.meaning: A process description has no story and no characters. It has a material that goes in at one end and comes out changed at the other, and every stage is something done to that material. So the whole answer stays in one time, the present, and every sentence reports a thing done rather than a person doing. The links between stages carry the sequence, and the material stays in the subject slot from beginning to end.

form.pattern: the material + is / are + past participle, repeated for every stage
notes: the present is used even for a process that happened yesterday or will happen tomorrow
sequence words open the stage: at this stage, once the sheets have dried, the mixture is then
a stage that follows a finished one takes once or after plus have been: once the pulp has been screened
a relative link keeps two stages in one sentence: a tank, where the water is held for two days
form.negative: the mixture is not heated again after this stage
form.question: Is the pulp screened before it is pressed?

left.text: waste paper, in bales

right.text: new board, in rolls

spec.caption: Everything between the two boxes is something done to the material. Nobody appears in the middle.

worked_example.sentence: Once the pulp has been screened, it is pressed into sheets and left to dry.
worked_example.why_this_form: One sentence carries two stages and a boundary between them, and the pulp holds the subject slot right through, so a reader never loses what is being tracked.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Once workers have screened the pulp, they press it into sheets would put two people into a diagram that has none, and the reader would start wondering how many there are.

notice_set.sentence: The cans are crushed into blocks and loaded onto a lorry.
notice_set.question: How many separate things happen to the cans here?
notice_set.why: Two stages share one subject, so the sentence covers more ground without repeating the noun.

notice_set.sentence: Once the blocks have been weighed, they are sent to the smelter.
notice_set.question: Which of the two things happens first?
notice_set.why: Once marks the boundary and the finished form on the left tells you that stage is over before the next begins.

notice_set.sentence: The molten metal is poured into a mould, where it cools for several hours.
notice_set.question: What is the word where pointing at?
notice_set.why: A link like this fastens a stage to the place it happens in, so a second sentence is not needed.

notice_set.sentence: The water evaporates and leaves a crust of salt behind.
notice_set.question: Is anybody making the water evaporate?
options: No, it happens on its own
notice_set.why: A natural step in a made process keeps its ordinary shape, because nothing is being done to the water at that moment.

notice_set.sentence: At this stage the sheets are trimmed to size.
notice_set.question: Where in the process are you standing when you read this?
notice_set.why: The opening phrase is doing the work of a signpost, which is what stops six stages from reading as six unrelated facts.

teach.rule_line: One time, one voice, one material followed from the first stage to the last.
teach.false_rule: That every verb in a process takes this shape. Steps that happen on their own, such as cooling and drying, keep their ordinary form, and forcing them breaks the sentence.

errors.wrong: The cans are crushed into blocks. Then the blocks were loaded onto a lorry.
errors.right: The cans are crushed into blocks. The blocks are then loaded onto a lorry.
errors.why_it_happens: A diagram feels like a report of something already seen, so the past creeps in as soon as the writer stops concentrating on the shape.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: were becomes are.

errors.wrong: The metal is cooled for several hours and then the mould is removed.
errors.right: The metal cools for several hours and then the mould is removed.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer has decided that everything in a process takes the same shape and applies it to a stage where nothing is being done at all.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: is cooled becomes cools.
errors.l1_note: Only where the stage genuinely happens on its own; a cooling tower does cool the metal.

errors.wrong: Once the pulp screened, it is pressed into sheets.
errors.right: Once the pulp has been screened, it is pressed into sheets.
errors.why_it_happens: Once feels like it has already marked the stage as finished, so the writer sees no work left for anything else to do.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one pair: has been.

used_in.quote: Six stages, one material, no people: the answer is a single chain built out of this point.
The tutorial walks through how the samples are handled, and every step arrives in this shape.

payload.sentence: The bales are broken open and the paper is fed into a shredder.
payload.question: Is the writer describing something happening this minute?

feedback.why_key: A process description reports a routine, not an occasion, which is why the present holds for the whole answer.
feedback.feed_forward: Treat every stage as something that happens each time.

payload.context: From a description of how metal parts are cast.
payload.sentence: The metal is cooled for several hours before the mould is opened.
reasons: nothing is doing the cooling here
the time is wrong
the mould cannot be opened
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Metal in a mould cools because it is left alone. Give the stage this shape and you have invented a machine that is not in the diagram.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether anything is acting before you reach for be.

payload.context: From a description of how aluminium cans are recycled.
payload.stem: The cans ___ (crush) into blocks before they leave the yard.

expected: are crushed

feedback.why_key: Cans crush nothing. They are what the machine flattens, and the plural subject picks are.
feedback.feed_forward: Check the subject is plural before you write are.

payload.context: From a description of how dried pasta is made.
payload.stem: Once the dough ___ (mix), it is pushed through a shaped die.

expected: has been mixed

feedback.why_key: Once opens a stage that has to be over before the next one starts, and only the finished form closes it.
feedback.feed_forward: After once, close the stage with has been.

payload.given: Workers weighed the blocks. Then they sent them to the smelter.
payload.instruction: Rewrite the two stages as one sentence with no people in it, in the time a diagram uses.

expected: have been weighed they are sent to the smelter
once the blocks have been weighed they are sent to the smelter

feedback.why_key: Two stages, one boundary, one sentence, and the blocks never leave the subject slot.
feedback.feed_forward: Join two stages with once rather than with then.

payload.context: One stage from a description of how sea water is turned into drinking water.

expected: the water is held in a tank for two days
the water is held for two days in a tank

feedback.why_key: Where and how long can trade places, and neither of them can come between is and the word after it.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the pair together and move the rest around it.

payload.audio_text: Once the salt has been removed the water is safe to drink.

expected: once the salt has been removed the water is safe to drink

feedback.why_key: Three weak syllables run together in the middle and they are the whole of the stage boundary.
feedback.feed_forward: Slow the replay and write the small words first.

payload.sentence: The panels are dried in a warm room, and then they were stacked ready for cutting.

expected: they are stacked

feedback.why_key: Two stages of one process cannot sit in two different times, and the reader notices the jolt even without knowing why.
feedback.feed_forward: Read your stages in a row and check they share one time.

payload.prompt_text: In a bottling plant, glass bottles are washed and then filled. Write one sentence covering both stages, keeping the bottles as the thing the sentence follows.

feedback.why_key: Two stages in one sentence with one subject is the sentence a process answer is made of.
feedback.feed_forward: Write one subject and hang both stages off it.

payload.prompt_text: Write the full body of the aluminium can recycling answer: every stage, one time throughout, and at least one sentence joined with once. Six minutes.

feedback.why_key: Six stages is where a chain either holds or comes apart, and no shorter task can show you which.
feedback.feed_forward: Read only your verbs at the end, in order, and check them.

title: Knowing where this shape is the wrong tool and using the ordinary one

point_json.grammar_name: When the passive is wrong

pays_in.note: Every chart answer is full of verbs that have nothing on the receiving end.
pays_in.model: Household numbers grew steadily until 2018 and then levelled off.

pays_in.note: An argument about responsibility needs people at the front of sentences.
pays_in.model: Councils cut the maintenance budget three years before the wall failed.

pays_in.note: Talking about your own life needs ordinary shapes, not report grammar.
pays_in.model: The whole thing got called off about an hour before we set out.

pays_in.note: Noticing that a passage says rose rather than was raised is often the whole answer.
pays_in.model: Water levels in the lower valley rose for three consecutive winters.

teach.can_do: I can tell when a sentence has nothing for this shape to move, and write it the ordinary way instead.
teach.why_it_matters: A module that only teaches when to reach for the passive produces writers who reach for it everywhere. Half of learning it is learning where it does not go.
teach.meaning: This shape works by taking the thing on the receiving end and moving it to the front. That only works if there is something on the receiving end. A great many verbs describe what something does rather than what is done to it: rise, fall, happen, occur, appear, evaporate, arrive. Nothing is receiving anything, so there is nothing to move, and the sentence has no version of this kind at all.

form.pattern: no be, no participle: the level rose, the meeting happened, the numbers fell
notes: test the verb by asking what comes after it: if nothing can, there is no version of this kind
a few verbs work both ways with two different meanings: the level rose, the level was raised
get instead of be belongs in speech, not in an essay: it got cancelled, it was cancelled
form.negative: the numbers did not fall after the charge came in
form.question: Did the numbers fall after the charge came in?

left.text: raise, cut, build, collect, monitor

right.text: rise, fall, happen, arrive, evaporate

spec.caption: Only the left box has anything to move to the front. The right box has no version of this kind, and forcing one produces a sentence with a hole in it.

worked_example.sentence: The water level rose by half a metre overnight.
worked_example.why_this_form: Rain fell and the level went up on its own. There is no one at the sluice, so the sentence has nothing to put on the receiving end.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Was raised would report a decision: someone at the sluice opened a gate and put the level up, which turns a weather event into an act.

notice_set.sentence: The water level rose by half a metre overnight.
notice_set.question: Did anyone make this happen?
options: No, it happened on its own
notice_set.why: Rain does this without anybody's help, and the sentence is shaped to say so.

notice_set.sentence: The water level was raised by half a metre overnight.
notice_set.question: Did anyone make this happen?
options: No, it happened on its own
notice_set.why: This one reports a decision. Somebody at the sluice did it, even though the sentence does not name them.

notice_set.sentence: The accident happened just after six in the morning.
notice_set.question: Could this sentence be built round somebody who caused it?
options: No, this verb takes nothing after it
notice_set.why: Happen has nothing after it to move anywhere, so there is no other version of the sentence to build.

notice_set.sentence: The committee chose the cheaper of the two designs.
notice_set.question: Who is this sentence about?
notice_set.why: The news is that these people made a choice, so they belong at the front where the reader can see them.

notice_set.sentence: The concert got cancelled about an hour before it was due to start.
notice_set.question: Where would you expect to hear this?
notice_set.why: Got instead of was is ordinary spoken English and reads as careless in an essay, which is a register problem rather than a mistake.

teach.rule_line: Ask what the verb does to something. If the answer is nothing, stop.
teach.false_rule: That processes take this shape, so every step in one does. Steps that happen on their own keep the ordinary form, and forcing them invents machinery.

contrast.question: Is there anything in this event on the receiving end?

fork.answer: Nothing at all: the subject acts and nothing is acted on
Yes, but the doer is the news of the sentence
Yes, and the doer is unknown, obvious or beside the point

a.text: The water level rose by half a metre overnight.
a.means: It went up on its own after rain. Nobody was involved.

b.text: The water level was raised by half a metre overnight.
b.means: Somebody at the sluice put it up. A decision was taken.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: Writing was risen where you mean rose is not a small slip. It hands the reader a sentence with a hole where the doer should be, and readers stop to look for the person who raised it before they can carry on.

edge_case.text: A handful of verbs work both ways with different meanings, and rise and raise are the pair you will meet most: things rise on their own, and people raise them. Grow, sink, increase and improve behave the same way.

contrast.stronger_test: Put the word something straight after the verb and read it aloud. Raise something works. Rise something does not, and that is your answer.

worked_pairs.a: Rainfall in the catchment fell sharply after 2016.
worked_pairs.b: Rainfall in the catchment was reduced sharply after 2016.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first reports weather. The second says somebody managed to reduce the rain, which is a claim no report would make.

worked_pairs.a: The committee chose the cheaper of the two designs.
worked_pairs.b: It was decided that the cheaper of the two designs would be used.
worked_pairs.gloss: The second version is not wrong and it is not neutral either. It removes the only people who could be asked why.

worked_pairs.a: The concert got cancelled an hour before the doors opened.
worked_pairs.b: The concert was cancelled an hour before the doors opened.
worked_pairs.gloss: Both are correct English. The first belongs in a conversation and the second belongs in a report, and swapping them is what makes a script sound out of place.
