errors.wrong: The number of visitors was increased sharply between 2015 and 2019.
errors.right: The number of visitors increased sharply between 2015 and 2019.
errors.why_it_happens: Data description feels formal, and this shape has been learned as the formal one, so it is applied to a verb that has nothing to act on.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: was.

errors.wrong: The accident was happened just after six in the morning.
errors.right: The accident happened just after six in the morning.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner reads the accident as a victim, because in the world it is one. The grammar does not agree: happen never takes anything after it.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: was.
errors.l1_note: Common where the first language marks events as things that befall people.

errors.wrong: The second reading of the bill got postponed until the following month.
errors.right: The second reading of the bill was postponed until the following month.
errors.why_it_happens: Get is the version the learner hears constantly and it feels more natural than be, because in speech it is. In an essay it drops the register by a whole level.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: got becomes was.

errors.wrong: Three sentences in a row: The samples are collected. They are labelled. They are stored.
errors.right: The samples are collected, labelled and stored, and the labels are checked twice.
errors.why_it_happens: Once the shape is learned it becomes the only shape, and a paragraph of it reads as flat because nothing in it ever changes.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one subject: join the three into one clause with a single subject.

used_in.quote: Almost every verb the line graph needs is one that has nothing on the receiving end.

payload.sentence: The reservoir level rose by nearly a metre overnight.
payload.question: Was anybody involved in this?

feedback.why_key: This is weather. The sentence is built to report something that happened without anybody's help.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether a person could have caused it before you decide.

payload.sentence: The reservoir level was raised by nearly a metre overnight.
payload.question: Was anybody involved in this one?

feedback.why_key: Somebody opened a gate. The sentence does not name them and it still tells you they exist.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the shape as a claim about whether anyone acted.

items.decision_cue: a line graph of rail passenger numbers

payload.context: From a paragraph describing a line graph of rail passenger numbers.
payload.sentence: The figure for weekday journeys was increased sharply after the line reopened.
reasons: nothing in the picture is doing this to it
the two halves are the wrong way round
the word after was is wrong
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: A graph reports what a figure did, not what somebody did to it. The extra word invents a hand nobody claimed.
feedback.feed_forward: Describe a trend with the plain verb and nothing else.

payload.context: From a paragraph about a chart of household spending.
payload.stem: Spending on transport ___ (fall) every year after the fuel duty came in.

expected: fell

feedback.why_key: Nothing is falling the spending. It went down, and the plain form is the only one the verb has.
feedback.feed_forward: Use the plain form for a trend with no one behind it.

payload.context: From a note about how a reservoir is managed.
payload.stem: In dry summers the level ___ (lower) deliberately to protect the dam wall.

expected: is lowered

feedback.why_key: Deliberately puts a person in the sentence whether they are named or not, so here the shape is right.
feedback.feed_forward: Look for a word like deliberately before you rule the passive out.

payload.given: It was decided by the committee that the cheaper design would be used.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it so the people who took the decision are at the front.

expected: chose the cheaper design
decided to use the cheaper design
the committee chose the cheaper design

feedback.why_key: Five words come out and nothing is lost, which tells you what those five words were doing.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the decider in front when a decision is the news.

payload.audio_text: The whole thing got cancelled an hour before the doors opened.

expected: the whole thing got cancelled an hour before the doors opened

feedback.why_key: What you hear in conversation is got, not was, and hearing the difference is the first step to keeping them apart on paper.
feedback.feed_forward: Note which of the two you heard, then decide where it belongs.

items.decision_cue: three days of heavy rain in the hills

payload.context: From a report on a river after three days of heavy rain in the hills.
payload.stem: The level ___ by half a metre overnight.

options.why_this_means: That it went up with nothing acting on it.
That somebody at the sluice put it up on purpose.

expected: rose

feedback.why_key: Rain in the hills is the cause the sentence has already given you, and rain is not a person.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the cause in the context before you choose the verb.

items.decision_cue: a controlled test of the new sluice gates

payload.context: From a report on a river during a controlled test of the new sluice gates.
payload.stem: The level ___ by half a metre overnight.

options.why_this_means: That it went up with nothing acting on it.
That somebody at the sluice put it up on purpose.

expected: was raised

feedback.why_key: A controlled test has operators in it, and the same half metre now reports what they did rather than what the weather did.
feedback.feed_forward: Let the situation, not the verb, decide whether anybody acted.

payload.context: Two friends on the phone about a festival that has fallen through.
payload.stem: Apparently the whole thing ___ at the last minute.

options.why_this_means: That the speaker is talking, not writing, and the news is the disappointment.
That the speaker is reporting for the record, in the register of a written notice.

expected: got called off

feedback.why_key: Both are correct. On the phone the shorter one is what a speaker reaches for, and using the other sounds like reading from a card.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the shape to whether you are speaking or writing.

items.decision_cue: the opening paragraph of a written report

payload.context: From the opening paragraph of a written report on the same festival.
payload.stem: Apparently the whole thing ___ at the last minute.

options.why_this_means: That the speaker is talking, not writing, and the news is the disappointment.
That the speaker is reporting for the record, in the register of a written notice.

expected: was called off

feedback.why_key: A report has no voice of its own, so the version that carries a speaking voice is the one that stands out for the wrong reason.
feedback.feed_forward: Write was in a report and save got for speech.

payload.context: Two lines taken from separate parts of one report on a national park.
sentences: Visitor numbers grew by a third over the decade.
Visitor numbers were capped at eight hundred a day.
meanings: Something happened and nobody arranged it.
Somebody made a decision and put a limit in place.

feedback.why_key: Two sentences about the same numbers, and only one of them has a person behind it.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether a decision is being reported or a trend.

items.decision_cue: rainfall has also been unusually high

payload.context: A note on a stretch of moorland where a drainage scheme has been running for two years and rainfall has also been unusually high.
payload.stem: Water levels in the peat ___ since the work began.

options.why_this_means: That the levels came up, and the sentence takes no view on whether the scheme or the weather did it.
That the scheme did it, and the sentence is giving the engineers the credit.

follow_up.question: Which one would you write if you did not want to claim the scheme caused it?

feedback.why_key: Both are correct English and they make different claims. One reports a measurement, the other awards a result.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose the version whose claim you can actually defend.

items.decision_cue: a change in hospital waiting times

payload.context: From a paragraph about a change in hospital waiting times.
payload.sentence: The waiting time was fallen by nearly two weeks after the new clinic opened.
reasons: this verb has nothing on the receiving end
the time is wrong
the clinic cannot open
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Nothing falls a waiting time. The word was is looking for a doer that this verb has no room for.
feedback.feed_forward: Test the verb with something after it before you add was.

payload.prompt_text: A chart shows household energy use dropping every year from 2016, with no policy behind it. Write one sentence reporting the drop. Do not put anybody into the sentence who is not there.

feedback.why_key: The hard part is resisting the shape you have just spent two lessons learning, which is exactly what this asks you to do.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the plain verb and leave the sentence short.

payload.prompt_text: Write three sentences of your renewable electricity answer. At least one must report a trend with a plain verb, and at least one must report a decision with the passive. Four minutes.

feedback.why_key: Mixing the two inside one paragraph is what a chart answer actually needs, and it is the only way to show you can tell them apart.
feedback.feed_forward: Mark which sentence is a trend and which is a decision.

title: Deciding whether a clause picks something out or just adds news about it

point_json.grammar_name: Non-defining relative clauses

teach.can_do: I can use commas to show whether a clause is telling my reader which one, or telling them something new about it.
teach.why_it_matters: A pair of commas changes how many people you are talking about. Your reader sees what you wrote, not what you meant.
teach.meaning: Both kinds of clause hang on a noun, and there the resemblance ends. One narrows the noun down until the right thing is left. The other assumes you already have the right thing and hands you a fact about it. Commas are the switch between those two jobs, and they are not decoration. Leave them out and you have quietly told your reader that other candidates exist. Put them in and you have said there are none.

form.pattern: noun , + who / which / whose + clause , + the rest of the sentence
notes: that is refused inside the commas; use who for people and which for things
the relative word can never be dropped here, however long the clause is
when the clause runs to the end of the sentence, one comma is enough: we walked to the depot, which shuts at six
form.negative: The inside goes negative as usual: the bridge, which does not carry lorries, reopened in April.
form.question: Before the comma goes in, ask whether your reader could already pick the thing out.

left.role: no commas: the clause says which one
left.text: the drivers who live in Marlow

right.role: commas: you already knew which, so this is news
right.text: the drivers, who live in Marlow,

spec.caption: Same seven words, two different head counts. The punctuation does all of it.

worked_example.sentence: The Sandmouth ferry, which stops running in November, carries about forty cars a trip.
worked_example.why_this_form: There is one ferry at Sandmouth and the reader already has it. The November detail is news about that ferry, not a way of telling it apart from another one.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Take the commas out and the sentence starts sorting Sandmouth's ferries into ones that stop in November and ones that do not, then picks the first kind.

notice_set.sentence: My aunt, who runs the bakery in Marlow, is retiring in June.
notice_set.question: How many aunts does the speaker have?
notice_set.why: The bakery detail is set apart, so it is not being used to tell one aunt from another. There is nobody to tell her apart from.

notice_set.sentence: My aunt who runs the bakery in Marlow is retiring in June.
notice_set.question: How many aunts does the speaker have?
notice_set.why: The bakery is doing the work of picking one aunt out, and picking out only makes sense when there is a choice.

notice_set.sentence: The two lifts, which were put in during 2019, keep breaking down.
notice_set.question: How many lifts does the building have?
notice_set.why: Nothing is being narrowed down, so the two named at the start are all there are.

notice_set.sentence: The staff, who were told on Friday, have already found other jobs.
notice_set.question: Were all the staff told on Friday?
notice_set.why: Setting the detail apart means the whole group is meant, so the telling reached every one of them.

notice_set.sentence: The staff who were told on Friday have already found other jobs.
notice_set.question: Were all the staff told on Friday?
notice_set.why: One part of the staff is being talked about. What happened to the rest is simply left outside the sentence.

discovery.prompt: Each pair below says something different about how many there are. Work out what is doing that.
pairs: My aunt, who runs the bakery in Marlow, is retiring in June.
My aunt who runs the bakery in Marlow is retiring in June.
The staff, who were told on Friday, have already found other jobs.
The staff who were told on Friday have already found other jobs.
The two lifts, which were put in during 2019, keep breaking down.
The two lifts that were put in during 2019 keep breaking down.

candidate_rules.text: On the left the group is already settled and the clause adds news; on the right the clause is what settles the group.
Commas go in when the noun is a person's relative or a named place.
Use which after a comma and that when there is no comma.

teach.rule_line: Ask whether the reader already knows which one. If they do, the clause takes commas.
teach.false_rule: That the commas are a style choice, or that they mark where you would pause. They mark how many things you are talking about.

contrast.question: Does my reader already know which one I mean?

fork.answer: No, and this clause is how they will find out: no commas
fork.selects: a clause welded straight onto the noun

fork.answer: Yes, it is already settled, and this is news about it: commas both sides
fork.selects: a clause fenced off by commas

a.text: The drivers who live in Marlow have been given parking permits.
a.means: Some drivers live in Marlow and those are the ones with permits. The others got nothing.

b.text: The drivers, who live in Marlow, have been given parking permits.
b.means: Every driver has a permit, and all of them happen to live in Marlow.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You fenced the clause off with commas. That tells your reader that every driver got a permit and that Marlow is a footnote. If only some of them got one, the commas have just handed over the wrong number.

edge_case.text: In speech there are no commas to see. The difference is carried by a small pause and a drop in the voice, and plenty of fluent speakers do not bother with either. Write them; do not lose sleep over hearing them.

contrast.stronger_test: Put your thumb over the clause. If what is left still names one particular thing, the clause is news and takes commas. If what is left names nothing in particular, the commas would be a lie.

worked_pairs.a: The tenants who complained about the damp have been rehoused.
worked_pairs.b: The tenants, who complained about the damp, have been rehoused.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first says a subset of the tenants moved. The second says all of them did, and mentions the damp on the way past.

worked_pairs.a: The two routes that lose money are being withdrawn.
worked_pairs.b: The two routes, which lose money, are being withdrawn.
worked_pairs.gloss: In the first, losing money is how you know which routes are meant. In the second you already knew, and losing money is the reason being offered.

worked_pairs.a: My cousin who trained as a nurse has moved to Sandmouth.
worked_pairs.b: My cousin, who trained as a nurse, has moved to Sandmouth.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first quietly tells you the speaker has several cousins. The second tells you there is one worth mentioning.

errors.wrong: Students, who fail the January test, must retake the module.
errors.right: Students who fail the January test must retake the module.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has been told that this kind of clause is extra information, so commas go round every one of them. The commas then quietly claim that the whole year group failed.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one pair of commas.

errors.wrong: Her sister who works at the clinic has offered to drive us.
errors.right: Her sister, who works at the clinic, has offered to drive us.
errors.why_it_happens: Nobody has ever told the learner that leaving the commas out makes a claim about how many sisters exist. The clause looks like ordinary detail, so it goes in bare.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one pair of commas.

errors.wrong: The Verdon bridge, that reopened in April, is still single-lane.
errors.right: The Verdon bridge, which reopened in April, is still single-lane.
errors.why_it_happens: That is the workhorse relative word and it goes in everywhere by default. Nothing in the way it is usually taught mentions that it will not sit inside a pair of commas.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: that becomes which.

errors.wrong: My uncle, lives in Ashfield, has offered us the flat.
errors.right: My uncle, who lives in Ashfield, has offered us the flat.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner knows the relative word can sometimes be dropped and carries that habit across. Inside commas there is nothing else holding the clause to its noun, so the sentence comes apart.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: who.

pays_in.note: It lets you name a thing and comment on it inside one sentence.
pays_in.model: Congestion charging, which has been tried in several large cities, shifts journeys rather than removing them.

pays_in.note: It attaches a figure to the thing the figure is about.
pays_in.model: Rail journeys, which had fallen sharply after the depot closed, were back to their earlier level within four years.

pays_in.note: A True or False stem often turns on whether the clause narrows or comments.
pays_in.model: The scheme, which had been running for eight years, was quietly dropped.

used_in.quote: The prompt asks about a group of people, and the first job of the essay is to say whether you mean all of them or some of them.
The passage names a district and then comments on it, and one question depends on reading the comment as a comment.

payload.sentence: My neighbours, who moved here from Ashfield, keep chickens.
payload.question: How many sets of neighbours is the speaker talking about?

feedback.why_key: Nothing is being narrowed down. The Ashfield detail is news about the neighbours the speaker already had in mind.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the fenced-off clause as news, never as a filter.

payload.sentence: Employees who joined before 2018 keep the old pension.
payload.question: Does everyone at the company keep the old pension?

feedback.why_key: The joining date is doing the work of picking a group out, so anyone outside that group is outside the promise.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask what the clause is filtering before you decide who benefits.

payload.context: From a report on the Ashfield line, which is the district's single railway.
payload.sentence: The Ashfield line, that carries the freight, has been closed for six weeks.
reasons: that is refused inside a pair of commas
the commas should not be there at all
the clause is next to the wrong noun
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: There is one line, so the commas are right. The word inside them is the problem, and only which will sit there.
feedback.feed_forward: Swap that for which as soon as commas go in.

payload.context: A note about the single road bridge over the Verdon.
payload.stem: The Verdon bridge, ___ reopened in April, still carries one lane of traffic.

expected: which

feedback.why_key: There is one bridge and the commas are already in place, and inside commas that has nowhere to stand.
feedback.feed_forward: Reach for which whenever the clause sits inside commas.

payload.given: Marlow has one secondary school. It was rebuilt after the flood of 2016. It now takes pupils from three villages.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence in which the rebuilding is a side note rather than a way of picking the school out.

expected: which was rebuilt after the flood of 2016, now takes pupils from three villages
which was rebuilt after the 2016 flood, now takes pupils from three villages

feedback.why_key: One school in the town means there is nothing to tell it apart from, so the rebuilding can only be news.
feedback.feed_forward: Count the candidates first, then decide about the commas.

payload.context: The station has one north platform. Build the sentence.

expected: the north platform, which floods every winter, is shut

feedback.why_key: Both commas are load-bearing: the clause is fenced off at each end so the reader knows it is not narrowing anything.
feedback.feed_forward: Close the fence at both ends before the main verb arrives.

payload.audio_text: My cousin, who's just qualified, is looking for work in Sandmouth.

expected: my cousin, who's just qualified, is looking for work in sandmouth
my cousin who's just qualified is looking for work in sandmouth
my cousin, who has just qualified, is looking for work in sandmouth
my cousin whos just qualified is looking for work in sandmouth

feedback.why_key: Who's is one squashed syllable in speech, and the two small pauses around it are all the punctuation you get to hear.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the dip in the voice that fences the clause off.

items.decision_cue: Every flat in the Brackenfield block changed hands last spring

payload.context: Every flat in the Brackenfield block changed hands last spring, and the landlord is writing to all of them.
payload.stem: The tenants ___ have been offered a rent reduction.

options.why_this_means: That the reduction is for the newcomers, and that longer-standing tenants are not included in it.
That every tenant gets the reduction, and that all of them arrived last year.

expected: , who moved in last year,

feedback.why_key: If every flat changed hands, there is no group left to narrow down, so the moving-in date can only be news.
feedback.feed_forward: Count who is left outside the clause before you choose.

items.decision_cue: the rest have had the same tenants for a decade

payload.context: Half the flats in that block were relet last spring; the rest have had the same tenants for a decade.
payload.stem: The tenants ___ have been offered a rent reduction.

options.why_this_means: That the reduction is for the newcomers, and that longer-standing tenants are not included in it.
That every tenant gets the reduction, and that all of them arrived last year.

expected: who moved in last year

feedback.why_key: Half the block has been there for ten years, so the clause has real work to do: it says which half the offer reaches.
feedback.feed_forward: Leave the commas out whenever a group is being separated.

payload.context: Halima has three brothers. One of them is on the council's maintenance team.
payload.stem: ___ has agreed to look at the drains.

options.text: Her brother who works for the council
options.why_this_means: That she has more than one brother, and this is the council one.

options.text: Her brother, who works for the council,
options.why_this_means: That she has one brother, and his job is a side note about him.

expected: her brother who works for the council

feedback.why_key: With three brothers in the room, the job is the only thing telling the listener which one turned up.
feedback.feed_forward: When several candidates exist, weld the clause on without commas.

payload.context: Halima has one brother. He is on the council's maintenance team.
payload.stem: ___ has agreed to look at the drains.

options.text: Her brother who works for the council
options.why_this_means: That she has more than one brother, and this is the council one.

options.text: Her brother, who works for the council,
options.why_this_means: That she has one brother, and his job is a side note about him.

expected: her brother, who works for the council,

feedback.why_key: There is nobody to tell him apart from, so leaving the commas out would invent brothers she does not have.
feedback.feed_forward: Fence the clause off once the person is already identified.

items.decision_cue: a hundred people across two sites

payload.context: Rasheed is describing a firm that employs a hundred people across two sites.
payload.stem: The staff ___ have been offered a shuttle bus.

options.why_this_means: That the bus is for the Ashfield half of the workforce and the other site gets nothing.
That the whole workforce gets the bus, and that all of them are based at Ashfield.

follow_up.question: Which version leaves the second site out of the offer?

feedback.why_key: Both sentences are correct English about a real firm. They describe two different firms, and the punctuation is the only thing telling them apart.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide the head count first, then punctuate to match it.

payload.context: Two sentences from different letters about the same college.
sentences: The lecturers who job-share have been given a shared office.
The lecturers, who job-share, have been given a shared office.
meanings: Some of the lecturers share a post, and those are the ones with the new office.
All the lecturers share a post, and all of them are moving into one office.

feedback.why_key: The first letter describes a subset of a staff room. The second describes an unusual college where nobody works full-time.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the punctuation to the number of people you mean.

items.decision_cue: who live more than three miles away

payload.context: From a draft paragraph about a village school and its catchment.
payload.sentence: Children, who live more than three miles away, qualify for free transport.
reasons: the commas claim that every child lives more than three miles away
the wrong relative word has been used
the clause has been attached to the wrong word
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The distance is what decides who gets the transport, so it has to be welded on. Fenced off, it becomes a claim about every child in the village.
feedback.feed_forward: Take the commas out when the clause decides who qualifies.

payload.sentence: The 14 bus, that runs hourly on Sundays, does not stop at the hospital.

expected: which runs hourly on sundays
which runs hourly on Sundays

feedback.why_key: There is one number 14, so the commas are doing the right job. It is the word between them that has to change.
feedback.feed_forward: Change that to which the moment the clause is fenced off.

payload.prompt_text: Your town has one railway station and it was rebuilt three years ago. Write one sentence that mentions the rebuilding as news, not as a way of picking the station out.

feedback.why_key: One station means there is nothing to distinguish it from, and that is exactly the situation the fenced-off clause exists for.
feedback.feed_forward: Fence the clause with a comma at each end, not just the first.

payload.prompt_text: Open your body paragraph on people living alone. Find the term you introduced first and rewrite that sentence so the definition sits inside a pair of commas. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: Defining a term once and then commenting on it is how an essay stops repeating itself, and it costs one sentence rather than two.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that the clause you fenced off is true of every case.

title: Putting the small word in the right place when a clause needs one

point_json.grammar_name: Relative clauses with prepositions

teach.can_do: I can keep the small word that a verb needs when the noun it belongs to has moved to the front.
teach.why_it_matters: The preposition carries the meaning here. Drop it and the sentence stops being English; move it wrongly and a spoken answer starts sounding like a legal document.
teach.meaning: Some verbs cannot stand alone: you depend on something, you complain to somebody, you look at a flat. When the thing they need becomes the noun that a clause hangs on, the verb still needs its small word. English gives you two places to put it. It can stay at the end of the clause, where the verb left it, or it can move to the front and take the relative word with it. The choice does not change the meaning at all. It changes how formal the sentence sounds.

form.pattern: noun + (that / who) + subject + verb ... + preposition    |    noun + preposition + which / whom + subject + verb
notes: the everyday shape leaves the preposition at the end: the supplier we ordered from
the formal shape moves it to the front, and then only which and whom will follow it: the supplier from whom we ordered
you cannot move it to the front and also leave it at the end, and you cannot delete it in either shape
form.negative: Negatives change nothing: the supplier we did not order from, the supplier from whom we did not order.
form.question: Say the clause as a plain sentence first. He ordered from them tells you the small word is from.

rungs.text: the team I worked with
the team that I worked with
the team with which I worked
the colleagues with whom I worked

spec.top_label: a report, a formal letter, an academic passage

worked_example.sentence: The supplier we ordered the parts from has gone into administration.
worked_example.why_this_form: The preposition stays where the verb dropped it, at the end of its own clause. That is ordinary written and spoken English and it costs nothing.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: From whom we ordered the parts says exactly the same thing in a colder voice. It suits a formal report and sounds strange in an interview answer.

notice_set.sentence: The colleague I share an office with is on leave until May.
notice_set.question: How many people use that office?
notice_set.why: Sharing takes two, and the small word at the very end is the thing that tells you the office is shared.

notice_set.sentence: The scheme we campaigned against went ahead anyway.
notice_set.question: Did the speakers want the scheme?
notice_set.why: Against is doing the whole job. Everything else in the sentence would be identical either way.

notice_set.sentence: The scheme we campaigned for went ahead anyway.
notice_set.question: Did the speakers want the scheme?
notice_set.why: One word has changed and it has reversed which side the speakers were on.

notice_set.sentence: The estate agent I complained to never replied.
notice_set.question: Who made the complaint?
notice_set.why: To points the complaint away from the speaker and towards the agent, so the speaker is the one who sent it.

notice_set.sentence: The bank from which the loan came has since closed its branch here.
notice_set.question: Where did the money come from?
notice_set.why: From has moved to the front, but it is still pointing at the bank as the source.

teach.rule_line: Leave the small word at the end unless you are writing something formal.
teach.false_rule: That a sentence must never end with a preposition. That rule was borrowed from Latin and English has never once obeyed it.

errors.wrong: The flat we looked on Saturday had already been let.
errors.right: The flat we looked at on Saturday had already been let.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner moves the noun to the front and the verb sounds finished without its small word, because the ear is listening for the end of the clause rather than for the verb.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: at.

errors.wrong: The colleague I shared an office to has left the firm.
errors.right: The colleague I shared an office with has left the firm.
errors.why_it_happens: The small word is picked from what the sentence means rather than from what the verb demands, and share happens to demand with in every context, however the sentence is arranged.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: to becomes with.
errors.l1_note: Learners often carry across whichever preposition their first language uses with the same verb.

errors.wrong: The supplier to that we sent the order has gone quiet.
errors.right: The supplier to whom we sent the order has gone quiet.
errors.why_it_happens: That is the default relative word, so it survives the move to the front. Nothing warns the learner that it is the one word which refuses to stand after a preposition.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: that becomes whom.

errors.wrong: That's the department in which I work, and the people with whom I deal are mostly in Marlow.
errors.right: That's the department I work in, and the people I deal with are mostly in Marlow.
errors.why_it_happens: The fronted shape has been learned as the correct one and the end-of-clause shape as a slip. In a spoken answer the effect is a candidate who sounds like a document being read out.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: in goes to the end of the clause.

pays_in.note: Answers about your job and your home run on these constantly.
pays_in.model: The team I work with is spread across two floors, so we mostly talk online.

pays_in.note: The fronted shape gives a formal register without any extra risk.
pays_in.model: The conditions under which the scheme was approved were never made public.

pays_in.note: Academic passages front the preposition, which hides where the clause starts.
pays_in.model: The period during which the readings were taken covered two unusually dry summers.

used_in.quote: Almost every follow-up on this card produces a sentence about the people you work with or the building you study in.

payload.sentence: The manager I report to has been off since March.
payload.question: Who is more senior?

feedback.why_key: Reporting to somebody points upwards, and the small word at the end is the whole of that direction.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the last word of the clause before you decide who does what.

payload.sentence: The fund from which the grants are paid was set up in the 1970s.
payload.question: Where does the grant money come from?

feedback.why_key: From has moved to the front of the clause but it is still pointing back at the fund as the source.
feedback.feed_forward: Track the small word to whichever noun it is pointing at.

payload.context: From a first draft about staff shortages.
payload.sentence: Most of the training we relied has now been cut.
reasons: the verb has lost the small word it needs
the wrong relative word has been chosen
the clause belongs to a different noun
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Rely never stands alone. With the training moved to the front, on has nowhere to go except the end of the clause.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the clause as a plain sentence and see which word disappeared.

payload.context: From a note about a delayed order at the Marlow depot.
payload.stem: The supplier we ordered the axles ___ has stopped answering the phone.

expected: from

feedback.why_key: Turn it back into a plain sentence and you get we ordered the axles from them, which puts from at the end when the noun moves.
feedback.feed_forward: Rebuild the plain sentence to find the missing word.

payload.context: Somebody describing a flat they nearly took.
payload.stem: The place I told you ___ turned out to have no heating at all.

expected: about

feedback.why_key: You tell somebody about something, so when the something moves to the front, about is left standing at the end of the clause.
feedback.feed_forward: Check what the verb demands, not what the meaning suggests.

payload.given: The readings were taken during a period. That period covered two dry summers.
payload.instruction: Write one formal sentence with the small word at the front of the clause.

expected: during which the readings were taken covered two dry summers
during which the readings were taken covered two dry summers.

feedback.why_key: Once during moves to the front, only which can follow it, and the sentence takes on the flat formality that a methods paragraph wants.
feedback.feed_forward: Front the small word first, then put which straight after it.

payload.context: Build a formal sentence about a grant.

expected: the conditions under which the grant was made were never published

feedback.why_key: Under and which travel to the front as a pair, and the sentence does not reach its own verb until the whole clause has gone by.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the small word and which side by side when you front them.

payload.audio_text: The firm we'd been dealing with pulled out in the end.

expected: the firm we'd been dealing with pulled out in the end
the firm we had been dealing with pulled out in the end
the firm wed been dealing with pulled out in the end

feedback.why_key: With is unstressed and sits next to another unstressed word, so it is exactly the kind of thing a listener writes straight past.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen right to the end of the clause, not to the main verb.

payload.sentence: Nobody has ever explained the standards we are judged in this department.

expected: the standards we are judged by
the standards by which we are judged

feedback.why_key: Judged demands by. Without it the sentence reads as though the standards themselves are being judged somewhere in the department.
feedback.feed_forward: Add the missing word at the end, or front it with which.

items.decision_cue: with whom I speak most often

payload.context: An examiner has asked who the candidate talks to most during the week.
payload.sentence: The person with whom I speak most often is my sister.
reasons: the small word has been left out
the wrong relative word follows the preposition
it is correct, but it sounds like a written document in a conversation
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Nothing here is broken. The sentence is simply dressed for a report, and a spoken answer wants the person I speak to most.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the small word at the end when you are speaking.

payload.prompt_text: Say one sentence about a person you work or study with regularly. Keep the small word at the end where a speaker would put it.

feedback.why_key: The end-of-clause shape is what a listener expects, and it leaves you nothing extra to get wrong while you are still thinking.
feedback.feed_forward: Finish the clause with the small word and then stop.

payload.prompt_text: In your four-day-week paragraph, find a sentence about the conditions or the people involved and rewrite it once with the small word fronted. Two minutes, then read both versions back.

feedback.why_key: Fronting the preposition is one of the few ways to raise the register of a sentence without adding anything new that could break.
feedback.feed_forward: Use the fronted shape once per paragraph, never twice.

title: Shrinking a whole clause down to one word and hanging it on the subject

point_json.grammar_name: Participle clauses (-ing and -ed)

teach.can_do: I can cut a clause down to a single verb form and attach it to the subject of my sentence.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the shortest complex structure in written English and it carries one hidden condition. Get the condition wrong and the sentence says something absurd.
teach.meaning: A participle clause is a clause with the subject and the auxiliary taken out. Living beside the river is a whole clause that has been reduced to two words, and it works because the sentence supplies the missing subject from its own. That is the deal: the clause borrows a subject and the sentence lends it. The -ing shape means the subject is doing it; the -ed shape means the subject is having it done to them.

form.pattern: -ing / -ed clause , + subject + main verb ...    |    noun + -ing / -ed clause + main verb
notes: -ing when the borrowed subject does the action: families living beside the river
-ed when the borrowed subject receives it: samples collected in June
having + past participle when the first action clearly finished before the second: having lost the contract, the firm cut fifteen jobs
when the clause opens the sentence it takes a comma; when it sits behind a noun it takes none
form.negative: Not goes in front: not having heard from the council, the residents wrote again.
form.question: Ask who or what is doing the shortened verb. That answer has to be the subject of the sentence.

left.role: a clause with no subject of its own
left.text: Having finished the survey,

right.text: the team packed up and left.

spec.caption: The clause has no subject. It takes whichever one comes next, whether you meant it to or not.

worked_example.sentence: Built on flood plain, the estate has been under water twice since 2015.
worked_example.why_this_form: The estate is the thing that was built and the thing that floods, so one subject serves both halves and the sentence saves six words without losing anything.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Building on flood plain would hand the building to the estate itself, turning a housing scheme into a construction firm.

notice_set.sentence: Left unlocked overnight, the depot lost two vans.
notice_set.question: What was unlocked?
notice_set.why: The shortened opening borrows its subject from the sentence, and that subject is the depot.

notice_set.sentence: Living beside the river, the Norland families keep sandbags in the shed.
notice_set.question: Who lives beside the river?
notice_set.why: The opening has no subject of its own, so it takes the one that arrives after the comma.

notice_set.sentence: Delayed by the storm, the survey team lost two days of work.
notice_set.question: What was held up?
notice_set.why: The -ed shape means the borrowed subject is on the receiving end, and the storm is the thing doing the holding up.

notice_set.sentence: Having lost the contract, the firm cut fifteen jobs.
notice_set.question: Who lost the contract?
notice_set.why: Having borrows the subject exactly like the plain -ing shape does, and the subject here is the firm.

notice_set.sentence: The samples collected in June were the only usable ones.
notice_set.question: Who did the collecting?
options: somebody the sentence does not name
notice_set.why: The -ed shape puts the samples on the receiving end and leaves the collector out altogether.

teach.rule_line: Whoever is doing the shortened verb must be the subject of the sentence that follows.
teach.false_rule: That an -ing opening can be bolted onto any sentence to make it sound academic. It only fits a sentence whose subject is doing the -ing.

errors.wrong: Walking along the Verdon path, the smell from the mill was overpowering.
errors.right: Walking along the Verdon path, we found the smell from the mill overpowering.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer knows perfectly well who was walking, so the sentence reads correctly inside their own head. English hands the opening clause to whatever subject turns up next, and here that is a smell.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one subject: the smell becomes we.

errors.wrong: Built in 1890, the council has never repaired the mill properly.
errors.right: Built in 1890, the mill has never been properly repaired.
errors.why_it_happens: The date belongs to the mill and the writer is thinking about the mill, but the sentence has put the council in the subject slot, so the council is what got built in 1890.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one subject: the council becomes the mill.

errors.wrong: The figures publishing last week show a small rise in rainfall.
errors.right: The figures published last week show a small rise in rainfall.
errors.why_it_happens: The -ing shape is the one learners meet first and it comes to stand for both directions. Nothing in it says who is acting, so the sentence sounds fine while claiming that figures publish themselves.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one ending: publishing becomes published.

errors.wrong: Having read the report twice. She still could not see the argument.
errors.right: Having read the report twice, she still could not see the argument.
errors.why_it_happens: The opening clause is long enough to feel like a sentence, and nothing inside it announces that it is unfinished. A full stop goes in and the borrowed subject never arrives.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one full stop into a comma.

pays_in.note: It attaches a date or a source to a figure in two words.
pays_in.model: Rainfall recorded at the Verdon gauge fell in every year after 2016.

pays_in.note: It packs a reason into the front of a sentence without a linker.
pays_in.model: Faced with a shrinking budget, most councils cut the services fewest people notice.

pays_in.note: Academic passages hide whole clauses in these, which makes them hard to unpack.
pays_in.model: Species introduced during the last century now outnumber those recorded in the original survey.

used_in.quote: The problem half of this answer is a list of things done to a river, which is exactly where the -ed shape earns its place.
The passage uses reduced clauses to attach dates and methods to its nouns, and a matching question turns on unpacking one.

payload.sentence: The trees planted along the embankment have all survived the winter.
payload.question: Who did the planting?
options: somebody the sentence does not name

feedback.why_key: The -ed shape puts the trees on the receiving end, and it says nothing at all about who held the spade.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the -ed shape as something done to the noun.

payload.sentence: Living on the top floor, we hear every one of those pipes.
payload.question: Who lives on the top floor?

feedback.why_key: Nothing in the opening says who did it, so the reader hands the job to whoever turns up first after the comma.
feedback.feed_forward: Look past the comma to find who is doing the opening verb.

payload.context: From a first draft about water quality at Sandmouth.
payload.sentence: Swimming in the estuary, the bacteria levels are a real worry.
reasons: the sentence has the bacteria doing the swimming
the wrong verb ending has been used
the comma should not be there
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The opening borrows the next subject, and the next subject is bacteria levels, which is not what anyone meant.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the swimmer as the subject straight after the comma.

payload.context: From the methods paragraph of a survey write-up.
payload.stem: The readings ___ (take) before dawn were the steadiest of the week.

expected: taken

feedback.why_key: Readings do not take anything. Somebody takes them, so the shape has to be the one that puts the noun on the receiving end.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the noun acts or is acted on, then choose the ending.

payload.context: From a passage about a reserve at Norland.
payload.stem: Birds ___ (nest) on the shingle are disturbed by dogs every weekend.

expected: nesting

feedback.why_key: The birds are doing the nesting themselves, so the shape that shows the noun acting is the one that fits.
feedback.feed_forward: Use the -ing shape when the noun is the one doing it.

payload.given: The samples which were collected in June were the only usable ones.
payload.instruction: Cut the clause down to a single verb form.

expected: collected in june were the only usable ones
collected in June were the only usable ones

feedback.why_key: Which and were are carrying no meaning of their own here, so both can go and the sentence keeps everything it was saying.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete the relative word and the auxiliary, and keep the ending.

payload.given: The council had already lost two appeals. It settled the third case out of court.
payload.instruction: Open the sentence with a shortened clause that shows the first event finished first.

expected: already lost two appeals, the council settled the third case out of court
lost two appeals already, the council settled the third case out of court
lost two appeals, the council settled the third case out of court

feedback.why_key: The council does both things, so it can lend its subject to the opening and keep it for the main clause.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that one subject can honestly do both verbs.

payload.context: Build one sentence that opens with the reason.

expected: faced with a smaller budget, the council cut two routes

feedback.why_key: The council is the thing facing the budget and the thing cutting the routes, which is what allows the opening to have no subject of its own.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the borrowing subject immediately after the comma.

payload.audio_text: The land drained in the 1950s is flooding again every winter.

expected: the land drained in the 1950s is flooding again every winter

feedback.why_key: Two endings in one short sentence point in opposite directions, and the -ed one is unstressed and easy to write straight past.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the ending on the word right after the noun.

items.decision_cue: the queue was already round the block

payload.sentence: Arriving at nine in the morning, the queue was already round the block.
payload.error_span: the queue was already round the block

expected: we found the queue already round the block
we found that the queue was already round the block
visitors found the queue already round the block

feedback.why_key: As written, the queue is the thing that arrived at nine. Naming the people who arrived fixes it without touching the opening.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the person who did the opening verb straight after the comma.

payload.context: From the opening of a research summary.
payload.sentence: Measured over ten years, the decline is smaller than the headline figures suggest.
reasons: the decline cannot be measured
the wrong verb ending has been used
the comma should not be there
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: A decline is exactly the sort of thing that gets measured, so the borrowed subject fits and the sentence holds together.
feedback.feed_forward: Accept the opening when the next subject can really receive that verb.

parts: The reserve was drained for farmland in the 1950s.
It is being deliberately flooded again.
Wading birds have returned to it within four years.
model_combinations: Drained for farmland in the 1950s and now deliberately flooded again, the reserve has drawn wading birds back within four years.
The reserve, drained for farmland in the 1950s, is being flooded again, and wading birds have returned within four years.
Having been drained for farmland in the 1950s, the reserve is now being flooded again, with wading birds back within four years.

feedback.why_key: All three facts are about one place, so one subject can carry every verb and the three sentences collapse into one.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the shared subject first, then hang the shortened clauses on it.

payload.prompt_text: A town has lost most of its shops to an out-of-town retail park. Write one sentence that opens with a shortened clause giving the reason.

feedback.why_key: The reason and the result share a subject here, which is the only condition under which the opening is safe.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the opening aloud and check who is doing it.

payload.prompt_text: Open your river pollution paragraph. Find two short sentences about the same thing and fold one into the other as a shortened clause. Then check who the opening belongs to. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: This is where the structure earns its keep and where it goes wrong: under time pressure the borrowed subject is the first thing to slip.
feedback.feed_forward: Reread your opening against the subject that follows it.

title: Deciding whether to move a reported verb back, instead of doing it automatically

point_json.grammar_name: Backshift as a choice

teach.can_do: I can decide whether a reported verb should step back, instead of stepping it back every time.
teach.why_it_matters: The step back is a claim about whether the thing is still true. Applied automatically it puts live facts quietly into the past.
teach.meaning: Moving the verb back is not a tax you pay for having written said. It is a small piece of distancing, and your reader feels it. The step back says: I am reporting this from outside the moment it was spoken, and I am not standing behind it as I write. Leaving the verb where it is says the opposite — the situation has not moved, and this is a statement that is still live. English offers you both, and whichever you take, the reader takes something from it.

form.pattern: said / told + (that) + [verb stepped back]  OR  said / told + (that) + [verb left alone]
notes: after a present-tense reporting verb — says, argues, claims, points out — nothing steps back at all
a past reporting verb makes the step available, never compulsory
will becomes would, can becomes could, may becomes might; must and should do not move
an event that finished before the speaking still steps back, because the order has to stay visible
form.negative: He said he did not think the figures were reliable. / He said he does not think the figures are reliable.
form.question: Before you write said, ask: is this still true as I write?

ends: still true as I write, and I will say so
sealed inside the moment it was spoken

marks.label: She said the fee is forty pounds — I am passing on a live fact
She said the fee was forty pounds — I take no position on today
She said the fee was forty pounds, though it has gone up since

worked_example.sentence: The tutor said the library opens at eight, so there is no rush.
worked_example.why_this_form: The opening time has not changed between her saying it and you passing it on, and the second half of your sentence is leaning on that.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Opened would seal the hours inside her sentence, and a reader would wonder whether they had since changed — which the rest of your sentence denies.

notice_set.sentence: Kemi said the tap water in Verdon is safe to drink.
notice_set.question: What has the person reporting committed themselves to?
options: that the water is safe as they write
that the water was safe only when Kemi spoke
notice_set.why: Leaving the verb alone hands the claim on as live, and the reporter has signed it on the way past.

notice_set.sentence: Kemi said the tap water in Verdon was safe to drink.
notice_set.question: Does this version say the water is unsafe today?
options: No, it simply declines to say
notice_set.why: The step back is a refusal to take a position, not a denial. It hands you Kemi's words and stops.

notice_set.sentence: The porter said the lift was out of order, but it seems fine to me.
notice_set.question: Why does the second half sit comfortably here?
options: because the report was sealed at the moment he spoke
notice_set.why: The step back left room for an update, and the second clause walks straight into it.

notice_set.sentence: The porter said the lift is out of order, so take the stairs.
notice_set.question: Is the lift broken as the speaker says this?
notice_set.why: The verb was left alone, so the report is a live instruction rather than a piece of history.

notice_set.sentence: The survey found that older houses lose more heat through the roof than through the walls.
notice_set.question: Is this claim tied to the moment of the survey?
options: No, it is offered as generally true
notice_set.why: Nothing about the claim has an end date, so there is nothing for the step back to mark.

notice_set.sentence: She said she was living in Marlow.
notice_set.question: Is she living in Marlow now?
notice_set.why: The stepped-back verb covers the moment she spoke and makes no offer about anything later.

discovery.prompt: Each pair reports exactly the same words. Work out what the right-hand version is refusing to claim.
pairs: Kemi said the tap water in Verdon is safe to drink.
Kemi said the tap water in Verdon was safe to drink.
The porter said the lift is out of order.
The porter said the lift was out of order.
The letter said the deposit is refundable.
The letter said the deposit was refundable.

candidate_rules.text: The left-hand version keeps the claim live as the writer writes; the right-hand version seals it inside the moment it was spoken.
The left-hand version is for facts and the right-hand version is for opinions.
A past reporting verb such as said forces every verb after it into a past form.

teach.rule_line: Ask whether it is still true as you write. If it is, you may leave the verb alone.
teach.false_rule: That said pushes every following verb one step back. It offers the step; it does not demand it, and taking it always tells your reader something.

contrast.question: Is what they said still true as I write this?

fork.answer: Still true, and I am content to stand behind it: leave the verb where it is
Over, changed, or not something I want to vouch for: step the verb back

a.text: The agent said the flat is available from the first of the month.
a.means: It is available as I write. I am passing on a fact I expect to hold.

b.text: The agent said the flat was available from the first of the month.
b.means: That is what he told me at the time. Whether it has since gone, I am not saying.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote was. A reader takes that as a deliberate step back: you are reporting what the agent said then and declining to say whether it holds now. If you meant the flat is there today, was has quietly withdrawn the only useful part of your sentence.

edge_case.text: After a reporting verb in the present — says, argues, claims, points out — nothing steps back at all, because there is no distance to mark and no choice to make. That is the single context where the question does not arise. Everything else you have read about compulsory shifts, leave it there.

contrast.stronger_test: Read the reported clause aloud on its own, as a statement of your own. If you would say it that way today, leave the verb alone. If saying it that way would make you a liar, step it back.

worked_pairs.a: The council said the footbridge is closed until the spring.
worked_pairs.b: The council said the footbridge was closed for most of last winter.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first closure is still running as you write. The second finished before you started, so there is nothing live left to keep.

worked_pairs.a: The letter said the deposit is refundable, so I have not paid the extra.
worked_pairs.b: The letter said the deposit was refundable, though the terms changed in April.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: so I have not paid the extra
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: though the terms changed in April
worked_pairs.gloss: In the first you are acting on the claim today, so you keep it live. In the second you already know it has expired.

worked_pairs.a: Dr Anand argues that rural bus funding is the cheapest lever available.
worked_pairs.b: Dr Anand argued that rural bus funding was the cheapest lever available.
worked_pairs.gloss: A present reporting verb leaves nothing to decide. Once the reporting verb itself goes back, the choice opens and you have to make it on purpose.

errors.wrong: My landlord said the boiler was fine, so I am not going to call anyone out.
errors.right: My landlord said the boiler is fine, so I am not going to call anyone out.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has been taught that said pushes the next verb back, and applies it without reading on. The step back then withdraws the very claim the second half of the sentence is relying on.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: was becomes is.

errors.wrong: A guest on the programme said vaccines cause more harm than good.
errors.right: A guest on the programme said vaccines caused more harm than good.
errors.why_it_happens: Learners are told the unshifted form is for general truths and apply it to anything phrased like one. Leaving the verb alone reads as the writer signing a claim they never meant to sign.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: cause becomes caused.

errors.wrong: He said he was tired and he wants to go home.
errors.right: He said he was tired and he wanted to go home.
errors.why_it_happens: Both clauses came out of one breath in the original and only the first got re-anchored. Nothing in the situation justifies the split, since he is not tired-then and wanting-now.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: wants becomes wanted.

pays_in.note: Every essay that reports supporters and critics makes this choice.
pays_in.model: Critics of the charge said the savings were speculative; supporters say they are already visible.

pays_in.note: Part 3 answers are full of what people say, and the choice shows where you stand.
pays_in.model: A lot of people said the app was a gimmick, but it is still the one everyone uses.

pays_in.note: A True or False stem often turns a sealed report into a live claim.
pays_in.model: The report said the pilot scheme was cheaper to run than the existing service.

used_in.quote: The essay has to report what each side says without accidentally agreeing with either, which is this choice made a dozen times.
Answers here report claims the speaker does not believe, and the stepped-back verb is how a speaker declines to endorse one.

payload.sentence: The surveyor said the roof is sound.
payload.question: What is the writer telling you about the roof today?
options: that it was sound only when the surveyor spoke

feedback.why_key: The verb was left alone, so the report arrives as a live fact and the writer has put their name to it.
feedback.feed_forward: Read an unshifted verb as a claim the writer is making now.

payload.sentence: The driver said the coast road was flooded.

options: No, only that the driver said so at the time
No, they say it is clear

feedback.why_key: The stepped-back verb seals the report inside the driver's moment and leaves the present entirely open.

items.decision_cue: so I have cancelled my order

payload.sentence: They said the print edition was ending in June, so I have cancelled my order.
reasons: the ending has not happened yet, so the verb should not have moved
the writer has cancelled, so the report is sealed and the step back is fine
was ending is the wrong form of end
there should be a that after said

feedback.why_key: Both versions would work here. The step back reports what they told him without promising the reader that June is still the date.
feedback.feed_forward: Accept the step back whenever the writer is only relaying.

payload.context: You are writing to the department this morning and you need the reader to act on the fee. Original, spoken yesterday: "The late fee is thirty pounds."
payload.stem: Your colleague said the late fee ___ (be) thirty pounds, so I have enclosed a cheque for that amount.

expected: is

feedback.why_key: You are asking the reader to act on the figure today, so the report has to arrive as a live one.

payload.context: Talking about a flat you looked at in the spring and did not take. Original: "The rent includes the water."
payload.stem: The agent told me the rent ___ (include) the water, but I never checked it.

expected: included

feedback.why_key: You are not living there and never verified it, so the report belongs sealed inside the viewing rather than offered as fact.
feedback.feed_forward: Step the verb back when you would not vouch for it.

payload.given: The archive told us: "The recordings are open to the public." They are open as you write, and you want your reader to go.
payload.instruction: Report it so the reader can act on it.

expected: the recordings are open to the public
that the recordings are open to the public

feedback.why_key: The reader is being sent somewhere, so the claim has to be live. A stepped-back verb would leave them wondering whether it had closed.
feedback.feed_forward: Leave the verb alone when the reader is meant to act.

payload.audio_text: He said he'd finish it tonight, so I'm not chasing him.

expected: he said he'd finish it tonight, so i'm not chasing him
he said he would finish it tonight, so i am not chasing him
he said hed finish it tonight, so im not chasing him

feedback.why_key: The 'd is the whole step back and it is one unstressed sound. Miss it and the report loses the distance the speaker put there.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the 'd, then decide what it is doing.

payload.stem: The agent said the flat ___ available from the first.

options.why_this_means: That it is available as you write, and you are prepared to be held to that.
That it was available when he spoke, and you take no position on today.

expected: is

feedback.why_key: You are asking someone to act, and an action needs a live fact. A sealed report would leave them chasing something that might have gone.

items.decision_cue: though somebody else took it in the end

options.why_this_means: That it is available as you write, and you are prepared to be held to that.
That it was available when he spoke, and you take no position on today.

expected: was

feedback.why_key: Somebody else has it, so a live report would be untrue. The step back puts the claim safely back where it was made.
feedback.feed_forward: Seal the report once the situation has moved on.

items.decision_cue: and I am about to start there myself

options.why_this_means: That this is how the depot runs, and you are passing it on as fact.
That this was how it ran when he told you, with no claim about the rota you will meet.

feedback.why_key: You are describing the job you are walking into, so the shifts are a live arrangement and not a piece of Dev's history.

items.decision_cue: before the whole rota was rewritten

payload.stem: Dev told me the shifts ___ eight hours long.

options.why_this_means: That this is how the depot runs, and you are passing it on as fact.
That this was how it ran when he told you, with no claim about the rota you will meet.

expected: were

feedback.why_key: The rota has been rewritten since, so a live report would describe a depot that no longer exists.
