items.decision_cue: an argument the writer goes on to build on

payload.context: From an essay paragraph, an argument the writer goes on to build on.
payload.stem: The panel argued that recycling rates ___ largely on collection frequency.

options.why_this_means: That the writer accepts the point and is taking it forward as their own.
That the writer is relaying the panel's view and reserving judgement on it.

expected: depend

feedback.why_key: The paragraph is built on this claim, so the writer has to hold it live. A sealed version would leave the argument standing on nothing.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep a claim live when your next sentence leans on it.

items.decision_cue: a view the writer spends the next paragraph dismantling

payload.context: From an essay paragraph, a view the writer spends the next paragraph dismantling.
payload.stem: The panel argued that recycling rates ___ largely on collection frequency.

options.why_this_means: That the writer accepts the point and is taking it forward as their own.
That the writer is relaying the panel's view and reserving judgement on it.

expected: depended

feedback.why_key: You are about to take the claim apart, so signing it in the previous sentence would leave you arguing with yourself.
feedback.feed_forward: Step back from a claim you are about to attack.

items.decision_cue: a documentary somebody watched last month

payload.context: Two people discussing a documentary somebody watched last month.
payload.stem: The programme said local papers ___ half their readers in ten years.

options.why_this_means: That the loss is a fact you are happy to repeat as your own.
That this was the programme's figure, and you are relaying it without checking it.

follow_up.question: Which version puts the figure on you rather than on the programme?

feedback.why_key: Both are correct English and they hand the reader a different author for the same number. That difference is the whole point of the choice.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide whose figure it is before you pick the form.

payload.context: Two sentences from different parts of a prospectus.
sentences: The department said the placement is compulsory.
The department said the placement was compulsory.
meanings: You should plan on doing a placement; the prospectus is standing behind it.
That is what the department said at the time; check before you plan anything.

feedback.why_key: One version is advice you can act on. The other is a record of something somebody once said. The reader is entitled to know which.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask which version a reader could safely act on.

items.decision_cue: and the samples arrive on Thursday

payload.context: From a draft essay paragraph about a delayed study.
payload.sentence: The team said the first results were disappointing and the samples arrive on Thursday.
reasons: half the report was re-anchored and half was left alone for no reason
the results were not disappointing
arrive is the wrong form of the verb
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Nothing in the situation separates the two clauses, so the split is an accident and the reader has to decide which frame is real.
feedback.feed_forward: Split the frames only when the meaning asks you to.

payload.prompt_text: Somebody told you last year that people would stop paying for news altogether. You think they were wrong. Write one sentence reporting them in a way that makes clear you do not agree.

feedback.why_key: The step back is how English lets you put somebody's claim on the page without adopting it, and that is exactly what you need here.
feedback.feed_forward: Step the verb back when you want the claim kept at arm's length.

payload.prompt_text: Open your last answer to this prompt and find one sentence reporting somebody else's view. Rewrite it twice: once so you are standing behind the claim, once so you are not. Then say which one the paragraph needs. Four minutes.

feedback.why_key: Seeing both versions of your own sentence side by side is the fastest way to feel that the step back is a decision rather than a reflex.
feedback.feed_forward: In the final read-through, check every reported verb against your own position.

title: Choosing a reporting verb that says what you think of the claim

point_json.grammar_name: Reporting verbs and their patterns

teach.can_do: I can choose a reporting verb that shows what I think of a claim, and get its pattern right.
teach.why_it_matters: Said is neutral and free. Claimed, argued, admitted and pointed out each add a judgement, and the judgement lands whether you meant it or not.
teach.meaning: Every reporting verb does two jobs in one word. It reports, and it rates. Argue says the person is building a case. Claim says they have asserted something you are not signing. Admit says the statement cost them something. Point out says it was a fact already lying there. Concede says they gave ground under pressure. The second job is why this is essay grammar and not vocabulary. Each verb also carries its own pattern, which cannot be worked out from the meaning and has to be stored with the word.

form.pattern: verb + that-clause | verb + -ing | verb + object + to-infinitive | verb + preposition + -ing
notes: that-clause: argue, claim, point out, insist, deny, admit, concede, warn, suggest
-ing form: admit, deny, suggest — she denied seeing the email
object + to-infinitive: urge, advise, warn, remind — they urged the council to reopen it
preposition + -ing: accuse someone of, warn against, insist on, object to
suggest never takes an object with to: not suggest us to wait
form.negative: He denied that the figures had been changed. / He denied changing the figures.
form.question: Which verb says what I actually think of this claim?

spec.label: how far am I standing behind this?

steps.gloss: it is a fact and I am with them
they demonstrated it and I accept it
they are making a case; I am neutral
they float it, and so do I
they assert it; I am not signing
they assert it and I have doubts

worked_example.sentence: Supporters of the charge point out that the money is ring-fenced for buses.
worked_example.why_this_form: Point out treats the ring-fencing as a fact already sitting there, so the writer has quietly agreed with it before the argument even starts.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Claim would hold the same words at arm's length: the money may or may not be ring-fenced, and the writer is not vouching for it.

notice_set.sentence: The company admitted that the data had been stored abroad.
notice_set.question: Was this comfortable for the company?
notice_set.why: Admit is only used when the statement costs the person making it something.

notice_set.sentence: The company claimed that the data had been stored securely.
notice_set.question: Is the writer standing behind this?
options: No, the writer is only reporting it
The writer says it is false
notice_set.why: Claim reports an assertion and declines to endorse it. It does not say the assertion is false.

notice_set.sentence: Ms Oduya pointed out that the two figures had been measured differently.
notice_set.question: Is this presented as something already true?
notice_set.why: Point out treats the difference as a fact lying in plain sight that somebody has drawn attention to.

notice_set.sentence: The panel conceded that the first estimate had been too low.
notice_set.question: Whose estimate was it?
notice_set.why: Concede means giving ground, and you can only give ground on your own position.

notice_set.sentence: The union urged the trust to reopen the ward.
notice_set.question: Who would reopen the ward?
notice_set.why: Urge takes an object and a to-infinitive, and the object is the one who would act.

notice_set.sentence: The developer denied cutting the number of affordable flats.
notice_set.question: What does the developer say happened?
notice_set.why: Deny takes an -ing form and reverses it: the developer's position is that no cut took place.

discovery.prompt: The same report is written two ways. Work out what the second verb in each pair is doing besides reporting.
pairs: The minister said the scheme would pay for itself.
The minister claimed the scheme would pay for itself.
Researchers said the effect was small.
Researchers found the effect was small.
The council said the consultation had been rushed.
The council admitted the consultation had been rushed.

candidate_rules.text: The second verb adds the writer's rating of the claim on top of the report.
The second verb in each pair is simply more formal than said.
Any reporting verb can replace said as long as a that-clause follows it.

teach.rule_line: Pick the verb that says what you think of the claim, then check its pattern.
teach.false_rule: That these verbs are synonyms of said that make writing look academic. Swapping one in without meaning its judgement is how an essay accidentally takes a side.

contrast.question: Am I signing this claim, staying neutral, or holding it away from me?

fork.answer: Signing it — it is a checkable fact and I am with them
Neutral — they are making a case and I am reporting it
At arm's length — they assert it and I am not vouching for it

a.text: The developer pointed out that the flats would be built on brownfield land.
a.means: The brownfield land is a fact, and the writer has accepted it on the way past.

b.text: The developer claimed that the flats would be built on brownfield land.
b.means: That is the developer's assertion, and the writer is not standing behind it.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote claimed. In one word you have told your reader you do not believe the developer, and the rest of your paragraph now has to earn that. If you had no reason to doubt them, claimed has picked a fight you did not intend to pick.

edge_case.text: Suggest is the trap of the set. It takes a that-clause or an -ing form and never an object with to, so suggest us to wait is wrong however natural it feels next to advise us to wait. Store suggest that and suggest doing as two fixed chunks and stop reasoning about it.

contrast.stronger_test: Read your sentence back as if you were the person being reported. If they would object to the verb you chose, you have taken a position. Decide whether you meant to take it.

worked_pairs.a: Campaigners point out that both consultations closed in August, which the council's own diary confirms.
worked_pairs.b: Campaigners claim that both consultations were deliberately timed to be missed.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: which the council's own diary confirms
worked_pairs.gloss: A date anybody can check invites point out. A statement about somebody's intentions is exactly what claim is for.

worked_pairs.a: The trust admitted that it had missed the target for a third year.
worked_pairs.b: The trust insisted that it had missed the target only because of the strike.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: it had missed the target for a third year
worked_pairs.gloss: Admit is for something that costs the speaker. Insist is for a defence they are holding on to while somebody pushes.

worked_pairs.a: Drawing on three small trials, the report suggests that shorter shifts reduce errors.
worked_pairs.b: Drawing on a decade of hospital records, the report shows that shorter shifts reduce errors.
worked_pairs.gloss: The strength of the evidence picks the verb. Suggest is honest about thin evidence; show over-claims on it.

errors.wrong: The committee suggested us to postpone the vote.
errors.right: The committee suggested postponing the vote.
errors.why_it_happens: Suggest sits in the same meaning space as advise and urge, and both of those take an object with to. The pattern cannot be worked out from the meaning, so it has to be stored with the word.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one span: us to postpone becomes postponing.

errors.wrong: The report accused the operator to cut corners on maintenance.
errors.right: The report accused the operator of cutting corners on maintenance.
errors.why_it_happens: Accuse looks like a verb that should take to, because so many verbs in this family do. Its preposition is of, and after of English takes only an -ing form.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one span: to cut becomes of cutting.

errors.wrong: She denied to send the message from the shared account.
errors.right: She denied sending the message from the shared account.
errors.why_it_happens: Deny is stored as a refusal verb and refuse takes to. Deny takes an -ing form or a that-clause and never an infinitive, which is a fact about the word rather than about refusing.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: to send becomes sending.

errors.wrong: The survey proves that shoppers prefer independent shops.
errors.right: The survey suggests that shoppers prefer independent shops.
errors.why_it_happens: Proves feels like the strongest available word and therefore the most persuasive. The reader hears a promise the evidence cannot keep, and the whole paragraph loses credit for it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: proves becomes suggests.

pays_in.note: It is how an essay gets other voices in without agreeing with all of them.
pays_in.model: Critics argue that the levy is regressive; the review concedes that its early years were poorly targeted.

pays_in.note: Paraphrase questions turn on whether the writer signed the claim or only reported it.
pays_in.model: The author notes that the two surveys used different age bands.

pays_in.note: Referring to what people argue lifts an answer off your own opinion.
pays_in.model: A lot of people argue that streaming has killed the album, though the sales figures suggest otherwise.

used_in.quote: A discussion essay on funding has to report two sides fairly, and the verb chosen for each side is where fairness is won or lost.
The card asks who gets believed and why, so answers report claims the speaker rates very differently.
The passage reports several researchers with different verbs, and one question depends on noticing which one the author endorses.

payload.sentence: The broadcaster conceded that the interview had been edited before transmission.
payload.question: Was this something the broadcaster wanted to say?

feedback.why_key: Concede reports a position given up under pressure, which is information about the situation and not just about the words.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the reporting verb as information about the speaker.

payload.sentence: The team leader urged the depot to keep two vans on standby.
payload.question: Who would keep the vans on standby?

feedback.why_key: Urge puts the person being pushed straight after it, and that person is the one who would act.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the object after urge; that is the doer.

payload.context: From an essay paragraph resting on a single pilot study.
payload.sentence: The pilot study proves that shorter lessons improve retention.
reasons: the verb claims more than one pilot study can support
shorter lessons do not improve retention
proves is the wrong form of the verb
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The verb writes a cheque the evidence cannot cash, and a reader who notices stops trusting the rest of the paragraph.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the verb's strength to the evidence you have.

payload.context: Original: "We did not release anything into the river."
payload.stem: The plant denied ___ (release) anything into the river.

expected: releasing
having released

feedback.why_key: Deny takes an -ing form, which is a fact about the word and not something the meaning can tell you.
feedback.feed_forward: Store deny with an -ing form attached.

payload.context: Original: "The channel has been burying corrections."
payload.stem: The regulator accused the channel ___ burying corrections.

expected: of

feedback.why_key: Accuse comes with of welded to it, and the -ing form after it is there because of arrived first.
feedback.feed_forward: Learn accuse of as one unit, never as two words.

payload.given: The panel said: "Screening should start five years earlier."
payload.instruction: Report it with suggest, using the pattern suggest takes.

expected: that screening should start five years earlier
screening should start five years earlier
starting screening five years earlier

feedback.why_key: Suggest takes a that-clause or an -ing form. It never takes an object with to, however much it feels like advise.
feedback.feed_forward: After suggest, write that or an -ing form.

payload.audio_text: They've admitted deleting the footage, but they've denied doing it deliberately.

expected: they've admitted deleting the footage, but they've denied doing it deliberately
they have admitted deleting the footage, but they have denied doing it deliberately
theyve admitted deleting the footage, but theyve denied doing it deliberately

feedback.why_key: Two verbs, two -ing forms, and two completely different admissions. Miss one and the sentence says the opposite of what was said.
feedback.feed_forward: Catch the -ing form that follows each reporting verb.

items.decision_cue: figures the council has published itself

payload.context: The writer is using figures the council has published itself and is not disputing them.
payload.stem: Residents' groups ___ that the estate has lost two of its four bus routes.

options.why_this_means: That the loss is a fact on the record and the writer accepts it.
That this is the groups' assertion and the writer is not vouching for it.

expected: point out

feedback.why_key: The figures are the council's own, so there is nothing to hold at arm's length and holding it there would look evasive.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the claim is checkable before you pick the verb.

items.decision_cue: a figure nobody has been able to check

payload.context: The writer is repeating a figure nobody has been able to check and intends to query it later.
payload.stem: Residents' groups ___ that the estate has lost two of its four bus routes.

options.why_this_means: That the loss is a fact on the record and the writer accepts it.
That this is the groups' assertion and the writer is not vouching for it.

expected: claim

feedback.why_key: You are about to query the figure, so signing it in the sentence before would leave you arguing against yourself.
feedback.feed_forward: Hold a claim at arm's length if you plan to query it.

payload.context: The study followed twelve volunteers over one week.
payload.stem: The authors ___ that daylight lamps improve winter concentration.

options.why_this_means: That the finding leans one way and the evidence is thin.
That the finding is established and the writer is treating it as settled.

expected: suggest

feedback.why_key: Twelve people over one week will support a lean, not a settlement, and the verb has to say which of those you have.
feedback.feed_forward: Size the verb to the study before you write it.

items.decision_cue: eleven thousand workers across four winters

payload.context: The study followed eleven thousand workers across four winters and has been repeated twice.
payload.stem: The authors ___ that daylight lamps improve winter concentration.

options.why_this_means: That the finding leans one way and the evidence is thin.
That the finding is established and the writer is treating it as settled.

expected: show

feedback.why_key: Hedging evidence this strong is its own kind of inaccuracy: the reader is told to doubt something the writer has no reason to doubt.
feedback.feed_forward: Do not hedge a finding the evidence fully supports.

items.decision_cue: which had been their own policy for years

payload.context: The board was defending a pay freeze which had been their own policy for years.
payload.stem: The board ___ that the freeze had held wages below inflation.

options.why_this_means: That the point went against them and they gave it up.
That they were holding a line while somebody pushed at it.

expected: admitted

feedback.why_key: The point damages their own policy, and a verb that damages the speaker is exactly what admit is for.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whose case the claim hurts, then choose.

items.decision_cue: against three hours of questions from the floor

payload.context: The board held the same line against three hours of questions from the floor.
payload.stem: The board ___ that the freeze had protected jobs at the plant.

options.why_this_means: That the point went against them and they gave it up.
That they were holding a line while somebody pushed at it.

expected: insisted

feedback.why_key: The claim helps their case and they repeated it under pressure, which is the situation insist exists to report.
feedback.feed_forward: Use insisted for a position defended under pressure.

items.decision_cue: a long piece about local newspapers

payload.context: From a long piece about local newspapers, where the writer has not yet declared a position.
payload.stem: The editor ___ that free distribution had kept the paper alive.

options.why_this_means: That she was making a case, and the writer is reporting it without judging it.
That she has held this view for a long time and has been challenged on it.

follow_up.question: Which version implies somebody has been arguing back?

feedback.why_key: Both are neutral and both are correct. They differ in whether the reader is told there is an opposing view in the room.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose on what the reader needs to know about the argument.

payload.context: Two sentences from different sections of the same review of a clinic.
sentences: The trust acknowledged that waiting times had risen.
The trust alleged that waiting times had been recorded incorrectly.
meanings: The trust accepted a point that did not help it, and the writer treats it as settled.
The trust made an accusation, and the writer is keeping well clear of it.

feedback.why_key: One verb records something conceded, the other records something asserted against somebody else. The writer's distance is different in each.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask who each claim damages before you read on.

payload.sentence: The waste review suggested residents to sort food waste separately, which most of them already did.

expected: suggested that residents sort
suggested that residents should sort
suggested sorting

feedback.why_key: Suggest will not take an object with to. The pattern has come across from advise, which means something similar and behaves differently.
feedback.feed_forward: Replace the object and to with a that-clause after suggest.

payload.prompt_text: Write two sentences about a change in how people get their news. In the first, report a view you accept. In the second, report a view you do not accept. Do not use said in either.

feedback.why_key: Two sentences of the same shape with two different verbs is the fastest way to feel how much of your position lives in the verb.
feedback.feed_forward: Check each verb against what you actually think.

payload.prompt_text: Write one body paragraph for this prompt that reports both sides. Use three different reporting verbs, none of them said, and make sure each one shows where you stand. Eight minutes.

feedback.why_key: A discussion paragraph that reports both sides with the same verb has not discussed anything. The verbs are where the discussion actually happens.
feedback.feed_forward: Read back the three verbs alone and check the pattern of each.

title: Keeping everything in a list the same shape as everything else

point_json.grammar_name: Parallel structure

teach.can_do: I can build a list where every item has the same shape, so my reader can take them in at one go.
teach.why_it_matters: Readers read a list by its pattern. Break the pattern in the third item and they go back to the beginning, which costs you far more than the words saved.
teach.meaning: When you join things with and, or, but or than, English expects the joined parts to be built the same way. Three nouns, or three -ing forms, or three whole clauses, but not two nouns and a clause. The shape is what tells a reader where each item ends and the next begins. When one item changes shape halfway through, the reader loses the thread and has to reread, and they will blame the sentence rather than themselves.

form.pattern: item + , + item + and / or + item, all built the same way
notes: the commonest break is the last item, because by then the writer is thinking about content and not about shape
the paired joiners are stricter still: both ... and, either ... or, not only ... but also, whether ... or
with the paired joiners, whatever follows the first half must match whatever follows the second
than and as are joiners too: better at running than at swimming, not better at running than to swim
form.negative: A negative list matches as well: the scheme covers neither travel nor equipment.
form.question: Read the joining word, then read each item on its own with the opening of the sentence. Do all of them fit?

left.role: the pattern breaks on the last item
left.text: fitness, concentration and it helps them sleep

right.text: fitness, concentration and sleep

spec.caption: A reader takes a list in by its shape. Change the shape and they start it again.

worked_example.sentence: The scheme pays for coaching, equipment and travel to away matches.
worked_example.why_this_form: Three nouns in a row let the reader take all three in one movement, because the shape itself says where each item begins and ends.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Coaching, equipment and it pays for travel turns the third item into a fresh sentence, and the reader goes back to check whether they missed something.

notice_set.sentence: The club offers coaching, equipment and transport to matches.
notice_set.question: How many things does the club offer?
notice_set.why: Three items of the same shape, so the counting happens without any effort at all.

notice_set.sentence: The club offers coaching, equipment and it will take children to away matches.
notice_set.question: How many things does the club offer?
notice_set.why: The third item has changed shape, so it no longer reads as part of the same list and the count comes apart.

notice_set.sentence: Children who play twice a week sleep better than those who play once.
notice_set.question: Which group sleeps better?
notice_set.why: Both sides of than are built the same way, so the comparison lines up and the answer falls out of it.

notice_set.sentence: The council will either build a new pool or refurbish the old one.
notice_set.question: How many of these will the council do?
notice_set.why: Either and or offer a choice of one, and the two matching verbs make it clear these are the two options.

notice_set.sentence: Not only does the club train children, but it also runs a holiday scheme.
notice_set.question: How many activities does the club run?
notice_set.why: The paired joiner promises a second item and delivers exactly one, in the same shape as the first.

teach.rule_line: Everything joined by and, or or than has to be built the same way.
teach.false_rule: That variety is a virtue, so items in a list should look different from one another. Variety belongs between sentences, never inside one list.

errors.wrong: The programme improves fitness, concentration and helps children sleep.
errors.right: The programme improves fitness and concentration, and helps children sleep.
errors.why_it_happens: By the third item the writer is thinking about what to say rather than about the shape they set up two items ago, and the sentence quietly changes gear.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one comma into and.

errors.wrong: Children learn more by playing regularly than to sit through a lesson about it.
errors.right: Children learn more by playing regularly than by sitting through a lesson about it.
errors.why_it_happens: Than feels like a link between two ideas rather than between two matching shapes, so the second half is built from scratch in whatever form comes to mind.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one form: to sit becomes by sitting.

errors.wrong: The club offers coaching, to hire equipment and free travel.
errors.right: The club offers coaching, equipment hire and free travel.
errors.why_it_happens: The middle item arrives as an action rather than as a thing, because that is how the writer thought of it, and nothing forces it back into the shape of its neighbours.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one item: to hire equipment becomes equipment hire.

errors.wrong: Not only the club trains children but also it runs a holiday scheme.
errors.right: The club not only trains children but also runs a holiday scheme.
errors.why_it_happens: Not only has been learned as a phrase that opens a sentence, so it goes to the front. From there it takes a whole clause on each side and the two halves stop matching.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one phrase: not only goes after the club.

pays_in.note: Any sentence listing reasons or benefits is a list, and lists break.
pays_in.model: Daily exercise improves concentration, attendance and behaviour in the afternoon.

pays_in.note: Chart answers list categories, and the categories have to match.
pays_in.model: Spending rose in housing, transport and education, and fell in everything else.

pays_in.note: A long turn is mostly lists, and a broken list is audible.
pays_in.model: It was cheap, easy to get to and open until quite late.

used_in.quote: The benefits paragraph on this prompt is one long list, which is exactly where a shape starts to slip.

payload.sentence: The centre runs classes in swimming, judo and climbing.
payload.question: How many activities does the centre run classes in?

feedback.why_key: Three items of the same shape count themselves, and the reader never has to stop and work anything out.
feedback.feed_forward: Count the items by their shape, not by the commas.

payload.sentence: She's better at running long distances than at sprinting.
payload.question: Which does she do better?

feedback.why_key: Both sides of than open with at and a verb form, so the two halves line up and the comparison is unmistakable.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that both sides of than start the same way.

payload.context: From a draft on school sport.
payload.sentence: Daily exercise improves concentration, attendance and it also builds confidence.
reasons: the last item is built differently from the first two
there are too many items in the list
the verb does not agree with the subject
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Two nouns set up a pattern and the third item arrives as a whole clause, so the reader loses the list and has to go back to the verb.
feedback.feed_forward: Make the last item match the shape of the first.

payload.context: From a paragraph about a village sports club.
payload.stem: The club depends on volunteers for coaching, fundraising and ___ (maintain) the pitches.

expected: maintaining

feedback.why_key: The first two items are -ing forms, so the third has to be one as well or the list changes gear on its last word.
feedback.feed_forward: Copy the shape of the first item into the last.

payload.given: The scheme pays for coaching. It pays for equipment. It also pays for travel to away matches.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence with all three items in the same shape.

expected: coaching, equipment and travel to away matches
coaching, equipment and travel

feedback.why_key: One verb serves all three items once they are the same shape, and the sentence drops from fifteen words to nine.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the verb once and hang matching items off it.

payload.given: Not only the college teaches languages but also it runs evening courses.
payload.instruction: Rewrite this so both halves match after the paired joiner.

expected: teaches languages but also runs evening courses
teaches languages, but also runs evening courses

feedback.why_key: With the subject in front, each half of the pair is now just a verb and its object, and the two halves finally match.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the subject first, then the paired joiner.

payload.context: Build one sentence about cheap ways of staying active.

expected: walking, cycling and swimming are all free or nearly free

feedback.why_key: Three -ing forms make one subject, and because they match, the verb after them can be a single word.
feedback.feed_forward: Set the shape with the first item and hold it.

payload.audio_text: It's cheap, easy to reach and open until ten.

expected: it's cheap, easy to reach and open until ten
it is cheap easy to reach and open until ten
its cheap easy to reach and open until ten

feedback.why_key: Three describing items hang off one squashed opening, and the and is the only signal that the list is about to close.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for and to know the list is ending.

items.decision_cue: and to reduce the cost of equipment

payload.sentence: The plan involves opening the pitches at weekends, training more volunteers and to reduce the cost of equipment.
payload.error_span: and to reduce the cost of equipment

expected: and reducing the cost of equipment
and cutting the cost of equipment

feedback.why_key: Two -ing forms have set the shape, and the third item arrives in a different one, which is where the reader stumbles.
feedback.feed_forward: Change the odd item to match the two before it.

payload.context: From a paragraph about the four-day week.
payload.sentence: Most staff would rather work five ordinary days than working four longer ones.
reasons: the two sides of the comparison are built differently
the comparison word is wrong
the subject and the verb do not match
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Would rather work sets a plain verb on the first side, so the second side needs work rather than working.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the verb form on both sides of than.

payload.prompt_text: Write one sentence giving three reasons why a school might make daily exercise compulsory. All three reasons must be built the same way.

feedback.why_key: Three reasons in one shape read as one argument. Three reasons in three shapes read as a writer thinking aloud.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the first item, then copy its shape twice.

payload.prompt_text: Open your answer on daily school exercise. Find every and and or in it, read the items on either side, and fix any pair that is not built the same way. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: Hunting for the joining words rather than reading for sense is what finds these, because a broken list still means what you intended.
feedback.feed_forward: Search for the joining words, then check both sides.

title: Not saying the same words twice, and leaving out what the reader can rebuild

point_json.grammar_name: Substitution and ellipsis: one, ones, do so, so, not

teach.can_do: I can avoid repeating myself by leaving a placeholder where the repeat would have been.
teach.why_it_matters: Repetition is the loudest sign of a writer with a small toolkit, and this is the cheapest way out of it. Nothing new has to be learned, only left out.
teach.meaning: English hates saying the same words twice in a row. Instead of repeating a noun it puts a placeholder there: one, ones, that one. Instead of repeating a verb and everything after it, it leaves only the auxiliary standing: does, did, has, will. Instead of repeating a whole clause it uses so or not. Every one of these is a promise to the reader that the missing words are recoverable from what came before, and the promise has to be kept.

form.pattern: one / ones for a noun · do, does, did, do so for a verb phrase · so / not for a whole clause
notes: one and ones need something to stand for: the small loaf, the fresh ones
the leftover auxiliary must match the kind of verb it replaces: cycle takes do, is takes is, has finished takes has
so and not follow think, hope, believe, expect and suppose: I hope so, I think not
after and, but, or and than, English deletes whatever is identical: Halima can drive and her brother cannot
form.negative: The negative lives on the leftover auxiliary: some cafés take cards and some do not.
form.question: Ask whether your reader can put the missing words back word for word. If not, put them back yourself.

left.text: I took the small loaf because the small loaf was fresher.

right.role: the repeat swapped for a placeholder
right.text: I took the small loaf because that one was fresher.

spec.caption: English does not repeat. It leaves a marker where the repeat would have gone.

worked_example.sentence: Some canteens still cook from scratch; most no longer do.
worked_example.why_this_form: Do stands in for cook from scratch, so the second half is four words long and the contrast between the two groups lands without anything in the way.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Most no longer cook from scratch repeats three words the reader already holds and buries the contrast somewhere in the middle of them.

notice_set.sentence: Some of the cafés take cards; the older ones don't.
notice_set.question: Can you pay by card in the older cafés?
notice_set.why: Don't is standing in for don't take cards, and the words it replaces are only two clauses back.

notice_set.sentence: Halima said the market would be open, and I hope so.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker know whether it is open?
notice_set.why: So stands in for the whole clause about the market, and hoping is what you do when you have no information.

notice_set.sentence: The big supermarkets deliver; the corner shop does too.
notice_set.question: Does the corner shop deliver?
notice_set.why: Does carries the whole of deliver across, and too adds the corner shop to the group.

notice_set.sentence: I asked for the brown loaf, but they'd sold the last one.
notice_set.question: Did the speaker get the brown loaf?
notice_set.why: One stands in for brown loaf, and the last one being sold means there was none left.

notice_set.sentence: Neither of the cafés opens before eight, and nor does the bakery.
notice_set.question: Can you buy bread at half past seven?
notice_set.why: Nor does carries the negative across to the bakery without repeating a single word of it.

teach.rule_line: Leave a word out only when your reader can rebuild it exactly.
teach.false_rule: That leaving words out looks careless and repeating them is the safe option. Repetition is what makes a paragraph read like a machine.

errors.wrong: There were two loaves left and I took the fresher.
errors.right: There were two loaves left and I took the fresher one.
errors.why_it_happens: In a great many languages an adjective can stand on its own as a noun. English needs a placeholder in that slot and the learner has no reason to suspect it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: one.
errors.l1_note: Common for speakers of Spanish, Italian, French, German and Russian.

errors.wrong: Some people cook every night and some are not.
errors.right: Some people cook every night and some do not.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner reaches for the auxiliary they use most rather than the one that matches the verb being replaced, and cook is not a be verb, so nothing can be borrowed from it.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: are becomes do.

errors.wrong: She said she would bring the bread, and I hope it.
errors.right: She said she would bring the bread, and I hope so.
errors.why_it_happens: It is the all-purpose placeholder in most learners' English, so it turns up wherever something has to be stood in for. So is the one that carries a whole clause, and it is the only one that will.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: it becomes so.

errors.wrong: I don't think the rules will change, and neither my colleagues.
errors.right: I don't think the rules will change, and neither do my colleagues.
errors.why_it_happens: Neither feels like a complete link on its own, and in several languages it is. English wants an auxiliary after it and then the subject, in that order.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: do.

pays_in.note: It keeps a comparison short enough to finish inside one breath.
pays_in.model: Older shoppers still use the market; younger ones mostly don't.

pays_in.note: It removes the repetition that makes a body paragraph read like a list.
pays_in.model: Some countries tax sugary drinks heavily; others have declined to do so.

pays_in.note: A short answer is often nothing but an auxiliary, with the meaning further back.
pays_in.model: The morning session does, but the afternoon one doesn't.

used_in.quote: This prompt sets two groups of schools against each other, and the second half of every comparison is where the words drop out.

payload.sentence: The northern schools kept their kitchens; the southern ones did not.
payload.question: Do the southern schools have kitchens?

feedback.why_key: Did not is carrying keep their kitchens across the semicolon, so the southern schools gave theirs up.
feedback.feed_forward: Rebuild the missing words from the clause before.

payload.sentence: I wanted the seeded rolls but they only had the plain ones.
payload.question: What did the speaker end up with?

feedback.why_key: Ones stands in for rolls, so plain ones is the only thing the shop had, whatever the speaker wanted.
feedback.feed_forward: Read ones as the noun from earlier in the sentence.

payload.context: Two people talking about who cooks at home.
payload.sentence: I cook most evenings and my brother is too.
reasons: the leftover word does not match the verb it is standing in for
the placeholder should be a noun
too should be at the front
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Cook has no be in it, so there is no is to leave behind. The verb that stands in for it is does.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the leftover auxiliary to the verb it replaces.

payload.context: From a paragraph comparing two kinds of school meal.
payload.stem: Both menus were cheap, but the cooked ___ was better balanced.

expected: one

feedback.why_key: Menus is already on the page, so English wants a placeholder rather than the noun again, and it will not accept the adjective on its own.
feedback.feed_forward: Put one after an adjective that is standing for a noun.

payload.context: Two colleagues comparing their weekends.
payload.stem: I swim on Saturdays and Marek ___ too, though he goes much earlier.

expected: does

feedback.why_key: Swim needs a do form to stand in for it, and Marek is one person, so the ending goes on.
feedback.feed_forward: Pick the auxiliary from the verb, then fix the ending.

payload.given: Some councils have banned fast food outlets near schools. Most councils have not banned fast food outlets near schools.
payload.instruction: Write the second sentence again without repeating anything.

expected: have not
have not, however
councils have not

feedback.why_key: Everything after have is identical, so the reader can rebuild all of it and none of it needs writing out.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete everything the previous sentence already supplied.

payload.context: Talking about a childhood street.

expected: my parents grew vegetables and so did everyone on the street

feedback.why_key: So and the auxiliary come first and the subject follows them, which is the one place in a plain sentence where that order is required.
feedback.feed_forward: Put so, then the auxiliary, then the subject.

payload.audio_text: Some of them deliver and some of them don't, honestly.

expected: some of them deliver and some of them don't, honestly
some of them deliver and some of them do not honestly
some of them deliver and some of them dont honestly

feedback.why_key: The whole of the second half is carried by one contracted word, and if you miss it the sentence says the opposite.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a single stressed auxiliary at the end of a clause.

payload.sentence: The trust does not publish waiting times, and neither the private clinics.

expected: and neither do the private clinics
nor do the private clinics

feedback.why_key: Neither carries the negative but it cannot carry the verb as well. Do has to arrive before the subject to finish the job.
feedback.feed_forward: Follow neither and nor with an auxiliary, then the subject.

items.decision_cue: some have declined to do so

payload.context: From a passage about how governments respond to a rise in food prices.
payload.sentence: Several governments have capped the price of staples, though some have declined to do so.
reasons: do so has nothing to stand for
the wrong auxiliary has been chosen
the two halves should be separate sentences
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Do so is standing in for cap the price of staples, which is six words back and rebuildable exactly, so the promise is kept.
feedback.feed_forward: Accept the shortening when the missing words are recoverable.

payload.prompt_text: Some schools teach children to cook and some have dropped it. Write one sentence comparing the two groups without repeating the verb.

feedback.why_key: The second half of a comparison is where repetition piles up, and it is also where it is easiest to remove.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the first half fully, then delete every repeated word.

payload.prompt_text: Open your paragraph on cooking lessons in schools. Find any noun or verb you have written twice within three lines and remove the second one. Then read the paragraph aloud and check nothing has gone missing. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: Reading it aloud is the test that matters: if a listener can rebuild the missing words, so can a reader.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete the second copy, then read the paragraph aloud.

title: Knowing when a linking word earns its place and when it costs you

point_json.grammar_name: Linker restraint: cohesion built into the sentence rather than bolted onto it

teach.can_do: I can tell when a linking word is doing real work and when it is only announcing that I know some linking words.
teach.why_it_matters: Stacking linkers is the single clearest sign of a memorised answer. It lowers the impression of your writing while feeling, as you do it, like an improvement.
teach.meaning: A linking word is a road sign. Its job is to stop a reader taking the wrong turning, and where there is only one turning it is clutter. Most connections between sentences are already carried by what the sentences say: a cause looks like a cause, a contrast looks like a contrast. Real cohesion comes from ordering ideas so each one grows out of the last, from pointing back with a noun, and from joining clauses. A sign nailed on afterwards is not the same thing.

form.pattern: add a marker only where a careful reader might otherwise join the ideas wrongly
notes: one signposted relation per two or three sentences is plenty in a short answer
never open more than one sentence in a paragraph with the same kind of marker
prefer the joins that live inside a sentence: although, because, which, and a noun that points back
if the sentence before already makes the relation obvious, the marker is only telling the reader what they know
form.negative: Not every contrast needs marking: two sentences that plainly disagree already disagree.
form.question: Cover the linking word. Does the paragraph still say the same thing? Then it was not doing anything.

spec.label: how much work is this linking word actually doing?

steps.gloss: three ways of saying keep reading; almost never needed
useful once in a long answer, ruinous once per sentence
earn their place when the turn would genuinely surprise a reader
the relation is built into the sentence, where nobody can skip it

worked_example.sentence: Rents in the capital doubled in a decade. Younger workers moved out to towns like Ashfield, where a flat still costs half as much.
worked_example.why_this_form: The second sentence follows from the first because of what it says. Nothing needs announcing when the content already points in one direction.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Opening with therefore would tell the reader something they had already worked out, and would quietly suggest you did not trust them to do it.

notice_set.sentence: Wages have not risen since 2015. Rents over the same period have gone up by a third.
notice_set.question: Are people better or worse off than they were?
notice_set.why: Nothing announced the contrast and you found it anyway, because the two facts do that work between them.

notice_set.sentence: Firstly, wages have stalled. Secondly, rents have risen. Thirdly, transport costs more. Moreover, food is dearer.
notice_set.question: Would you have known these were four separate points without the numbering?
notice_set.why: Four full stops already told you there were four points. The numbering repeats what the punctuation had covered.

notice_set.sentence: The scheme cost forty million pounds. It cut journey times by nine minutes.
notice_set.question: Which two numbers is the writer inviting you to weigh against each other?
options: the cost against the time saved
notice_set.why: Setting a very large figure beside a very small one is an argument, and no word had to make it.

notice_set.sentence: Many governments have promised to cut emissions. Few have met the targets they set themselves.
notice_set.question: Have the promises been kept?
notice_set.why: The turn is inside what the second sentence says, and a reader takes it without needing to be warned.

notice_set.sentence: Visitor numbers have risen every year. However, visitor spending has risen too.
notice_set.question: Do the two sentences disagree with each other?
notice_set.why: The word promised a turn that never came, so the reader spends a second hunting for a disagreement that is not there.

teach.rule_line: Add a linking word only when a reader could take the wrong relation without it.
teach.false_rule: That more linking words show better organisation. They show that the ideas underneath were never organised.

errors.wrong: Firstly, tourism creates jobs. Secondly, it brings money in. Moreover, it funds restoration. Furthermore, it raises the town's profile.
errors.right: Tourism creates jobs and brings money into a town with little other income. Some of that money funds restoration, and the town's profile rises with it.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has been told that linking words show cohesion, so more of them ought to show more of it. What they show is four sentences that were never joined in any other way, and taking the markers out is what forces the joining to happen.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete four words: Firstly, Secondly, Moreover and Furthermore.

errors.wrong: In conclusion, to sum up, it is clear that tourism brings both benefits and problems.
errors.right: On balance, tourism brings more to a small town than it takes away.
errors.why_it_happens: Two closing phrases were memorised separately as the way to finish, so both arrive. Together they announce the ending twice and say nothing at all about the argument.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one phrase: to sum up.

errors.wrong: Although tourism creates jobs, however most of them last only four months.
errors.right: Although tourism creates jobs, most of them last only four months.
errors.why_it_happens: The contrast has already been marked once at the front, but the second half feels unmarked to a writer whose first language marks both ends of it.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: however.
errors.l1_note: Very common for speakers of Chinese, Turkish and Vietnamese.

errors.wrong: Visitor numbers have risen every year. However, visitor spending has also risen.
errors.right: Visitor numbers have risen every year, and spending has risen with them.
errors.why_it_happens: However has been stored as the word that joins two sentences rather than as the word that warns of a turn. Here nothing turns, so the reader stops and looks for a disagreement.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: however becomes and.

pays_in.note: A stack of memorised openers is the loudest signal of a rehearsed answer.
pays_in.model: Cheap flights opened the coast to weekend visitors, and the town has been rebuilt around them.

pays_in.note: A long turn stacked with markers sounds rehearsed rather than fluent.
pays_in.model: The flat was tiny, so we spent most of our time out on the balcony.

pays_in.note: Good writing links by content, which is what makes summary questions hard.
pays_in.model: Rents doubled in a decade. Younger workers left for the towns along the line.

used_in.quote: An advantages and disadvantages answer invites a list, and a list invites four memorised openers in a row.

payload.sentence: Factories moved abroad through the 1990s. The town lost two thirds of its manufacturing jobs in fifteen years.
payload.question: Why did the town lose the jobs?

feedback.why_key: You read the cause straight off the content. No word had to point at it, and adding one would have told you what you already had.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the content has already made the relation plain.

payload.sentence: Firstly the hotel was lovely, and secondly the beach was quiet, and moreover the food was excellent.
payload.question: How does this speaker come across?
options: as though they are reading a list they prepared
as though they are describing something they remember
as though they disliked the holiday

feedback.why_key: Three markers in one breath announce that the answer was assembled beforehand, which is the opposite of what a long turn is meant to sound like.
feedback.feed_forward: Drop the numbering and let one detail lead to the next.

items.decision_cue: Furthermore, teaching in English also attracts

payload.context: From a body paragraph about degrees taught in English.
payload.sentence: Teaching in English opens a course to students from anywhere. Furthermore, teaching in English also attracts staff from abroad.
reasons: the marker adds nothing that the second sentence was not already saying
the marker points the relation the wrong way
the two sentences should be joined by a comma
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Also is already inside the sentence doing that job, so the opener is the second sign on the same road.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete the opener when the sentence already signals addition.

payload.given: Firstly, container shipping made distance cheap. Secondly, factories moved to wherever labour was cheapest.
payload.instruction: Write this as one sentence with the relation built into it.

expected: container shipping made distance cheap, factories moved to wherever labour was cheapest
shipping made distance cheap, factories moved to wherever labour was cheapest

feedback.why_key: Once carries the whole relation inside the sentence, so neither number is needed and the two facts become one idea.
feedback.feed_forward: Replace two openers with one joining word inside the sentence.

payload.given: The town gets two million visitors a year. Moreover, it has only nine hundred residents.
payload.instruction: Rewrite this as one sentence and let the figures do the work.

expected: nine hundred residents takes two million visitors a year
nine hundred people takes two million visitors a year
nine hundred residents receives two million visitors a year

feedback.why_key: Putting the two numbers in one sentence makes the contrast unmissable, which is more than any opener could have done for it.
feedback.feed_forward: Let two figures sit side by side and delete the marker.

payload.context: The paragraph has already given three reasons why small exporters struggle. This is the last sentence of it.
payload.stem: ___ these pressures, a handful of firms in Brackenfield have doubled their overseas sales.

expected: despite
in spite of

feedback.why_key: This is a genuine turn after three sentences going the other way, which is exactly the situation in which a marker earns its place.
feedback.feed_forward: Save the marker for the sentence that actually turns.

payload.context: Build one sentence. Mark the contrast once and only once.

expected: while the festival draws crowds, few of them stay overnight

feedback.why_key: The contrast is marked at the front and the second half carries nothing, which is the shape English wants.
feedback.feed_forward: Mark a contrast at one end only and then stop.

payload.audio_text: It rained all week, so we've booked somewhere inland this time.

expected: it rained all week, so we've booked somewhere inland this time
it rained all week so we have booked somewhere inland this time
it rained all week so weve booked somewhere inland this time

feedback.why_key: One unstressed syllable does the whole job here, which is what natural cohesion sounds like when nobody is performing it.
feedback.feed_forward: Notice how small the join is when the content already fits.

payload.sentence: Although foreign firms brought work to the district, but however these jobs paid less than the ones lost.

expected: these jobs

feedback.why_key: Although at the front has already marked the contrast. Two more markers behind it say the same thing twice and hold up the sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete every marker after the first one.

items.decision_cue: Even so, the paper kept its Sunday edition

payload.context: The three sentences before this one all described falling print sales.
payload.sentence: Even so, the paper kept its Sunday edition and hired two more reporters.
reasons: the marker adds nothing the content did not already carry
the phrase sends the reader in the wrong direction
two markers are doing the same job
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Three sentences of decline set up an expectation, and this sentence breaks it, so the reader genuinely needs the warning.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the marker when the sentence goes against what came before.

payload.prompt_text: Write three sentences about why a small exporter might struggle to sell abroad. Use no sentence-opening linking word at all, and make each sentence grow out of the one before it.

feedback.why_key: Taking the signs away forces the ordering to do the work, and ordering is what cohesion actually is.
feedback.feed_forward: Begin each sentence with something the sentence before mentioned.

payload.prompt_text: Open your answer on English-medium degrees. Cross out every sentence-opening linking word, then read the paragraph. Put back only the ones whose absence made you stumble. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: Most of them will not go back in, and the paragraph will read faster and sound less rehearsed for their absence.
feedback.feed_forward: Restore only the markers whose loss you actually noticed.

title: Starting a sentence with what the reader already has and ending with the news

point_json.grammar_name: Information order: given before new

teach.can_do: I can order a sentence so it begins with something my reader already holds and ends with the part they do not.
teach.why_it_matters: This is the reason some paragraphs read as one argument and others as a pile of true sentences. It is also the real reason the passive exists.
teach.meaning: A reader is always holding something from the sentence before. English expects the next sentence to start from that and to put the new part at the end, where the voice falls and the weight lands. When a sentence opens with a brand-new noun, the reader has to hold it up in the air until they find out what it has to do with anything. Do that four times in a paragraph and the paragraph stops joining up, whatever linking words you nail onto it.

form.pattern: old information + verb + new information
notes: a pronoun or the plus a known noun is the cheapest way to open from what is already there
the passive exists partly for this: it lets the known thing take the front and pushes the doer to the end
there is and there are exist to bring something in for the first time, which is why they cannot open with the
the last few words of a sentence are the loudest, so put there whatever you want remembered
form.negative: The rule survives the negative: what is known still comes first, and the denial lands at the end.
form.question: Look at the first four words of your sentence. Did your reader already have them?

ends: what the reader has not been told yet

marks.label: the subject slot: known things live here
the end of the sentence: the news lands here

worked_example.sentence: The council opened a new footbridge in March. It was paid for out of the parking surplus.
worked_example.why_this_form: The second sentence starts from something the first one handed over and ends with the part nobody knew, so the paragraph moves forward instead of starting again.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Opening with the parking surplus puts a brand-new noun in the first four words and leaves the reader holding it until the sentence finally explains itself.

notice_set.sentence: The trust bought the old mill in 2019. It has stood empty ever since.
notice_set.question: What has stood empty?
notice_set.why: The second sentence opens from the thing the first one has just handed over, so there is nothing to work out.

notice_set.sentence: Rents doubled between 2013 and 2023. The sharpest rise came in the last two years.
notice_set.question: When did rents rise fastest?
notice_set.why: The news sits at the end of the sentence, which is where the weight falls and where a reader looks for it.

notice_set.sentence: There is a new bus shelter outside the surgery.
notice_set.question: Had the listener heard about the shelter before?
notice_set.why: There is exists to bring something into a conversation for the first time, so it announces that this is new.

notice_set.sentence: The shelter outside the surgery has been vandalised twice this year.
notice_set.question: Had the listener heard about the shelter before?
notice_set.why: Opening with the shelter treats it as shared property, which only works if the listener already has it.

notice_set.sentence: Two of the blocks are coming down. Asbestos in the stairwells is the reason.
notice_set.question: Which part of the second sentence is the news?
notice_set.why: The news has been put at the front, which is why the sentence reads slightly backwards even though nothing in it is wrong.

teach.rule_line: Start with what your reader already has. Finish with what they do not.
teach.false_rule: That the most important idea should come first so nobody misses it. English puts its weight at the end of a sentence, not at the beginning.

errors.wrong: The footbridge was opened by the council in March, and the parking surplus was used by them to pay for it.
errors.right: The council opened the footbridge in March and paid for it out of the parking surplus.
errors.why_it_happens: The passive has been learned as the formal option and goes in everywhere. Here the council is the thing the paragraph is already about, so pushing it to the end hides the one familiar noun in the sentence.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one verb: was opened becomes opened.

errors.wrong: The survey report on the stairwells was buried for two years.
errors.right: The housing department buried the survey report on the stairwells for two years.
errors.why_it_happens: The passive lets you leave the doer out, and a writer who has been told that formal English avoids naming people leaves everybody out. Here who did it is the entire point of the sentence.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one agent: by the housing department.

errors.wrong: Rents in Ashfield doubled in a decade. However, a two-bedroom flat now costs more than a house did in 2015.
errors.right: Rents in Ashfield doubled in a decade. A two-bedroom flat now costs more than a house did in 2015.
errors.why_it_happens: The flat price is new information arriving in a new sentence, and new information feels as though it needs announcing. It does not: it already grows out of the rent rise, and however tells the reader to brace for a disagreement that never arrives.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: however.

pays_in.note: A chart description that restarts every sentence is exhausting to read.
pays_in.model: Coal supplied a third of the total in 2000. By 2020 that share had fallen to a twentieth.

pays_in.note: It is why a paragraph reads as one argument rather than five true facts.
pays_in.model: Most new flats are built for sale. Those that are not go to housing associations.

pays_in.note: Matching-information questions turn on which idea a sentence starts from.
pays_in.model: The scheme was extended in 2019. Two years later it was quietly dropped.

used_in.quote: The answer moves from a problem to a cause to a remedy, and each step has to start from the step before it.

payload.sentence: The estate was finished in 1974. Half of it was sold to private landlords twenty years later.
payload.question: Which part of the second sentence is the news?
options: sold to private landlords twenty years later

feedback.why_key: The estate is already on the page, so the fresh information is everything after the verb, where English lets it land.
feedback.feed_forward: Look for the news in the last few words of a sentence.

payload.sentence: There's a leak in the ceiling of the back bedroom.
payload.question: Had the listener been told about the leak before?

feedback.why_key: There's is how English opens the door for something the listener has not met yet, so it marks the leak as fresh news.
feedback.feed_forward: Read there is as a door opening on something new.

payload.context: The sentence before this one said that young people in Ashfield are staying at home into their thirties.
payload.sentence: A shortage of small units is the underlying cause.
reasons: the sentence opens with a noun the reader has not met yet
the doer of the action has been left out
the two sentences need a linking word between them
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: A shortage of small units is brand-new, and the only familiar words, the underlying cause, have been left to the end where the news should have been.
feedback.feed_forward: Open with the cause word and close with the shortage.

payload.given: Two of the tower blocks are coming down. Asbestos in the stairwells is the reason.
payload.instruction: Rewrite the second sentence so it opens from what the reader already has.

expected: is asbestos in the stairwells
is asbestos in the stairwells.

feedback.why_key: A reason has already been implied by the first sentence, so it belongs at the front, and the asbestos lands at the end where it hits hardest.
feedback.feed_forward: Move the known word to the front and the news to the end.

payload.given: The samples arrived in March. A laboratory in Norland analysed them.
payload.instruction: Rewrite the second sentence so it keeps the samples at the front.

expected: were analysed by a laboratory in norland
were analysed by a laboratory in Norland
were then analysed by a laboratory in norland

feedback.why_key: This is the honest reason for the passive: it lets the known thing keep the front of the sentence and sends the new laboratory to the end.
feedback.feed_forward: Reach for the passive when the doer is the news.

payload.context: The paragraph has been describing a single housing scheme in Brackenfield.
payload.stem: ___ was finally approved in 2021, eight years after the first application.

expected: it
the scheme

feedback.why_key: The scheme is what the paragraph has been discussing, so it takes the front and the eight-year wait lands at the end.
feedback.feed_forward: Open with the noun the paragraph is already about.

payload.context: The sentence before said that terraced housing made up half the stock in 1990.

expected: that share had fallen to a fifth by 2020

feedback.why_key: That share reaches back to the half from the previous sentence, so the reader starts on solid ground and the new figure arrives last.
feedback.feed_forward: Open with a pointing word that reaches back one sentence.

payload.audio_text: It's been empty since the trust bought it in 2019.

expected: it's been empty since the trust bought it in 2019
it has been empty since the trust bought it in 2019
its been empty since the trust bought it in 2019

feedback.why_key: The sentence opens with two squashed syllables carrying old information, which is exactly why they are unstressed and easy to miss.
feedback.feed_forward: Expect the opening words to be small and already known.

items.decision_cue: The grant was withdrawn in June

payload.context: The paragraph is arguing that a particular department cannot be trusted with the money.
payload.sentence: The grant was withdrawn in June with no explanation.
reasons: the sentence leaves out the one thing the paragraph is trying to prove
the sentence opens with a noun nobody has met
the news has been put at the front
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The paragraph is about who is responsible, and this sentence quietly removes them. The passive is hiding the only thing being argued for.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the doer whenever your point is about who acted.

items.decision_cue: A private management company was appointed by the trust

payload.sentence: The trust took over the estate in 2016. A private management company was appointed by the trust to run it.
payload.error_span: A private management company was appointed by the trust

expected: it appointed a private management company
the trust appointed a private management company
it then appointed a private management company

feedback.why_key: The trust is already known and the company is new, so the sentence currently has them the wrong way round and the passive is what put them there.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the known noun first and drop the by phrase.

payload.prompt_text: Write three sentences about why first-time buyers struggle in a small town. Every sentence after the first must open with something the sentence before it gave you.

feedback.why_key: Once each sentence opens from the one before, you will find you no longer need a marker between them at all.
feedback.feed_forward: Copy one word from the end of each sentence into the start of the next.

payload.prompt_text: Open your answer on first homes. Underline the first four words of every sentence in one body paragraph and mark each one old or new. Rewrite any sentence that starts on something new. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: Marking your own openings old or new takes two minutes and finds the disjointed paragraph that reading for meaning never catches.
feedback.feed_forward: Rewrite any sentence whose first four words are new.

title: Loading detail onto a noun instead of writing three short sentences

point_json.grammar_name: Expanding the noun phrase

teach.can_do: I can load several pieces of information onto one noun so that a sentence makes a single point rather than three.
teach.why_it_matters: This is the cheapest complexity in English. A long noun phrase raises the level of a sentence with almost nothing in it that can break.
teach.meaning: A noun can carry a great deal before it and a great deal after it. In front go the determiner and the describing words. Behind go the small phrases and the clauses: by the harbour, with twelve rooms, that the guidebooks recommend, opened last spring. All of it belongs to one noun, and that noun is still the subject of the sentence, however far the verb has been pushed back. Filling this space is how a writer packs three facts into one sentence without stacking clauses.

form.pattern: determiner + describing words + NOUN + small phrase + clause
notes: before the noun, English fixes the order and nobody has to be taught it: a lovely old stone cottage, never a stone lovely old cottage
after the noun you can stack a small phrase and then a clause: the path along the cliff that floods at high tide
the verb agrees with the head noun, which is the one everything else is hanging on, not the nearest word to it
keep the items in a list the same shape as each other, or the reader has to start again halfway through
form.negative: The negative goes on the verb, not inside the phrase: the hostel by the harbour has not reopened.
form.question: Find the one word everything else is describing. That is the word the verb has to agree with.

rungs.text: the hostel
the hostel by the harbour
the cheap hostel by the harbour
the cheap hostel by the harbour that the guidebooks all recommend

spec.top_label: as much as one noun can carry

worked_example.sentence: The steady rise in weekend visitors that followed the new rail link has emptied the car parks by nine in the morning.
worked_example.why_this_form: Everything the reader needs about the rise is packed in before the verb, so the sentence makes one point instead of three and never has to name the rise twice.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Three short sentences would carry the same facts and would make the reader hold the rise in mind while the other two arrived and joined on.

notice_set.sentence: The hostel by the harbour that the guidebooks recommend is shut all winter.
notice_set.question: Is every hostel in the town shut all winter?
notice_set.why: One hostel has been picked out with two pieces of detail. What the others do is outside the sentence altogether.

notice_set.sentence: The number of visitors staying more than two nights has fallen since 2019.
notice_set.question: What has fallen?
notice_set.why: Everything after number is describing it, so number is the word the verb belongs to.

notice_set.sentence: Cheap flights from the northern cities have filled the town every August.
notice_set.question: Where do the flights come from?
notice_set.why: The small phrase after flights says where they start, and the town is where they end up.

notice_set.sentence: The path along the cliff above the old lifeboat station floods at high tide.
notice_set.question: What floods?
notice_set.why: Two small phrases have stacked up behind path, but path is still the thing the sentence is about.

notice_set.sentence: A converted warehouse with twelve rooms and a shared kitchen opened last spring.
notice_set.question: How many rooms does it have?
notice_set.why: The rooms and the kitchen are both hanging off warehouse, so both belong to the same building.

teach.rule_line: Pack the detail behind the noun and keep the verb agreeing with the noun itself.
teach.false_rule: That range means long sentences. Long noun phrases show range; long sentences with three clauses show how many ways there are to break one.

errors.wrong: The number of visitors arriving at the coastal towns in August have doubled.
errors.right: The number of visitors arriving at the coastal towns in August has doubled.
errors.why_it_happens: Eight words separate the noun from its verb, and the last thing in the writer's ear was towns in August. The verb copies whatever plural was nearest.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: have becomes has.

errors.wrong: Increase in weekend visitors that followed the new line has strained the car parks.
errors.right: The increase in weekend visitors that followed the new line has strained the car parks.
errors.why_it_happens: The clause behind the noun has already identified exactly which increase is meant, so the phrase feels complete. English still wants the word at the front that says the reader can now find it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: the.
errors.l1_note: Frequent for learners whose first language marks no articles.

errors.wrong: The town offers cheap accommodation, good transport and it has a long beach.
errors.right: The town offers cheap accommodation, good transport and a long beach.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer runs out of the list shape halfway through and finishes the third item as a fresh sentence, because by then they are thinking about the beach rather than about the list.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one phrase: it has.

pays_in.note: It names a category exactly, in one phrase rather than a sentence.
pays_in.model: The share of households with no car rose in every district outside the centre.

pays_in.note: Complexity you can risk, because so little of it can go wrong.
pays_in.model: Towns dependent on a single summer season have the least room to absorb a bad year.

pays_in.note: A long subject hides the verb, which is often exactly what the question tests.
pays_in.model: The decision to close the two smallest sites was taken without any consultation.

used_in.quote: This prompt is about a kind of traveller and a kind of place, and both have to be named precisely before the argument can start.

payload.sentence: The ferry to the islands that runs twice a day was cancelled all week.
payload.question: What was cancelled?

feedback.why_key: Everything after ferry is describing it, so ferry is what the main verb at the end belongs to.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the noun everything else is hanging on.

payload.sentence: The little place by the station we found last year has closed.
payload.question: How does the speaker know the place?

feedback.why_key: We found last year is a second piece of detail stacked behind the noun, and it tells you how the place got into the conversation.
feedback.feed_forward: Read every phrase after the noun as more about that noun.

items.decision_cue: The cost of the ferry crossings during the summer months

payload.context: From a draft about island communities.
payload.sentence: The cost of the ferry crossings during the summer months are now beyond most families.
reasons: the verb has agreed with the wrong word
the word the is missing from the front
the list does not match itself
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Cost is what the sentence is about and it is one thing. Crossings and months are only describing it, however close they are to the verb.
feedback.feed_forward: Trace the verb back to the head noun before you write it.

payload.context: From a description of a chart on overnight stays.
payload.stem: The number of visitors booking more than three nights ___ (have) fallen every year since 2018.

expected: has

feedback.why_key: Number is one thing and it is what the sentence is about. Visitors and nights are only describing it from behind.
feedback.feed_forward: Cover everything after the head noun, then choose the verb.

payload.given: A hostel stands by the harbour. It is cheap. The guidebooks all recommend it.
payload.instruction: Write one noun phrase carrying all three facts, then finish the sentence.

expected: by the harbour that the guidebooks all recommend is shut in winter
by the harbour that the guidebooks recommend is full every august
by the harbour that all the guidebooks recommend is shut in winter

feedback.why_key: One phrase, one small phrase and one clause, and the whole of it is still just the subject waiting for its verb.
feedback.feed_forward: Stack the small phrase first, then the clause.

payload.given: The district has cheap rents. It has good transport. It also has a lot of empty units.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence with a list of three items in the same shape.

expected: cheap rents, good transport and a lot of empty units
cheap rents, good transport and plenty of empty units

feedback.why_key: Three noun phrases in a row read as one list. Two noun phrases and a clause make the reader start the sentence again.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that every item in a list is the same shape.

payload.context: Build one sentence about a coastal walk.

expected: the path along the cliff above the bay floods twice a month

feedback.why_key: Two small phrases stack up behind path in the order you would walk them, and the verb still belongs to path at the front.
feedback.feed_forward: Stack the phrases behind the noun in the order they narrow it.

payload.audio_text: The café by the harbour that we liked has closed.

expected: the café by the harbour that we liked has closed
