the cafe by the harbour that we liked has closed

feedback.why_key: Two unstressed words are holding the whole phrase together, and losing either one leaves you with three nouns and no idea how they connect.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the small joining words between the nouns.

items.decision_cue: The share of beaches meeting the water quality standard

payload.sentence: The share of beaches meeting the water quality standard have risen every year since 2017.

expected: has risen

feedback.why_key: Share is the head of the phrase and it is singular. Beaches is doing nothing but describing it from behind.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the verb to the first noun in the phrase.

items.decision_cue: Studies carried out before 2015 tend to

payload.context: From the opening of a research summary.
payload.sentence: Studies carried out before 2015 tend to report much larger effects than later ones.
reasons: this phrase needs the in front of it
the ending on the verb does not match the head noun
the detail should come before the noun
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: This is a claim about a class rather than about particular studies, and a class opens without the. The clause behind it narrows the class without identifying members.
feedback.feed_forward: Leave the off a class you are generalising about.

parts: A ferry serves the three outer islands.
It runs twice a day in summer.
It has carried the same number of passengers since 2015.
model_combinations: The ferry serving the three outer islands twice a day in summer has carried the same number of passengers since 2015.
The twice-daily summer ferry to the three outer islands has carried the same number of passengers since 2015.
Passenger numbers on the summer ferry to the three outer islands have not moved since 2015.

feedback.why_key: Two of the three facts are describing the ferry, so they belong inside the subject and only the third one needs a verb.
feedback.feed_forward: Put every describing fact inside the subject, then write one verb.

payload.prompt_text: A chart shows how many visitors to a coastal town stayed overnight rather than coming for the day. Write one sentence naming that group precisely and saying what happened to it.

feedback.why_key: Naming the group exactly is most of the work in a chart answer, and it all happens inside the subject before the verb arrives.
feedback.feed_forward: Check the verb against the first noun, not the last.

payload.prompt_text: Open your answer on photo-led travel. Find three consecutive short sentences that all describe one noun and pack two of them into the subject of the third. Then check the verb against the head noun. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: This is the safest way to raise the level of a paragraph under time pressure, because nothing in it depends on a clause you might not finish.
feedback.feed_forward: Fold the describing sentences into the subject, then reread the verb.

title: Building the first sentence of a paragraph so the rest of it has a job

point_json.grammar_name: The grammar of a topic sentence

teach.can_do: I can open a paragraph with a claim that is narrow enough for the next four sentences to prove.
teach.why_it_matters: The first sentence sets the size of the job. Make the claim too big and nothing you write underneath it will be enough.
teach.meaning: A paragraph opener is a claim about a class of things, and its grammar shows that. The subject names the class rather than one example of it, so it is usually plural and usually has no the in front. The verb is present simple, because the claim is meant to hold generally rather than to report one occasion. And it carries a word that says how far the claim reaches, because a claim with no limit on it is the easiest thing in the world to knock down.

form.pattern: general noun phrase + present simple verb + a limit on how far the claim reaches
notes: the subject names the class: short prison sentences, community schemes, first offenders
the verb stays in the present simple even when your evidence is about the past
tend to, most, generally and rarely narrow the claim without weakening the writing
keep the example out of this sentence; it belongs in the next one
form.negative: A negative claim needs the same limit: short sentences rarely reduce crime, not short sentences never reduce crime.
form.question: Ask whether four sentences could prove what you have just written. If not, narrow it.

spec.label: how much of this claim could you actually defend?

steps.gloss: a whole essay's worth of claim in three words, and nothing below it can carry that
still absolute; one contrary case sinks the paragraph

steps.text: Community sentences tend to reduce reoffending among first offenders.
steps.gloss: narrow enough that four sentences can hold it up

worked_example.sentence: Short prison sentences tend to make reoffending more likely rather than less.
worked_example.why_this_form: The subject names the class the paragraph is about, the verb is general because the claim is general, and tend to leaves room for the cases that go the other way.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Short prison sentences made reoffending more likely would report one particular occasion, and a paragraph under it would have nothing left to prove.

notice_set.sentence: Community sentences tend to work better for first offenders.
notice_set.question: Is the writer saying this is true in every case?
notice_set.why: Tend to admits the exceptions in advance, which is what stops one contrary case from sinking the paragraph.

notice_set.sentence: Community sentences work better for first offenders.
notice_set.question: Is the writer saying this is true in every case?
notice_set.why: With no limit on it, the claim covers every first offender everywhere, and the writer has to defend all of them.

notice_set.sentence: Last year the Marlow scheme cut reoffending by a fifth.
notice_set.question: Is this about schemes in general or about one of them?
notice_set.why: A named scheme and a named year make this an example, and an example is what a paragraph offers second, not first.

notice_set.sentence: Most magistrates prefer to keep first offenders out of custody.
notice_set.question: Do all magistrates prefer this?
notice_set.why: Most says the majority and quietly concedes the rest, which is exactly the amount a paragraph can carry.

notice_set.sentence: Prison costs the taxpayer far more than supervision in the community.
notice_set.question: What will the rest of the paragraph be about?
options: the cost of the two options
notice_set.why: The claim names cost, so cost is the debt the paragraph now owes its reader.

teach.rule_line: Name the class, keep the verb general, and leave the example for the next sentence.
teach.false_rule: That an opening claim should be as strong as you can make it. A claim you cannot defend in four sentences costs more than it earns.

errors.wrong: Prison never reduces crime.
errors.right: Long prison sentences rarely reduce crime on their own.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has been told to state a clear position, and never feels clearer than usually does. It is also the one word a reader can disprove with a single case, after which the whole paragraph is defending the indefensible.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: never becomes rarely.

errors.wrong: Everybody agrees that community sentences are better for society.
errors.right: Community sentences have wide support among magistrates and probation staff.
errors.why_it_happens: Everybody agrees has been memorised as a confident opening. It makes a claim about the entire world, which one disagreeing voice destroys, and it says nothing about who actually holds the view.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one phrase: everybody agrees that.

errors.wrong: Firstly, the first advantage of community sentences is that they are cheaper.
errors.right: Community sentences cost the state far less than custody.
errors.why_it_happens: Two openers and a scaffolding phrase have each been memorised as the way to begin, so all three arrive, and the actual claim starts seven words into the sentence.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one phrase: the first advantage of.

errors.wrong: This is a serious problem in many countries.
errors.right: Overcrowding in prisons is a serious problem in many countries.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer has the topic in their head from reading the prompt, so this feels anchored to them. On the page it is the first sentence of a paragraph and there is nothing behind it to point at.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word for its noun: this becomes overcrowding.

pays_in.note: The first sentence of a paragraph decides what the rest has to do.
pays_in.model: Short custodial sentences tend to break up work and housing without reducing crime.

pays_in.note: Heading-matching questions are usually answered by one sentence per paragraph.
pays_in.model: Community supervision has expanded steadily since the 1990s.

pays_in.note: An answer that opens with a limited claim has somewhere to go next.
pays_in.model: On the whole, tougher sentences change what people are given rather than what they do.

used_in.quote: Each body paragraph on this prompt lives or dies on whether its first sentence is a claim or a stray fact.

payload.sentence: Electronic tagging generally costs a fraction of what a prison place costs.
payload.question: Is the writer claiming this holds everywhere without exception?

feedback.why_key: Generally admits the exceptions before a reader can produce one, which is what makes the claim survivable.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the limiting word to see how far the claim reaches.

payload.sentence: Nobody comes out of prison better than they went in.
payload.question: How easy would it be to argue against this?
options: very easy, one example is enough

feedback.why_key: Nobody covers every person who has ever been released, so a single counterexample is all anybody needs.
feedback.feed_forward: Narrow a claim before a listener narrows it for you.

items.decision_cue: This is getting worse every year

payload.context: This is the opening sentence of the second body paragraph.
payload.sentence: This is getting worse every year in almost every region.
reasons: the opening word has nothing behind it to point at
the claim has no limit on it
the verb should be in the past
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: A paragraph opener is where the reader is most lost, so it is the one place a pointing word has nothing to stand on.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the topic in full in a paragraph's first sentence.

payload.context: The paragraph beneath this sentence gives two examples and one counterexample.
payload.stem: Community schemes ___ keep first offenders out of the system altogether.

expected: tend to
often
usually
generally

feedback.why_key: The paragraph itself contains a case that goes the other way, so the opening claim has to leave room for it.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the size of the claim to the evidence below it.

payload.given: Prison never works.
payload.instruction: Rewrite this as a claim four sentences could actually prove.

expected: rarely reduce reoffending
rarely reduce reoffending among first offenders
tend to have little effect on reoffending

feedback.why_key: Naming the kind of sentence and softening the verb turns an unwinnable position into one that four sentences can hold.
feedback.feed_forward: Narrow the subject first, then soften the verb.

payload.given: Firstly, the first advantage of longer school days is that parents can work full time.
payload.instruction: Write the claim on its own, with nothing bolted on the front.

expected: let parents work full time
allow parents to work full time
make full-time work possible for parents

feedback.why_key: The claim was always there. It was just buried under seven words of scaffolding that told the reader nothing.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete everything before the subject of the claim.

payload.context: Build the opening sentence of a paragraph about cost.

expected: supervised release usually costs less than a prison place

feedback.why_key: The class comes first, the general verb second, and the limiting word sits between them where it can catch the exceptions.
feedback.feed_forward: Place the limiting word directly before the verb.

payload.audio_text: They're far more likely to reoffend within the first year.

expected: they're far more likely to reoffend within the first year
they are far more likely to reoffend within the first year
theyre far more likely to reoffend within the first year

feedback.why_key: More likely is the whole limit on this claim, and both words are unstressed enough to disappear if you are only listening for reoffend.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the words that measure how far a claim goes.

payload.sentence: Everyone knows that tagging is cheaper and safer than custody.

expected: tagging
electronic tagging

feedback.why_key: Everyone knows adds no evidence and makes a claim about the whole population, which a reader can refuse simply by not knowing it.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete the appeal to everybody and start from the claim.

payload.context: This is the opening sentence of a body paragraph in an essay about daily exercise in schools.
payload.sentence: In 2019 the Ashfield club opened its pitches to two local primary schools.
reasons: it reports one occasion instead of making a claim about a class
the claim has no limit on it
the opening word points at nothing
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: A named club and a named year make this an example. An example is the second sentence of a paragraph, and it needs a claim above it to be an example of.
feedback.feed_forward: Move the example down and write the claim above it.

payload.prompt_text: You are arguing that community sentences suit some offenders and not others. Write the opening sentence of that paragraph, with a limit on it you could defend in four more sentences.

feedback.why_key: The size of this sentence is the size of the debt you take on, and a smaller debt is easier to pay off in four lines.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the claim, then ask what would disprove it.

payload.prompt_text: Open your answer on community sentences. Read only the first sentence of each body paragraph, one after the other. If they do not form a summary of your argument on their own, rewrite them until they do. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: Reading only your openers is the fastest structural check there is, and it takes less than a minute in a real timed answer.
feedback.feed_forward: Read your opening sentences in sequence and check they cohere.

title: Writing long sentences that hold together under time pressure

point_json.grammar_name: Control of the complex sentence

teach.can_do: I can write long sentences that stay in one piece, and I know which long sentences are worth the risk.
teach.why_it_matters: A higher score asks for more clean complex sentences, not for fewer mistakes. Writing short and safe is not the cautious option; it is a decision to score lower.
teach.meaning: Two things are being marked at once, and learners usually protect one at the expense of the other. Range means sentences that carry more than one idea and join them properly. Accuracy means those sentences arriving whole. The way to have both is not to write more carefully; it is to reach for structures that have very little in them to go wrong, use two of them per sentence at most, and check three specific things at the end. Long is not the risk. Uncontrolled is.

form.pattern: main clause + one or two supporting clauses, each doing exactly one job
notes: the low-risk workhorses are the relative clause, the because and although clause, the shortened clause and the loaded noun phrase
two supporting clauses in one sentence is plenty; a third rarely adds anything a reader notices
vary the length on purpose, because a short sentence after two long ones is the strongest thing on the page
the three end checks: does every sentence have a main verb, does each verb match its own subject, and did every clause you opened get closed
form.negative: A negative main clause changes nothing about the joins: because nobody else was free, my grandmother collected us.
form.question: Read your sentence back and find the main verb. If you cannot, the sentence has not finished.

spec.label: how much is there in this structure to get wrong?

steps.text: a relative clause, a because clause, an although clause
steps.gloss: one or two things to get right, so use them constantly

steps.text: a shortened clause, a loaded noun phrase
steps.gloss: two or three things, and safe once you have checked whose subject it borrowed

steps.text: an inverted opening, a mixed unreal sentence
steps.gloss: four things at once, under time pressure, for one sentence's worth of credit

worked_example.sentence: Because both my parents worked shifts, the person who actually raised me was my grandmother, who lived three streets away.
worked_example.why_this_form: Two supporting clauses, each doing one job, and both of the kinds that hardly ever break. The sentence is plainly long and has very little inside it that can fail.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Three short sentences would carry every one of those facts and would leave a reader with no evidence that the writer can join anything at all.

notice_set.sentence: Because both my parents worked shifts, my grandmother was the one who actually raised me.
notice_set.question: Who raised the speaker?
notice_set.why: The opening explains why, and the part after the comma is the sentence's real news.

notice_set.sentence: My grandmother moved in when I was nine she stayed for eleven years.
notice_set.question: How many separate things is the speaker reporting?
notice_set.why: Nothing marks where the first report ends, so the reader has to hunt for the join and may find it in the wrong place.

notice_set.sentence: Although both my parents worked full time and my grandmother lived three streets away.
notice_set.question: What does the speaker end up telling you happened?
notice_set.why: Everything here is background. The part it was building towards never arrives, so the sentence makes no claim.

notice_set.sentence: We ate together every evening, a habit that has completely disappeared.
notice_set.question: Does the family still eat together?
notice_set.why: The noun after the comma names the practice and the clause behind it reports that it has gone.

notice_set.sentence: Having grown up in a house of six, I found sharing a room completely normal.
notice_set.question: Who grew up in a house of six?
notice_set.why: Nobody is named in the first half, so the reader waits for the comma and gives the growing-up to whoever turns up next, which here is the speaker.

teach.rule_line: Two supporting clauses per sentence, and check every sentence still has a main verb.
teach.false_rule: That a higher score means making fewer mistakes. It means more clean complex sentences, so short safe writing scores lower rather than higher.

errors.wrong: My grandmother moved in with us when I was nine she stayed for eleven years.
errors.right: My grandmother moved in with us when I was nine, and she stayed for eleven years.
errors.why_it_happens: One subordinate clause has already gone in, so the sentence feels complex enough and the second main idea gets attached with nothing joining it at all.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one joining word after nine.

errors.wrong: Although both my parents worked full time and my grandmother lived three streets away.
errors.right: Although both my parents worked full time, my grandmother lived three streets away.
errors.why_it_happens: Two clauses feel like enough for one sentence. Neither of them is the main one, because and pulled the second clause inside the although along with the first.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: and.

errors.wrong: We ate together every evening, that has completely disappeared now.
errors.right: We ate together every evening, a habit that has completely disappeared.
errors.why_it_happens: The comment plainly belongs with the sentence in front of it, so a full stop feels too heavy. A comma cannot hold two sentences, and there is nothing else in the sentence doing the work.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one noun: a habit, in front of that.

errors.wrong: Having grown up in a house of six, sharing a room felt completely normal.
errors.right: Having grown up in a house of six, I found sharing a room completely normal.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer is thinking about their own childhood, so the opening is anchored inside their head. On the page it borrows the subject that follows, and that subject is an activity rather than a person.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one subject: sharing a room becomes I.

pays_in.note: It is the difference between an answer that is correct and one that shows range.
pays_in.model: Because rents rose faster than wages, the young people who stayed had to live at home.

pays_in.note: Longer answers need joins that hold while you are still deciding what to say.
pays_in.model: The people who moved out were mostly the ones who had young children.

pays_in.note: Dense passages are two-clause sentences, and finding the main one is the skill.
pays_in.model: Although the scheme proved popular, the council that introduced it lost the following election.

used_in.quote: This prompt pulls answers towards long sentences about families, which is exactly where the joins start giving way.
A two-minute turn about a change in your life is where a candidate either joins their sentences or lists them.

payload.sentence: Because the flat was too small and my sister had just started school.
payload.question: What does this tell you actually happened?

feedback.why_key: Two pieces of background have arrived and the thing they were explaining never turns up, so no event has been reported at all.
feedback.feed_forward: Look for the clause that is not explaining anything.

payload.sentence: Living so far from my parents, I only see them twice a year.
payload.question: Who lives far away?

feedback.why_key: The opening takes the subject that comes after the comma, and that subject is the speaker rather than the parents.
feedback.feed_forward: Take the opening's subject from the clause after the comma.

items.decision_cue: when I was nine she stayed

payload.context: From a first draft about growing up.
payload.sentence: My grandmother moved in with us when I was nine she stayed for eleven years.
reasons: two whole sentences have been run together with nothing joining them
the sentence has no main verb at all
the opening clause has borrowed the wrong subject
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: She stayed for eleven years could stand alone, which is exactly why it cannot simply be laid against the sentence in front of it.
feedback.feed_forward: Add a joining word wherever two whole sentences meet.

payload.given: My parents both worked shifts. My grandmother lived three streets away. She was the one who raised me.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence using no more than two supporting clauses.

expected: both my parents worked shifts, i was raised by my grandmother, who lived three streets away
my parents both worked shifts, i was raised by my grandmother, who lived three streets away
both my parents worked shifts, the person who raised me was my grandmother

feedback.why_key: One reason and one piece of description are enough. A third clause would add length without adding anything the reader notices.
feedback.feed_forward: Stop at two supporting clauses and find your main verb.

payload.given: Evening classes were free until 2019. That has completely changed.
payload.instruction: Join these into one sentence without using a full stop or a semicolon.

expected: a situation that has completely changed
an arrangement that has completely changed
which has completely changed

feedback.why_key: Either a naming noun or a relative word turns the second sentence into part of the first, and a bare comma does neither.
feedback.feed_forward: Add a noun or a relative word before the comma can hold.

payload.context: From a paragraph about older relatives living with a family.
payload.stem: The flat was already crowded, ___ nobody suggested that my aunt should move out.

expected: but
yet
and yet

feedback.why_key: Both halves are whole sentences, so a comma on its own cannot join them and the word after it has to do the work.
feedback.feed_forward: Put a joining word after the comma between two full clauses.

payload.context: Build one sentence with a concession and a relative clause.

expected: although the house was small, nobody who visited ever complained

feedback.why_key: Two supporting clauses and one main verb at the very end, which is what a long sentence looks like when it is under control.
feedback.feed_forward: Finish with the main verb so you can see it is there.

payload.audio_text: She'd moved in by the time I started school.

expected: she'd moved in by the time i started school
she had moved in by the time i started school
shed moved in by the time i started school

feedback.why_key: One contracted auxiliary sets the order of two events, and by the time is the join. Miss either and you have two loose facts.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the squashed auxiliary that orders the events.

items.decision_cue: and my brother was still at school

payload.sentence: Because my mother had gone back to work and my brother was still at school.
payload.error_span: and my brother was still at school

expected: my brother was still at school
, my brother was still at school

feedback.why_key: And pulled the second clause inside the reason, leaving the sentence with two explanations and nothing to explain.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete the and so the second clause becomes the main one.

items.decision_cue: the families who stayed were the ones

payload.context: From the middle of a body paragraph about a district losing its younger residents.
payload.sentence: When the two factories closed within a year of each other, the families who stayed were the ones with nowhere else to go.
reasons: two whole sentences have been run together
the sentence has no main verb
there are too many supporting clauses in it
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Two supporting clauses, one main verb, both joins marked. This is a long sentence with almost nothing in it that could have failed.
feedback.feed_forward: Accept a long sentence once you can find its main verb.

parts: Older people in Brackenfield used to live with their children.
Most of them now live alone or in sheltered flats.
Housing built in the last twenty years has almost no room for a second household.
model_combinations: Older people in Brackenfield, who once lived with their children, now live alone or in sheltered flats, largely because housing built in the last twenty years has no room for a second household.
Because almost nothing built in the last twenty years has room for a second household, the older people of Brackenfield, who once lived with their children, now live alone.
Housing built in the last twenty years leaves no room for a second household, which is why older people in Brackenfield now live alone rather than with their children.

feedback.why_key: Three facts, one main verb, and two supporting clauses of the kinds that rarely break. Three ways of arranging it and all three are fine.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose the main verb first and hang the rest around it.

payload.prompt_text: Write two sentences about why fewer families now live with an older relative. Make the first one long, with two supporting clauses, and the second one short.

feedback.why_key: The short sentence is doing work here. After a long one it lands hard, and varying the length on purpose is part of what range means.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the main verb in the long sentence before you submit.

payload.prompt_text: Open your answer on residential care. Run the three end checks over one body paragraph: a main verb in every sentence, every verb matching its own subject, and every clause you opened closed again. Fix what fails. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: These three checks take under two minutes on a real answer and they catch almost everything that breaks a long sentence under time pressure.
feedback.feed_forward: Run the three checks in order, one pass each.

title: Reporting what people generally think without saying who thinks it

point_json.grammar_name: The impersonal reporting passive

pays_in.note: It opens the paragraph where you set out a view before disagreeing with it.
pays_in.model: It is often argued that longer school days improve results, though the evidence is thin.

pays_in.note: It is how you report a general view in a discussion without claiming it as yours.
pays_in.model: It's generally thought that people read less than they used to.

pays_in.note: Passages mark their own hedged claims this way, and questions test whether you saw the hedge.
pays_in.model: The settlement is believed to have been abandoned within a generation.

teach.can_do: I can put a claim into an essay without owning it and without inventing somebody to blame for it.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the difference between an essay that asserts and an essay that positions. It buys credit for the argument as well as for the grammar.
teach.meaning: Sometimes you need a claim in your paragraph that you are not prepared to sign your name to. This structure puts the claim on the page and leaves the believing to people in general. Nobody is named, no source is invented, and the sentence is honest about where it stands. It also lets you introduce a view in order to disagree with it in the next line, which is what most argument paragraphs are made of.

form.pattern: It is thought that + a full clause  —  or  —  X is thought to + verb
notes: the two carry the same meaning: It is thought that the scheme works, and The scheme is thought to work
an adverb in the middle sharpens it: widely accepted, generally assumed, commonly held
for something already over, the second pattern takes to have: the wall is thought to have failed in the storm
the verbs that fit are the reporting ones: think, believe, say, argue, assume, accept, suggest, know
form.negative: it is not generally accepted that the scheme has worked
form.question: Is it generally accepted that the scheme has worked?

spec.label: how far am I standing behind this claim?

steps.gloss: I am saying it, and you can hold me to it

steps.text: It is widely accepted that small classes raise attainment.
steps.gloss: other people say it and I am not arguing with them

steps.text: It has been suggested that small classes raise attainment.
steps.gloss: somebody has said it once, and I am about to look at whether it holds

worked_example.sentence: It is generally accepted that class size matters less than the quality of teaching.
worked_example.why_this_form: The claim needs to be in the paragraph so the next sentence can qualify it, and the writer has no study to point at and should not pretend to.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Stated flat, it would put the writer's own name on a finding they have not defended, which is a bigger promise than the paragraph can keep.

notice_set.sentence: It is widely accepted that early reading habits shape later attainment.
notice_set.question: Is the writer saying this is their own view?
options: No, they are reporting what people hold
notice_set.why: The claim is in the paragraph and the writer is standing beside it rather than behind it.

notice_set.sentence: Early reading habits shape later attainment.
notice_set.question: Who is answerable for this claim?
notice_set.why: With nothing in front of it, a claim belongs to whoever wrote it down.

notice_set.sentence: The sea wall is thought to have failed during the November storm.
notice_set.question: Is the failure certain?
options: No, it is what people believe
notice_set.why: The structure reports a belief about the past, which is exactly what you need when the cause is still being argued over.

notice_set.sentence: It has been suggested that the charge simply moved the traffic elsewhere.
notice_set.question: How many people hold this view, on the evidence of the sentence?
options: At least one, and possibly few
notice_set.why: Suggested is the weakest verb in the set, and it is the one to use before you take a claim apart.

notice_set.sentence: It is generally assumed that new roads reduce congestion, but the evidence is mixed.
notice_set.question: What is the second half of the sentence doing?
options: Pushing back against the first half
notice_set.why: Introducing a view in order to argue with it is the commonest reason to reach for this structure at all.

teach.rule_line: Report the claim, name nobody, then say what you think of it.
teach.false_rule: That this is a way of sounding academic. It shows where you stand, and a paragraph that uses it and never comes off the fence has used it wrongly.

errors.wrong: The scheme is thought that it reduces congestion.
errors.right: The scheme is thought to reduce congestion.
errors.why_it_happens: The two patterns are learned as one and then blended. Once the subject is at the front, the clause has nowhere to attach and the sentence carries the claim twice.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one join: that it reduces becomes to reduce.

errors.wrong: It widely accepted that early reading habits shape later attainment.
errors.right: It is widely accepted that early reading habits shape later attainment.
errors.why_it_happens: The adverb sits where the small word belongs and fills the gap to the eye, so the sentence looks complete while it is being written.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: is.

errors.wrong: Everyone knows that new roads simply fill up with new traffic.
errors.right: It is widely argued that new roads simply fill up with new traffic.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer wants weight behind the claim and reaches for the biggest available number of believers, which a reader immediately doubts.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one opening: Everyone knows that becomes It is widely argued that.

used_in.quote: A discussion answer needs both views on the page before either can be judged, and this is how the first one arrives.
Answers about what people generally do need a way to report a view without pretending to have counted.

payload.sentence: It is widely assumed that reading at home lifts later results.
payload.question: Whose view is this?

feedback.why_key: The writer has put the claim on the page without signing it, which leaves them free to qualify it next.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the opening words to see who is answerable.

payload.context: From an essay paragraph about road building.
payload.sentence: It is obvious to everyone that widening a motorway never eases congestion for long.
reasons: it claims more agreement than anybody can show
the verb form is wrong
the time is wrong
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: A reader who has not met this claim immediately becomes the exception, and the sentence has lost them in seven words.
feedback.feed_forward: Report a claim as widely held rather than as beyond argument.

payload.context: From the opening of a report on a coastal collapse.
payload.stem: It ___ (think) that the wall failed during the November storm.

expected: is thought

feedback.why_key: The small word before the participle is the whole structure, and it is the one most often left out.
feedback.feed_forward: Write is before the reporting word, always.

payload.context: From a summary of research into sleep.
payload.stem: Short sleep is believed ___ (increase) the risk of several long-term conditions.

expected: to increase

feedback.why_key: This pattern hands the claim to the subject and then needs an infinitive to carry the rest. Nothing else fits after believed here.
feedback.feed_forward: Join the second pattern with to, not with that.

payload.given: It is thought that the market improves footfall in the surrounding streets.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it so the market is the subject, keeping the same meaning.

expected: is thought to improve footfall in the surrounding streets
the market is thought to improve footfall in the surrounding streets

feedback.why_key: The claim does not change. Only the way in changes, and the two ways are worth having because paragraphs need both.
feedback.feed_forward: Move the subject forward and turn that into to.

payload.context: One sentence from a report on an abandoned settlement.

expected: the site is believed to have been abandoned within a generation

feedback.why_key: Four small words run in a fixed order in the middle, and none of them can be dropped or swapped.
feedback.feed_forward: Build the middle from the left, one word at a time.

payload.audio_text: It's generally thought that people read less than they used to.

expected: it's generally thought that people read less than they used to
it is generally thought that people read less than they used to
its generally thought that people read less than they used to

feedback.why_key: In speech the opening shrinks to a single syllable, and that syllable is the entire hedge.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the short opening even when you barely hear it.

payload.sentence: The scheme is thought that it reduces congestion in the centre.

expected: to reduce

feedback.why_key: Two ways in have been used at once, so the sentence announces its claim twice and finishes neither.
feedback.feed_forward: Pick one of the two patterns and finish it.

payload.prompt_text: Write the opening sentence of a paragraph that sets out the popular view that online courses are as good as classroom teaching, so that the next sentence can disagree with it.

feedback.why_key: A view you are about to argue with has to be on the page first, and it has to be somebody else's when it gets there.
feedback.feed_forward: Set the claim up so you can still walk away from it.

payload.prompt_text: Write the first three sentences of your online courses paragraph: the popular view reported without a named source, one qualification, and your own position stated plainly. Four minutes.

feedback.why_key: The structure only earns its place if the paragraph eventually comes off the fence, so the third sentence is the test.
feedback.feed_forward: End the three sentences with your own view, unhedged.

title: Using this shape in places where a verb cannot carry a time

point_json.grammar_name: Passive infinitives and passive -ing forms

pays_in.note: It states what has to happen without naming who has to do it.
pays_in.model: Older housing stock needs to be insulated before any of this is worth doing.

pays_in.note: It joins two stages of a process into one sentence.
pays_in.model: The sheets are stacked without being trimmed at this stage.

pays_in.note: Dense academic sentences are dense largely because of these forms.
pays_in.model: Having been abandoned twice, the site was finally cleared in the 1970s.

teach.can_do: I can use this shape after another verb, or after a preposition, where a full sentence will not fit.
teach.why_it_matters: It is what lets one sentence carry two events. Without it, learners write two short sentences and lose the connection between them.
teach.meaning: Not every verb in a sentence carries a time. After another verb, and after a preposition, English uses a form that has no time of its own and takes it from the sentence around it. This shape has those forms too, and they let you say that something has to be done, is about to be done, or happened without anybody noticing, all inside a sentence that has already started.

form.pattern: to be + past participle  ·  being + past participle  ·  having been + past participle
notes: after another verb: the roof needs to be replaced, the gate has to be locked
after a preposition: the lorry left without being weighed
for something finished first: having been signed off in the spring, the scheme went to tender
the time is carried by the first verb in the sentence, never by this part
form.negative: the report does not need to be rewritten
form.question: Does the report need to be rewritten?

rungs.text: The roof needs to be replaced.
The lorry left without being weighed.
Having been approved in March, the plan went out to tender.

worked_example.sentence: The old cabling has to be replaced before the building can be let again.
worked_example.why_this_form: Has to already carries the time, so the verb after it has none of its own, and the cabling is on the receiving end of the work.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: The old cabling has to replace would say the cabling goes off and replaces something else, which is a sentence about very unusual wiring.

notice_set.sentence: The pumps need to be serviced before the wet season starts.
notice_set.question: Are the pumps doing the servicing or having it done?
notice_set.why: The small word before the last one is what puts the pumps on the receiving end.

notice_set.sentence: The lorry left the yard without being weighed.
notice_set.question: Did anybody weigh the lorry?
notice_set.why: After a preposition the -ing form is the only one allowed, and this shape has its own version of it.

notice_set.sentence: Having been approved in March, the plan went out to tender in May.
notice_set.question: Which happened first?
notice_set.why: The opening phrase reports the earlier event, which is how one sentence can hold two dates without saying either of them twice.

notice_set.sentence: The old panels are due to be removed next month.
notice_set.question: Have the panels gone yet?
notice_set.why: Due carries the time and points forward, so the whole sentence sits ahead of now.

notice_set.sentence: Nobody likes being told what to do at short notice.
notice_set.question: Who is doing the telling in this sentence?
notice_set.why: The teller is left out, exactly as in a full sentence of this kind, and the shape survives inside another verb.

teach.rule_line: Keep be in the sentence even when it cannot carry a time.
teach.false_rule: That the small word can go because the sentence is long already. It is the only thing putting the subject on the receiving end, and without it the sentence reverses.

errors.wrong: The roof needs to replaced before the winter.
errors.right: The roof needs to be replaced before the winter.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has to hold three verbs at once and the smallest of the three drops out. It carries no meaning of its own, so nothing warns them.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: be.

errors.wrong: The lorry left the yard without be weighed.
errors.right: The lorry left the yard without being weighed.
errors.why_it_happens: The rule that a preposition takes the -ing form is known, but it is applied to the last verb rather than to the first one, which is where it belongs.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: be becomes being.

errors.wrong: Having been approve in March, the plan went out to tender.
errors.right: Having been approved in March, the plan went out to tender.
errors.why_it_happens: Three words have already been produced correctly and attention has run out by the fourth, which is where the meaning actually lives.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one ending: approve becomes approved.

used_in.quote: A solutions paragraph is a list of things that need to be done, which is this structure repeated.

payload.sentence: The filters need to be changed before the dry season starts.
payload.question: Are the filters cleaning something else?
options: No, something is being done to them

feedback.why_key: Two small words in the middle turn the filters from the worker into the thing worked on.
feedback.feed_forward: Check for be before the last word of the pair.

payload.context: From a note about weighbridge procedure at a depot.
payload.sentence: No lorry may leave the yard without be weighed.
reasons: the word after without is in the wrong shape
may cannot be used here
the yard cannot be left
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: After a preposition English allows one shape only, and it is the first of the two verbs that has to take it.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the -ing on the first verb after a preposition.

payload.context: From a surveyor's report on an empty flat.
payload.stem: The wiring needs ___ (replace) before the flat can be let again.

expected: to be replaced

feedback.why_key: Need carries the time, so all three of the words after it are fixed and none of them can be spared.
feedback.feed_forward: Write all three words after need, every time.

payload.context: From a note on a fault in a sorting line.
payload.stem: Several boxes went through without ___ (scan) at all.

expected: being scanned

feedback.why_key: Without takes the -ing shape, and the boxes are what somebody failed to scan, so both parts are needed.
feedback.feed_forward: Combine the -ing with the participle after a preposition.

payload.given: The plan was approved in March. It went out to tender in May.
payload.instruction: Join the two into one sentence that opens with the earlier event.

expected: been approved in march the plan went out to tender in may
having been approved in march the plan went out to tender in may

feedback.why_key: One sentence now carries both events and their order, which is what a reader was working out for themselves before.
feedback.feed_forward: Open with the earlier event, then give the main clause.

payload.context: One line from a maintenance schedule.

expected: the old panels are due to be removed next month
next month the old panels are due to be removed

feedback.why_key: Five words run in one fixed order in the middle, and the only thing that can move is the time phrase.
feedback.feed_forward: Lock the middle, then place the time phrase.

payload.audio_text: Nobody likes being told what to do at short notice.

expected: nobody likes being told what to do at short notice

feedback.why_key: Being runs into the word after it and the pair sounds like one word, which is how it disappears from writing.
feedback.feed_forward: Split what you heard into two words before you write it.

payload.sentence: The roof needs to replaced before the winter, and the gutters need clearing.

expected: needs to be replaced

feedback.why_key: The second half of the sentence is fine, which is what makes the first half easy to read past.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the short words in the middle before you submit.

payload.prompt_text: Offices with long sitting hours are unhealthy. Write one sentence saying what has to change, without naming who should change it.

feedback.why_key: A solution stated this way commits to what must happen and leaves the argument about who out of the sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Say what must happen; leave out who must do it.

payload.prompt_text: Write the solutions paragraph of your sedentary working day answer. At least two sentences must say what needs to happen without naming an actor. Five minutes.

feedback.why_key: A whole paragraph of solutions is where the shape either becomes automatic or keeps losing its small words.
feedback.feed_forward: Count the small words in each sentence before you stop.

title: Splitting a sentence in two so one part cannot be missed

point_json.grammar_name: Cleft sentences: it is X that ... and what ... is

teach.can_do: I can split a sentence so that the part I care about cannot be read past.
teach.why_it_matters: English has almost no way of underlining a word in speech or in an essay. This structure is the way, and it does the job of a raised voice.
teach.meaning: A cleft takes one ordinary sentence and breaks it into two pieces so that one piece stands alone in the light and the rest is pushed into a clause behind it. Nothing new is being said. What changes is which part your reader treats as the news and which part they treat as already agreed. That makes it the tool for correcting an assumption, for setting two things against each other, and for holding the important word back until the end.

form.pattern: It + is / was + the part you want heard + that / who + the rest    |    What + clause + is / was + the part you want heard
notes: the it shape puts the spotlight early: it is the running costs that worry people
the what shape holds it back to the end: what worries people is the running costs
that works for people and things in the it shape; who is available for people
the verb after that agrees with the spotlit part, not with the it at the front
form.negative: The negative usually sits in the spotlight itself: it is not the rent that people object to.
form.question: Ask which single part of your sentence your reader might otherwise skim past. That part goes in the light.

left.text: The timing worries people.

right.role: one part moved into the light
right.text: It is the timing that worries people.

spec.caption: Nothing new has been said. One piece has been moved into the light and everything else into the shade.

worked_example.sentence: It is the running costs, not the building work, that will decide whether the scheme survives.
worked_example.why_this_form: The reader arrives expecting an argument about construction, so the sentence has to put the running costs where they cannot be skimmed and shove everything else back.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: The running costs will decide whether the scheme survives reports the same fact and quietly lets the reader go on assuming the building work matters too.

notice_set.sentence: It was the noise that made them move, not the rent.
notice_set.question: Why did they move?
notice_set.why: The noise has been put in the light and the rent has been ruled out by name.

notice_set.sentence: What the council has not explained is where the money went.
notice_set.question: Has the council explained where the money went?
notice_set.why: The gap is held back to the very end, which is what makes it land.

notice_set.sentence: It was in March that the depot closed.
notice_set.question: What is the speaker putting right?
notice_set.why: March is standing in the light, so the date is the part the speaker thinks somebody has wrong.

notice_set.sentence: What surprised everybody was how quickly the shops emptied.
notice_set.question: Were people expecting the shops to empty that fast?
notice_set.why: Surprise means the speed was not expected, and the speed is the part held back until last.

notice_set.sentence: It is small firms that carry most of the cost.
notice_set.question: Who carries most of the cost?
notice_set.why: Small firms have been lifted out and put in front, which is where a reader looks first.

teach.rule_line: Use it when one part has to be corrected, set against something, or held back.
teach.false_rule: That this structure makes writing sound advanced. It sounds argumentative, and where nothing is in dispute it simply reads as odd.

errors.wrong: It is the timing what worries people, not the cost.
errors.right: It is the timing that worries people, not the cost.
errors.why_it_happens: Many languages use their question word to open this second half, and what is the closest English match, so the writer's ear raises no objection at all.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: what becomes that.
errors.l1_note: Frequent where the learner's first language uses its question word here.

errors.wrong: It is the delays that worries commuters most.
errors.right: It is the delays that worry commuters most.
errors.why_it_happens: The verb has to agree with the spotlit part, but the writer's ear is still holding the singular it is from three words earlier, and that is what the ending copies.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one letter: the s on worries.

errors.wrong: What most people object to. The way the charge was brought in.
errors.right: What most people object to is the way the charge was brought in.
errors.why_it_happens: The opening feels heavy enough to stand alone and the second part feels like the answer to it, so a full stop goes between them and the sentence never gets a main verb at all.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one full stop into the word is.

errors.wrong: It is my brother who taught me to cook.
errors.right: My brother taught me to cook.
errors.why_it_happens: The frame has been learned as a way of sounding impressive rather than as a way of singling one thing out against a rival. With nothing in dispute it adds four words and makes an ordinary sentence sound like a correction of somebody.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one frame: It is ... who.

pays_in.note: It corrects an assumption the prompt has planted in the reader's head.
pays_in.model: It is the shortage of small flats, not the price of large ones, that keeps young people at home.

pays_in.note: It marks which half of a long answer you actually want heard.
pays_in.model: What really changed things was the new bus route, not the car park.

pays_in.note: A writer's real claim often sits in the clause after that.
pays_in.model: It was the delay in publishing the figures that provoked most of the complaints.

used_in.quote: Both sides of this prompt rest on saying which factor really does the work, which is what this structure is for.

payload.sentence: It is the smallest firms that lose most when a payment is late.
payload.question: Who is worst affected?

feedback.why_key: The smallest firms have been lifted to the front and stood in the light, which is where the reader's eye goes first.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the part before that as the writer's real claim.

payload.sentence: What puts people off is the deposit, not the monthly rent.
payload.question: Which of the two is the bigger obstacle?

feedback.why_key: The deposit is held back to the end and the rent is ruled out by name, so the sentence is choosing between them.
feedback.feed_forward: Wait for the end of a what sentence before deciding.

payload.context: From a paragraph about town centre shops.
payload.sentence: It is the empty units what people notice first when they walk down the street.
reasons: the second half has been opened with the wrong word
the verb does not agree with the units
a comma belongs in front of the second half
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The second half of this structure opens with that or who. What has its own job elsewhere and English will not lend it out here.
feedback.feed_forward: Open the second half with that after it is.

payload.context: From a paragraph about household budgets.
payload.stem: It is the fixed bills that ___ (make) a small income impossible to plan around.

expected: make

feedback.why_key: The verb agrees with the fixed bills, which is the part in the light, and not with the it at the front of the sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the verb to the spotlit part, not to it is.

payload.given: Late payment closes small firms. Your reader assumes it is low demand.
payload.instruction: Put late payment where it cannot be missed.

expected: late payment that closes small firms
late payment, not low demand, that closes small firms

feedback.why_key: The reader has arrived with the wrong culprit in mind, and the only way to shift it is to stand the right one in front of them.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the corrected part straight after it is.

payload.given: Councils cannot find enough builders. That is the real obstacle to new housing.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that holds the obstacle back until the end.

expected: holds up new housing is the shortage of builders
stops councils building is the shortage of builders
councils cannot find is enough builders

feedback.why_key: Holding the answer back keeps the reader with you to the last word, which is the whole advantage of the what shape.
feedback.feed_forward: Join the two halves with is, never with a full stop.

payload.context: Build a sentence that keeps the answer until the end.

expected: what worries shoppers is the price of basics

feedback.why_key: Is is the hinge between the two halves, and without it the sentence is two pieces lying side by side.
feedback.feed_forward: Place is between the two halves before anything else.

payload.audio_text: It's the deposit that stops most people, not the rent.

expected: it's the deposit that stops most people, not the rent
it is the deposit that stops most people, not the rent
its the deposit that stops most people not the rent

feedback.why_key: Both hinges are unstressed in speech, so the whole frame can vanish and leave the listener with a list of two nouns.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a small unstressed that in the middle.

payload.sentence: It is the entry costs that keeps them out of the market altogether.

expected: that keep them out

feedback.why_key: Costs is the part in the light and the verb belongs to it, however far away the singular it is now looks.
feedback.feed_forward: Trace the verb back to the spotlit noun, not to it.

items.decision_cue: It was my sister who suggested

payload.context: The examiner has simply asked how the candidate chose their job. Nobody has disagreed with anything.
payload.sentence: It was my sister who suggested it, and it was the hours that appealed to me.
reasons: the second half opens with the wrong word
the verb does not agree
it is correct, but nothing is in dispute, so the sentence sounds like an argument
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Nothing here is broken. The structure exists to correct somebody, and there is nobody to correct, so the answer sounds defensive.
feedback.feed_forward: Save this structure for a point somebody might dispute.

payload.prompt_text: Most people blame online shopping for empty high streets. You think business rates matter more. Write one sentence that puts the reader right.

feedback.why_key: A correction is exactly the situation this structure was built for, and a plain sentence would let the reader keep their original culprit.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the thing you are ruling out as well as the one you are choosing.

payload.prompt_text: Open your paragraph on very high salaries. Find the one sentence where you disagree with the other side and rewrite it as a split sentence. Use it once in the paragraph and no more. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: One of these in a paragraph marks your real claim. Two of them cancel each other out, because everything cannot be the important part.
feedback.feed_forward: Use it once, at the point of disagreement, then stop.

title: Saying how much of a group you mean without starting a new sentence

point_json.grammar_name: Relative clauses after a quantifier: most of which, several of whom

teach.can_do: I can give a total and then say what happened to part of it, inside one sentence.
teach.why_it_matters: This is the structure that turns the commonest punctuation error in academic writing into a complex sentence. One word is the whole difference.
teach.meaning: You often need to say two things about the same group: how many there were, and what happened to some of them. Written English lets you do both in one sentence by hanging the second fact on the first with a quantifier and a relative word. The clause is always news rather than a way of picking the group out, so it is always fenced off by a comma, and the relative word can never be dropped.

form.pattern: noun phrase , + quantifier + of + which / whom + verb ...
notes: which for things, whom for people, and after of there is no third option: that and who are both refused
any quantifier fits in the slot: most, some, several, three, half, none, all, the last of
the same shape works with a noun instead of a quantifier: the cost of which, the results of which
form.negative: None of which and neither of whom carry the negative on their own: the panel heard six witnesses, none of whom were named.
form.question: Ask how many out of how many. The answer is the phrase that goes in front of of.

left.role: two sentences taped together with a comma
left.text: ..., most of them came from one street.

right.text: ..., most of which came from one street.

spec.caption: One word turns a punctuation error into a complex sentence.

worked_example.sentence: The trial produced fourteen readings, three of which had to be discarded.
worked_example.why_this_form: The total and the exception arrive together, so the reader never has to hold two separate facts side by side and work out how they connect.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Three of them had to be discarded is a second sentence wearing a comma. It says the same thing while telling the reader you cannot hear a sentence boundary.

notice_set.sentence: The department interviewed forty applicants, most of whom had never worked in a laboratory.
notice_set.question: How many of the applicants had laboratory experience?
notice_set.why: Most is counting the ones without experience, which leaves the smaller share on the other side.

notice_set.sentence: The survey used six instruments, two of which failed in the first week.
notice_set.question: How many instruments were still working after that week?
notice_set.why: Six minus the two that failed. The second half of the sentence is arithmetic on the first half.

notice_set.sentence: The scheme, the cost of which has never been published, is now in its fifth year.
notice_set.question: Do we know what the scheme cost?
notice_set.why: The whole point of the fenced-off clause is that the figure has been withheld.

notice_set.sentence: The team submitted three reports, none of which reached the minister.
notice_set.question: Did the minister see any of the reports?
notice_set.why: None covers all three, so nothing at all arrived on that desk.

notice_set.sentence: The clinic wrote to nine families, all of whom replied within a week.
notice_set.question: How many families did not reply?
notice_set.why: All of them replied, so the number left over is zero.

teach.rule_line: After of, use which for things and whom for people. Nothing else fits there.
teach.false_rule: That whom is old-fashioned and who will always do instead. After of, who is not available at all.

errors.wrong: The council received two hundred objections, most of them came from one street.
errors.right: The council received two hundred objections, most of which came from one street.
errors.why_it_happens: The second fact clearly belongs with the first, so a full stop feels too heavy and a comma goes in instead. A comma cannot hold two sentences together, and the writer has no other tool to hand.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: them becomes which.

errors.wrong: The panel heard six witnesses, two of who were never named.
errors.right: The panel heard six witnesses, two of whom were never named.
errors.why_it_happens: Who is the familiar word and whom feels like decoration, so it gets quietly dropped. After of, English offers no choice at all, whatever the writer thinks of the word.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one letter: the m on the end of who.

errors.wrong: The trial produced fourteen readings, three of that had to be discarded.
errors.right: The trial produced fourteen readings, three of which had to be discarded.
errors.why_it_happens: That is the default relative word everywhere else, so it survives into a slot where it has never been allowed. Nothing in the sentence sounds wrong to the writer's own ear.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: that becomes which.

errors.wrong: The clinic wrote to nine families, much of whom replied at once.
errors.right: The clinic wrote to nine families, most of whom replied at once.
errors.why_it_happens: Much is stored as the general word for a large amount, and nobody checks whether the group it points back at can be counted. Families can be counted, so much has nothing to measure.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: much becomes most.

pays_in.note: A total and a striking part of it belong in one sentence, not two.
pays_in.model: Eleven countries were included, four of which accounted for almost the whole rise.

pays_in.note: It concedes a point and keeps the sentence moving at the same time.
pays_in.model: Several remedies have been proposed, none of which addresses why the shortage began.

pays_in.note: Passages hide their exceptions in this clause, and the questions live there.
pays_in.model: The programme trained sixty inspectors, half of whom left within two years.

used_in.quote: Describing four lines on one chart invites exactly this sentence: four sources, two of which rose steadily throughout.

payload.sentence: The laboratory ran twelve tests, five of which produced no reading at all.
payload.question: How many tests produced a reading?

feedback.why_key: The clause counts the failures, so what is left over is the number that worked.
feedback.feed_forward: Subtract the number in the clause from the total in front of it.

payload.sentence: We had about thirty on the course, half of whom dropped out by Christmas.
payload.question: Roughly how many finished the autumn term?

feedback.why_key: Half the group left, so half of the original thirty is what remained by the end of term.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the quantifier as a share of the group in front of it.

items.decision_cue: most of them closed within a year

payload.context: From a paragraph about new businesses in a small town.
payload.sentence: Nineteen shops opened on that street, most of them closed within a year.
reasons: a comma has been asked to hold two complete sentences together
the wrong quantifier has been chosen
the share has been hung on the wrong noun
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Most of them closed within a year could stand on its own, which is precisely why a comma cannot be the thing joining it on.
feedback.feed_forward: Turn them into which and the join becomes legal.

payload.context: From the methods section of a field report.
payload.stem: The team deployed eight sensors, three of ___ stopped transmitting within a fortnight.

expected: which

feedback.why_key: Sensors are things, and after of only which is available, however natural that may feel.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose which for things and whom for people after of.

payload.context: From a paragraph about community sentences.
payload.stem: The scheme supervised ninety offenders, none of ___ reoffended in the first year.

expected: whom

feedback.why_key: Offenders are people, and after of the only form English will take is the one ending in m.
feedback.feed_forward: Write whom whenever of points back at people.

payload.given: The council planted four hundred trees along the Verdon. About sixty of them did not survive the summer.
payload.instruction: Join these into one sentence.
payload.starter: The council planted four hundred trees along the Verdon, ___

expected: about sixty of which did not survive the summer
sixty of which did not survive the summer

feedback.why_key: The second fact is arithmetic on the first, so the two belong inside one sentence rather than side by side.
feedback.feed_forward: Replace them with which to join the two facts.

payload.context: Build one sentence about a small grants fund.

expected: the fund backed twelve projects, half of which ran over budget

feedback.why_key: The quantifier, of and which travel as a block, and the verb of the clause comes after all three of them.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep half of which together as one unit when you build.

payload.audio_text: We visited nine clinics, two of which had already shut.

expected: we visited nine clinics, two of which had already shut
we visited nine clinics two of which had already shut

feedback.why_key: Of and which are both unstressed and run together in speech, which is why they get heard as one blurred syllable and written as of them.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for two small words between the number and the verb.

items.decision_cue: several of them were never occupied

payload.sentence: The district built two thousand flats in a decade, several of them were never occupied.
payload.error_span: several of them were never occupied

expected: several of which were never occupied
several of which have never been occupied

feedback.why_key: The words after the comma make a whole sentence, and a comma is not strong enough to hold two of those together.
feedback.feed_forward: Change them to which and the comma becomes legal.

payload.context: Two sentences from different summaries of the same programme.
sentences: The programme funded thirty studies, few of which were ever completed.
The programme funded thirty studies, a few of which were ever completed.
meanings: Almost none of them finished, and the writer thinks that is the story.
A small number did finish, and the writer is pointing at those ones.

feedback.why_key: Few counts what is missing; a few counts what is there. One small word swaps disappointment for a modest success.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide whether you are counting the gap or the survivors.

payload.prompt_text: A research group applied for eleven grants and was turned down for eight of them. Write one sentence carrying both facts.

feedback.why_key: Two numbers about one group belong in one sentence, and this is the join that makes it possible without a semicolon.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the total first and hang the share on it with of which.

payload.prompt_text: Go back to your chart description of renewable electricity. Find a place where you gave a total and then a share, and rewrite the two sentences as one. Ninety seconds.

feedback.why_key: Chart answers are full of totals followed by shares, which is why this one structure lifts the whole paragraph rather than one sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Scan your draft for a comma followed by a number and them.

title: Commenting on the whole thing you just said, without starting again

point_json.grammar_name: Sentential which: a relative clause commenting on a whole clause

teach.can_do: I can add a comment about what I have just said, and make sure my reader knows what the comment is about.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the difference between a sentence that comments on your own point and a sentence that says something about a bridge you never meant to mention.
teach.meaning: Which does not always point at the noun in front of it. It can reach back and take the whole event you have just described, so that the clause comments on what happened rather than on any single thing inside it. Your reader decides which by asking what could plausibly have done what the clause says. When both answers are plausible, the sentence has two meanings, and you will never find out which one your reader took away.

form.pattern: a complete clause , + which + verb ...
notes: the comment clause always comes last; it cannot be lifted into the middle of the sentence
the comma is compulsory, because without it which fastens straight onto the nearest noun
that is refused here, and so is what, however natural what may feel
form.negative: The comment goes negative like any clause: ..., which did not surprise anybody who works there.
form.question: Ask which noun could plausibly have done it. If two candidates could, name the one you mean.

ends: which lands on the nearest noun
which lands on the whole event

marks.label: the deadline, which had been extended twice
the memo, which the lawyers had advised against

worked_example.sentence: The depot closed six weeks early, which left the drivers without a rota for October.
worked_example.why_this_form: A depot cannot leave anybody without a rota. Only the early closing can, so the reader carries which back over the whole event without noticing they did it.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Had the clause said which had been rebuilt in 2019, nothing but the depot could fit, and the comment would have stopped dead at the noun.

notice_set.sentence: Marek turned down the promotion, which had been advertised internally.
notice_set.question: What had been advertised?
notice_set.why: Only a job can be advertised, so the words after the comma can belong to nothing else in the sentence.

notice_set.sentence: Marek turned down the promotion, which nobody in the office understood.
notice_set.question: What did the office fail to understand?
notice_set.why: People fail to understand actions rather than job titles, so the comment reaches back over the whole thing he did.

notice_set.sentence: The clinic moved to a smaller building, which was cheaper to heat.
notice_set.question: What was cheaper to heat?
notice_set.why: Buildings are heated and moves are not, so there is only one candidate here.

notice_set.sentence: The clinic moved to a smaller building, which saved four jobs.
notice_set.question: What saved the four jobs?
notice_set.why: A building does not save jobs. The decision to move into it does, so the comment travels back over the whole event.

notice_set.sentence: The board approved the merger, which the unions had opposed for months.
notice_set.question: What had the unions been opposing?
notice_set.why: Both readings work here and nothing in the sentence chooses between them. That is the trap this whole point is about.

discovery.prompt: Each pair below ends differently. Work out what decides where the comment lands.
pairs: Marek turned down the promotion, which had been advertised internally.
Marek turned down the promotion, which nobody in the office understood.
The clinic moved to a smaller building, which was cheaper to heat.
The clinic moved to a smaller building, which saved four jobs.
The depot closed six weeks early, which had been rebuilt in 2019.
The depot closed six weeks early, which left the drivers without a rota.

candidate_rules.text: What comes after the comma decides it: the comment lands on whatever could plausibly have done that.
The comment lands on the whole event whenever the clause is about how people reacted.
A comma in front of which always sends the comment back to the whole sentence.

teach.rule_line: Ask what could have done it. If two things could, name the one you mean.
teach.false_rule: That a comma in front of which always throws it back to the whole sentence. The comma only frees it; the verb decides where it lands.

contrast.question: Does the comment fit the nearest noun, or only the whole event?

fork.answer: It fits the nearest noun, and only that noun: leave it where it lands
fork.selects: a clause commenting on the noun

fork.answer: It only makes sense about the whole event: put it at the very end after a comma
fork.selects: a clause commenting on everything before it

fork.answer: Both work, so your reader cannot tell: replace which with a noun that names it
fork.selects: a summary noun such as a decision, a move, a refusal

a.text: Ivo missed the deadline for the grant, which had already been extended twice.
a.means: The deadline had been extended twice. The comment stops at the noun in front of it.

b.text: Ivo missed the deadline for the grant, which surprised everybody in the office.
b.means: Missing it is what surprised people. The comment reaches back over the whole event.

minimal_pair.only_difference: had already been extended twice / surprised everybody in the office

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You left which where it lands on the nearest noun. A reader takes it there first and only comes back if that reading collapses. If it does not collapse, they never come back, and they have read something you did not write.

edge_case.text: You will find a sentence-final which frowned on in a few style guides and used constantly by good writers. It is standard English. What is not standard is a which whose target the reader has to guess at.

contrast.stronger_test: Read only the words after the comma and ask what could have done that. If exactly one thing in your sentence could, you are safe. If two could, name it with a noun instead.

worked_pairs.a: The clinic moved to a smaller building, which was cheaper to heat.
worked_pairs.b: The clinic moved to a smaller building, which saved the trust four jobs.
worked_pairs.gloss: A building can be cheaper to heat; only a move can save jobs. The words after the comma say what was grabbed.

worked_pairs.a: Marek turned down the promotion, which had been advertised internally.
worked_pairs.b: Marek turned down the promotion, which nobody in the office understood.
worked_pairs.gloss: The post was advertised. The refusal was the thing nobody could follow. Same eight opening words, two different targets.

worked_pairs.a: The paper printed the leaked memo, which ran to forty pages.
worked_pairs.b: The paper printed the leaked memo, a decision that cost the editor her job.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: a decision that cost the editor her job
worked_pairs.gloss: In the second sentence both readings were live, so the writer named the thing outright and the ambiguity vanished.

errors.wrong: The board approved the merger, which the staff had been warning about for months.
errors.right: The board approved the merger, a decision the staff had been warning about for months.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer knows perfectly well which idea they meant, so the sentence reads cleanly to them. The reader has two candidates, takes the nearer one, and nothing later in the sentence corrects them.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word for a naming noun: which becomes a decision.

errors.wrong: Half the staff resigned in one week, what nobody had expected.
errors.right: Half the staff resigned in one week, which nobody had expected.
errors.why_it_happens: A great many languages use their question word for exactly this job, and what is the closest English match to it. English keeps what for a different job and will not lend it out.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: what becomes which.
errors.l1_note: Very common for speakers of Romance, Slavic and Germanic languages.

errors.wrong: They closed the ticket office which meant nobody could buy a ticket after six.
errors.right: They closed the ticket office, which meant nobody could buy a ticket after six.
errors.why_it_happens: Without the comma there is nothing to free which from the noun beside it, so the clause fastens onto the office and the reader is briefly told that an office meant something. The writer hears their own intended meaning and never sees the other one.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one comma in front of which.

pays_in.note: It comments on your own example without spending a whole new sentence.
pays_in.model: Fares rose twice in a single year, which pushed a good many regular passengers back into their cars.

pays_in.note: Part 3 answers comment on what you have just said, and this is the join.
pays_in.model: A lot of people work from home now, which has emptied the town centre at lunchtime.

pays_in.note: Writers bury their own view in this clause, and questions go looking for it.
pays_in.model: The scheme was extended for a further decade, which few of its early critics had predicted.

used_in.quote: Both sides of this prompt need a sentence that reports what happened and then says what the writer makes of it.

payload.sentence: The channel dropped the late bulletin, which had run since the 1970s.
payload.question: What had run since the 1970s?

feedback.why_key: A programme can run for fifty years. A single decision cannot, so the comment can only belong to the bulletin.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask what could have done the thing the clause describes.

payload.sentence: The channel dropped the late bulletin, which upset a lot of older viewers.
payload.question: What upset the viewers?
